note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: משנת הקנוי והסתירה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on witnesses for kinuy and setirah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: Rabbi Eliezer requires two witnesses for the warning (kinuy) but allows one witness or the husband's own testimony for the seclusion (setirah) that leads to the water ordeal; Rabbi Yehoshua requires two witnesses for both. The Mishnah then explains the process of warning and the consequences of seclusion.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי אליעזר לרבי יהושע על מספר העדים הנדרשים לקנוי ולסתירה, ומפרטת את ההלכות הנובעות מקנוי וסתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the number of witnesses required for kinuy (warning) and setirah (seclusion).
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי אליעזר לרבי יהושע בדיני קנוי וסתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah explains the process of kinuy: the husband warns his wife in front of two witnesses not to speak with a certain man, and if she speaks with him, she remains permitted to her husband and to eat תרומה (priestly portion).
sub.desc: המשנה מבארת כיצד מתבצע הקנוי: אזהרה בפני שנים, ואם דיברה עמו – עדיין מותרת.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that if she enters a secluded place with him and stays long enough for טומאה (ritual impurity) to occur, she becomes forbidden to her husband and to eat תרומה, and if he dies, she performs חליצה (levirate release) rather than יבום (levirate marriage).
sub.desc: המשנה מפרטת את דין כניסה לסתר: איסור לביתה ולתרומה, ואם מת – חולצת ולא מתייבמת.

items.text: טעם סמיכות סוטה לנזיר
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is Sotah placed after Nazir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the tractate Sotah follows Nazir, since the previous chapter dealt with Nazir. It answers with a baraita from Rabbi: the juxtaposition teaches that one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should become a nazir and abstain from wine. The Gemara further explains the order of the tractates: after Ketubot and 'HaMadir' (Nedarim), the Tanna taught Nedarim, then Nazir (similar to Nedarim), and then Sotah because of Rabbi's teaching.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע סדר המסכתות הוא נזיר ואחריו סוטה, ומסבירה על פי רבי שפרשת נזיר סמוכה לפרשת סוטה לומר שהרואה סוטה בקלקולה יזיר עצמו מן היין. עוד מסבירה את סדר המסכתות מנזיר לכתובות לנדרים לנזיר לסוטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna placed Sotah after Nazir, given that the previous chapter ended with Nazir.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע מסכת סוטה נסמכה לנזיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the juxtaposition follows Rabbi's teaching: one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should become a nazir and abstain from wine.
sub.desc: הגמרא משיבה שזה משום שרבי אומר שכל הרואה סוטה בקלקולה יזיר עצמו מן היין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the order: after Ketubot and 'HaMadir' (Nedarim), the Tanna taught Nedarim, then Nazir (similar to Nedarim), and then Sotah because of Rabbi's teaching.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, היה ראוי לשנות סוטה קודם נזיר כסדר התורה.

items.text: איסור קנוי לכתחילה
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Kinuy is only after the fact
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses the past tense 'ha-mekanei' (one who warned), implying it is only after the fact, not initially. It concludes that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds that it is forbidden to warn one's wife (to cause her to undergo the ordeal).
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת מלשון המשנה 'המקנא' שדיעבד אין לכתחילה, ומסיקה שהתנא סובר שאסור לקנאות לכתחילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's use of the past tense 'ha-mekanei' that the action is only described after the fact (בדיעבד), not as an initial directive (לכתחילה).
sub.desc: הגמרא דנה בלשון המשנה 'המקנא' שמשמעו דיעבד, ומסיקה שהתנא סובר שאסור לקנאות לכתחילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds that it is forbidden to warn one's wife (לקנאות) in the first place.
sub.desc: הגמרא דנה בלשון המשנה 'המקנא' שמשמעו דיעבד, ומסיקה שהתנא סובר שאסור לקנאות לכתחילה.

items.text: זיווג לפי מעשים וזיווג ראשון
items.text_en: Aggadic discussion: Matchmaking is difficult and predetermined
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish opens the tractate with an aggadic statement: a person is only matched with a spouse according to his deeds, citing Psalms. Rabbi Yochanan adds that matchmaking is as difficult as the splitting of the Red Sea. The Gemara challenges this with Rav's statement that forty days before conception a bat kol announces who will marry whom. The resolution distinguishes between a first marriage (predetermined) and a second marriage (based on merit).
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מאמרי אמוראים על זיווג: ריש לקיש אומר שמזווגים לאדם אשה לפי מעשיו, ורבי יוחנן אומר שקשה לזווגם כקריעת ים סוף. הקושיה מרב יהודה שאומר שבת קול מכריזה על זיווגים לפני יצירת הוולד, והתירוץ: הא בזוג ראשון הא בזוג שני.

sub.text: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק בשם ריש לקיש
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish opens the tractate with an aggadic statement that a person is only matched with a spouse according to his deeds, citing Psalms.
sub.desc: פתיחה: ריש לקיש אומר שזיווג אשה לאדם הוא לפי מעשיו.

sub.text: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק בשם ריש לקיש
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that matchmaking is as difficult as the splitting of the Red Sea, citing Psalms.
sub.desc: פתיחה: ריש לקיש אומר שזיווג אשה לאדם הוא לפי מעשיו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with Rav's statement that forty days before conception a bat kol announces who will marry whom, implying predetermination.
sub.desc: קושיה: והרי רב יהודה אמר רב שבת קול מכריזה על זיווג 40 יום לפני יצירת הוולד, משמע שזיווג נקבע מראש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a first marriage (predetermined) and a second marriage (based on merit).
sub.desc: קושיה: והרי רב יהודה אמר רב שבת קול מכריזה על זיווג 40 יום לפני יצירת הוולד, משמע שזיווג נקבע מראש.

items.text: עד אחד בטומאת סוטה
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: A single witness is trusted for impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua only dispute regarding kinuy and setirah, but both agree that a single witness is trusted for the actual impurity (tum'ah). It supports this with a Mishnah that a single witness who says 'I saw her become impure' prevents her from drinking. The Gemara then derives this from the Torah: the verse 'and there is no witness against her' refers to two witnesses, and the verse 'one witness shall not rise up against a man' teaches that a single witness is not sufficient for punishment but is trusted for prohibitions.
items.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שהמחלוקת במשנה היא רק בקנוי וסתירה, אבל בטומאה כולי עלמא מודו שעד אחד נאמן. מביאה ראיה ממשנה אחרת ומבררת מקור מהתורה: 'ועד אין בה' בשנים הכתוב מדבר, ומדין 'לא יקום עד אחד באיש' למדים שעד אחד נאמן בטומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua only dispute regarding kinuy (warning) and setirah (seclusion), but agree that a single witness is trusted for tum'ah (impurity).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שהמחלוקת במשנה היא רק בקנוי וסתירה, אבל בטומאה כולם מודים שעד אחד נאמן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a single witness who says 'I saw her become impure' prevents her from drinking the bitter water.
sub.desc: מובאת ראיה ממשנה אחרת שעד אחד בטומאה נאמן ואינה שותה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from the Torah, how do we derive that a single witness is trusted?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה המקור מהתורה שעד אחד נאמן בטומאה, ומביאה ברייתא הדורשת 'ועד אין בה' בשניים.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbanan taught that the verse 'and there is no witness against her' refers to two witnesses, and the verse 'one witness shall not rise up against a man' teaches that a single witness is not sufficient for punishment but is trusted for prohibitions.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה המקור מהתורה שעד אחד נאמן בטומאה, ומביאה ברייתא הדורשת 'ועד אין בה' בשניים.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'lo yakum ed echad' and its application to sotah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'lo yakum ed echad' and its application to sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah needed to specify 'echad' in the verse about a single witness, establishing that 'ed' generally implies two witnesses unless specified otherwise. It then addresses the unique case of sotah, where a single witness might be believed due to the circumstances of warning and seclusion, but the verse 'vehi lo nitpasah' indicates she is forbidden, requiring at least one witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'לֹא יָקוּם עֵד בְּאִישׁ' (a single witness shall not rise up) needs to specify 'אֶחָד' (one), and answers that it establishes a general rule: wherever 'עֵד' (witness) is stated, it implies two witnesses unless the verse explicitly says 'אֶחָד' (one).
The Gemara explains that the Torah says there are not two witnesses but only one, and the phrase 'וְהִיא לֹא נִתְפָּשָׂה' (and she was not seized) indicates she is forbidden.

The Gemara objects that if not for the verse 'לֹא יָקוּם עֵד אֶחָד' (a single witness shall not rise up), one might think that 'עֵד' (witness) in the case of sotah means a single witness, and if there is not even one witness, how is she forbidden?

The Gemara answers that it is necessary, because one might have thought that 'עֵד אֵין בָּהּ' (there is no witness against her) means that a witness is not believed regarding her, and then the Gemara questions what else the verse would require.

The Gemara objects that if the requirement is for two witnesses, the verse could have been silent, since a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from monetary law would teach that all testimonies in the Torah require two witnesses.
The Gemara answers that it is necessary because one might have thought that sotah is different, since there is a basis for suspicion (warning and seclusion), so a single witness should be believed.
The Gemara objects: how can you say that a witness is not believed and she is permitted, when the verse 'וְהִיא לֹא נִתְפָּשָׂה' (and she was not seized) implies she is forbidden?

The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that a witness is not believed until there are two, and even with two she is not seized, so the verse teaches that she is forbidden.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer on the exclusion of kinuy or setirah
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer on the exclusion of kinuy or setirah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the word 'bah' excludes both kinuy and setirah from requiring two witnesses, while Rabbi Eliezer only excludes kinuy. The Gemara questions why setirah is not excluded, and the discussion weighs whether kinuy or setirah is more fundamental, concluding that setirah is the beginning of impurity and thus more stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehoshua, and answers that the verse 'בָּהּ' (in her) excludes warning (קִינּוּי) and seclusion (סְתִירָה) from requiring two witnesses.
Rabbi Eliezer says that the verse 'בָּהּ' (in her) excludes only warning (קִינּוּי) from requiring two witnesses, but not seclusion.

The Gemara objects: why not say that 'בָּהּ' (in her) excludes seclusion? It answers that seclusion is linked to טומאה (impurity) by the verse 'וְנִסְתְּרָה וְהִיא נִטְמָאָה' (and she was secluded and she became impure).

The Gemara objects that warning (קִינּוּי) is also linked to טומאה (impurity) by the verse 'וְקִנֵּא אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ וְהִיא נִטְמָאָה' (and he warned his wife and she became impure), so the Merciful One excluded it with 'בָּהּ' (in her).
The Gemara answers: what did you see? It is logical that seclusion is more stringent, because it forbids her like טומאה (impurity).
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, warning (קִינּוּי) is more important, because it is the primary cause for her.
The Gemara objects: without seclusion, is there warning? And without warning, what benefit is seclusion?
The Gemara resolves that even so, seclusion is more important, because it is the beginning of טומאה (impurity).
The Gemara asks what reason supports preferring one exclusion over the other.
The Gemara reasons that סתירה is more stringent because it directly prohibits her like טומאה.
The Gemara objects that קינוי is more fundamental because it is the primary cause of the prohibition.
The Gemara rejects the objection by showing that קינוי and סתירה are interdependent.
The Gemara resolves that סתירה is still more stringent because it is the beginning of impurity (אתחלתא דטומאה).

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages' objection
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages' objection
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah's opinion that kinuy can be based on a single witness or the husband himself, while the Sages object that this leads to no end (ein ladavar sof). The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei derives this from 'bah' excluding setirah, and the Sages' concern is that a husband might falsely claim to have warned his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that contradicts the Mishnah, attributed to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a husband may issue a kinuy (warning) based on a single witness or his own testimony, but the sotah (suspected adulteress) is made to drink only on the testimony of two witnesses.
The Sages object that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah's position, there would be no end to the matter (ein ladavar sof), as a husband could falsely claim to have warned his wife.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah derives his ruling from the word 'בָּהּ' (in her), which excludes the requirement of setirah (seclusion) for the kinuy, but not for the drinking.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why the word 'בָּהּ' should exclude setirah rather than kinuy, and answers that the connection of setirah to tum'ah (impurity) is only for the duration of seclusion, not for the exclusion itself.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of the Sages' objection
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Sages' objection
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Sages' concern: a husband might falsely claim to have issued a kinuy even when he did not, leading to endless disputes.

items.text: Clarification of the objection: comparison between Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Clarification of the objection: comparison between Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's position also has the problem of 'no end', and Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah, even the Mishnah has no end, as the husband could falsely claim seclusion. The discussion corrects an earlier version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's position has a definitive end, noting that a husband could falsely claim seclusion.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah, there is no end to the matter.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah has a foundation (the wife's actual seclusion) while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah's position lacks such a foundation, so the statement seems backwards.
The Gemara corrects the earlier version: Rabbi Yochanan actually said that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah, even the Mishnah has no end.

items.text: Practical halachic ruling: Rav Chanina from Sura warns against kinuy today
items.text_en: Practical halachic ruling: Rav Chanina from Sura warns against kinuy today
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina from Sura rules that a husband should not warn his wife not to seclude herself with a specific man nowadays, because we might follow Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehudah that kinuy can be by the husband himself, and without the sotah waters to test her, she would be permanently forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina from Sura rules that a man should not tell his wife nowadays 'do not seclude yourself with so-and-so', because we might hold like Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda that warning can be on his own, and if she secludes herself, there are no sotah waters to test her, and he would forbid her forever.

items.text: Etymology of 'kinuy' and its implications for the dispute
items.text_en: Etymology of 'kinuy' and its implications for the dispute
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rav Yeimar bar Rabbi Shelemya in the name of Abaye debate the meaning of 'kinuy': Reish Lakish says it means something that causes jealousy between her and others, implying kinuy by the husband alone, while Rav Yeimar says it means jealousy between him and her, implying kinuy by two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish defines 'kinuy' as something that causes jealousy between her and others, implying kinuy is done by the husband alone without witnesses.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar bar Rabbi Shelemya in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar bar Rabbi Shelemya in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Rabbi Shelemya in the name of Abaye defines 'kinuy' as something that causes jealousy between him and her, implying kinuy is done before two witnesses.

items.text: The meaning of 'kinuy' according to the one who permits it
items.text_en: The meaning of 'kinuy' according to the one who permits it
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that it is permitted to warn one's wife (kinuy), what is the meaning of the word 'kinuy'? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that 'kinuy' is a term of warning, citing the verse 'The Lord was jealous for His land'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that warning one's wife (קינוי) is permitted, what is the meaning of the word 'קינוי'?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that 'קינוי' is a term of warning, citing the verse 'וַיְקַנֵּא ה׳ לְאַרְצוֹ' (The Lord was jealous for His land).

items.text: Two interpretations of the 'spirit of jealousy'
items.text_en: Two interpretations of the 'spirit of jealousy'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a person who sins in secret is publicly proclaimed by God, as the verse says 'a spirit of jealousy passed over him'. Resh Lakish says that a person only commits a sin if a spirit of foolishness enters him, as the verse says 'if his wife goes astray' (written as 'tishgeh').

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that a person who sins in secret is publicly proclaimed by God, as the verse says 'a spirit of jealousy passed over him' and the word 'passed' implies public proclamation.
Resh Lakish says that a person only commits a sin if a spirit of foolishness enters him, as the verse says 'if his wife goes astray' (written as 'tishgeh').

items.text: Why the Torah believes one witness in the case of a sotah
items.text_en: Why the Torah believes one witness in the case of a sotah
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the Torah trusts a single witness in the case of a sotah because there is a basis for the suspicion: the husband warned her, she secluded herself, and a witness testifies she is defiled. Rav Pappa questions Abaye: the warning (kinuy) is written after the seclusion and defilement in the Torah! Abaye answers that the verse 'and passed' means it already passed. The Gemara challenges this with another verse, and concludes that if kinuy were after defilement, it would be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael states that the Torah trusts a single witness in the case of a sotah because there is a basis for the suspicion: the husband warned her, she secluded herself, and a witness testifies she is defiled.
Rav Pappa questions Abaye: the warning (kinuy) is written in the Torah after the seclusion and defilement, so how can it be a basis for trusting the witness?
Abaye answers that the verse 'וְעָבַר' (and passed) means it already passed, so the warning preceded the seclusion and defilement.
The Gemara objects: if 'וְעָבַר' means past, then the verse 'וְעָבַר לָכֶם כׇּל חָלוּץ' (and every armed man passed) would also refer to the past, contradicting its context.
The Gemara resolves that in the other verse, the context shows it refers to the future, but here, if kinuy were after defilement, it would be superfluous, so it must be interpreted as past.

items.text: The nature of the 'spirit' that enters the husband
items.text_en: The nature of the 'spirit' that enters the husband
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that a man only warns his wife if a spirit enters him. The Rabbis say it is a spirit of impurity, while Rav Ashi says it is a spirit of purity. The Gemara concludes that it is more reasonable to say it is a spirit of purity, based on a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael says kinuy is optional and Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory; if it were a spirit of impurity, how could one bring impurity upon oneself?

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that a man only warns his wife if a spirit enters him, citing the verse 'וְעָבַר עָלָיו רוּחַ קִנְאָה' and then asks what kind of spirit this is.
The Rabbis say it is a spirit of impurity (רוח טומאה).
Rav Ashi says it is a spirit of purity (רוח טהרה).

The Gemara concludes that it is more reasonable to say it is a spirit of purity, based on a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael says kinuy is optional (רשות) and Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory (חובה); if it were a spirit of impurity, how could one bring impurity upon oneself?

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'kinuy' and 'itama'
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'kinuy' and 'itama'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the baraita: Rabbi Yishmael says 'and he warned his wife' is optional, Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory. Similarly, 'to her he shall become impure' is optional according to Rabbi Yishmael and obligatory according to Rabbi Akiva. Rav Pappa asks Abaye if they disagree throughout the entire Torah on this principle, but Abaye answers that here they disagree based on the specific verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited: Rabbi Yishmael says 'and he warned his wife' is optional, Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory.
The baraita continues: similarly, 'to her he shall become impure' is optional for Rabbi Yishmael and obligatory for Rabbi Akiva.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva disagree throughout the entire Torah on this principle of optional vs. obligatory.
Abaye answers that here they disagree based on the specific verses, not as a general principle.

items.text: The scriptural basis for the dispute on 'kinuy'
items.text_en: The scriptural basis for the dispute on 'kinuy'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasons: Rabbi Yishmael holds like the tanna who says that the verse 'and he warned his wife' comes to permit warning despite the prohibition of hatred. Rabbi Akiva says another 'kinuy' is written. Rabbi Yishmael responds that the repetition is due to the need to write 'and she was defiled' and 'and she was not defiled'. This is in line with the school of Rabbi Yishmael's principle that every repeated paragraph is only for something new.

sub.text: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'and he warned his wife' as a permission (רשות), while Rabbi Akiva interprets it as an obligation (חובה).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who says the verse 'and he warned his wife' comes to permit warning despite the prohibition of hatred (לא תשנא).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds that another 'kinuy' (warning) is written in the Torah, implying an obligation.

The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yishmael accounts for the repetition of 'and he warned his wife', and answers that it is needed because the Torah also writes 'and she was defiled' and 'and she was not defiled'.
The Gemara cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael's principle that every repeated paragraph is only for something new, supporting Rabbi Yishmael's position.

items.text: The scriptural basis for the dispute on 'lah yitama'
items.text_en: The scriptural basis for the dispute on 'lah yitama'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains: Rabbi Yishmael says the verse 'to her he shall become impure' is needed because of the general prohibition for priests to become impure. Rabbi Akiva derives the obligation from 'to his close relative', and the verse 'to her' teaches it is obligatory. Rabbi Yishmael counters that 'to her' means he becomes impure to her entire body, not to individual limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding the verse 'to her he shall become impure' — Rabbi Yishmael says it is optional, Rabbi Akiva says it is obligatory.

The Gemara asks: What is Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning? It answers: Since the general prohibition 'to a person he shall not become impure' is written, the verse 'to her' was needed to permit impurity for a close relative.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains: Rabbi Akiva derives the obligation to become impure for a close relative from the verse 'only to his close relative', so the verse 'to her' teaches that it is obligatory.
Rabbi Yishmael counters: The verse 'to her' teaches that he becomes impure to her entire body, but not to her individual limbs.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's question and Rabbi Yishmael's answer regarding the extra word 'yitama'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's question and Rabbi Yishmael's answer regarding the extra word 'yitama'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that if the Torah only intended to permit a suspected adulteress to her husband, it would have written 'lah' and stopped; the extra 'yitama' teaches that she is forbidden to the adulterer. Rabbi Yishmael responds that since 'lah' was written, 'yitama' was also written, and he cites the principle of his school that any passage that is repeated is only repeated because of a new element.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva argues that if the Torah only intended to permit the suspected adulteress to her husband, it would have written only 'lah' and been silent, so the extra word 'yitama' must teach that she is forbidden to the adulterer.
Rabbi Yishmael responds that since 'lah' was written, 'yitama' was also written, and he cites the principle of his school that any passage that is repeated is only repeated because of a new element.

items.text: Debate on 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' – permission or obligation
items.text_en: Debate on 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' – permission or obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding the verse 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu': Rabbi Yishmael says it is a permission, while Rabbi Akiva says it is an obligation. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning, citing a baraita about purchasing a child born from a non-Jew and a Canaanite woman. Rabbi Akiva derives the permission from another verse and uses 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' for obligation. Further derivations are made regarding the exclusion of Israelites from this servitude.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael interprets the verse 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' as a permission, while Rabbi Akiva says it is an obligation.

The Gemara explains Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning: since the verse 'Lo techayeh kol neshama' commands destruction, the verse 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' is needed to permit purchasing a child born from a non-Jew and a Canaanite woman.
A baraita is cited to support Rabbi Yishmael's position, deriving from the verse 'Mehem tiknu' that one may purchase such a child as a slave.
The baraita further limits the permission: a Canaanite who fathers a child with a non-Canaanite woman is not purchasable, as derived from 'Asher holidu be'artzchem'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva derives the permission from 'Mehem tiknu' itself, so 'Le'olam bahem ta'avodu' must teach obligation.
Rabbi Yishmael derives from 'Bahem' that the servitude applies to Canaanites but not to fellow Israelites.
Rabbi Akiva objects that the exclusion of Israelites is already derived from the end of the verse 'Uve'acheikhem... lo tirdah bo befarech'.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via School of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via School of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yishmael holds the verse was repeated only for the novel point of 'Bahem' excluding Israelites, applying the principle of the School of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rav Chisda's aphorisms about promiscuity and strength in the home
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's aphorisms about promiscuity and strength in the home
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that promiscuity in the home is like a worm in a sesame seed, and similarly, strength in the home is like a worm in a sesame seed. He adds that both of these apply to a woman, but not to a man.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that promiscuity in the home is like a worm in a sesame seed.
Rav Chisda adds that strength in the home is also like a worm in a sesame seed, and both apply only to a woman, not to a man.

items.text: Rav Chisda on the Divine Presence dwelling with Israel
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on the Divine Presence dwelling with Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that before Israel sinned, the Divine Presence dwelled with each individual, as per the verse 'For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp.' After they sinned, the Divine Presence departed, as per the verse 'And He will not see in you any indecent thing and turn away from you.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that before Israel sinned, the Divine Presence dwelled with each individual, and after they sinned, it departed.

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Elazar on the reward and punishment of mitzvot and aveirot
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Elazar on the reward and punishment of mitzvot and aveirot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that one who performs a mitzvah in this world has it precede him to the World to Come, while one who commits a transgression has it entangle him for the Day of Judgment. Rabbi Elazar adds that a transgression is tied to a person like a dog, citing the verse about Joseph and Potiphar's wife.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that a mitzvah precedes a person to the World to Come, while a transgression entangles him for the Day of Judgment, citing verses.
Rabbi Elazar adds that a transgression is tied to a person like a dog, citing the verse about Joseph and Potiphar's wife to show it follows him in this world and the next.

items.text: The law of testimony for sotah: first and second testimony
items.text_en: The law of testimony for sotah: first and second testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's kal vachomer regarding testimony: the first testimony (of seclusion) requires two witnesses, but the second testimony (of defilement) should logically require two as well, yet the verse 've'ed ein bah' teaches that any witness suffices. A counter kal vachomer is then presented, but the verse 'ki matza bah ervat davar' is used to require two witnesses for the first testimony. The Gemara clarifies that the derivation is from 'bah', excluding cases without warning (kinuy) or seclusion. Finally, a baraita defines the first testimony as testimony of seclusion and the second as testimony of defilement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, presenting a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that the first testimony (of seclusion) requires two witnesses, so the second testimony (of defilement) should also require two.
The Mishnah counters with the verse 'וְעֵד אֵין בָּהּ' (and there is no witness against her), teaching that any witness suffices for the second testimony.

A counter kal vachomer is presented: since the second testimony (which prohibits her forever) is established by one witness, the first testimony (which does not prohibit forever) should logically also be established by one witness.

The Mishnah counters with the verse 'כִּי מָצָא בָהּ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר' (for he found in her a matter of nakedness), which is linked via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) to the verse 'עַל פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים' (by the mouth of two witnesses), requiring two witnesses for the first testimony.

The Gemara objects that the derivation should come from the word 'בָּהּ' (in her), which excludes cases of kinuy (warning) and setirah (seclusion), not from the full phrase 'כִּי מָצָא בָהּ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר'.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah indeed derives from 'בָּהּ' (in her), meaning that the requirement of two witnesses applies only to the case of seclusion, not to kinuy or setirah.

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a mere claim of defilement without kinuy or setirah requires two witnesses? It answers via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'דָּבָר' (matter) in the verses.
A baraita is cited to define the terms: the first testimony is testimony of seclusion, and the second testimony is testimony of defilement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Listing the measures of seclusion
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Listing the measures of seclusion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the measure of seclusion is the time for tum'ah, bi'ah, or ha'ara'ah. It then lists the opinions of Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Ben Azzai, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, Rabbi Elazar ben Yirmeya, Chanin ben Pinchas, and P'leimo, each offering a different measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks: What is the measure of seclusion? It answers: The time for טומאה (ritual impurity), ביאה (intercourse), or העראה (preliminary contact).
Rabbi Yishmael defines the measure as the time to encircle a palm tree.
Rabbi Eliezer defines the measure as the time to mix a cup of wine.
Rabbi Yehoshua defines the measure as the time to drink the cup.
Ben Azzai defines the measure as the time to roast an egg.
Rabbi Akiva defines the measure as the time to swallow the egg.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira defines the measure as the time to swallow three eggs consecutively.
Rabbi Elazar ben Yirmeya defines the measure as the time for a weaver to tie a thread.
Chanin ben Pinchas defines the measure as the time for a woman to reach into her mouth to remove a splinter.
P'leimo defines the measure as the time for a woman to reach into a basket to take a loaf.
The Mishnah cites a verse from Proverbs (6:26) as a mnemonic for P'leimo's measure: 'For a harlot is sought until a loaf of bread.'

items.text: Gemara's question: Why all these measures?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why all these measures?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists multiple measures (tum'ah, bi'ah, ha'ara'ah) and explains that each is necessary to avoid misinterpretation. It also clarifies that the measure of ha'ara'ah is the time for circling a palm tree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists multiple measures (tum'ah, bi'ah, ha'ara'ah) and begins explaining that each is necessary to avoid misinterpretation.
The Gemara continues explaining that if only the measure of bi'ah were taught, one might think it means the full completion of the act, so the measure of ha'ara'ah is needed.

The Gemara completes the explanation: if only ha'ara'ah were taught, one might think it includes the time for the woman to become impure, so the measure of tum'ah is needed; it then clarifies that the measure of ha'ara'ah is the time for circling a palm tree.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot regarding Rabbi Eliezer's measure
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot regarding Rabbi Eliezer's measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists different measures for seclusion, including 'chazarat dekel' (return of the palm) attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, while the Mishnah attributes 'hakafat dekel' (circling the palm) to Rabbi Yishmael. Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'hakafah' is with the foot, while 'chazarah' is with the wind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that lists 'chazarat dekel' (return of the palm) as Rabbi Eliezer's measure for seclusion, whereas the Mishnah attributes 'hakafat dekel' (circling the palm) to Rabbi Yishmael.
The baraita continues listing the measures of other sages: Rabbi Yehoshua, Ben Azzai, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
The Gemara objects that 'hakafat dekel' and 'chazarat dekel' appear to be the same measure, yet Rabbi Eliezer disputes Rabbi Yishmael in the Mishnah but uses 'chazarat dekel' in the baraita.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'hakafah' (circling) is done with the foot, while 'chazarah' (return) is done by the wind, so they are different measures.

items.text: Rav Ashi's query on chazarah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query on chazarah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether 'chazarah' with the wind means the wind goes and returns, or goes and returns and stands in its place. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether 'chazarah' with the wind means the wind goes and returns, or goes and returns and stands in its place.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Reconciling other contradictory measures between the baraitot
items.text_en: Reconciling other contradictory measures between the baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses discrepancies between the measures attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Ben Azzai, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in the two sources. It explains that some measures are identical, while others are combined or reinterpreted to avoid redundancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the contradiction between Rabbi Eliezer's measure in the first baraita (מזיגת הכוס) and his measure in the second baraita (חזרת דקל), and resolves that both are the same measure.

The Gemara questions the contradiction between Rabbi Yehoshua's measure in the first baraita (לשתותו) and his measure in the second baraita (מזיגת הכוס), and resolves that he means the time to mix and drink, otherwise he would be identical to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Ben Azzai's measure in the first baraita (לצלות ביצה) and his measure in the second baraita (לשתותו), stating they are the same measure.

The Gemara questions the contradiction between Rabbi Akiva's measure in the first baraita (לגומעה) and his measure in the second baraita (לצלות ביצה), and resolves that he means the time to roast an egg and swallow it, otherwise he would be identical to Ben Azzai.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's measure in the first baraita (לגמוע שלוש ביצים) and his measure in the second baraita (לגומעה), explaining that he was speaking to Rabbi Akiva's position, stating that the measure of a single swallow is actually the time to swallow three eggs one after another, which is the combined time of roasting and swallowing.

items.text: Rav Ashi's queries on the remaining opinions
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's queries on the remaining opinions
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises unresolved questions about the measures of Rabbi Elazar ben Yirmeya (tying a thread), Chanin ben Pinchas (taking a splinter), and P'leimo (taking a loaf), asking about specific details such as distance, tightness, and freshness of the bread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Elazar ben Yirmeya's measure for סתירה (seclusion) as the time to tie a weaver's thread.
Rav Ashi asks whether the tying is done with the thread close to the weaver or far away.
The gemara concludes with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand unresolved).
The Mishnah cites Chanin ben Pinchas's measure as the time to extend a hand into the mouth to remove a splinter.
Rav Ashi asks whether the splinter is tightly wedged or loose.
The gemara concludes with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand unresolved).
The Mishnah cites P'leimo's measure as the time to extend a hand to a basket to take a loaf.
Rav Ashi asks multiple questions: whether the loaf is tightly packed or loose, whether it is fresh or stale, and whether it is hot or cold.
The gemara concludes with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Unresolved question about measuring the bitter water
items.text_en: Unresolved question about measuring the bitter water
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of unresolved questions about the measurement of the bitter water given to the suspected adulteress, such as whether it is measured by dry or liquid measure, and whether the ingredients are soft or hard. The discussion concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions about whether the bitter water is measured by dry or liquid measure and whether the ingredients are soft or hard, concluding with 'teiku' (let it stand).

items.text: Explanation of how each sage estimated the measure
items.text_en: Explanation of how each sage estimated the measure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that each sage estimated the measure himself. The Gemara questions how Ben Azzai could have estimated since he never married. Three answers are offered: he married and then separated, he heard it from his teacher, or it is a secret of God.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that each sage estimated the measure himself.
The Gemara questions how Ben Azzai could have estimated the measure since he never married.
First answer: Ben Azzai married and then separated from his wife.
Second answer: Ben Azzai heard the measure from his teacher.
Third answer: It is a secret of God revealed to those who fear Him.

items.text: Eating without washing hands compared to adultery
items.text_en: Eating without washing hands compared to adultery
items.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches in the name of Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi that eating bread without washing hands is like having relations with a harlot, citing Proverbs 6:26. Rava objects to the verse's wording and reinterprets it to mean that one who has relations with a harlot will eventually seek a loaf of bread.

sub.text: Rav Avira citing Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Avira citing Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches in the name of Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi that eating bread without washing hands is like having relations with a harlot, citing Proverbs 6:26.
Rava objects that the verse's wording should be reversed to 'for a loaf of bread until a harlot'.
Rava reinterprets the verse to mean that one who has relations with a harlot will eventually seek a loaf of bread.

items.text: Laws of hand-washing: raising and lowering hands
items.text_en: Laws of hand-washing: raising and lowering hands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that one who treats hand-washing lightly is uprooted from the world. Rav Chiya bar Ashi quotes Rav that for the first washing one must raise hands, and for the final washing one must lower them. A baraita supports this to prevent water from flowing back and defiling the hands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that one who treats hand-washing lightly is uprooted from the world.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quotes Rav that for the first washing one must raise hands, and for the final washing one must lower them.
A baraita supports Rav's ruling, explaining that raising hands prevents water from flowing back and defiling the hands.

items.text: Eating without drying hands compared to eating impure bread
items.text_en: Eating without drying hands compared to eating impure bread
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches that eating bread without drying hands is like eating impure bread, citing Ezekiel 4:13.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches that eating bread without drying hands is like eating impure bread, citing Ezekiel 4:13.

items.text: Haughtiness leads to adultery
items.text_en: Haughtiness leads to adultery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a haughty person will eventually stumble with a married woman, citing Proverbs 6:26. Rava objects to the wording and reinterprets the verse to mean that one who has relations with a married woman, even if he studied Torah, will be caught by her for judgment in Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'וְאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ נֶפֶשׁ יְקָרָה תָצוּד' (a man's wife hunts a precious soul).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that a haughty person will eventually stumble with a married woman, citing the verse.
Rava objects that the verse should have said 'נֶפֶשׁ גְּבוֹהָה' (haughty soul) and 'הִיא תָּצוּד' (she hunts) instead of the current wording.
Rava reinterprets the verse to mean that one who has relations with a married woman, even if he studied Torah which is called 'יְקָרָה' (precious), will be caught by her for judgment in Gehinnom.

items.text: Haughtiness equated to idolatry, heresy, incest, and building a high place
items.text_en: Haughtiness equated to idolatry, heresy, incest, and building a high place
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says a haughty person is like an idolater. Rabbi Yochanan himself says such a person is like one who denies the fundamental principle. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says it is like one who has relations with all forbidden relatives. Ulla says it is like one who builds a high place for idolatry.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai equates a haughty person to an idolater, using a verbal analogy on the word 'תועבה' (abomination).
Rabbi Yochanan independently states that a haughty person is like one who denies the fundamental principle (כפירה בעיקר), citing the verse about forgetting God.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina equates a haughty person to one who has relations with all forbidden relatives (עריות), using the same verbal analogy on 'תועבה'.
Ulla equates a haughty person to one who builds a high place (במה) for idolatry, by reinterpreting the word 'במה' (what) as 'במה' (high place).

items.text: Interpretation of 'hand to hand' regarding adultery
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'hand to hand' regarding adultery
items.desc_en: Rav interprets Proverbs 11:21 to mean that one who commits adultery will not be absolved even if he gave God heaven and earth like Abraham. The school of Rabbi Sheila objects to the wording and says even if he received the Torah like Moses he will not be absolved. Rabbi Yochanan objects and reinterprets the verse to mean that one who commits adultery will not be absolved from judgment in Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'יָד לְיָד לֹא יִנָּקֶה' (hand to hand will not be absolved), and Rav answers that it refers to one who commits adultery, who will not be absolved from Gehinnom even if he gave God heaven and earth like Abraham.

The school of Rabbi Sheila objects to Rav's interpretation, arguing that the verse should have said 'יָדִי' (my hand) if it meant Abraham, and instead reinterprets it to mean that even one who received the Torah like Moses will not be absolved from Gehinnom.

Rabbi Yochanan objects to the school of Rabbi Sheila's interpretation, arguing that the verse should have said 'יָד מִיָּד' (hand from hand) if it meant receiving the Torah, and instead reinterprets it to mean that one who commits adultery will not be absolved from judgment in Gehinnom.

items.text: Opening statement on the severity of hidden charity
items.text_en: Opening statement on the severity of hidden charity
items.desc_en: Even one who gives charity in secret will not be spared from Gehinnom if he is arrogant.

items.text: Source for warning against arrogance
items.text_en: Source for warning against arrogance
items.desc_en: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derive a warning against arrogance from verses, and Rabbi Avin cites a principle that 'hishamer', 'pen', and 'al' indicate a negative commandment.

items.text: The fate of the arrogant: diminishment and possible redemption
items.text_en: The fate of the arrogant: diminishment and possible redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches that an arrogant person will ultimately be diminished, but if he repents, he is gathered in like the patriarchs; otherwise, he is cut off like a stalk.

items.text: Interpretation of 'like the top of a stalk'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'like the top of a stalk'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate the meaning of 'like the top of a stalk', with one saying it means like a reed of grain and the other like the stalk itself. Rav Asi and the school of Rabbi Yishmael explain it as a parable of a man picking the tallest stalks.

items.text: God dwells with the lowly
items.text_en: God dwells with the lowly
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate the meaning of 'et daka' in the verse, concluding that God is with the lowly. Rav Yosef teaches that one should learn from God's attribute of choosing the lowly, as He chose Mount Sinai and the bush.

items.text: Three statements of Rabbi Elazar on the arrogant
items.text_en: Three statements of Rabbi Elazar on the arrogant
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that an arrogant person deserves to be cut down like an asherah, his dust will not be stirred (resurrection), and the Shekhinah laments over him.

items.text: God's attribute differs from man's
items.text_en: God's attribute differs from man's
items.desc_en: Rav Avira or Rabbi Elazar teaches that unlike man, God who is high sees the lowly, as the verse says 'For the Lord is high, and He sees the lowly'.

items.text: God cannot dwell with the arrogant or slanderer
items.text_en: God cannot dwell with the arrogant or slanderer
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda or Mar Ukva says that God says He and the arrogant cannot dwell together, and some apply this to slanderers.

items.text: The arrogant are easily disturbed
items.text_en: The arrogant are easily disturbed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri says that an arrogant person is disturbed by even a small wind, as the sea is disturbed by a small wind.

items.text: The proper measure of arrogance for a scholar
items.text_en: The proper measure of arrogance for a scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi says a Torah scholar should have an eighth of an eighth of arrogance. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says it adorns him like a reed to a stalk. Rava curses one who has it and one who lacks it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says one should have none at all.

items.text: Prayer requires humility like flesh
items.text_en: Prayer requires humility like flesh
items.desc_en: Chizkiya says prayer is only heard if one makes his heart like flesh. Rabbi Zeira notes that 'basar' (flesh) is written with 'venirpa' (healed), but 'adam' is not. Rabbi Yochanan lists the components of adam and basar.

items.text: Final statement on the fate of the arrogant
items.text_en: Final statement on the fate of the arrogant
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says that an arrogant person will ultimately be diminished.

items.text: Opening exposition on the terms 'שאת' and 'ספחת'
items.text_en: Opening exposition on the terms 'שאת' and 'ספחת'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical terms 'שאת' and 'ספחת' from the Torah portion regarding skin ailments, deriving 'שאת' from the language of height and 'ספחת' from the language of attachment, citing verses to support each.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'שאת' (a skin ailment) derives from the language of height, citing a verse about high mountains, and 'ספחת' (a secondary ailment) derives from the language of attachment, citing a verse where someone asks to be attached to the priesthood.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on humility and setting one's ways
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on humility and setting one's ways
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi delivers two homilies: first, that the humble are considered as if they offered all sacrifices, and their prayer is not rejected; second, that one who sets their ways in this world merits to see God's salvation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the humble are considered as if they offered all sacrifices, and their prayer is not rejected.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who sets their ways in this world merits to see God's salvation.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction on the effect of speech in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction on the effect of speech in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies that speech (talking with a designated man) is a violation, but the later clause states that if she merely spoke with him, she remains permitted, implying speech is meaningless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies that speech (talking with a designated man) is a violation, but the later clause states that if she merely spoke with him, she remains permitted, implying speech is meaningless.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the Mishnah's intent: if the husband said 'do not speak' and she spoke, or 'do not speak' and she secluded herself, it is nothing; but if he said 'do not seclude yourself' and she merely spoke, she is still permitted; only if she entered a secluded place and stayed long enough for defilement does she become forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's cases are distinct: if the husband said 'do not speak' and she spoke or secluded herself, it is nothing; if he said 'do not seclude yourself' and she merely spoke, she is still permitted; only if she entered a secluded place and stayed long enough for defilement does she become forbidden.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's ruling 'if he dies, she performs חליצה'
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's ruling 'if he dies, she performs חליצה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that if the husband dies, the sotah performs חליצה (removal of the shoe) rather than being eligible for יבום (levirate marriage), asking why she cannot enter levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that if the husband dies, the sotah performs חליצה (removal of the shoe) rather than being eligible for יבום (levirate marriage).

items.text: Rav Yosef's first answer and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's first answer and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a verse to show that the sotah is forbidden to the yavam, as the verse says 'to another man' and not to the yavam. Abaye objects that if so, she should not even require חליצה, but Rav Yosef responds that just as she would need a get from the living husband, so she needs חליצה from the yavam.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the verse 'וְיָצְאָה מִבֵּיתוֹ וְהָלְכָה וְהָיְתָה לְאִישׁ אַחֵר' teaches that the sotah goes to 'another man' and not to the yavam, so she is forbidden to the yavam.
Abaye objects that if the sotah is forbidden to the yavam, then she should not even require חליצה (release from yibbum).
Rav Yosef resolves that just as the sotah would need a גט (bill of divorce) from her living husband, so too she needs חליצה from the yavam.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's answer and Abaye's further objection
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's answer and Abaye's further objection
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rav Yosef citing the verse to mean that the sotah should not cause her husband's house to be destroyed, so she certainly cannot enter levirate marriage. Abaye objects that by that logic she should not be allowed to marry any other man, but Rav Yosef's response is cut off.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Rav Yosef citing the verse 'ויצאה מביתו' (and she departs from his house) to argue that the sotah should not cause her husband's house to be destroyed, so she certainly cannot enter levirate marriage.
Abaye objects that by that logic she should not be allowed to marry any other man either, lest she destroy the second husband's house.
Rav Yosef begins to respond to Abaye's objection, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav Yosef's argument against yibbum for the sotah
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's argument against yibbum for the sotah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the sotah who married another man is called 'another' in Scripture, indicating she is not a proper match for the first husband, so she certainly cannot enter yibbum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the sotah who married another man is called 'אחר' (another) in Scripture, indicating she is not a proper match for the first husband, so she certainly cannot enter yibbum.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: if the sotah is called 'another' and thus cannot enter yibbum, then if she married another man and he died childless, she should also not enter yibbum with that second husband's brother, which is absurd.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: if the sotah is called 'another' and thus cannot enter yibbum, then if she married another man and he died childless, she should also not enter yibbum with that second husband's brother, which is absurd.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: Rava argues with a kal vachomer: if the sotah was forbidden to her husband (who was permitted to her), then she is certainly forbidden to the yavam (who is forbidden to her).

sub.desc_en: Rava argues with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) inference: if the sotah was forbidden to her husband, who was permitted to her, then she is certainly forbidden to the yavam, who is forbidden to her.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding Rava's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding Rava's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rava's kal vachomer is flawed because the sotah was already forbidden to her husband. The Gemara refines the case to a kohen's wife who was raped and whose husband died, leaving a chalal brother, but then notes that rape is permitted for an Israelite, so there is no prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's kal vachomer by proposing a parallel case: a High Priest who betrothed a widow and died, leaving a regular priest brother—should she not undergo יבום (levirate marriage) by the same kal vachomer?
The Gemara rejects Abaye's objection, pointing out that the widow was already forbidden to the High Priest, so the kal vachomer's premise—'if she was forbidden by what was permitted'—does not apply.
The Gemara refines the case to a kohen's wife who was raped and whose husband died, leaving a חלל (disqualified priest) brother—arguing by kal vachomer that she should not undergo יבום.
The Gemara rejects even the refined case, noting that rape is permitted (מותר) for an Israelite woman, so there is no prohibition to ground the kal vachomer.

items.text: Mishnah: Women forbidden from eating terumah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women forbidden from eating terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists women who are forbidden from eating terumah: one who says she is defiled, one who has witnesses that she is defiled, one who refuses to drink, one whose husband does not want to give her the water, and one whose husband had relations with her on the way.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five categories of women forbidden from eating תרומה (priestly portion): one who declares herself defiled, one with witnesses of defilement, one who refuses to drink, one whose husband refuses to give her the water, and one whose husband had relations with her on the way.

items.text: Rav Amram's teaching from Rav Sheshet: witnesses overseas prevent water test
items.text_en: Rav Amram's teaching from Rav Sheshet: witnesses overseas prevent water test
items.desc_en: Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught from the Mishnah that a sotah with witnesses overseas is not tested by the water, because the verse requires that there be no witness who knows of her defilement. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's case of witnesses coming after she drank implies that the water would not have tested her, otherwise the witnesses would be proven false.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram reports that Rav Sheshet taught from the Mishnah that a sotah with witnesses overseas is not tested by the water, because the verse requires that there be no witness who knows of her defilement.
Rav Amram clarifies that the Mishnah's case of witnesses coming after she drank implies that the water would not have tested her, otherwise the witnesses would be proven false.
Rav Amram concludes that if the water does not test her, the Mishnah's case is consistent; if it did test her, the witnesses would be proven false retroactively.

items.text: Rav Yosef's response: merit can suspend the water's effect
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's response: merit can suspend the water's effect
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the water still tests her, but merit can suspend the punishment, causing her to wither. The Gemara explains that Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef disagree about whether Rabbi's opinion that merit suspends the water applies only to Rabbi or to the Rabbis as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef responds to Rav Sheshet that the water still tests the sotah, but merit can suspend the punishment.
The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef revolves around Rabbi's opinion that merit suspends the water's effect, causing the woman to wither (מתנוונה).
The Gemara resolves that Rav Sheshet holds that both Rabbi and the Rabbis agree the woman withers, while Rav Yosef holds that only Rabbi holds she withers, but the Rabbis do not.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi cites Rabbi Shimon who says merit does not suspend the water, otherwise it would cast aspersions on all pure women who drank. The Gemara deflects: Rabbi Shimon holds that merit does not suspend, so witnesses also do not suspend, but the debate is only between Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef regarding Rabbi's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that merit does not suspend the bitter waters, because that would cast aspersions on all pure women who drank.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi extends the objection: if witnesses in a distant land suspend the water, the same aspersion would be cast on pure women.

The Gemara deflects: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection is only according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that merit does not suspend, so witnesses also do not suspend — the debate between Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef is only regarding Rabbi's view.

items.text: Transition to next Mishnah: whose meal-offerings are burned
items.text_en: Transition to next Mishnah: whose meal-offerings are burned
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic with a citation from a Mishnah listing those whose meal-offerings are burned.

sub.desc_en: Rav cites the Mishnah listing those whose meal-offerings are burned.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of a woman who says 'I am impure' and witnesses arrive. It considers whether the witnesses came before or after the meal-offering was sanctified, and whether the water tests her, leading to a contradiction about the offering's status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's case of a woman who says 'I am impure' and witnesses arrive, then asks whether the witnesses came before or after the meal-offering was sanctified, concluding that if before, the offering should be redeemed to חולין (non-sacred status).

The Gemara considers the alternative that the witnesses came after sanctification, and argues that if the water does not test her, the sanctification was retroactively mistaken, so the offering should be redeemed to חולין (non-sacred status).

items.text: Rav Yehuda of Disakarta's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda of Disakarta's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda from Disakarta resolves the contradiction by specifying that the woman committed adultery in the Temple courtyard, so the initial sanctification was valid and the water tests her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Disakarta resolves the contradiction by specifying that the woman committed adultery in the Temple courtyard, so the initial sanctification was valid and the water tests her.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's objection
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects that priests' attendants accompany the woman, so she could not have committed adultery in the courtyard unless it was with those attendants themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects that priests' attendants accompany the woman, so she could not have committed adultery in the courtyard unless it was with those attendants themselves.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests the case is where she needed to relieve herself, and the attendants do not accompany her there, allowing for adultery.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by proposing that the woman needed to relieve herself, and the young priests would not accompany her there, allowing for adultery.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution based on rabbinic decree
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution based on rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa maintains the original assumption that the water does not test her, but explains that the offering is not released to non-sacred use due to a rabbinic decree preventing people from saying sacred items are taken out to common use.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by maintaining the original assumption that the water does not test her, but explains that the offering is not released to non-sacred use due to a rabbinic decree (גזירה) preventing people from saying sacred items are taken out from Temple service to common use.

items.text: Rav Mari's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Mari's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Mari objects by citing a baraita that details the laws of a meal-offering that became impure or was not yet offered, concluding that if witnesses of adultery arrive, the offering is burned, contradicting Rav Pappa's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects by citing a baraita that rules that if a meal-offering became impure after being sanctified in a vessel, it is burned, implying that the offering is validly sanctified.
The baraita continues with the case where the handful was sanctified but not yet offered, and the woman died, ruling that the offering is burned.
The baraita rules that if the handful was offered but the leftovers were not yet eaten, the leftovers are eaten, because the offering atoned for her doubt.
The baraita concludes that if witnesses of adultery arrive, the offering is burned, but if the witnesses are found to be conspiring, the offering becomes חולין (non-sacred).

items.text: Gemara's clarification on witnesses
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's mention of conspiring witnesses, noting that such witnesses are well-known and thus the case is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's mention of conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין) is irrelevant because such witnesses are notorious and thus the case is different.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Sheshet and additional derivations
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Sheshet and additional derivations
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Sheshet's view, though not for his reason. It then derives from the Mishnah's wording that the woman must be pure, not have witnesses in a distant land, not have merit to suspend her, and not have women discussing her case, with Rabbi Shimon's opinion noted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Sheshet's position, though not for his reasoning.
The baraita derives from the word 'טהורה' (pure) that the woman must be pure, not that she has witnesses in a distant land.
The baraita derives from the extra 'ו' in 'וּטְהוֹרָה' that the woman does not have merit to suspend her punishment.
The baraita derives from the word 'הִיא' (she) that women should not discuss her case.
The gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon, who does not expound the word 'וי

items.text: Gemara's question on witnesses in a distant province
items.text_en: Gemara's question on witnesses in a distant province
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's earlier statement about witnesses being in a distant province, explaining that such a situation is uncommon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's earlier statement about witnesses being in a distant province.
The Gemara answers that such a situation is uncommon.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for bringing the sotah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for bringing the sotah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that the husband brings his wife to the local court, which appoints two Torah scholars to accompany them to Jerusalem, lest the husband have relations with her on the way. Rabbi Yehuda says the husband is trusted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for bringing the sotah: the husband brings her to the local court, which appoints two Torah scholars to accompany them to Jerusalem, lest the husband have relations with her on the way; Rabbi Yehuda says the husband is trusted.

items.text: Gemara: Why two scholars? Supporting Rav's statements
items.text_en: Gemara: Why two scholars? Supporting Rav's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two scholars are needed, noting that with the husband there are three. It suggests this supports Rav's ruling that on the road three are needed in case one needs to relieve himself. The Gemara rejects this, explaining the reason is to have witnesses. It then questions why specifically Torah scholars, supporting another of Rav's rulings that only upright people are suitable, not permissive ones, but rejects that too, saying the reason is that scholars know how to admonish him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two scholars are needed, noting that with the husband there are three.
The Gemara suggests this supports Rav's ruling that on the road three are needed in case one needs to relieve himself.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining the reason is to have witnesses.
The Gemara questions why specifically Torah scholars, supporting another of Rav's rulings that only upright people are suitable.
The Gemara rejects that support, saying the reason is that scholars know how to admonish him.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's kal vachomer: if a husband is trusted regarding a niddah (which carries karet), he should certainly be trusted regarding a sotah (which carries only a negative commandment). The Rabbis respond that a niddah has a permitted end, so the husband is reliable, but a sotah does not, so he is not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's kal vachomer: if a husband is trusted regarding a niddah (which carries karet), he should certainly be trusted regarding a sotah (which carries only a negative commandment).
The Rabbis respond that a niddah has a permitted end, so the husband is reliable, but a sotah does not, so he is not.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's source is a verse, not kal vachomer
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's source is a verse, not kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yehuda actually derives his ruling from a verse, not a kal vachomer, as a baraita states: 'And the man shall bring his wife to the priest' — from the Torah the husband brings her, but the Sages said to appoint two scholars. Rabbi Yosei then presents the kal vachomer, and the Sages refute it. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda first presented the kal vachomer, they refuted it, and then he cited the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yehuda derives his ruling from a verse, not a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument), citing a baraita.

The baraita presents Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer: if a husband is trusted regarding a niddah (menstruant) who is subject to karet (extirpation), then certainly he should be trusted regarding a sotah (suspected adulteress) who is only subject to a negative commandment.
The Sages refute the kal vachomer: niddah has a permitted remedy (immersion), but sotah does not, and they cite the verse 'Stolen waters are sweet' (Proverbs 9:17).
The baraita concludes that Rabbi Yehuda cites the verse 'And the man shall bring his wife to the priest' (Numbers 5:15) as his source.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda first presented the kal vachomer, the Sages refuted it, and then he cited the verse.

items.text: Difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda's opinion seems identical to the first Tanna, and explains that the difference lies in the phrase 'but they said' — whether the Sages' enactment overrides the Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda's position differs from the first Tanna (תנא קמא), since both seem to say the husband brings his wife.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the phrase 'but they said' (אבל אמרו) — whether the Sages' enactment overrides the Torah law, which the first Tanna includes but Rabbi Yehuda omits.

items.text: Mishnah: Bringing the sotah to the Great Court and the intimidation procedure
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bringing the sotah to the Great Court and the intimidation procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that they bring the sotah to the Great Court in Jerusalem and intimidate her like witnesses in capital cases. They tell her that wine, laughter, and youth lead to sin, and urge her to confess for the sake of God's name. If she admits guilt, she forfeits her ketubah; if she claims innocence, they bring her to the Nicanor Gate for the ordeal. The priest tears her clothes and loosens her hair, though Rabbi Yehuda says if she is beautiful, he does not do so. If she wears white, they dress her in black, and remove her jewelry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that they bring the sotah to the Great Court in Jerusalem and intimidate her like witnesses in capital cases.

The Mishnah details the intimidation speech: they tell her that wine, laughter, youth, and bad neighbors lead to sin, and urge her to confess for the sake of God's name, saying things not fit to be heard by her and her family.
The Mishnah states that if the woman admits guilt, she forfeits her ketubah and leaves.
The Mishnah states that if she claims innocence, they bring her to the Nicanor Gate for the ordeal, where sotot are given to drink and where women after childbirth and lepers are purified.
The Mishnah describes that the priest tears her clothes and loosens her hair, though Rabbi Yehuda says if her heart or hair is beautiful, he does not do so.
The Mishnah concludes that if she wears white, they dress her in black, and remove her jewelry.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Stripping and Public Viewing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Stripping and Public Viewing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that ornaments are removed from the Sotah to disgrace her, and a rope is tied above her breasts. All may come to see her except her own slaves, because she is brazen with them, but all women are permitted to see her, as it is said: 'And all women shall be warned and not do as your lewdness.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that ornaments are removed from the Sotah to disgrace her, a rope is tied above her breasts, all may view her except her own slaves, and all women are permitted to see her as a warning.

items.text: Gemara: Source for Court of 71
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for Court of 71
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the requirement that the Sotah be judged by a court of 71. Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina derives it from a verbal analogy of 'Torah' to 'Torah' from the verse about the high court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the requirement of a court of 23 for the Sotah procedure) derived?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תורה' to the verse about the Great Sanhedrin of 71, teaching that the Sotah procedure requires a court of 71.

items.text: Gemara: Encouragement to Drink and Resolution of Contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara: Encouragement to Drink and Resolution of Contradiction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they intimidate her not to drink, but a baraita says they also encourage her to drink, telling her that if she is pure, she should drink, as the bitter waters are like a dry bandage that only affects a wound. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the intimidation is before the scroll is erased, the encouragement is after.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement about intimidating her and raises a contradiction from a baraita that says they also encourage her to drink, using the analogy of a dry bandage on healthy flesh.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before the scroll is erased (intimidation) and after (encouragement).

items.text: Gemara: Homiletical Stories of Judah and Reuben
items.text_en: Gemara: Homiletical Stories of Judah and Reuben
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says the priest speaks to her words of aggadah. The Tanna taught that he recounts events from early writings, such as 'which wise men have told and have not hidden from their fathers.' The Gemara elaborates that Judah confessed and was not ashamed, and his reward was inheriting the World to Come; similarly Reuben. Their reward in this world is that the land was given to them alone.
