sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates that Judah confessed and was not ashamed, inheriting the World to Come, and similarly Reuben; their reward in this world is that the land was given to them alone.

items.text: Gemara: Source for Reuben's Confession and Judah's Suffering
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for Reuben's Confession and Judah's Suffering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for Reuben's confession, since only Judah's confession is explicit in the Torah. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that during the years in the desert, Judah's bones were rolling in the coffin until Moses prayed, asking who caused Reuben to confess—Judah. Then God heard Judah's voice, brought him to the heavenly academy, enabled him to debate, and ensured his rulings aligned with halakha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: It is understandable that Judah confessed, as the Torah records it, but from where do we know that Reuben confessed?

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that during the years in the desert, Judah's bones were rolling in the coffin until Moses prayed, asking who caused Reuben to confess—Judah; then God heard Judah's voice, brought him to the heavenly academy, enabled him to debate, and ensured his rulings aligned with halakha.

items.text: Gemara: Why Reuben Confessed
items.text_en: Gemara: Why Reuben Confessed
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Reuben confessed, since it is not like Judah who confessed to save Tamar from burning. Rav Sheshet says it is brazen to detail one's sin, but Reuben confessed to clear his brothers from suspicion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: It is understandable that Judah confessed to save Tamar from burning, but why did Reuben confess, given that Rav Sheshet said it is audacious to specify one's sin?
The Gemara answers: Reuben confessed so that his brothers would not be suspected of the incident with Bilhah.
The Gemara answers: Reuben confessed so that his brothers would not be suspected.

items.text: Gemara: If She Says 'I am Defiled' or 'I am Pure'
items.text_en: Gemara: If She Says 'I am Defiled' or 'I am Pure'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if she says 'I am defiled,' she writes a receipt (for her ketubah). Abaye teaches that she tears it, but Rava objects that the Mishnah says 'breaks.' Rava explains that we are dealing with a place where they do not write a ketubah. If she says 'I am pure,' they bring her up to the Eastern Gate. The Gemara questions this procedure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that when she says 'I am defiled,' they write a receipt for her ketubah.
Abaye proposes that the Mishnah should read 'she tears' the receipt, not 'breaks.'
Rava objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'breaks,' not 'tears.'
Rava resolves that the Mishnah deals with a place where they do not write a ketubah, so she physically breaks the receipt.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's procedure: if she says 'I am pure,' why do they bring her up to the Eastern Gate?

items.text: Moving witnesses to confuse them
items.text_en: Moving witnesses to confuse them
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the court moves witnesses from place to place to confuse them and cause them to retract their testimony, citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the court moves witnesses from place to place to confuse them and cause them to retract their testimony, citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

items.text: Why the sotah is brought to the Nicanor Gate
items.text_en: Why the sotah is brought to the Nicanor Gate
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the sotah is brought to the Nicanor Gate, noting that it is written 'and the priest shall stand the woman before the Lord' for sotahs, and similarly for lepers. It then asks why a woman after childbirth is also brought there, and answers that it is because her offering must be present, but then questions why zavim and zavot are not also brought, concluding that the tanna only mentioned one category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a woman after childbirth (יולדת) must be brought to the Temple gate, given that the verses for sotah and lepers are explicit.
The Gemara suggests that the reason is because the woman stands by her offering, and then notes that the same would apply to zavim and zavot, so the tanna only mentioned one case.

items.text: Two sotahs are not administered together
items.text_en: Two sotahs are not administered together
items.desc_en: A baraita states that two sotahs are not administered together to prevent her heart from being bold toward her friend. Rabbi Yehuda says the reason is from the verse 'her' alone. The Tanna Kamma is identified as Rabbi Shimon, who derives the reason from the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that two sotahs are not given the bitter water together, so that one woman's heart not be emboldened by her companion.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) disagrees, saying the prohibition is not for that reason but because the verse states 'אֹתָהּ' (her) — her alone.
The Gemara asks: but the first tanna — isn't 'אֹתָהּ' (her) also written, so why does he not derive the law from it?

The Gemara answers that the first tanna is רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon), who interprets the reason of the verse, and the verse's 'אוֹתָהּ' (her) alone teaches the reason: so that her heart not be emboldened by her companion.

items.text: The difference between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages: a trembling woman
items.text_en: The difference between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages: a trembling woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages, and answers: a trembling woman. It then questions whether a trembling woman can be administered the water, since we do not perform mitzvot in bundles. Abaye or Rav Kahana resolves that one case is with one priest, the other with two priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference there is between the position of רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) and that of the Sages, and answers that the difference concerns a רותתת (trembling woman).
The Gemara objects: can a רותתת (trembling woman) really be given to drink together with another, given the principle that one does not perform מצוות (commandments) in bundles?

A baraita is cited to support the objection, listing the pairs that may not be done simultaneously — two סוטות (sota women), two מצורעים (lepers), two עבדים (slaves), two עגלות (heifers) — because one does not perform מצוות in bundles.

sub.text: Abaye, and some say Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Abaye, and some say Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: אביי (Abaye), and some say רב כהנא (Rav Kahana), resolves the contradiction: the baraita forbidding simultaneous drinking refers to one כהן (priest), while רבי שמעון's permission for a trembling woman refers to two כהנים (priests).

items.text: The priest holds her garments and uncovers her hair
items.text_en: The priest holds her garments and uncovers her hair
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'and he shall uncover the head of the woman' includes her body, but the specific phrase teaches that the priest loosens her hair.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'ופרע את ראש האשה' (and he shall uncover the woman's head) to teach that the kohen loosens her hair, and that 'האשה' includes her body.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's concern for improper thoughts vs. the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's concern for improper thoughts vs. the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda is concerned for improper thoughts regarding the sotah, but in a baraita about stoning, he requires more covering for a woman, while the Sages allow her to be stoned naked. Rabba resolves that in the sotah case, she might leave the court innocent and priests might become aroused, but in stoning she is being killed. Rava then notes that Rabbi Yehuda's positions are not contradictory as explained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda is concerned for improper thoughts (הרהור) while the Sages are not.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires more covering for a woman being stoned, while the Sages allow her to be stoned naked, showing the opposite concern.
Rabba explains that in the sotah case, she might leave the court innocent and priests might become aroused, but in stoning she is being killed, so no arousal occurs.
Rava resolves that Rabbi Yehuda's positions are not contradictory, as already explained.

items.text: Reconciling the rabbinic opinions on humiliation and the principle of a beautiful death
items.text_en: Reconciling the rabbinic opinions on humiliation and the principle of a beautiful death
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction between two rabbinic statements by explaining that the principle of 'choose a beautiful death' (from Rav Nachman) applies here, based on the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself'. This is used to justify why the Sotah is not subjected to both humiliation and physical pain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between rabbinic statements by explaining that one context requires humiliation for deterrence, while the other considers the humiliation itself the greatest suffering.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers the potential objection that both humiliation and physical pain should be applied, citing the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself' to justify choosing a beautiful death.

items.text: Debate between Tannaim regarding the preference for humiliation vs. physical pain
items.text_en: Debate between Tannaim regarding the preference for humiliation vs. physical pain
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman's principle is disputed by Tannaim, but concludes that all agree with it. The actual dispute is about whether a person prefers humiliation (bizyon) over physical pain (tza'ar) or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman's principle is disputed by Tannaim.
The Gemara answers that all agree with Rav Nachman's principle, but they dispute whether humiliation or physical pain is worse for the woman.

items.text: Clothing the Sotah in ugly garments and removing her jewelry
items.text_en: Clothing the Sotah in ugly garments and removing her jewelry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the Sotah was wearing white, she is covered in black; if she had gold jewelry, it is removed. The Gemara clarifies that even if she had black clothes that were attractive, they are replaced with ugly ones. It then questions the necessity of removing jewelry, explaining that it is to increase her humiliation, as per the folk saying about a naked messenger wearing shoes.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna adds that even if the Sotah had attractive black clothes, they are replaced with ugly ones.
The Gemara questions why it is necessary to explicitly mention removing her gold jewelry, given that she is already being humiliated.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought the jewelry adds to her humiliation, as per the folk saying about a naked messenger wearing shoes, so the Mishnah teaches that it is removed.

items.text: The requirement of an Egyptian rope for the Sotah
items.text_en: The requirement of an Egyptian rope for the Sotah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether the Egyptian rope is essential for the Sotah ritual. The question is whether its purpose is merely to prevent her clothes from slipping (in which case a small cord would suffice) or if it is required because it corresponds to her sin of girding herself with a belt for her lover. Rav Huna answers that the Mishnah explicitly states the rope is used to prevent her clothes from falling, implying it is not essential.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether the Egyptian rope is essential for the Sotah ritual or if a small cord suffices.
Rav Huna answers by citing the mishnah that the Egyptian rope is tied above her breasts to prevent her clothes from slipping off.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding who may see the Sotah
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding who may see the Sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the Mishnah: it first says 'anyone who wants to see her may see', implying both men and women, but then says 'all women are permitted to see her', implying only women. Abaye suggests the first clause refers to men, but Rava objects that it says 'anyone'. Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first clause permits both men and women to see her, while the second clause obligates women to see her, based on the verse 'And all women shall be admonished'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the mishnah: first it says anyone may see her, then it says only women may see her.
Abaye suggests that the mishnah means 'anyone' refers to men, but Rava objects that the mishnah explicitly says 'anyone who wants to see may see'.
Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'anyone who wants to see may see' applies to both men and women, but women are obligated to see her for the purpose of deterrence.

Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first clause permits both men and women to see her, while the second clause obligates women to see her, based on the verse 'And all women shall be admonished'.

items.text: Mishnah: Measure for measure in the Sotah ritual
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measure for measure in the Sotah ritual
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that a person is measured with the same measure they used. It applies this to the Sotah: she adorned herself for sin, so God disgraces her; she uncovered herself, so God exposes her; she began with the thigh and then the belly, so she is punished in that order, and the rest of the body does not escape.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the principle of measure-for-measure and applies it to the Sotah's punishment.

items.text: Gemara: The principle of measure for measure remains even after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Gemara: The principle of measure for measure remains even after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that although the formal measure (the Sotah ritual) has ceased, the principle of measure-for-measure punishment still applies. He supports this with a baraita that even after the Sanhedrin ceased, the four death penalties were not abolished but are carried out by divine means: one liable for stoning falls from a roof or is trampled by an animal, etc.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that although the formal measure-for-measure punishment is nullified, the principle itself remains.
Rav Yosef supports his statement with a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya that although the Sanhedrin is nullified, the four death penalties still apply in principle.
A baraita details how the four death penalties are carried out by divine means after the Temple's destruction.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the principle of measure for measure
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the principle of measure for measure
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi deriving the principle from the verse 'In measure, when it is sent forth, you contend with it'. The Gemara then expands this to include all measures, from a se'ah to a perutah, citing additional verses. It concludes by applying this to the Sotah, listing how her actions are mirrored in the ritual: she stood at her door to be seen, so the priest stands her at the Nikanor Gate; she spread a fine cloth on her head, so the priest removes her headdress; she adorned her face, so...

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi deriving the principle of measure-for-measure from the verse 'בְּסַאסְּאָה בְּשַׁלְּחָהּ תְּרִיבֶנָּה' (In measure, when it is sent forth, you contend with it).

The Gemara expands the principle to include all measures from a se'ah down to an ukhla, citing the verse 'כִּי כׇּל סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ' (for every boot of the booted warrior in the din of battle).
The Gemara adds that even each perutah (small coin) joins to a great account, citing the verse 'אַחַת לְאַחַת לִמְצֹא חֶשְׁבּוֹן' (one to one to find the account).

The Gemara applies the principle to the Sotah, listing how her actions are mirrored in the ritual: she stood at her door to be seen, so the priest stands her at the Nikanor Gate; she spread a fine cloth on her head, so the priest removes her headdress; she adorned her face, so...

items.text: Measure-for-measure punishments of the sotah
items.text_en: Measure-for-measure punishments of the sotah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the sotah's sins and corresponding punishments, each introduced by 'הִיא... לְפִיכָךְ'. A second interpretation (דָּבָר אַחֵר) adds that her secret sin is publicly exposed by God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the sotah's sins and their corresponding measure-for-measure punishments, each introduced by 'הִיא... לְפִיכָךְ'.
The Mishnah continues listing additional sins and punishments, including the sotah's belly swelling and the offering being animal fodder.
The Mishnah states that because the sotah sinned in secret, God, who dwells in secret, exposes her, citing the verse about the adulterer's eye.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: because the sotah sinned in secret, God publicizes her sin openly, citing the verse that concealed hatred is eventually revealed in public.

items.text: Gemara's questions on redundant verses
items.text_en: Gemara's questions on redundant verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why additional verses (כִּי כׇל סְאוֹן סֹאֵן and בְּסַאסְּאָה) are needed if the principle of measure-for-measure is already derived from 'אַחַת לְאַחַת לִמְצֹא חֶשְׁבּוֹן'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'כִּי כׇל סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ' is needed if the measure-for-measure principle is already derived from 'אַחַת לְאַחַת לִמְצֹא חֶשְׁבּוֹן'.
The Gemara further asks why the verse 'בְּסַאסְּאָה בְּשַׁלְּחָהּ תְּרִיבֶנָּה' is needed if the principle is already derived from the previous verse.

items.text: Rav Chinana bar Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa explains that the verse 'בְּסַאסְּאָה' teaches that God does not punish a nation until the time of its exile.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa explains that the verse 'בְּסַאסְּאָה' teaches that God does not punish a nation until the time of its exile.

items.text: Objection and revised statement
items.text_en: Objection and revised statement
items.desc_en: Rava objects with a tradition about three cups of punishment for Egypt, implying earlier punishments. The Gemara resolves by citing a baraita about a convert, then revises Rav Chinana bar Pappa's statement to refer to a king rather than a nation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Chinana bar Pappa's statement by citing Rava's tradition that Egypt drank three cups of punishment, implying earlier punishments occurred before the nation's dismissal.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that these are different cups by citing a baraita where Minyamin the Egyptian convert discusses the status of Egyptian converts, implying a single continuous nation.

sub.text: Revised statement of Rav Chinana bar Pappa
sub.text_en: Revised statement of Rav Chinana bar Pappa
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by revising Rav Chinana bar Pappa's statement to refer to a king (מלך) rather than a nation (אומה), so that punishment is deferred until the king's dismissal.

items.text: Amemar's teaching on God's unchanging nature
items.text_en: Amemar's teaching on God's unchanging nature
items.desc_en: Amemar applies Rav Chinana bar Pappa's statement to a verse about God not changing and Israel not being consumed, explaining that God's arrows are spent but Israel is not.

sub.desc_en: Amemar applies Rav Chinana bar Pappa's statement to a verse about God not changing and Israel not being consumed, explaining that God's arrows are spent but Israel is not.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna on God's delayed punishment of individuals
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna on God's delayed punishment of individuals
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches that God does not punish a person until his measure is full, citing the verse 'בִּמְלֹאות שִׂפְקוֹ יֵצֶר לוֹ'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches that God does not punish a person until his measure is full, citing the verse 'בִּמְלֹאות שִׂפְקוֹ יֵצֶר לוֹ'.

items.text: Rav Chinana bar Pappa's homily on Moses and David
items.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa's homily on Moses and David
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa interprets a verse to refer to Moses and David, whose works were not destroyed by enemies. The Gemara explains that David's gates sank into the earth and Moses' Tabernacle was hidden under the Temple chambers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Pappa interprets the verse 'לַיְשָׁרִים נָאוָה תְהִלָּה' as referring to Moses and David, whose works were not destroyed by enemies.
The Gemara explains that David's gates sank into the earth, preventing enemies from destroying them.
The Gemara explains that Moses' Tabernacle was hidden under the Temple chambers when the First Temple was built, as stated by Mar and cited by Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi.

items.text: Baraita on the sotah's punishment
items.text_en: Baraita on the sotah's punishment
items.desc_en: A baraita summarizes that the sotah, who set her eyes on one not meant for her, neither received what she sought nor kept what she had, illustrating the principle that one who covets another's loses both.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the sotah, who set her eyes on one not meant for her, neither received what she sought nor kept what she had, and generalizes that anyone who covets another's loses both.

items.text: Principle of measure-for-measure: the primordial serpent and other sinners
items.text_en: Principle of measure-for-measure: the primordial serpent and other sinners
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that one who desires what is not theirs loses what they have, citing the primordial serpent as the first example, followed by Cain, Korah, Balaam, and others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle of measure-for-measure punishment, citing the primordial serpent and other sinners who desired what was not theirs and lost what they had.

items.text: Gemara's question on the order of curse and testing
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the order of curse and testing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the curse mentions the thigh first while the test mentions the belly first. Abaye explains that the curse began with the thigh, but the test follows its natural order, and the verse in the curse is to inform the priest to mention the belly first to avoid slander against the bitter waters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the order 'thigh first, then belly' in the curse, and raises a contradiction from the verse that mentions belly first.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the curse begins with the thigh, but the priest announces the order of belly first to avoid disparaging the bitter waters.
The Gemara objects that the curse itself also mentions the belly before the thigh.
Abaye resolves that the verse in the curse is to inform the priest to mention the belly first, to avoid slander against the bitter waters.

items.text: Mishnah: Measure-for-measure for Samson, Absalom, and righteous figures
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measure-for-measure for Samson, Absalom, and righteous figures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Samson followed his eyes, so the Philistines gouged them out. Absalom was proud of his hair, so he was hanged by it; he slept with his father's concubines, so ten spears pierced him; he stole three hearts, so three darts struck him. The Mishnah then gives positive examples: Miriam waited for Moses, so Israel waited for her; Joseph buried his father, and Moses buried Joseph, and God buried Moses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the principle of measure-for-measure: Samson followed his eyes, so the Philistines gouged them out.

The Mishnah continues with Absalom: he was proud of his hair, so he was hanged by it; he slept with his father's concubines, so ten spears pierced him; he stole three hearts, so three darts struck him.
The Mishnah gives a positive example: Miriam waited for Moses, so Israel waited for her.
The Mishnah concludes with Joseph and Moses: Joseph buried his father, Moses buried Joseph, and God buried Moses, extending the principle to all righteous.

items.text: Gemara: Samson's rebellion and divine providence
items.text_en: Gemara: Samson's rebellion and divine providence
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that Samson rebelled with his eyes, so his eyes were gouged out. It questions this, citing the verse that his parents did not know it was from God, and explains that he went after his own inclination.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Samson rebelled with his eyes, so the Philistines gouged them out, citing the verse about his request for a woman and the subsequent punishment.
The Gemara questions the baraita by citing the verse that Samson's parents did not know his desire was from God, implying divine orchestration rather than rebellion.
The Gemara resolves that although the initial match was divinely ordained, Samson's subsequent actions followed his own inclination (יַשְׁרוּתֵיהּ), justifying the punishment.

items.text: Rabbi's statement: Samson's downfall began in Gaza
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement: Samson's downfall began in Gaza
items.desc_en: Rabbi teaches that Samson's corruption began in Gaza, so he was punished in Gaza, citing verses about his visit to a prostitute there and his later capture. The Gemara questions a verse about Timnah, and clarifies that the initial corruption was in Gaza.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi teaches that Samson's initial corruption was in Gaza, so he was punished in Gaza, and the Gemara clarifies that despite his earlier visit to Timnah, the corruption began in Gaza.
The Gemara questions Rabbi's statement by citing a verse that Samson went down to Timnah, implying an earlier corruption.
The Gemara resolves that the initial corruption was indeed in Gaza, while the Timnah episode was a later event.

items.text: Delilah's name and Samson's confession
items.text_en: Delilah's name and Samson's confession
items.desc_en: Rabbi explains that Delilah's name indicates she weakened his strength, heart, and deeds. The Gemara then discusses how Delilah knew Samson told the truth: Rabbi Chanin says true words are recognizable, and Abaye says she knew he would not utter God's name in vain, so when he said 'I am a Nazirite of God,' she knew it was true.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi explains that Delilah's name indicates she weakened Samson's strength, heart, and deeds.
Rabbi cites three verses to prove that Delilah weakened Samson's strength, heart, and deeds (the departure of the Divine Presence).
The Gemara asks how Delilah knew that Samson had told her the truth.
Rabbi Chanin in the name of Rav answers that true words are recognizable.
Abaye answers that Delilah knew Samson would not utter God's name in vain, so when he said 'I am a Nazirite of God,' she knew it was true.

items.text: Samson's coercion and the jawbone
items.text_en: Samson's coercion and the jawbone
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that 'וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ' means she slipped away from under him at the moment of climax. He also explains that the angel's command to Samson's mother not to eat anything 'טָמֵא' refers to things forbidden to a nazirite, and that Samson desired something impure, so his life was sustained by something impure (the jawbone).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ' (and she pressed him) means in the context of Delilah's coercion of Samson.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that 'וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ' means she slipped away from under him at the moment of climax.
The Gemara asks what 'כׇּל טָמֵא' (anything impure) means in the angel's command to Samson's mother, and questions how she could have been eating impure things before.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that 'כׇּל טָמֵא' refers to things forbidden to a nazirite, not general impurity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that because Samson desired something impure (a Philistine woman), his life was sustained by something impure (the jawbone of a donkey).

items.text: Samson's prophecy and strength
items.text_en: Samson's prophecy and strength
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina says that the spirit of God began to 'impel' Samson, fulfilling Jacob's prophecy about Dan. Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami says the Shekhinah 'tinkled' before him like a bell. Rabbi Assi says that Samson uprooted two mountains and ground them together. The Gemara concludes with Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's statement about Samson beginning to save Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina says that the spirit of God began to impel Samson, fulfilling Jacob's prophecy about Dan being a serpent.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains that the Divine Presence 'tinkled' before Samson like a bell, based on a verbal analogy between 'lefa'amo' and 'pa'amon'.
Rabbi Assi says that Zorah and Eshtaol were two large mountains, and Samson uprooted them and ground them together.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina begins a statement about Samson beginning to save Israel, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Abimelech's oath and its consequences
items.text_en: Abimelech's oath and its consequences
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that Abimelech's oath was initiated, citing the verse where he asks for loyalty from his descendants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that Abimelech's oath was initiated, citing the verse where he asks for loyalty from his descendants.

items.text: Samson's blessing and prayer
items.text_en: Samson's blessing and prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that Samson was blessed with his measure being like that of other men but his seed like a rushing stream. Then, Samson's prayer for strength is cited, where he reminds God of his 22 years of judging Israel without imposing personal burdens.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With what did God bless Samson?
Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers that God blessed Samson with his measure: his measure was like other men, but his seed was like a rushing stream.
Rav cites Samson's prayer, where he reminds God of his 22 years of judging Israel without imposing personal burdens.

items.text: Why foxes?
items.text_en: Why foxes?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagdi in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that Samson used foxes because they turn back, symbolizing the Philistines who reneged on their oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why specifically foxes were chosen for Samson's revenge.

sub.text: Rabbi Ayyevu bar Nagdi said Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ayyevu bar Nagdi said Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ayyevu bar Nagdi in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that Samson said: let the one who turns back (the fox) come and exact punishment from the Philistines who reneged on their oath.

items.text: Samson's width
items.text_en: Samson's width
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon the Pious states that Samson's shoulders were sixty cubits wide, based on the verse about him carrying the gates of Gaza, and the tradition that Gaza's gates were no less than sixty cubits.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon the Pious that Samson's shoulders were sixty cubits wide, based on the gate of Gaza being at least sixty cubits.

items.text: Samson's grinding and its implications
items.text_en: Samson's grinding and its implications
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'grinding' as a euphemism for sin, teaching that each Philistine brought his wife to Samson in prison to become pregnant. He further states that one who commits adultery will have his own wife commit adultery, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'grinding' (טחינה) as a euphemism for sin, citing the verse 'תִּטְחַן לְאַחֵר אִשְׁתִּי' (let my wife grind for another).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that each Philistine brought his wife to Samson in prison to become pregnant from him.

sub.text: Rav Pappa citing a popular saying
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa citing a popular saying
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a popular saying: before a wine drinker, wine; before a grinder, a duvla (a type of cake).
Rabbi Yochanan states that one who commits adultery will have his own wife commit adultery, citing verses and a popular saying.

items.text: Samson judged like God and named after God
items.text_en: Samson judged like God and named after God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that Samson judged Israel like their Father in heaven, and that his name reflects God's name, as God is a sun and shield. The Gemara clarifies that he is not literally named after God but in a similar sense of protection.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Samson judged Israel like their Father in Heaven, citing the verse 'Dan shall judge his people as one'.
Rabbi Yochanan says Samson was named after God, but clarifies it is only analogous: as God protects the whole world, so Samson protected Israel in his generation.
The Gemara objects: if Samson is literally named after God, his name should not be erasable (as God's name is not erased).
The Gemara resolves: Samson's name is only analogous (מעין) to God's name — just as God protects the entire world, so Samson protected Israel in his generation.

items.text: Balaam and Samson's lameness; five who were created with superior traits and punished through them
items.text_en: Balaam and Samson's lameness; five who were created with superior traits and punished through them
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states Balaam was lame in one foot and Samson in both. The Sages list five people created with a semblance of the supernal and were punished through those traits: Samson (strength), Saul (neck), Absalom (hair), Zedekiah (eyes), Asa (feet). Each is supported by verses, and the Gemara discusses Asa's ailment and its cause.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Balaam was lame in one foot and Samson in both, citing verses.
The Sages list five people created with a semblance of the supernal who were punished through those traits: Samson (strength), Saul (neck), Absalom (hair), Zedekiah (eyes), Asa (feet).
A verse is cited showing Samson's strength was removed.
A verse is cited showing Saul fell on his sword, affecting his neck.

sub.text: Supporting verse for Absalom and Zedekiah
sub.text_en: Supporting verse for Absalom and Zedekiah
sub.desc_en: Verses are cited for Absalom (hair) and Zedekiah (eyes).

sub.text: Supporting verse for Asa and discussion
sub.text_en: Supporting verse for Asa and discussion
sub.desc_en: A verse is cited for Asa's foot ailment; Rav Yehuda says it was פָּדַגְרָא (gout), and Mar Zutra asks Rav Nachman to describe it, with various explanations of how Rav Nachman knew.

items.text: Asa's punishment for conscripting scholars
items.text_en: Asa's punishment for conscripting scholars
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Asa was punished because he conscripted Torah scholars for forced labor, as the verse says he summoned all Judah with no exemption, even bridegrooms and brides.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds that Asa was punished because he conscripted Torah scholars, as the verse says 'and King Asa summoned all of Judah, none was exempt', including even a bridegroom from his chamber and a bride from her canopy.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse and explains that 'אֵין נָקִי' (no one was exempt) included even bridegrooms and brides, showing the severity of the conscription.

items.text: The descent and ascent of Timnah
items.text_en: The descent and ascent of Timnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar notes that for Samson, who was degraded through Timnah, the verse uses 'descent', while for Judah, who was elevated through Timnah, it uses 'ascent'. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says there were two Timnahs, and Rav Pappa says it was one place, with descent from one side and ascent from the other, like certain locations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar contrasts the language of 'descent' for Samson and 'ascent' for Judah regarding Timnah, reflecting their respective degradation and elevation.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani resolves the contradiction by positing two distinct places named Timnah, one approached by descent and the other by ascent.
Rav Pappa offers a third resolution: it is a single Timnah, but the direction of approach determines whether one descends or ascends, analogous to known locales.

items.text: The location of 'Einayim' and Tamar's conversation
items.text_en: The location of 'Einayim' and Tamar's conversation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri says Tamar sat at the entrance of Abraham, where all eyes look to him. Rabbi Chanin says it is a place named Einayim. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says she gave 'eyes' to her words, explaining her responses to Judah's questions about her status.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri interprets 'פתח עינים' as the entrance of Abraham, where all eyes look to him.
Rabbi Chanin says 'עינים' is a place name, citing a verse from Joshua.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says Tamar gave 'eyes' to her words, explaining her responses to Judah's questions about her status.

items.text: Abraham's planting: orchard or inn?
items.text_en: Abraham's planting: orchard or inn?
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says Abraham planted an orchard with all kinds of delicacies. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia debate whether it was an orchard or an inn, with the Gemara supporting the orchard from the word 'planted' and the inn from a similar usage in Daniel.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets Abraham's planting of an אשל (a tamarisk tree) as planting an orchard (פרדס) containing all kinds of delicacies.
The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia: one says it was an orchard (פרדס), the other says it was an inn (פונדק).
The Gemara notes that for the one who says 'orchard', the word 'וַיִּטַּע' (and he planted) fits naturally.
The Gemara objects: for the one who says 'inn', what does 'וַיִּטַּע' (and he planted) mean?
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a verse in Daniel where 'וַיִּטַּע' (and he planted) is used idiomatically for pitching tents, supporting the interpretation of an inn.

items.text: Calling in God's name
items.text_en: Calling in God's name
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'and he called there in the name of the Lord, God of the world' as a directive to read it differently, implying Abraham caused others to call upon God.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish begins a homiletic interpretation of the verse 'and he called there in the name of the Lord', suggesting a different reading.

items.text: Abraham's proclamation of God's name
items.text_en: Abraham's proclamation of God's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abraham made God's name known to all passersby by telling them to bless God after eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abraham made God's name known by telling passersby to bless God after eating.

items.text: Why Judah thought Tamar was a harlot
items.text_en: Why Judah thought Tamar was a harlot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Judah thought Tamar was a harlot just because she covered her face. Rabbi Elazar explains that she covered her face in her father-in-law's house, and a modest daughter-in-law merits kings and prophets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Judah thought Tamar was a harlot just because she covered her face.

Rabbi Elazar explains that Tamar covered her face in her father-in-law's house, and a modest daughter-in-law merits kings and prophets, citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, Rabbi Yonatan, and Rabbi Levi.

items.text: The removal and return of Tamar's signs
items.text_en: The removal and return of Tamar's signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the unusual spelling of 'she is brought out' and explains that after Tamar's signs were found, Samael distanced them and Gabriel brought them back. This is connected to the psalm 'For the conductor, upon the silent dove of distant ones.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the unusual spelling 'הִיא מוּצֵאת' (she is brought out) instead of the expected 'הִיא מִיתּוֹצֵאת' (she is being brought out).
Rabbi Elazar explains that after Tamar's signs were found, Samael (the angel of death) distanced them, and Gabriel brought them back, accounting for the unusual spelling.

Rabbi Yochanan connects this to the psalm 'עַל יוֹנַת אֵלֶם רְחוֹקִים' (upon the silent dove of distant ones), explaining that when her signs were distanced, Tamar became like a silent dove, and David, who emerged from her, was humble and perfect to all.

The Gemara offers two alternative interpretations of 'מִכְתָּם': that David's wound was complete (he was born circumcised), and that in his smallness he humbled himself before greater people to learn Torah, and so in his greatness.

items.text: The lesson of not embarrassing others publicly
items.text_en: The lesson of not embarrassing others publicly
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Tamar sent a message to Judah rather than telling him directly, citing a teaching that it is better to be thrown into a fiery furnace than to embarrass someone publicly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Tamar sent a message to her father-in-law instead of telling him directly.
The Gemara cites a tradition that it is better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to publicly shame another, with proof from Tamar.

items.text: The word 'Haker na' and its significance
items.text_en: The word 'Haker na' and its significance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina notes that the word 'haker' (recognize) was used both to inform Jacob about Joseph's coat and to inform Judah about his signet. The word 'na' is a request, and Tamar asked Judah to recognize his Creator and not ignore her.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina notes that the word 'הכר' (recognize) was used both to inform Jacob about Joseph's coat and to inform Judah about his signet.
The gemara explains that 'נא' is a term of request, and Tamar asked Judah to recognize his Creator and not ignore her.

items.text: Judah's public sanctification of God's name
items.text_en: Judah's public sanctification of God's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Joseph, who sanctified God's name in private and had a letter added to his name, with Judah, who sanctified God's name in public and was named entirely after God. A heavenly voice declared that Judah saved Tamar and her sons from fire, so God would save three of his sons from fire.

sub.text: Rav Chanin bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chanin bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida states that Joseph, who sanctified God's name in private, merited having a letter from God's name added to his own name, as it is written 'עדות ביהוסף שמו' (a testimony in Joseph He placed).

sub.text: Same authority (Rav Chanin bar Bizna / Rabbi Shimon Chasida)
sub.text_en: Same authority (Rav Chanin bar Bizna / Rabbi Shimon Chasida)
sub.desc_en: The same authority contrasts Judah, who sanctified God's name in public, meriting that his entire name is composed of letters from God's name, and because he admitted 'צדקה ממני' (she is more righteous than I), a heavenly voice declared that just as he saved Tamar and her two sons from fire, so too God would save three of his descendants from fire.

The Gemara identifies the three saved descendants as Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, and adds that a heavenly voice declared that from Judah himself emerged those who were subdued (i.e., the three youths who were thrown into the furnace).

items.text: Judah never ceased from knowing Tamar
items.text_en: Judah never ceased from knowing Tamar
items.desc_en: Shmuel Sava explains that once Judah knew Tamar, he never stopped having relations with her, as the verse 'and he did not continue further to know her' is interpreted like 'a great voice and did not cease.'

sub.desc_en: Shmuel Sava teaches that once Judah knew Tamar, he never ceased from her, using a verbal analogy from the verse about the great voice that did not cease.

items.text: Absalom's pride and downfall
items.text_en: Absalom's pride and downfall
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Absalom's pride in his hair, which led to his death by being caught in a tree. It describes how he was suspended between heaven and earth, and how David's eight cries of 'my son' were to raise him from the seven levels of Gehinnom and bring him to the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Absalom rebelled through his hair, citing the verse about his beauty and the weight of his hair.
The Gemara explains that therefore Absalom was hanged by his hair, citing the verse of his capture, and adds that the abyss of Gehinnom opened beneath him.
The Gemara asks what the purpose of David's eight cries of 'my son' was.
The Gemara answers that seven cries raised Absalom from the seven levels of Gehinnom, and the eighth either brought his head to his body or brought him to the World to Come.

sub.text: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets 'Absalom took' as taking a bad acquisition for himself, and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explains 'the King's Valley' as the deep counsel of the King of the World.

items.text: Midrash on 'from the valley of Hebron'
items.text_en: Midrash on 'from the valley of Hebron'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa interprets 'from the valley of Hebron' as referring to the deep counsel of the righteous one buried in Hebron (Abraham), who was told that his descendants would be strangers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa interprets 'from the valley of Hebron' as referring to the deep counsel of Abraham, who was told his descendants would be strangers.

items.text: Why Absalom said 'I have no son'
items.text_en: Why Absalom said 'I have no son'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Absalom said he had no son, given that he had three sons. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains he had no son fit for kingship. Rav Chisda cites a tradition: one who burns another's produce leaves no heir, referencing Absalom's burning of Yoav's field.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions how Absalom could say he had no son, since the verse states he had three sons.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi answers that Absalom had no son fit for kingship.
Rav Chisda answers that one who burns another's grain does not leave a son to inherit, citing Absalom's burning of Yoav's field.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about good measure
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about good measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: regarding punishment, Miriam was leprous for one hour, but regarding good, the reward is seven days. Abaye suggests emending the text to say 'regarding good it is not so.' Rava objects that the text explicitly says 'and so regarding good,' and explains that the measure of good is always greater than the measure of punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's comparison: regarding punishment Miriam was leprous for one hour, but regarding good the reward is seven days, so the analogy is inconsistent.
Abaye proposes emending the text to read 'regarding good it is not so,' thereby removing the contradiction.
Rava objects that the baraita explicitly states 'and so regarding good,' so emending the text is impossible.

Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita means the same measure applies, but the measure of good (מידה טובה) is always greater than the measure of punishment (מידת פורענות), so the seven days are consistent with the principle.

items.text: The verse 'And his sister stood afar' refers to the Shekhinah
items.text_en: The verse 'And his sister stood afar' refers to the Shekhinah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the entire verse 'And his sister stood afar' as referring to the Divine Presence, citing scriptural parallels for each word.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that the entire verse 'and his sister stood at a distance' is said with reference to the Divine Presence.
Each word of the verse is linked to a verse about God, demonstrating the verse refers to the Divine Presence.

items.text: Dispute over 'a new king'
items.text_en: Dispute over 'a new king'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether 'a new king' means literally new or one whose decrees were renewed. The one who says literally new cites the word 'new'; the other notes that it does not say 'and he died and reigned.' The verse 'who did not know Joseph' means he acted as if he did not know him.

sub.desc_en: One opinion holds that 'a new king' means literally a new king.
The other opinion holds that his decrees were renewed, not that he was a new king.
The gemara provides scriptural support for each opinion: the literal reading from 'new' and the renewed decrees from the absence of 'and he died and reigned'.
The gemara explains that 'who did not know Joseph' means he acted as if he did not know him at all.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the phrase 'who did not know Joseph'
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the phrase 'who did not know Joseph'
sub.desc_en: The verse 'who did not know Joseph' means he acted as if he did not know him at all.

items.text: Pharaoh began the evil counsel and was punished first
items.text_en: Pharaoh began the evil counsel and was punished first
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: Pharaoh began the evil counsel, so he was punished first, as the verse says 'upon you and your people.'

sub.desc_en: The tanna states that Pharaoh began with the evil counsel first, so he was punished first.
The gemara supports this with verses: 'he said to his people' shows he began, and 'upon you and your people and all your servants' shows he was punished first.

items.text: The counsel to afflict Israel with water
items.text_en: The counsel to afflict Israel with water
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the unusual wording 'to him' instead of 'to them.' Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains: they sought to outsmart the savior of Israel. They considered punishing Israel by fire or sword, but concluded to use water, since God swore not to bring a flood on the world, though they did not know He would bring it on one nation. Alternatively, they would fall into it. Rabbi Elazar notes the principle: in the pot they cooked, they were cooked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the unusual wording 'לוֹ' (to him) instead of 'לָהֶם' (to them) in Pharaoh's statement.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the verse means they sought to outsmart the savior of Israel (God).
The Gemara considers punishing Israel by fire or sword, but rejects both because God will use them against Egypt in the future.
The Gemara concludes that they chose to punish Israel by water, exploiting God's oath not to bring a flood on the whole world, unaware that He could bring it on one nation.
An alternative explanation: God does not bring the flood, but the Egyptians themselves fall into the water, as the verse says 'and Egypt fled toward it.'

Rabbi Elazar states the principle: in the pot they cooked (the water), they were cooked (drowned), citing the verse 'וַיָּזֶד יַעֲקֹב נָזִיד' (and Jacob cooked a stew) to show that 'זָדוּ' relates to a pot.

items.text: The three advisors: Balaam, Job, and Jethro
items.text_en: The three advisors: Balaam, Job, and Jethro
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai: three were in that counsel. Balaam who advised was killed, Job who was silent was afflicted with suffering, Jethro who fled merited that his descendants sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Simai that three individuals were present at Pharaoh's counsel against Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.desc_en: The tradition details the outcomes: Balaam who advised was killed, Job who was silent was afflicted with suffering, and Jethro who fled merited that his descendants sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, as supported by verses.

items.text: Pharaoh's self-curse: 'and go up from the land'
items.text_en: Pharaoh's self-curse: 'and go up from the land'
items.desc_en: The verse says 'and go up from the land' instead of 'and we will go up.' Rabbi Abba bar Kahana explains: like one who curses himself and attributes the curse to another.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse says 'and go up from the land' (וְעָלָה) instead of 'and we will go up' (וְעָלִינוּ).
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana answers that Pharaoh cursed himself and attributed the curse to others.

items.text: The taskmasters and the humiliation of Pharaoh
items.text_en: The taskmasters and the humiliation of Pharaoh
items.desc_en: The verse says 'upon him' instead of 'upon them.' The school of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon teaches: they brought a brick mold and hung it on Pharaoh's neck, and when an Israelite claimed to be delicate, they said: are you more delicate than Pharaoh? 'Taskmasters' refers to something that makes bricks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse says 'upon him' (עליו) instead of 'upon them' (עליהם), questioning the irregular wording.

sub.text: Tanna debei Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Tanna debei Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon teaches that the Egyptians brought a brick mold and hung it on Pharaoh's neck, so that when an Israelite claimed to be delicate, they would say: are you more delicate than Pharaoh?
The Gemara explains that the term 'שרי מסים' (taskmasters) refers to something that makes bricks (משים לבנים), supporting the previous teaching.

items.text: The unusual wording 'to afflict him'
items.text_en: The unusual wording 'to afflict him'
items.desc_en: The verse says 'to afflict him' instead of 'to afflict them.' The Gemara explains: to afflict Pharaoh with the burdens of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse says 'to afflict him' (עַנּוֹתוֹ) instead of 'to afflict them' (עַנּוֹתָם).
The gemara answers that 'to afflict him' refers to afflicting Pharaoh through the burdens of Israel.

items.text: Dispute over 'store cities'
items.text_en: Dispute over 'store cities'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute: one says they endanger their owners, the other says they impoverish their owners, citing the principle that one who engages in building becomes impoverished.

sub.desc_en: One opinion holds that 'עָרֵי מִסְכְּנוֹת' means cities that endanger their owners.
The other opinion holds that they are cities that impoverish their owners, as one who engages in building becomes poor.

items.text: Dispute over the names Pitom and Raamses
items.text_en: Dispute over the names Pitom and Raamses
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute: one says its name was Pitom, and it was called Raamses because one by one it crumbles; the other says its name was Raamses, and it was called Pitom because one by one the mouth of the deep swallows it.

sub.desc_en: One opinion holds that the city was named Pithom, and it was called Raamses because each building crumbled.
The other opinion holds that the city was named Raamses, and it was called Pithom because each building was swallowed by the mouth of the deep.

items.text: The Holy Spirit's prophecy: 'so will it increase'
items.text_en: The Holy Spirit's prophecy: 'so will it increase'
items.desc_en: The verse says 'so will it increase' instead of 'so it increased.' Reish Lakish explains: the Holy Spirit was announcing to them: 'so will it increase and so will it spread.' 'They were distressed' teaches that they were like thorns in their eyes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the verse says 'so it will multiply and so it will burst forth' (יִרְבֶּה וְיִפְרוֹץ) instead of 'so they multiplied and so they burst forth' (רַבּוּ וּפָרְצוּ).
Reish Lakish answers that the Holy Spirit was announcing to them that 'so it will multiply and so it will burst forth'.
The gemara explains that 'they were disgusted' means they were like thorns in their eyes.

items.text: Interpretations of "בְּפָרֶךְ" and the progression of labor
items.text_en: Interpretations of "בְּפָרֶךְ" and the progression of labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the meaning of "בְּפָרֶךְ" (with harsh labor): Rabbi Elazar says it means "with a soft mouth" (persuasion), Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it means "with crushing" (backbreaking work). Rava notes that the labor began with clay and bricks and ended with field work. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that the Egyptians swapped men's and women's work to make it harder.

items.text: The righteous women's merit and the miracles of redemption
items.text_en: The righteous women's merit and the miracles of redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches that the Israelites were redeemed from Egypt due to the righteous women of that generation. He describes how they would go to draw water, find small fish in their jugs, prepare meals for their husbands, and attend to them. They gave birth in the field under apple trees, and God miraculously cared for the newborns. When Egyptians tried to kill the infants, they were swallowed into the ground. The women recognized God first at the sea.

items.text: The identities of the midwives Shifrah and Puah
items.text_en: The identities of the midwives Shifrah and Puah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the identities of the midwives. One says they were a woman and her daughter (Yocheved and Miriam), the other says a daughter-in-law and mother-in-law (Yocheved and Elisheva). A baraita supports the view that Shifrah is Yocheved and Puah is Miriam, explaining their names: Shifrah because she beautifies the child, Puah because she coaxes the child out or prophesies.

items.text: The meaning of "אבניים" and the sign for the child's gender
items.text_en: The meaning of "אבניים" and the sign for the child's gender
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan explains that "אבניים" (the birthstool) refers to a sign given to the midwives: when a woman is about to give birth, her thighs become cold as stones. Another interpretation compares it to a potter's wheel. Rabbi Chanina adds that a male child faces downward and a female faces upward.

items.text: The midwives' fear of God and their actions
items.text_en: The midwives' fear of God and their actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse says "וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדוֹת אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים" (the midwives feared God). Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains that Pharaoh tried to seduce them but they refused. A baraita adds that they not only spared the children but also provided them with water and food.

items.text: The midwives' response to Pharaoh: Israel compared to animals
items.text_en: The midwives' response to Pharaoh: Israel compared to animals
items.desc_en: The midwives tell Pharaoh that Hebrew women are like animals (חיות) and do not need midwives. The Gemara explains that the tribes are compared to various animals: Judah to a lion, Dan to a serpent, etc. Even tribes not explicitly compared are included through the verse about the lioness.

items.text: The reward of the midwives: houses of priesthood, Levites, and kingship
items.text_en: The reward of the midwives: houses of priesthood, Levites, and kingship
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of "בָּתִּים" (houses) given to the midwives. One says houses of priesthood and Levites (Aaron and Moses), the other says houses of kingship (David, descended from Miriam through Caleb). The Gemara clarifies that Caleb is called "ben Chetzron" because he turned from the spies' advice, and Rava explains that he was the stepson of Kenaz.

items.text: Conclusion of previous midrash
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous midrash
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse supports the identification of the Kenizzite with Caleb, as previously argued.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse supports the identification of the Kenizzite with Caleb.

items.text: Midrashic interpretations of names in Chronicles
items.text_en: Midrashic interpretations of names in Chronicles
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets various names from the genealogy in I Chronicles, explaining why Miriam is called Azuvah, the meaning of the names of her sons, and the significance of Ashhur and his wives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Azuvah as Miriam and explains she was called so because everyone abandoned her at first.
The Gemara questions why the verse says 'he fathered' regarding Caleb marrying Miriam, since he merely married her.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that one who marries a woman for the sake of Heaven is credited as if he fathered her.
The Gemara explains the name Yeriot as referring to Miriam's face being like curtains (beautiful).
The Gemara interprets the sons' names as describing their character: Yesher straightened himself, Shovav subdued his inclination, and Ardon ruled his inclination.
An alternative explanation: the names refer to Miriam's face being like a rose.
The Gemara identifies Ashhur as Caleb, explaining his name as one whose face was darkened by fasts, and Tekoa as one who fixed his heart to his Father in Heaven.
The Gemara explains that Miriam was considered like two women, initially repulsive (חֶלְאָה) and later youthful (נַעֲרָה).
The Gemara explains the names of the sons: Tzeret as one who became a rival to her friends, Tzo'har as having a face bright as noon, and Etnan as causing every viewer to bring a gift to his wife.

items.text: Pharaoh's three decrees
items.text_en: Pharaoh's three decrees
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that Pharaoh decreed three progressively harsher decrees against the Israelites: first against male newborns, then to throw all male newborns into the Nile, and finally against his own people.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that Pharaoh decreed even against his own people.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina details the three decrees Pharaoh made: first on males, then on all newborns, then on his own people.

items.text: Amram's separation from Yocheved and his daughter's rebuke
items.text_en: Amram's separation from Yocheved and his daughter's rebuke
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Amram, the leader of the generation, divorced his wife due to Pharaoh's decree, but his daughter (Miriam) rebuked him, arguing that his decree was harsher than Pharaoh's. Amram then remarried her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the man from the house of Levi went, introducing the story.
Rav Yehuda bar Zevina answers that Amram followed his daughter's advice.
A Tanna relates that Amram, the leader of the generation, divorced his wife due to Pharaoh's decree, and all the others followed suit.

Miriam rebukes Amram, arguing that his decree to separate from Yocheved is harsher than Pharaoh's, as it affects both genders and both worlds, and since he is righteous, his decree is certain to be fulfilled.
Amram accepts the rebuke and remarries Yocheved, and all the other men follow his example.

items.text: The marriage of Amram and Yocheved and Yocheved's age
items.text_en: The marriage of Amram and Yocheved and Yocheved's age
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse uses the term 'took' instead of 'returned', describing a wedding ceremony. It then discusses Yocheved's age, noting she was 130 years old and called a 'daughter' because she regained youthful signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses the term 'took' (וַיִּקַּח) instead of 'returned' (וַיַּחְזִיר), since Amram was already married to Yocheved.

Rav Yehuda bar Zevina answers that the verse uses 'took' because Amram performed a formal wedding ceremony (מעשה ליקוחין) for Yocheved, seating her in a bridal canopy with Aaron and Miriam dancing and angels proclaiming her joy.
The Gemara questions how Yocheved, who was 130 years old at the time, can be called a 'daughter' (בת).

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina identifies the woman as Yocheved, explaining that she was conceived on the journey and born between the walls, so the verse emphasizes her birth in Egypt but not her conception there.
Rabbi Yehuda resolves the difficulty by explaining that Yocheved was called a 'daughter' because she regained the signs of youth (סימני נערות) at that time.

items.text: Moses' birth without pain and the meaning of 'good'
items.text_en: Moses' birth without pain and the meaning of 'good'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Moses' birth was painless, like his conception, and that righteous women are not subject to Eve's curse. It then records various interpretations of 'ki tov' regarding Moses: his name, his fitness for prophecy, his being born circumcised, and the light that filled the house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the verse can say she conceived and gave birth, since she was already three months pregnant.
Rav Yehuda bar Zevina explains that the verse equates her birth to her conception: just as conception was painless, so too was the birth.
The Gemara derives from this that righteous women were not included in Eve's decree of painful childbirth.
The Gemara introduces a baraita that offers multiple interpretations of the phrase 'ki tov' regarding Moses.
Rabbi Meir says 'tov' refers to Moses' name itself.
Rabbi Yehuda says his name was 'Toviyah'.
Rabbi Nechemya says 'tov' indicates he was fit for prophecy.
Acherim says he was born circumcised.
The Sages say that at Moses' birth the entire house was filled with light, as derived from the parallel use of 'tov' with light in creation.

items.text: Details of Moses' concealment and the ark
items.text_en: Details of Moses' concealment and the ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Moses was hidden for only three months, how the Egyptians discovered hidden babies, why the ark was made of reeds, and the application of pitch inside and tar outside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Moses was hidden for three months because the Egyptians counted the pregnancy only from the time Amram remarried Jochebed, but she was already three months pregnant.
The Gemara asks why Jochebed could no longer hide Moses, suggesting she could have continued hiding him.
The Gemara answers that the Egyptians would bring babies to the location of a hidden infant so that the crying would reveal it, citing a verse about little foxes.
The Gemara asks why Jochebed specifically chose bulrushes for the ark.
Rabbi Elazar (רבי אלעזר) explains that righteous people value their money more than their bodies, so she used an inexpensive material, because they do not steal.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani (רבי שמואל בר נחמני) offers an alternative reason: bulrushes are soft and can withstand impact against both soft and hard objects.
A Tanna (תנא) teaches that she applied bitumen on the inside and pitch on the outside so that the righteous child would not smell the foul odor of pitch.
Rabbi Elazar (רבי אלעזר) interprets 'bassuf' as the Sea of Reeds (ים סוף).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani (רבי שמואל בר נחמני) begins his alternative interpretation of 'bassuf', but the text is cut off.

items.text: Conclusion of the story of Moses's birth and the prophecy of his sister
items.text_en: Conclusion of the story of Moses's birth and the prophecy of his sister
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the earlier narrative about Moses's birth, describing how his father Amram kissed his daughter for her prophecy that Moses would save Israel, but later slapped her when he was thrown into the river. The verse 'And his sister stood afar off' is interpreted as her desire to know the outcome of her prophecy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the story of Moses's birth, describing Amram's reaction to Miriam's prophecy and the interpretation of the verse about his sister standing afar.

items.text: Question about the order of Joseph's funeral procession
items.text_en: Question about the order of Joseph's funeral procession
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verses describing Joseph's funeral for Jacob list the Egyptian dignitaries before Joseph's family initially, but later list Joseph and his brothers first. Rabbi Yochanan answers that initially the Egyptians did not honor the Israelites, but after seeing their honor, they did.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what accounts for the difference in the order of the funeral procession for Jacob, where initially the Egyptian servants are listed before Joseph's family, but later Joseph and his brothers are listed first.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that initially the Egyptians did not honor the Israelites, but after witnessing their honor at the funeral, they began to show respect.

items.text: The thorns and the crowns at Jacob's funeral
items.text_en: The thorns and the crowns at Jacob's funeral
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'until the threshing floor of Atad' — Rabbi Abahu says that the non-Israelite nations surrounded Jacob's coffin with crowns like a threshing floor surrounded by thorns. A baraisa states they all came for war but upon seeing Joseph's crown hanging on the coffin, they hung their own crowns, totaling 36 crowns. Another baraisa says even animals mourned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the threshing floor of Atad and Rabbi Abahu's explanation that the nations surrounded Jacob's coffin with crowns like a threshing floor surrounded by thorns.
A baraisa reports that all nations came for war but upon seeing Joseph's crown on Jacob's coffin, they hung their own crowns, totaling 36 crowns.
Another baraisa states that even animals, including horses and donkeys, participated in the great mourning.

items.text: Esau's objection and the resolution with the document
items.text_en: Esau's objection and the resolution with the document
items.desc_en: When they reached the Cave of Machpelah, Esau obstructed the burial, claiming the remaining plot was his. They argued he had sold his birthright, but he countered that he had only sold the birthright, not the plain inheritance. They cited a verse interpreted by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that 'kirah' means sale. Esau demanded a deed, which was in Egypt. Naftali was sent to retrieve it, but Chushim ben Dan, who was hard of hearing, killed Esau for delaying Jacob's burial. This fulfilled Rebecca's prophecy that they would not both die on the same day, but they were buried on the same day.

sub.desc_en: When they reached the Cave of Machpelah, Esau obstructed the burial, claiming the remaining plot was his based on Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of the verse.

The brothers argued that Esau had sold his birthright, but Esau countered that he had only sold the birthright, not the plain inheritance; they cited a verse interpreted by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that 'כירה' means sale.
Esau demanded a deed, which was in Egypt; they proposed sending Naftali, who is swift as a deer, as explained by Rabbi Abahu's wordplay.
Chushim ben Dan, who was hard of hearing, killed Esau for delaying Jacob's burial, and Jacob's eyes opened and smiled, fulfilling the verse.
This fulfilled Rebecca's prophecy that they would not both die on the same day, but they were buried on the same day.

items.text: Joseph's honor in burial
items.text_en: Joseph's honor in burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Joseph's brothers would not have buried him if he had not, citing the verse that his sons carried him. They answer that they left it to him because his honor is greater with kings than with commoners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Joseph's brothers would not have buried Jacob if Joseph had not been involved, citing the verse that they carried him.
The Gemara answers that Joseph's honor among kings was greater than that of commoners, so he was given precedence.

items.text: Moses's search for Joseph's coffin
items.text_en: Moses's search for Joseph's coffin
items.desc_en: The Gemara praises Moses for occupying himself with the mitzvah of Joseph's bones while others took spoils. It recounts how Serach bat Asher told Moses that the Egyptians had sunk Joseph's coffin in the Nile. Moses called to Joseph, and the coffin floated. A kal vachomer from Elisha proves iron can float. Rabbi Nathan says Joseph was buried in the royal mausoleum; Moses called and the coffin shook. For all the years in the desert, two arks — one of the dead (Joseph) and one of the Shechinah — traveled together, and people marveled that a dead person traveled with the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: The baraita praises Moses for occupying himself with the mitzvah of Joseph's bones while all Israel took spoils.
The Gemara asks how Moses knew where Joseph was buried.
Serach bat Asher tells Moses that the Egyptians sank Joseph's metal coffin in the Nile to bless its waters.
Moses stands at the Nile, calls to Joseph, and the coffin floats up.
The Gemara proves iron can float via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from Elisha's miracle, all the more so for Moses.
Rabbi Natan says Joseph was buried in the royal mausoleum; Moses calls and the coffin shakes, then Moses takes it.
The Gemara describes how two arks—Joseph's and the Shechinah's—traveled together in the desert, and people marveled that a dead person accompanied the Divine Presence.

items.text: Moses and Israel's involvement with Joseph's bones
items.text_en: Moses and Israel's involvement with Joseph's bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Moses alone was involved with Joseph's bones, citing verses that show Israel and Joseph's sons also participated. The response is that it is more honorable for a great person to be buried by many or by great people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Moses alone was involved with Joseph's bones, citing verses that show Israel and Joseph's sons also participated.
The first answer states that it is more honorable for a great person to be buried by many rather than by few.
The second answer states that it is more honorable for a great person to be buried by great people rather than by lesser ones.

items.text: Why Joseph was buried in Shechem
items.text_en: Why Joseph was buried in Shechem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that Joseph was buried in Shechem because he was stolen from there, and his lost item should be returned there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Joseph was specifically buried in Shechem.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that Joseph was buried in Shechem because he was stolen from there, and his lost item should be returned there.

items.text: Contradiction between verses about Joseph's bones
items.text_en: Contradiction between verses about Joseph's bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one verse says Moses took Joseph's bones, another says Israel brought them. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina resolves it: one who starts a task and another completes it is credited as if the completer did it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two verses: one says Moses took Joseph's bones, another says the Israelites brought them up from Egypt.

Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction by stating that Scripture credits the one who completes a task as if he did it entirely, so the Israelites who completed the burial are credited.

items.text: Consequences for one who does not complete a task
items.text_en: Consequences for one who does not complete a task
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani add that one who does not complete a task is demoted from greatness and buries his wife and children, citing verses about Judah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that one who does not complete a task is also demoted from greatness, citing the verse about Judah's descent.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that such a person also buries his wife and children, citing the deaths of Judah's wife and sons.

items.text: Why Joseph was called 'bones' and died early
items.text_en: Why Joseph was called 'bones' and died early
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains Joseph was called 'bones' in life because he did not protest when his brothers called Jacob 'your servant'. Another reason: Joseph died before his brothers because he acted with authority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav asks why Joseph was called 'bones' during his lifetime and answers that it was because he did not protest when his brothers referred to Jacob as 'your servant'.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav (or alternatively Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina) explains that Joseph died before his brothers because he acted with authority (הנהיג עצמו ברבנות).

items.text: Joseph's descent to Egypt and Potiphar
items.text_en: Joseph's descent to Egypt and Potiphar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'hured' as 'horid'—Joseph brought down Pharaoh's astrologers. Rav says Potiphar bought Joseph for himself, but Gabriel castrated and 'unfurled' him, changing his name to Potifera.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'hured' as 'horid'—Joseph brought down Pharaoh's astrologers from their greatness.
Rav explains that Potiphar bought Joseph for himself, but Gabriel castrated and unfurled him, changing his name to Potifera.

items.text: Interpretations of 'Rav lach'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'Rav lach'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi says 'Rav' was used both for good news (to the spies) and bad (to Moses). Another interpretation: 'Rav lach' means you have a greater one—Joshua. A third: so people won't say the teacher is harsh and the student rebellious, as per the measure of the camel is the load.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the verse 'Rav lach' and cites Rabbi Levi's interpretation that the word 'Rav' was used both for good news (to the spies) and bad (to Moses).
The Gemara offers a second interpretation: 'Rav lach' means 'you have a greater one'—Joshua.
The Gemara offers a third interpretation: 'Rav lach' means so people won't say the teacher is harsh and the student rebellious, as per the measure of the camel is the load.

items.text: Moses' statement 'I am 120 years old today' and 'I can no longer go out and come in'
items.text_en: Moses' statement 'I am 120 years old today' and 'I can no longer go out and come in'
