items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'today' means his days were completed. 'Go out and come in' refers to Torah study, as the gates of wisdom were sealed from him, despite his physical strength.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'today' indicates his days were completed, teaching that God completes the years of the righteous precisely.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'go out and come in', rejecting a literal interpretation because Moses retained his physical strength.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that 'go out and come in' refers to Torah study, as the gates of wisdom were sealed from Moses.

items.text: Moses' death and burial location
items.text_en: Moses' death and burial location
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where Moses died (in Reuben's territory) and was buried (in Gad's territory, four mil away, carried by the Divine Presence). Various sages offer verses about his burial, including a tradition that a bat kol announces his death over twelve mil, and some say he never died.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that on the Shabbat of the 'twosome' (דיו זוגי), authority was transferred from Moses to Joshua.
Rabbi Yehuda states that Moses died in Reuben's territory, citing the verse about Mount Nebo being in Reuben's portion.
The Gemara notes that Nebo is where three prophets—Moses, Aaron, and Miriam—died.
The Gemara asks: Moses was buried in Gad's territory, four mil from Reuben's; who carried him those four mil?
The Gemara answers that Moses was carried by the wings of the Divine Presence (שכינה), with ministering angels and God reciting verses.

sub.text: Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rav Nachman, Semalyon
sub.text_en: Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rav Nachman, Semalyon
sub.desc_en: Various sages (Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, Rav Nachman, Semalyon) cite verses about Moses' death and burial.
Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol says a bat kol announces Moses' death over twelve mil, and some say Moses never died but stands and serves like at Sinai.

items.text: The hidden burial place of Moses
items.text_en: The hidden burial place of Moses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Berechya notes that even with a sign within a sign, no one knows Moses' burial place. The daf ends with a mention that the evil kingdom once sent...

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Berechya states that even with a sign within a sign, no one knows Moses' burial place.
The gemara begins to relate that the evil kingdom once sent agents to find Moses' grave, but the daf ends mid-sentence.

items.text: Moses' burial place and its concealment
items.text_en: Moses' burial place and its concealment
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the site of Moses' grave was hidden from people, and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that even Moses himself did not know where he was buried. He explains that Moses was buried near Beit Pe'or to atone for the sin of Pe'or.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the site of Moses' grave was hidden from people, appearing differently to those above and below.

items.text: The mitzvah to follow God's attributes
items.text_en: The mitzvah to follow God's attributes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains the verse 'After the Lord your God you shall walk' — since God is a consuming fire, one cannot literally follow Him. Rather, one should imitate His attributes: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, comforting mourners, and burying the dead.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that even Moses did not know his burial place, and that he was buried near Beth Peor to atone for the sin of Peor.

items.text: Interpretation of 'kotnot or' and Torah's bookends of gemilut chasadim
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'kotnot or' and Torah's bookends of gemilut chasadim
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'kotnot or' (garments of skin). Rabbi Simlai then teaches that the Torah begins and ends with acts of kindness: God clothing Adam and Eve and God burying Moses.

sub.text: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, explains that 'following God' means imitating His attributes: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, consoling mourners, and burying the dead, with scriptural proof for each.

The Gemara cites the verse 'כתנות עור' (garments of skin) and presents the debate between Rav and Shmuel: one says it means something that comes from skin, the other says it means something from which the skin benefits.
Rav holds that 'כתנות עור' (garments of skin) refers to something that comes from the skin, i.e., animal hide.
Shmuel holds that 'כתנות עור' (garments of skin) refers to something from which the skin benefits, such as wool or linen.

items.text: Moses' desire to enter the Land of Israel
items.text_en: Moses' desire to enter the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai explains that Moses wanted to enter the Land not for its physical bounty but to fulfill the many commandments that depend on the land. God responds that He will credit Moses as if he performed them, citing the verse from Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: רבי שמלאי (Rabbi Simlai) teaches that the Torah begins and ends with acts of kindness: clothing the naked (Adam and Eve) and burying the dead (Moses).
רבי שמלאי (Rabbi Simlai) asks why Moses desired to enter the Land of Israel, rejecting the possibility that it was for its physical bounty.
רבי שמלאי (Rabbi Simlai) answers that Moses wanted to enter the land to fulfill the many commandments that depend on the Land of Israel.

items.text: Exegesis of the verse from Isaiah regarding Moses' reward
items.text_en: Exegesis of the verse from Isaiah regarding Moses' reward
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets each phrase of the verse: Moses will receive a portion like the patriarchs; he exposed himself to death (by pleading for Israel); he was counted among the sinners of the desert; he atoned for the Golden Calf; and he prayed for sinners to repent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the verse from Isaiah (53:12) as God's response to Moses' desire to enter the land for reward.
The Gemara interprets the first two phrases: Moses will receive a portion like the patriarchs (עצומים), and he exposed himself to death by pleading for Israel.
The Gemara interprets the remaining phrases: Moses was counted among the desert sinners, atoned for the Golden Calf, and prayed for sinners to repent.

items.text: Mishnah: Unique laws of the sotah offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Unique laws of the sotah offering
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists the differences between the sotah offering and other meal offerings: it is placed in a wicker basket, not a service vessel; it lacks oil and frankincense; it is made of barley, not wheat; it is coarse flour, not fine; and Rabban Gamliel compares her act to an animal's, so her offering is animal feed.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the topic of the sotah offering, stating that the husband brings her meal offering in a wicker basket and places it on her hands to weary her.
The mishnah specifies that the offering is brought in a wicker basket, not a service vessel, to weary her.
The mishnah contrasts the sotah offering with other meal offerings: all others begin and end in a service vessel, but this one begins in a wicker basket and ends in a service vessel.

The mishnah lists further differences: the sotah offering lacks oil and frankincense, is made of barley not wheat, is coarse flour not fine, and Rabban Gamliel compares her act to an animal's, so her offering is animal feed.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for exhausting the sotah
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for exhausting the sotah
items.desc_en: Abba Chanin cites Rabbi Eliezer: all these measures are to exhaust her so she might confess. The Gemara questions whether this is out of mercy or to prevent the scroll from being erased, and leaves the matter unresolved.

sub.text: Baraita citing Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Abba Chanin says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that all these measures are to exhaust the sotah so she might confess, and then draws a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) about God's mercy.
The Gemara questions whether the reason is truly mercy (חסה) or rather to prevent the scroll from being erased.
The Gemara leaves the matter unresolved, indicated by the incomplete phrase 'קסבר' (he holds), implying the discussion is cut off or inconclusive.

items.text: Opening statement: Sotah offering order
items.text_en: Opening statement: Sotah offering order
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that for the sotah, the woman is made to drink the bitter water first, and then her meal-offering is sacrificed, because the scroll has already been erased.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for the sotah, the woman is made to drink the bitter water first, and then her meal-offering is sacrificed, because the scroll has already been erased.

items.text: Baraita on the order of meal-offerings
items.text_en: Baraita on the order of meal-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the procedure for a standard meal-offering: the person brings it in baskets of silver or gold, then the priest performs the kemitzah, and the remainder is eaten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that describes the procedure for bringing a meal-offering, from the person's home to the priest's presentation at the altar.
The baraita details the priest's actions: removing the frankincense, performing the kemitzah (taking a handful), and offering it on the altar.
The baraita concludes that once the kemitzah is offered, the remainder is eaten by the priests, who may add wine, oil, or honey but may not leaven it.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about vessels
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to vessels fit for service, implying that wicker baskets are unfit. This is challenged by Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view that wooden service vessels are valid, but the Gemara limits his view to important vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita explicitly mentions wicker baskets of silver and gold, which are not service vessels.
Rav Pappa resolves: say the baraita refers to vessels fit for service vessels, implying wicker baskets are unfit.
The Gemara infers that wicker baskets are unfit, which contradicts Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda who validates wooden service vessels.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi invalidates wooden service vessels, but Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda validates them.
The Gemara objects: even according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, he only validates important wooden vessels, not insignificant ones like wicker baskets.
The Gemara rejects this limitation: does Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda not apply the verse 'Offer it now to your governor' (Malachi 1:8), implying that even insignificant vessels are unfit for service?

items.text: Sanctification requires intent
items.text_en: Sanctification requires intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that a service vessel sanctifies only with intent, but then reinterprets the phrase to mean placing it in a vessel for sanctification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita's phrasing that a service vessel (כלי שרת) sanctifies only with intent (מדעת).
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita's phrase to mean 'placing it in a service vessel for sanctification,' not that the vessel itself sanctifies with intent.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the offering steps
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the offering steps
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides biblical verses for each step: pouring oil, bringing to the priest, bringing to the altar, and presenting at the southwest corner, derived from a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse for pouring oil and placing frankincense on the meal-offering.
The Gemara cites the verse for bringing the meal-offering to the priest.
The Gemara cites the verse for the priest bringing the meal-offering to the altar.
The Gemara asks for the source that the meal-offering is presented at the southwest corner of the altar.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the southwest corner from the verses 'before the Lord' and 'in front of the altar'.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar argues that the presentation should be at the south of the corner, based on a principle of reconciling verses. Rav Ashi explains that this Tanna holds the entire altar is in the north.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) introduces a principle for reconciling two verses: one should prefer the verse that fulfills itself and also fulfills the other, and he applies it to the location of the meal-offering presentation.

רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) applies the principle to conclude that the priest presents the meal-offering at the southern side of the corner, since that location fulfills both 'before the Lord' (west) and 'in front of the altar' (south).
The Gemara asks: But where have you fulfilled the phrase 'before the Lord' in this southern location?
רב אשי (Rav Ashi) answers that this Tanna holds the entire altar stands in the north, so the southern side of the altar is opposite the Holy of Holies in the west, fulfilling 'before the Lord'.

items.text: The meaning of 'and that is enough'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'and that is enough'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the phrase 'and that is enough' teaches that only presentation is required, not waving. The Gemara questions this, but a verse shows that presentation is done in a vessel, like the bringing to the priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'וְדַיּוֹ' (and that is enough) teaches, suggesting that one might think the presentation of the meal-offering itself requires waving.
Rav Ashi explains that the phrase is necessary to teach that only presentation is required, not waving.
The Gemara objects that perhaps waving is indeed required, citing the verse about bringing the offering to the priest and presenting it to the altar.
The Gemara resolves by citing a verse that compares bringing to the priest (done in a vessel) to presenting at the altar, showing that presentation is also done in a vessel, not by hand.

items.text: Details of kemitzah and remaining steps
items.text_en: Details of kemitzah and remaining steps
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the frankincense is set aside, the source for taking from the oil-rich part, the need for a second sanctification, and the scriptural basis for placing the frankincense on top.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the frankincense is set aside to prevent it from being taken up with the kemitzah (handful), citing a Mishnah that if a pebble, salt grain, or frankincense lump is taken up, the kemitzah is invalid.
The Gemara derives from the verses 'מִסׇּלְתָּהּ וּמִשַּׁמְנָהּ' (from its fine flour and from its oil) that the kemitzah is taken from the oil-rich part of the meal offering.
The Gemara questions why a second sanctification in a service vessel is needed, since the meal offering was already sanctified once.
The Gemara answers by analogy to blood: just as blood is sanctified by the knife at the animal's neck and then again in a service vessel, so too the kemitzah requires a second sanctification.

The Gemara cites the verse 'וְאֶת כׇּל הַלְּבוֹנָה אֲשֶׁר עַל הַמִּנְחָה' (and all the frankincense that is on the meal offering) as the scriptural basis for placing the frankincense on top of the kemitzah.
The Gemara notes the final step of bringing the kemitzah up to the altar.

items.text: Procedure for the handful and salt
items.text_en: Procedure for the handful and salt
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the handful is brought up to the altar in a service vessel, not burned directly, and salt is added as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the handful is actually burned in a service vessel, given the Mishnah's phrasing.
The Gemara corrects the Mishnah: the handful is brought up in a service vessel to the altar, not burned in it.
The Gemara adds that the handful is salted and placed on the altar fire, citing the verse requiring salt on every meal-offering.

items.text: Source for eating the remainder
items.text_en: Source for eating the remainder
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that after the handful is burned, the remainder is eaten by the priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that after the handful (קומץ) is offered, the remainder is eaten?
The Gemara answers by citing two verses: one about the priest burning the memorial portion, and another stating that the remainder of the meal-offering is for Aaron and his sons.

items.text: Dispute on when the handful permits the remainder
items.text_en: Dispute on when the handful permits the remainder
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yoḥanan about when the handful permits the remainder to be eaten: when fire takes hold of it or when most of it is consumed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about when the handful permits the remainder, noting that each authority follows his own view.
The gemara poses the question: from when does the handful permit the remainder to be eaten?
Rabbi Ḥanina answers: from when fire takes hold of it.
Rabbi Yoḥanan answers: from when most of it is consumed by fire.

items.text: Permitted additives and prohibition of leavening
items.text_en: Permitted additives and prohibition of leavening
items.desc_en: The priests may add wine, oil, and honey to the remainder as a mark of honor, but they are forbidden from leavening it, as derived from the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that priests may add wine, oil, and honey to the remainder as a mark of honor, and the Gemara explains the scriptural basis for this practice.

sub.text: Gemara's citation and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse prohibiting leavening the remainder and adds Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's statement that even the priests' portion may not be baked as leaven.

items.text: Clarifying the mishnah's statement about all meal-offerings
items.text_en: Clarifying the mishnah's statement about all meal-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah's claim that all meal-offerings require oil and frankincense is contradicted by the sin-offering meal-offering. It explains that the mishnah means all meal-offerings require oil and frankincense except the sin-offering, and the sotah offering is unique in being barley flour without oil or frankincense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah's claim that all meal-offerings require oil and frankincense is contradicted by the sin-offering meal-offering, which the Torah explicitly excludes from oil and frankincense.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah means all meal-offerings require oil and frankincense except the sin-offering, and the sotah offering is unique in being barley flour without oil or frankincense.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and discussion on libations
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and discussion on libations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon explains why the sin-offering meal-offering lacks oil and frankincense: to prevent the sinner from benefiting. The Gemara extends this logic to the sin-offering for fat, but notes that the offerings of a leper require libations because they are not for sin. An objection about leprosy being a punishment is resolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that logically the sin-offering meal-offering should require oil and frankincense to prevent the sinner from benefiting, but it lacks them so that his offering is not adorned.

sub.text: Gemara's extension of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's extension of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends Rabbi Shimon's logic to the sin-offering for fat, which should logically require libations but lacks them so the offering is not adorned.
The Gemara notes that the sin-offering and guilt-offering of a leper require libations because they do not come for sin.

sub.text: Objection citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Objection citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that leprosy comes for seven sins, implying it is a punishment for sin.
The Gemara resolves: the leper's atonement is achieved through the affliction itself, and the offerings are brought only to permit him to eat sacred food.

items.text: Exception for the nazirite's sin-offering
items.text_en: Exception for the nazirite's sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the nazirite's sin-offering does not require libations, and answers that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar considers a nazirite a sinner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the nazirite's sin-offering, which does not come for sin, should not require libations.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who considers a nazirite a sinner.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's statement and baraita
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's statement and baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabban Gamliel telling the Sages to let him expound the sotah offering like a type of clay.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabban Gamliel's statement that the sotah offering is like a type of clay.
A baraita records Rabban Gamliel telling the Sages to let him expound the sotah offering like a type of clay.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's reason for the sotah's offering
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's reason for the sotah's offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Meir, because the sotah fed her husband delicacies, her offering is animal feed. The Gemara then refines this: just as her deeds are animal-like, so is her offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir says: because the sotah fed her husband delicacies, her offering is animal feed.

items.text: Mishnah: The vessel and the water
items.text_en: Mishnah: The vessel and the water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes bringing an earthenware vessel, putting half a log of water from the laver into it (Rabbi Yehuda says a quarter log), and then taking earth from the Temple floor and placing it on the water.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one brings an earthenware vessel and puts half a log of water from the laver into it.
Rabbi Yehuda says a quarter log, just as he minimizes the writing, so he minimizes the water.
The Mishnah describes entering the Temple, turning right, taking earth from under a marble slab, and placing it on the water.

items.text: Gemara: The vessel must be new
items.text_en: Gemara: The vessel must be new
items.desc_en: A beraita teaches that the vessel must be new, according to Rabbi Yishmael, derived from a gezerah shavah with the metzora. The Gemara questions this derivation and provides answers, including Rava's distinction regarding the vessel's condition.

sub.desc_en: A beraita teaches that the vessel must be new, according to Rabbi Yishmael, derived from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with the metzora.
The Gemara asks: from where do we know that the metzora's vessel must be new, and answers by citing the verse and the analogy to fresh water.
The Gemara objects: if the analogy is strict, then the sotah water should also require living spring water like the metzora.
The Gemara answers that indeed Rabbi Yishmael holds the water must be from a spring, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara objects further: the metzora's ritual also requires cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool, which the sotah does not.
Rabbah answers that the verse itself hints at the requirement by saying 'בכלי חרס' (in an earthen vessel), implying a vessel already designated for this purpose.
Rava resolves that the requirement of 'new' applies only when the vessel's surface has not discolored, analogous to water that has not changed.

items.text: Rava's query about a restored vessel
items.text_en: Rava's query about a restored vessel
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a vessel that became discolored and was then fired again in a kiln is valid. The Gemara attempts to answer from a ruling of Rabbi Elazar about other items, but distinguishes the cases.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a vessel whose discolored face was restored by firing in a kiln is valid or permanently invalid.

sub.text: Gemara's attempted answer from Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted answer from Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to answer Rava's query by citing Rabbi Elazar's ruling that cedar wood, hyssop, and crimson wool that were used and then straightened out are invalid, implying that restoration does not restore validity.
The Gemara rejects the attempted proof by distinguishing the case: there the items were merely peeled back, not fundamentally restored, so the analogy does not apply.

items.text: Gemara: The location of the earth and its source
items.text_en: Gemara: The location of the earth and its source
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the priest turns right, and then discusses the source of the earth: it must be from the floor of the Sanctuary, and if there is none, he must place it there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the priest turns right upon entering the Sanctuary.
Mar explains that all turns should be to the right, citing a general rule.
A baraita derives from the verse that the earth must come from the Sanctuary floor, and if none is present, the priest must place it there.

items.text: Another beraita on the earth
items.text_en: Another beraita on the earth
items.desc_en: A second beraita teaches that the priest prepares the earth outside and brings it in, and Isi ben Yehuda says the verse includes the floor of the Sanctuary.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita teaches that the priest prepares the earth outside and brings it in, citing the verse 'וּמִן הֶעָפָר אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה' (from the earth that shall be).
Isi ben Yehuda states that the phrase 'בְּקַרְקַע הַמִּשְׁכָּן' (in the floor of the Sanctuary) includes the floor itself as a source of earth.

items.text: Isi ben Menachem's derivation
items.text_en: Isi ben Menachem's derivation
items.desc_en: Isi ben Menachem argues that the phrase 'in the ground of the Tabernacle' is unnecessary for excluding ash, since a fortiori reasoning from a light impurity suffices; rather, it teaches that the woman must bring earth from her own property, not from the Temple treasury.

sub.desc_en: Isi ben Menachem argues that the phrase 'in the ground of the Tabernacle' is unnecessary for excluding ash, since a fortiori reasoning from a light impurity suffices; rather, it teaches that the woman must bring earth from her own property, not from the Temple treasury.

items.text: Inquiry about ash when no earth is available
items.text_en: Inquiry about ash when no earth is available
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if there is no earth, may one use ash? According to Beit Shammai, who hold that ash is never called 'earth', the question is moot. The inquiry is only according to Beit Hillel, who find that ash is sometimes called 'earth'. The question is whether the verse 'in the ground of the Tabernacle' restricts the substance to earth, or whether it only serves Isi's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if there is no earth available, may one use ash instead?
The Gemara clarifies that according to Beit Shammai, who hold that ash is never called 'עפר (earth)', the question is moot.
The Gemara refines the inquiry: according to Beit Hillel, who hold that ash is sometimes called 'עפר (earth)', what is the ruling?

The Gemara presents two possibilities: either the verse 'בקרקע המשכן (in the ground of the Tabernacle)' restricts the substance to earth, or it only serves the teaching of Isi ben Yehudah and Isi ben Menachem.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's list of three places where halakhah overrides Scripture
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's list of three places where halakhah overrides Scripture
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael states that in three places halakhah overrides Scripture: the Sotah water may be in any vessel (not just earthenware), the Nazirite may shave with anything (not just a razor), and the bill of divorce may be written on any material (not just a scroll). The Gemara objects: if ash could be used for Sotah, that would be a fourth case, so why isn't it listed?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael introduces a list of three places where halakhah overrides Scripture.

The list details three cases: the Sotah water may be in any vessel (not just earthenware), the Nazirite may shave with anything (not just a razor), and the bill of divorce may be written on any material (not just a scroll).
The Gemara objects: if ash could be used for Sotah, that would be a fourth case, so why isn't it listed?

items.text: Answer: the Tanna omitted the leper's case
items.text_en: Answer: the Tanna omitted the leper's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna omitted some cases, specifically the leper's shaving, which is derived from a general-particular-general hermeneutic. The halakhah for the leper is that he shaves like a gourd (all hair), which is an addition to the Scriptural text. The Mishnah explicitly states that the leper passes a razor over all his flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna omitted the leper's case from the list of three places where halakha overrides Scripture.
A baraita is cited that derives the leper's shaving from a general-particular-general hermeneutic, including hair of the legs and excluding hidden places.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that the leper shaves like a gourd, passing a razor over all his flesh, and the second shaving is like the first.

items.text: Three resolutions: the Sotah ash case is different
items.text_en: Three resolutions: the Sotah ash case is different
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yochanan's list only includes cases where halakhah overrides a Scriptural law, but the Sotah ash case is a rabbinic enactment. Rav Pappa says the list includes only cases where halakhah overrides and uproots, but the ash case adds to the Scriptural law. Rav Ashi says the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who uses general-particular-general, but the Sotah earth requirement is not derived that way.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that Rabbi Yochanan's list only includes cases where halakhah overrides a Scriptural law, but the Sotah ash case is a rabbinic enactment, so it is excluded.
Rav Pappa answers that the list includes only cases where halakhah overrides and uproots the Scriptural law, but the Sotah ash case adds to the Scriptural law, so it is not included.

Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who uses the hermeneutic principle of general-particular-general, but the Sotah earth requirement is not derived that way, so it is excluded from the list.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah's ruling about 'like a gourd' follows Rabbi Akiva, who interprets the Torah using the method of amplification and limitation. It cites a baraita about the nazirite's shaving to illustrate this method.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the Mishnah's ruling about 'like a gourd' follows Rabbi Akiva, who interprets the Torah using the method of amplification and limitation, and cites a baraita about the nazirite's shaving to illustrate this method.
The Gemara clarifies that the amplification includes all body hair, and the limitation excludes hair inside the nose.

items.text: Dust from decayed vegetation
items.text_en: Dust from decayed vegetation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ruling is regarding using decayed vegetation as dust. Rav Huna bar Ashi quotes Rav that if there is no actual dust, one may bring decayed vegetation and sanctify it. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to decayed vegetation that has become dust, not to ash.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ruling is regarding using decayed vegetation as dust for the sotah ritual.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Ashi quotes Rav that if there is no actual dust, one may bring decayed vegetation and sanctify it.
The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to decayed vegetation that has become dust, not to ash.

items.text: Things that must be visible on water
items.text_en: Things that must be visible on water
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three things that must be visible on water: the dust of the sotah, the ash of the red heifer, and the saliva of the yevamah. Rabbi Yishmael adds the blood of the bird used in the purification of a leper.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three items that must be visible on water: the dust of the sotah, the ash of the red heifer, and the saliva of the yevamah; Rabbi Yishmael adds the blood of the bird used in the purification of a leper.

items.text: Debate about the blood of the bird
items.text_en: Debate about the blood of the bird
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that the blood of the bird must be visible on the water, and the Rabbis' counterarguments. The debate involves interpreting the verses about dipping the bird in blood and water, with each side offering different derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what scriptural basis Rabbi Yishmael has for requiring the bird's blood to be visible on the water.

Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'וְטָבַל אוֹתָם בְּדַם הַצִּפֹּר' that the blood must be mixed with water in a way that the blood is recognizable, and the minimum measure is a רְבִיעִית (quarter-log).
The Rabbis object that the verse simply requires dipping in both blood and water, without any requirement of visibility.
Rabbi Yishmael counters that if the Torah only intended dipping in both, it would have written 'וְטָבַל בָּהֶם'; the extra phrase 'בְּדַם וּבַמַּיִם' teaches that the blood must be recognizable.
The Rabbis respond that the phrase 'בְּדַם וּבַמַּיִם' teaches that the blood and water must be mixed together, not dipped separately.
Rabbi Yishmael argues that the requirement of mixing is already taught by another verse, so the current verse must teach the visibility requirement.

The Rabbis respond that without the current verse, one might have thought the bird must be slaughtered directly over the vessel and the blood collected separately; the verse teaches that the blood must be mixed with water.

items.text: Size of the bird for the purification ritual
items.text_en: Size of the bird for the purification ritual
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about a bird that is too large and displaces the water, or too small and is displaced by the water. Rabbi Zeira rebukes him, stating that the Sages set the measure as a 'bird of freedom' (דרור), which is neither too large nor too small.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about the halachic status of a bird that is too large and displaces the water, or too small and is displaced by the water.
Rabbi Zeira rebukes Rabbi Yirmeya for straying from halacha, and answers that the Sages set the measure as a ציפור דרור (bird of freedom), which is neither too large nor too small.

items.text: Order of placing dust and water
items.text_en: Order of placing dust and water
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon regarding whether placing the dust before the water invalidates the ritual. Rabbi Shimon derives from a gezerah shavah that the order is flexible, while the Rabbis argue that the verses indicate a fixed order.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that if one placed the dust before the water, the ritual is invalid, while Rabbi Shimon validates it.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, and cites his own statement that the Torah changed the term from 'אפר' (ash) to 'עפר' (dust) to derive a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy).

Rabbi Shimon applies the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) to show that just as in the case of the red heifer (להלן) the dust can be placed before water and still be valid, so too in the sotah ritual (כאן) the order is flexible.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification for the red heifer
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification for the red heifer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the red heifer case, two verses — one saying 'עליו' (upon it) and another saying 'מים חיים אל כלי' (living water into a vessel) — indicate that either order is acceptable.
The Rabbis counter that the verse 'אל כלי' (into a vessel) indicates the water must be placed first, while 'עליו' (upon it) only teaches that the ash and water must be mixed together.
The Gemara raises an alternative interpretation: perhaps 'עליו' (upon it) is the fixed order (ash first), and 'אל כלי' (into a vessel) merely teaches that the water must be in a vessel.

The Gemara resolves the dispute by invoking a general principle: wherever the Torah uses the term 'עליו' (upon it), it validates placing the substance on top, so here too the ash can be placed on top of the water.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: What the priest writes in the scroll
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: What the priest writes in the scroll
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies that the priest writes only the curses and the oath, starting from 'If no man has lain with you...' and 'But you who have strayed...', and includes the verses about the bitter waters causing the curse. He does not write the introductory adjuration or the woman's response 'Amen, amen'. Rabbi Yosei says he does not interrupt, and Rabbi Yehuda says he writes only the core curse verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking from which point in the Torah passage the priest writes the scroll for the sota.
The Mishnah states that the priest writes from the blessing and curse verses but omits the adjuration and the woman's 'Amen, amen'.
Rabbi Yosei says the priest does not interrupt the verses but writes the entire passage without omissions.
Rabbi Yehuda says the priest writes only the core curse verses and does not write the woman's 'Amen, amen'.

items.text: Gemara: The tannaitic dispute over the source verse
items.text_en: Gemara: The tannaitic dispute over the source verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute among Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Yehuda is based on the verse 'And the priest shall write these curses in a book'. Rabbi Meir interprets the words to include actual curses and exclude others, Rabbi Yosei includes the commands and acceptances via the word 'et', and Rabbi Yehuda interprets all terms as exclusions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the tannaitic dispute in the mishna is based on, and identifies the source verse.
Rabbi Meir interprets the words of the verse to include actual curses and curses from blessings, and to exclude curses from Mishne Torah and the commands and acceptances.
Rabbi Yosei agrees with Rabbi Meir's interpretation but adds that the word 'et' includes the commands and acceptances.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir does not interpret the word 'et' as an amplifier.
Rabbi Yehuda interprets all the terms in the verse as exclusions, excluding curses from blessings, curses from Mishne Torah, and commands and acceptances.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's method
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's method
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir uses some terms for inclusion and others for exclusion, and answers that proximity to a term of inclusion makes it inclusive, and proximity to a term of exclusion makes it exclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir interprets the letter heh in 'ha'alot' as inclusive and the heh in 'ha'eleh' as exclusive.
The Gemara answers that a heh near an amplifier amplifies, and a heh near a restrictor restricts.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Meir's principle
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Meir's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir does not accept the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive', but Rabbi Tanchum resolves that the word 'hinaki' (innocent) is written, implying a different derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir does not accept the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive' (מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן), questioning how he can derive a positive from a negative in the context of the sotah scroll.

Rabbi Tanchum resolves the objection by noting that the word 'הינקי' (innocent) is written in the verse, indicating a different derivation that does not rely on the principle of 'from a negative you hear a positive'.

items.text: Homilies on the sotah procedure: dust and reward
items.text_en: Homilies on the sotah procedure: dust and reward
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva teaches that if a husband and wife are worthy, the Divine Presence dwells between them; if not, fire consumes them. Rava explains that the woman's letter is superior to the man's because it joins them. Rava also explains that the Torah requires dust for the sotah because if she is worthy, she will produce a son like Abraham, who said 'dust and ashes'; if not, she returns to dust. Rava further teaches that in reward for Abraham's 'dust and ashes', his children received the mitzvot of the red heifer's ash and the sotah's dust, excluding the dust for covering blood which has no benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva teaches that if a husband and wife are worthy, the Divine Presence dwells between them; if not, fire consumes them.
Rava explains that the woman's letter is superior to the man's because it joins them.
Rava explains that the Torah requires dust for the sotah because if she is worthy, she will produce a son like Abraham, who said 'dust and ashes'; if not, she returns to dust.

items.text: Homily on the reward for Abraham's 'thread and shoelace'
items.text_en: Homily on the reward for Abraham's 'thread and shoelace'
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that in reward for Abraham saying 'from a thread to a shoelace', his children received the mitzvot of the blue thread (tekhelet) and the strap of tefillin. The Gemara explains the tefillin strap is derived from a verse about God's name being called upon Israel, and the tekhelet is explained by Rabbi Meir as resembling the sea, which resembles the firmament, which resembles the Throne of Glory.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that in reward for Abraham saying 'I am dust and ashes', his children received the mitzvot of the ashes of the red heifer and the dust of the sotah.
The Gemara objects: there is also the mitzvah of covering the blood with dust, which should be included.
Rava answers that covering the blood is only a preparation for a mitzvah, not a direct benefit, so it is not counted.
Rava teaches that in reward for Abraham saying 'from a thread to a shoelace', his children received the mitzvot of the blue thread (tekhelet) and the strap of tefillin.

The Gemara explains that the tefillin strap is derived from the verse 'and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you', which Rabbi Eliezer the Great interprets as referring to the head-tefillin.
The Gemara explains the tekhelet by citing Rabbi Meir, who says the blue thread resembles the sea, which resembles the firmament, which resembles the Throne of Glory, as supported by verses.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah: Materials on which the scroll is not written
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah: Materials on which the scroll is not written
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing materials on which the scroll for the sotah may not be written, such as a board, paper, or unfinished parchment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing materials on which the scroll for the sotah may not be written, such as a board, paper, or unfinished parchment.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Writing materials for the sotah scroll
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Writing materials for the sotah scroll
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the sotah scroll is written on a scroll (not a tablet), and only with ink that can be erased, as derived from the verse 'and he shall blot out'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the sotah scroll must be written on a scroll (not a tablet) and only with erasable ink, as derived from the verse 'and he shall blot out'.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's derivation that the scroll must be written by day
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's derivation that the scroll must be written by day
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if the scroll was written at night it is invalid, using a גזירה שווה from the word 'Torah' to the verse about judgment, which must be by day.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a sotah scroll written at night is invalid, deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תורה' (Torah) to the word 'משפט' (judgment), which must be performed by day.

items.text: Gemara: Writing out of order invalidates the scroll
items.text_en: Gemara: Writing out of order invalidates the scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the scroll was written out of order (למפרע) it is invalid, as the verse says 'and he shall write these curses' — implying when they are written as they are.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that writing the scroll out of order (before the curses are written) invalidates it, as the verse requires writing 'the curses' at the time of writing.

items.text: Gemara: Writing before the oath invalidates the scroll
items.text_en: Gemara: Writing before the oath invalidates the scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if the scroll was written before the woman accepted the oath, it is invalid, based on the sequence in the verse: 'and he shall adjure' and then 'and he shall write'.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that writing the scroll before the woman accepts the oath invalidates it, as the verse prescribes the oath before the writing.

items.text: Gemara: Writing as a letter invalidates the scroll
items.text_en: Gemara: Writing as a letter invalidates the scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the scroll was written as a letter (איגרת) it is invalid, because the Torah said 'in a book' (בספר), implying a proper scroll format.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that writing the scroll as a letter (not in the prescribed scroll format) invalidates it, as the Torah requires a 'ספר' (scroll).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Invalid writing of the scroll
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Invalid writing of the scroll
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the sotah scroll is written on two separate pages, it is invalid, as the Torah requires a single 'book'. Similarly, if the priest wrote and erased one letter at a time, it is invalid, as the verse requires writing the entire Torah at once.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that writing the sotah scroll on two separate pages invalidates it, as the Torah requires a single 'book'.
The Mishnah adds that writing and erasing one letter at a time invalidates the scroll, citing the verse requiring the entire Torah to be written at once.

items.text: Rava's series of questions about erasure and mixing
items.text_en: Rava's series of questions about erasure and mixing
items.desc_en: Rava raises a series of unresolved questions (teiku) about the validity of the sotah water when the scroll is written for two women and erased into one cup, or erased into two cups and then mixed, or mixed and then divided. The final question touches on the principle of bereirah (retroactive clarification).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether writing two scrolls for two women and erasing them into one cup is valid, questioning if the erasure must also be done lishmah (for her sake).
Rava asks if the erasures were made into two separate cups and then mixed, whether each woman drinks from the other's portion, invalidating the procedure.
Rava asks if he mixed and then divided the water, whether the principle of ברירה (retroactive clarification) applies, and leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rava's question about drinking through a fiber or tube
items.text_en: Rava's question about drinking through a fiber or tube
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether administering the sotah water through a fiber (siv) or a tube (shfoferet) is considered a valid act of drinking. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether administering the sotah water through a fiber (סיב) or a tube (שפופרת) is considered a valid act of drinking, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Ashi's question about spilled and remaining water
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question about spilled and remaining water
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the sotah water is valid if some of it spilled and only a portion remained. This question is also left unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the sotah water is valid if some of it spilled and only a portion remained.
The gemara records that the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Debate about the two oaths in the sotah ritual
items.text_en: Debate about the two oaths in the sotah ritual
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Rav taught there are two oaths in the sotah ritual: one before the scroll is erased and one after. Rava objects that both are written before erasure, and instead explains one is with an imprecation (alah) and one without. Rav Amram and Rav Ashi offer further refinements about the wording of the oath and imprecation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Rav taught there are two oaths (שבועות) in the sotah ritual: one before the scroll is erased and one after.
Rava objects that both oaths are written before the scroll is erased, and instead explains that one oath includes an imprecation (אלה) and one does not.
Rav Amram citing Rav defines the oath with an imprecation (אלה) as: 'I adjure you that you were not defiled, and if you were defiled may these waters bring affliction upon you.'
Rava objects that the imprecation (אלה) and the oath (שבועה) are separate, and instead proposes the wording: 'I adjure you that if you were defiled may these waters bring affliction upon you.'

Rav Ashi resolves that the imprecation (אלה) is present but the oath (שבועה) is absent, and proposes the wording: 'I adjure you that you were not defiled, and if you were defiled may these waters bring affliction upon you.'

items.text: Mishnah: The woman's response of 'Amen, Amen'
items.text_en: Mishnah: The woman's response of 'Amen, Amen'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that the woman says 'Amen, Amen' to affirm the imprecation and the oath, and also to affirm that she did not stray while betrothed or married.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the various affirmations the woman expresses by saying 'Amen, Amen': acceptance of the curse, the oath, the husband's identity, and that she did not stray while betrothed or married.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conditions for the Sotah's oath
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conditions for the Sotah's oath
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a yevamah and a married woman (kenusah) both recite 'Amen' to the oath. Rabbi Meir adds an extra clause about future impurity. The Mishnah rules that a husband cannot stipulate conditions regarding periods before betrothal or after divorce, nor if she was unfaithful with another man and then remarried him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a yevamah and a married woman (kenusah) both recite 'Amen' to the oath: 'Amen that I did not become defiled, and if I did become defiled, may all these curses come upon me.'
Rabbi Meir adds an extra clause: 'Amen that I did not become defiled, amen that I will not become defiled in the future.'
All agree that the husband cannot stipulate conditions regarding periods before betrothal or after divorce.
If a woman was divorced, secluded herself with another man and became defiled, and then her husband remarried her, he cannot stipulate regarding that period.
The Mishnah states the principle: In any case where if she engaged in sexual intercourse she would not become forbidden to her husband, he may not stipulate with her.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's inference: Yevamah who committed adultery is forbidden
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's inference: Yevamah who committed adultery is forbidden
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna argues that a yevamah who committed adultery is forbidden to her yavam, based on the Mishnah's inclusion of 'shomeret yavam' alongside 'kenusah'. If she were permitted, the husband could not stipulate conditions, contradicting the Mishnah's rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asserts that a יבמה (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who committed adultery is forbidden to her יבם (levir), deriving this from the Mishnah's pairing of 'shomeret yavam' with 'kenusah'.

The Gemara supports Rav Hamnuna's inference: if the יבמה were not forbidden, the husband could not stipulate conditions, contradicting the Mishnah's rule that stipulation is only possible when the act would render her forbidden.

items.text: Rejection of Rav Hamnuna's ruling: The Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav Hamnuna's ruling: The Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara in the West says the halakha does not follow Rav Hamnuna. Instead, the Mishnah's inclusion of 'shomeret yavam' is explained as following Rabbi Akiva, who holds that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments, making her like a forbidden relative.

sub.desc_en: The Sages of the West rule that the halakha does not follow Rav Hamnuna's position.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's inclusion of 'shomeret yavam' follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that betrothal does not take effect for those liable for negative commandments, making her like a forbidden relative.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: Stipulating on first marriage (brother's marriage)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: Stipulating on first marriage (brother's marriage)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a husband can stipulate conditions regarding the first marriage (i.e., his brother's marriage to her). The Gemara resolves from the Mishnah's rule that if she would be forbidden, he can stipulate.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a husband can stipulate conditions regarding the first marriage (i.e., his brother's marriage to her).
The Gemara resolves from the Mishnah's rule that if she would be forbidden, he can stipulate.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's statement
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that Rabbi Meir's addition of 'Amen that I will not be defiled' does not mean the waters test her immediately, but rather that if she becomes defiled later, the waters will cause her distress and test her.

sub.desc_en: A baraita clarifies that Rabbi Meir's addition of 'אמן שלא אטמא' (Amen that I will not be defiled) does not mean the waters test her immediately, but rather that if she becomes defiled later, the waters will cause her distress and test her.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question: Stipulating on later marriages (after divorce)
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question: Stipulating on later marriages (after divorce)
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a husband can stipulate conditions regarding later marriages (after divorce and remarriage). The Gemara resolves from the Mishnah that if she is divorced and then remarried, he cannot stipulate, but if he remarries her and she becomes defiled, he can.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a husband can stipulate conditions regarding later marriages (after divorce and remarriage), considering that currently she is not forbidden to him, but perhaps he might divorce and remarry her.
The Gemara resolves from the Mishnah that if she is divorced and then remarried, he cannot stipulate, but if he remarries her and she becomes defiled, he can.

items.text: Dispute on whether a woman drinks and repeats (sotah drinking twice)
items.text_en: Dispute on whether a woman drinks and repeats (sotah drinking twice)
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma learns from 'zot torat hakena'ot' that a woman can drink the bitter waters and then drink again (if suspected again). Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages argue she cannot. Rava resolves the dispute by distinguishing between one witness and one lover (all agree she cannot repeat) versus other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאֹת' (this is the law of jealousies) that a woman may drink the bitter waters and then drink again if suspected a second time.
Rabbi Yehuda objects, interpreting the word 'זֹאת' (this) to exclude repetition, meaning a woman does not drink and then drink again.
Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent: Nehunya Chofer Sichin testified that a woman drinks and repeats, but they accepted his testimony only with two witnesses, not one.
The Sages rule that a woman never drinks and repeats, whether the suspicion arises from one witness or two.
The Gemara questions how the Tanna Kamma and the later Sages each interpret the limiting words 'זֹאת' (this) and 'תּוֹרַת' (the law) in the verse.
Rava resolves the dispute: in the case of one witness and one lover, all agree that a woman does not drink and repeat; the dispute is limited to other scenarios.

items.text: Dispute over the scope of 'zot' and 'torat'
items.text_en: Dispute over the scope of 'zot' and 'torat'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Tanna Kamma, the later Sages, and Rabbi Yehuda regarding how the words 'zot' and 'torat' in the Torah limit or expand the cases where a woman drinks and repeats. Tanna Kamma holds that 'torat' includes all cases and 'zot' excludes only one man and one paramour; the later Sages hold that 'zot' excludes all and 'torat' includes only two men and two paramours; Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'zot' excludes two cases and 'torat' includes two cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that in the case of two husbands and two paramours, all agree the woman drinks and repeats, citing the verse 'תּוֹרַת' (the law).
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is about cases of one husband with two paramours, or two husbands with one paramour.
Tanna Kamma holds that 'תּוֹרַת' (the law) includes all cases, and 'זֹאת' (this) excludes only the case of one husband and one paramour.
The later Sages hold that 'זֹאת' (this) excludes all cases, and 'תּוֹרַת' (the law) includes only the case of two husbands and two paramours.

Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'זֹאת' (this) excludes two cases (one husband with one paramour, and one husband with two paramours), and 'תּוֹרַת' (the law) includes two cases (two husbands with one paramour, and two husbands with two paramours).

items.text: Mishnah: Order of the meal-offering and the drinking
items.text_en: Mishnah: Order of the meal-offering and the drinking
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the sotah's meal-offering: the priest takes it from a wicker basket, places it in a service vessel, puts it on her hand, waves it, brings it near, takes a handful, burns it, and the remainder is eaten by priests. Then it states that the drinking precedes the offering, but Rabbi Shimon says the offering precedes the drinking, citing the verse 'and afterward he shall make the woman drink'. If he drank first and then offered, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the sotah's meal-offering: the priest takes it from a wicker basket, places it in a service vessel, puts it on her hand, waves it, brings it near, takes a handful, burns it, and the remainder is eaten by priests.
The Mishnah states the anonymous view that the priest forces the woman to drink first and then sacrifices her meal-offering.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the meal-offering is sacrificed first and then the woman drinks, citing the verse 'and afterward he shall make the woman drink'.
Rabbi Shimon concedes that if the priest forced her to drink first and then sacrificed the meal-offering, it is still valid.

items.text: Derivation of tenufah for the sotah's meal-offering
items.text_en: Derivation of tenufah for the sotah's meal-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoshiya to explain the source for the requirement of waving (tenufah) for the sotah's meal-offering. The Gemara answers that it is derived from a gezerah shavah of 'yad' from the peace-offering (shelamim): just as there the owner waves, so too here the owner waves, with the priest placing his hand under the owner's hand.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's question to Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question to Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoshiya to explain the source for the requirement of waving (תנופה) by the owner for the sotah's meal-offering.
The Gemara answers that the requirement is derived from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'יד' (hand) from the peace-offering (שלמים).
The Gemara resolves the analogy: just as here the priest places his hand under the owner's hand, so too there the priest places his hand under the owner's hand, and the owner waves.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's order and the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's order and the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the drinking precedes the offering, asking how the offering could have already been brought. It explains that the Mishnah is describing the order of the meal-offering itself, not the drinking. Then it notes that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages is about the order of the drinking and the offering, with the Sages holding that drinking comes first and Rabbi Shimon holding that the offering comes first, based on the verse 'and afterward he shall make the woman drink'. If he drank first, it is still valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the drinking precedes the offering, pointing out that the offering has already been brought (הניף והגיש קמץ והקטיר).
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is describing the order of the meal-offering itself (סדר מנחות), not the drinking, and the drinking clause is a separate statement.

The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages is about the order of the drinking and the offering itself, with the Sages holding that drinking comes first and Rabbi Shimon holding that the offering comes first, based on the verse 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה' (and afterward he shall make the woman drink).
The Mishnah concludes that if he drank first and then offered her meal-offering, it is still valid (כשרה).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the extra verses
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the extra verses
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Akiva) and Rabbi Shimon each derive a different halacha from the extra verses 'וְהִשְׁקָה' and 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה'. Rabbi Akiva learns that if the scroll is erased and she refuses to drink, they force her; Rabbi Shimon learns that three things delay the procedure: before the handful is offered, before the scroll is erased, and before she accepts the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Akiva) asks why the extra verse 'וְהִשְׁקָה' is needed, and answers that if the scroll is erased and she refuses to drink, they force her to drink against her will.

Rabbi Shimon asks why the extra verse 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה' is needed, and answers that it teaches three things that delay the procedure: before the handful is offered, before the scroll is erased, and before she accepts the oath.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Shimon's three delays
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Shimon's three delays
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each of Rabbi Shimon's three delays. The first delay (before the handful is offered) aligns with his own view that the offering precedes drinking. The second delay (before the scroll is erased) is clarified by Rav Ashi to mean before the erasure is recognizable. The third delay (before she accepts the oath) raises a contradiction with Rava's ruling that writing the scroll before the oath is invalid, which is resolved by saying the verse refers to the case where they wrote it after the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon's first delay (before the handful is offered) aligns with his own view that the offering precedes the drinking.
The Gemara asks what drinking could occur before the scroll is erased, since the scroll must be erased for the water to take effect.
Rav Ashi answers that the delay refers to before the erasure is recognizable, meaning the writing is still visible.
The Gemara questions the third delay (before she accepts the oath), noting that while she may not drink, the scroll could still be written.
The Gemara objects with Rava's ruling that writing the scroll before the oath is invalid, contradicting the possibility of writing it before the oath.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the verse refers to a case where they wrote the scroll after she accepted the oath, not before.

items.text: The dispute over the three verses
items.text_en: The dispute over the three verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the tannaitic dispute: there are three verses ('וְהִשְׁקָה' first, 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה', and 'וְהִשְׁקָהּ' last). The Rabbis (Tanna Kamma) use the first for the basic law (drinking before offering), the second for recognizable erasure, and the third for forced drinking. Rabbi Shimon uses the second for the basic law (offering before drinking), the first for post-facto validity, and the third for forced drinking. The Rabbis hold that the verse does not open for post-facto cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon, noting that three verses are written: 'וְהִשְׁקָה' first, 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה', and 'וְהִשְׁקָהּ' last.

The Rabbis hold that the first 'וְהִשְׁקָה' teaches the basic law (drinking before offering), the second 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה' teaches recognizable erasure, and the third 'וְהִשְׁקָהּ' teaches forced drinking if the scroll is erased and she refuses.
Rabbi Shimon holds that 'וְאַחַר יַשְׁקֶה' teaches the basic law (offering before drinking), the first 'וְהִשְׁקָה' teaches post-facto validity, and the third 'וְהִשְׁקָהּ' teaches forced drinking.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold that the verse does not open for post-facto (בדיעבד) cases, so they cannot derive post-facto validity from the first verse.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's position on forced drinking and the point of no return
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position on forced drinking and the point of no return
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda describes forcing her with an iron clasp, and Rabbi Akiva objects: why check her if she is already checked? Rather, before the handful is offered she can retract, but after it is offered she cannot. The Gemara challenges this: after the handful is offered, she is still checked? The answer distinguishes between retracting due to trembling (fear) and retracting due to health (illness).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Akiva really holds that she is forced to drink, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda describes forcing her with an iron clasp.

The baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's view of forcing her with an iron clasp, and Rabbi Akiva's objection that she is already checked, concluding that before the handful is offered she can retract but after it is offered she cannot.
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Akiva's own reasoning, after the handful is offered she should still be considered checked and unable to retract.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between retracting due to trembling (fear) and retracting due to health (illness), explaining that after the handful is offered, if the scroll was erased properly she cannot retract.

items.text: Final clarification of the distinction
items.text_en: Final clarification of the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains: if she retracts due to illness, she will never drink; if due to trembling, before the handful is offered (when the scroll may have been erased improperly) she can retract, but after the handful is offered (when the erasure was proper) she cannot retract.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the distinction: if she retracts due to illness (בריותא), she will never drink; if due to trembling (רתיתא), before the handful is offered she can retract, but after the handful is offered she cannot retract.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's views resolved by two Tannaim
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's views resolved by two Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Akiva said erasure is essential (in the sotah scroll), but here he says the handful is essential. The resolution is that there are two Tannaitic sources aligned with Rabbi Akiva's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Akiva's consistency: there he said erasure is essential (מחיקה מעכבא), but here he says the handful is essential (קומץ מעכב).
The Gemara resolves that there are two Tannaim who both follow Rabbi Akiva's opinion, one holding erasure essential and the other holding the handful essential.

items.text: Question about retracting refusal due to illness
items.text_en: Question about retracting refusal due to illness
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a woman says 'I will not drink' due to illness (not claiming impurity), then retracts, is she considered impure because she admitted impurity, or is her retraction valid because she was just scared? The Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a question: if a woman initially says 'I will not drink' on the grounds of illness, then retracts and says 'I will drink,' what is the law?
One possible reasoning: by saying 'I will not drink,' she effectively says 'I am impure,' and once she established her own impurity she cannot retract.
An alternative possibility: since she now says 'I will drink,' it reveals that her initial refusal was merely due to intimidation, so her retraction is effective.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Avuh deShmuel requires bitter substance in the water
items.text_en: Avuh deShmuel requires bitter substance in the water
items.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel states that one must put a bitter substance into the water, citing the verse 'mei hamarim' (bitter waters) meaning they are already bitter.

sub.desc_en: Avuha d'Shmuel rules that one must put bitter substance (מר) into the water.
He derives this from the verse 'מי המרים' (the bitter waters), implying that the water is already bitter.

items.text: Mishnah: Stages of the sotah procedure and the debate on teaching Torah to daughters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stages of the sotah procedure and the debate on teaching Torah to daughters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details what happens if the woman refuses to drink before or after the scroll is erased, and describes her physical reaction. It then discusses the concept of merit suspending punishment, leading to a dispute between Ben Azzai (who says one should teach his daughter Torah so she knows merit can suspend) and Rabbi Eliezer (who says teaching Torah to a daughter is like teaching her frivolity). Rabbi Yehoshua adds that a woman prefers a kab of frivolity to nine kavs of abstinence, and lists types of people who destroy the world.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by detailing the procedure when the woman refuses to drink before or after the scroll is erased, and when she admits guilt after erasure.
The Mishnah describes the woman's physical reaction as she drinks and the order to remove her from the Temple courtyard.
The Mishnah introduces the concept of merit suspending punishment, and Ben Azzai states that one must teach his daughter Torah so she knows merit can suspend.
Rabbi Eliezer objects that teaching Torah to a daughter is like teaching her frivolity (תפלות).
Rabbi Yehoshua supports Rabbi Eliezer's view by stating that a woman prefers a kab of frivolity to nine kavs of abstinence.
Rabbi Yehoshua lists types of people who destroy the world: a foolish pietist, a cunning wicked person, a woman who is a פרושה (ascetic), and the plagues of the פרושים (ascetics).

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Meir's story about adding vitriol to ink
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Meir's story about adding vitriol to ink
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Meir, when studying with Rabbi Akiva, added vitriol to the ink without objection. When he went to Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yishmael warned him to be careful with his scribal work, and Rabbi Meir explained that he adds vitriol to prevent errors from flies. Rabbi Yishmael objected, citing the verse 'umachah' (and he shall erase), requiring erasable writing.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Meir (first story)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel citing Rabbi Meir (first story)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir recounts that when he studied with Rabbi Akiva, he added kantharos to the ink (making it erasable) and Rabbi Akiva did not object.
When Rabbi Meir went to Rabbi Yishmael, he identified himself as a scribe; Rabbi Yishmael warned him to be careful not to add or omit a letter, lest he destroy the entire world.
Rabbi Meir replied that he adds kantharos to the ink; Rabbi Yishmael questioned the practice, citing the verse 'ומחה' (and he shall erase) requiring erasable script.
Rabbi Yishmael objects, citing the verse 'וּמָחָה' (and he shall erase), requiring that the writing be erasable, which vitriol would prevent.

items.text: Explanation of the dialogue between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Explanation of the dialogue between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies what Rabbi Meir meant: he was not only careful about missing or extra letters, but even about a fly that might sit on the tag of a dalet and erase it, making it a resh. That is why he added vitriol to fix the ink.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Meir meant by his response to Rabbi Yishmael and what Rabbi Yishmael's original concern was.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir was not only careful about missing or extra letters, but even about a fly that might erase a dalet into a resh, so he added vitriol (קנקנתום) to fix the ink.

items.text: Contradiction in the stories about Rabbi Meir's teachers
items.text_en: Contradiction in the stories about Rabbi Meir's teachers
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a contradiction: Rabbi Meir said he added vitriol when studying with Rabbi Yishmael without objection, but when he went to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva forbade it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction about the order of study (first with Rabbi Akiva, then Rabbi Yishmael, then back to Rabbi Akiva), but the contradiction about the prohibition remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita quotes Rabbi Meir saying that when he studied with Rabbi Yishmael he added vitriol without objection, but when he went to Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Akiva forbade it.
The Gemara identifies two contradictions: one about the order of study (which teacher was first) and one about the prohibition itself (who forbade it).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction about the order of study: Rabbi Meir first studied with Rabbi Akiva, then went to Rabbi Yishmael for the plain text, then returned to Rabbi Akiva for reasoning.
The Gemara concludes that the contradiction about who forbade the vitriol (Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva) remains unresolved.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Meir that vitriol is permitted for all
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Meir that vitriol is permitted for all
items.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Yehuda saying that Rabbi Meir ruled that one may add vitriol to ink for all purposes.

sub.text: Baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Meir that everyone adds kantharos to ink (i.e., it is universally permitted).

items.text: Dispute over erasing the sotah passage from a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Dispute over erasing the sotah passage from a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yosei says the sotah passage is erased only from a Torah scroll in the Temple, while the first Tanna says it is erased from any Torah scroll. Rabbi Yirmeya explains the difference is whether one may erase it from a Torah scroll at all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that only the sotah passage is excluded from the rule that sacred writings may not be erased.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yosei limits the exception to a Torah scroll in the Temple.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the difference is whether one may erase the passage from a Torah scroll at all.

items.text: Parallel Tannaitic dispute about the scroll's reuse
items.text_en: Parallel Tannaitic dispute about the scroll's reuse
items.desc_en: A related Tannaitic dispute is cited: the first Tanna says a sotah scroll cannot be used for another sotah, while Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya permits it. Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each suggest that the dispute about the Torah scroll may not align with this one, due to different considerations of intent and purpose.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a parallel Tannaitic dispute: the first Tanna says a sotah scroll cannot be reused for another sotah, while Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya permits it.

Rav Pappa suggests the dispute about the Torah scroll may not align with this one, because the first Tanna's concern is that the scroll was designated for a specific woman (Rachel) and cannot be reassigned to another (Leah), whereas a Torah scroll is written generically and may be erased.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a different objection: Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya permits reuse only because the scroll was written for the sake of the curses in general, but a Torah scroll written for study purposes may not be erased.

items.text: Objection from the law of a get written for another woman
items.text_en: Objection from the law of a get written for another woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya would reject the law that a get written for one woman cannot be used for another if the names match. The answer distinguishes between a get, which requires writing for her sake, and the sotah passage, where the act is erasure for her sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya rejects the principle that a get written for one woman cannot be used for another.
The Gemara answers that a get requires writing for her sake, while here the Torah says 'וְעָשָׂה לָהּ' (and he shall do for her), which refers to erasing for her sake.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's Tanna regarding merit and the bitter waters
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's Tanna regarding merit and the bitter waters
