items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if she cannot finish drinking before her face turns green, it is because she is guilty. The Gemara first identifies this as Rabbi Shimon, who says the meal-offering is offered before she drinks, but then notes the Mishnah also says merit suspends, which contradicts Rabbi Shimon. Rav Chisda resolves this by identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Akiva, who agrees with Rabbi Shimon on the order but with the Rabbis on merit suspending.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's ruling that she cannot finish drinking before her face turns green as following Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the meal-offering is offered before she drinks, since the waters only test her after the offering is brought.

The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's continuation, which says merit suspends the punishment, contradicts Rabbi Shimon, who explicitly holds that merit does not suspend the effect of the bitter waters.

Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Akiva, who agrees with Rabbi Shimon on the order of the meal-offering but holds like the Rabbis that merit suspends the punishment.

items.text: Reason for removing the sotah from the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Reason for removing the sotah from the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says they remove her from the courtyard lest she die and cause impurity. The Gemara questions whether a corpse is forbidden in the Levite camp, citing a baraita that even a corpse is permitted there. Abaye answers that the concern is she might menstruate from fear, and explains that sudden terror causes bleeding, while constant fear stops it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the reason for removing the sotah from the Temple courtyard is due to fear that she might die, implying that a corpse is forbidden in the Levite camp.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a corpse is permitted in the Levite camp, citing the verse that Moses brought Joseph's bones with him, within his own partition.
Abaye answers that the concern is not death but that she might menstruate from sudden terror, and explains that sudden terror causes bleeding while constant fear stops it.

items.text: Dispute over how long merit suspends the bitter waters
items.text_en: Dispute over how long merit suspends the bitter waters
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's statement that merit suspends as not aligning with Abba Yosei ben Chanan, Rabbi Elazar ben Yitzchak, or Rabbi Yishmael. A baraita records their opinions: Abba Yosei says three months (to recognize pregnancy), Rabbi Elazar says nine months (based on verses about seed), and Rabbi Yishmael says twelve months (with a mnemonic from Daniel).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah's statement that merit suspends punishment, and rules out Abba Yosei ben Chanan and Rabbi Elazar ben Yitzchak.

sub.text: Baraita citation — Abba Yosei ben Chanan
sub.text_en: Baraita citation — Abba Yosei ben Chanan
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Abba Yosei ben Chanan who says merit suspends punishment for three months.
Rabbi Elazar ben Yitzchak says merit suspends punishment for nine months, based on a verbal analogy from the verse 'וְנִקְּתָה וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע'.
Rabbi Yishmael says merit suspends punishment for twelve months, citing a verse from Daniel as a mnemonic.

items.text: Gemara's question about the source for 'no proof but a memory'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the source for 'no proof but a memory'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier proof from Daniel that a verse can serve as a memory even without direct proof, suggesting that perhaps gentiles are different because they are not judged by the same standard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier proof from Daniel by citing verses that explicitly state the fulfillment of the prophecy, suggesting that the case of Daniel provides direct proof, not merely a memory.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael's principle is still valid, citing the verse about Edom as an example where a verse provides a memory without direct proof.
The Gemara objects that perhaps gentiles are different because they are not subject to divine judgment, so the verse about Edom cannot serve as a general precedent for Israel.

items.text: Question about the merit that suspends punishment
items.text_en: Question about the merit that suspends punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what kind of merit can suspend punishment for three years: if it is merit of Torah, a woman is not commanded; so it must be merit of a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what kind of merit can suspend punishment for three years, rejecting the possibility of Torah merit because a woman is not commanded to study Torah.
The Gemara concludes that the merit must be that of a מצוה (commandment), not Torah study.

items.text: Objection: Mitzvah does not protect like Torah
items.text_en: Objection: Mitzvah does not protect like Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a mitzvah cannot provide such long-lasting protection, citing Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei's drasha that mitzvah is like a lamp which protects only temporarily, while Torah is like light which protects forever, and brings a mashal of a person walking in darkness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the merit of a mitzvah cannot provide such long-lasting protection, citing a baraita where Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei interprets that a mitzvah is like a lamp which protects only temporarily.
The baraita continues that Torah is like light which protects forever, and cites verses showing Torah protects in this world, at death, and in the future.
A parable is given of a man walking in darkness: a torch (mitzvah) saves from thorns and pits, dawn (Torah) saves from wild animals and bandits, and a crossroads (Torah scholar) saves from all.
The baraita adds an alternative interpretation: a transgression extinguishes the merit of a mitzvah but not the merit of Torah, citing the verse 'Many waters cannot extinguish the love'.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction between Torah and mitzvah
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction between Torah and mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that a mitzvah protects and saves only when one is engaged in it, but when not engaged, it only protects but does not save; Torah always protects and saves whether engaged or not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef distinguishes between a מצוה (commandment) and Torah: a מצוה protects and saves only when one is engaged in it, but when not engaged it only protects without saving; Torah always protects and saves whether engaged or not.

items.text: Rabbah's objection and Rava's alternative
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and Rava's alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects that Doeg and Achitophel studied Torah yet were not protected; Rava reverses the distinction: Torah protects only when engaged, while mitzvah always protects but never saves.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects that if Torah protects even when not engaged, why did Doeg and Achitophel, who studied Torah, not receive protection?
Rava reverses the distinction: Torah protects and saves only when engaged, while mitzvah always protects but never saves.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: women earn merit through Torah indirectly
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: women earn merit through Torah indirectly
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that the merit is indeed of Torah, because although women are not commanded, they earn reward by having their children taught Torah and by waiting for their husbands from the study hall.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the difficulty by arguing that women indeed earn merit of Torah, because although not commanded, they share in the reward by having their children taught Torah and by waiting for their husbands from the study hall.

items.text: Interpretations of 'crossroads' and the drasha of Rabbi Menachem
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'crossroads' and the drasha of Rabbi Menachem
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim explain the mashal's 'crossroads': Rav Chisda says it is a Torah scholar and the day of death; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is a Torah scholar and fear of sin; Mar Zutra says it is a Torah scholar whose rulings align with halakha. The Gemara then returns to the drasha that sin extinguishes mitzvah but not Torah, and notes that Doeg and Achitophel would not have pursued David had they understood this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the 'crossroads' in the parable?
Rav Chisda says: This is a Torah scholar and the day of death.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: This is a Torah scholar and fear of sin.
Mar Zutra says: This is a Torah scholar whose rulings align with the halakha.
The Gemara returns to the drasha that a transgression extinguishes the merit of a mitzva but does not extinguish the merit of Torah.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei interpreted this verse as given at Sinai, and had Doeg and Achitophel understood it, they would not have pursued David.
The Gemara asks: What verse did Doeg and Achitophel interpret incorrectly?

The Gemara answers: They interpreted the verse 'וְלֹא יִרְאֶה בְךָ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר' (that He see no licentious matter in you) to mean God abandons one who sins, but they did not know that a transgression extinguishes a mitzva but not Torah.

items.text: Explanation of 'they will utterly despise him'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'they will utterly despise him'
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the verse does not refer to Shimon brother of Azaryah or Rabbi Yochanan of the Patriarch's house, but to Hillel and Shavna, who were brothers; Hillel engaged in Torah, Shavna in business, and a bat kol declared that all wealth cannot compare to Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'they will utterly despise him' refers to, and Ulla answers that it does not refer to Shimon brother of Azaryah or Rabbi Yochanan of the Patriarch's house.

Ulla explains that the verse refers to Hillel and Shevna, who were brothers; Hillel engaged in Torah, Shevna in business, and when Shevna proposed to share wealth for Torah reward, a bat kol declared that all wealth cannot compare to Torah.

items.text: Ben Azzai's teaching and Rabbi Eliezer's objection
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's teaching and Rabbi Eliezer's objection
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai states that a person is obligated to teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer objects, saying that teaching a daughter Torah is like teaching her frivolity. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer means it is as if he taught her frivolity.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai states that a person is obligated to teach his daughter Torah.
Rabbi Eliezer objects, saying that teaching a daughter Torah is teaching her frivolity.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer means it is as if he taught her frivolity, not that he literally teaches frivolity.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning and the Sages' alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning and the Sages' alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning based on the verse "I, wisdom, dwell with cunning" (Proverbs 8:12), meaning that when wisdom enters a person, cunning enters with it. The Sages interpret the same verse differently, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan, who say that Torah endures only with one who makes himself bare (or as if he does not exist) over it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning by citing the verse 'אני חכמה שכנתי ערמה' (I, wisdom, dwell with cunning), meaning that when wisdom enters a person, cunning enters with it.

sub.text: Sages' interpretation via Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Sages' interpretation via Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Sages interpret the same verse differently, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan, who say that Torah endures only with one who makes himself bare (or as if he does not exist) over it.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about a woman's preference
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about a woman's preference
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua says that a woman prefers a kab (a small measure) of food with frivolity over nine kabs of food with abstinence. The Gemara clarifies that this means a woman prefers a modest living with some frivolity over a more abundant life with strict separation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that a woman prefers a kab (a small measure) of food with frivolity over nine kabs of food with abstinence.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehoshua means by his statement.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehoshua means a woman prefers a modest living with some frivolity over a more abundant life with strict separation.

items.text: Definition of a foolish pious person
items.text_en: Definition of a foolish pious person
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines a foolish pious person as one who sees a woman drowning in a river and refrains from saving her because it would be improper to look at her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing the category of a foolish pious person.
The Gemara asks for a concrete example of a foolish pious person.
The Gemara answers: one who sees a woman drowning in a river and refrains from saving her because it would be improper to look at her.

items.text: First definitions of a cunning wicked person
items.text_en: First definitions of a cunning wicked person
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines a cunning wicked person as one who presents his arguments to the judge before the other litigant arrives. Rabbi Avahu defines it as one who gives a dinar to a poor person to complete his 200 zuz, thereby disqualifying him from receiving charity, based on the Mishnah that one with 200 zuz may not take gleanings, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah, or poor man's tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a concrete example of a cunning wicked person (רשע ערום).
Rabbi Yochanan defines a cunning wicked person as one who presents his arguments to the judge before the other litigant arrives.
Rabbi Avahu defines a cunning wicked person as one who gives a dinar to a poor person to complete his 200 zuz, thereby disqualifying him from receiving charity.

Rabbi Avahu supports his definition by citing the Mishnah that one with 200 zuz may not take gleanings, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah, or poor man's tithe, but if he lacks one dinar, even if given a thousand at once, he may take.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan defines a cunning wicked person as one who advises orphans to sell limited property, because if they sell it first, the sale is valid, even though normally they cannot sell such property.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines a cunning wicked person as one who advises orphans to sell limited property, because if they sell it first, the sale is valid.

items.text: Abaye's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.text_en: Abaye's definition of a cunning wicked person
items.desc_en: Abaye defines a cunning wicked person as one who advises selling property according to the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that in a case of 'my property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' if the first recipient sells and consumes, the second recipient can only take what remains, unlike Rabbi who allows the second to reclaim from the buyers.

sub.desc_en: Abaye defines a cunning wicked person as one who advises selling property according to the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

A baraita is cited: in a case of 'my property to you, and after you to so-and-so,' if the first recipient sells and consumes, Rabbi holds the second can reclaim from buyers, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the second only takes what remains.

items.text: Additional definitions of a cunning wicked person
items.text_en: Additional definitions of a cunning wicked person
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet defines a cunning wicked person as one who tips others in his ways. Rabbi Zerika quoting Rav Huna defines it as one who is lenient with himself and strict with others. Ulla's definition is cut off.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama in the name of Rav Sheshet defines a cunning wicked person as one who tips others in his ways.
Rabbi Zerika in the name of Rav Huna defines a cunning wicked person as one who is lenient with himself and strict with others.
Ulla begins his definition of a cunning wicked person, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Definitions of one who read and repeated but did not serve Torah scholars
items.text_en: Definitions of one who read and repeated but did not serve Torah scholars
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute among Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, Rabbi Yannai, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov regarding the status of one who read Scripture and repeated Mishnah but did not serve Torah scholars. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports Rav Acha bar Yaakov's view that such a person is a magosh (sorcerer), comparing the mumbling of a sorcerer to a tanna who recites without understanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of one who read Scripture and repeated Mishnah but did not serve Torah scholars.
Rabbi Elazar states that such a person is an am ha'aretz (ignoramus).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says such a person is a bur (an ignoramus of a lower level).
Rabbi Yannai says such a person is a Kutian (Samaritan).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says such a person is a magosh (sorcerer).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports Rav Acha bar Yaakov's view by comparing the mumbling of a sorcerer to a tanna who recites without understanding.

items.text: Baraita defining 'am ha'aretz' and related categories
items.text_en: Baraita defining 'am ha'aretz' and related categories
items.desc_en: A baraita presents multiple definitions of an am ha'aretz: Rabbi Meir says one who does not recite the Shema morning and evening with its blessings; the Sages say one who does not don tefillin; Ben Azzai says one who has no tzitzit on his garment; Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef says one who has children but does not raise them to study Torah; Acheirim says even one who reads and repeats but does not serve Torah scholars is an am ha'aretz. The baraita then distinguishes a 'bor' (one who read but did not repeat) and applies a verse to one who neither read nor repeated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking who is an am ha'aretz and gives Rabbi Meir's definition: one who does not recite the Shema morning and evening with its blessings.
The Sages define an am ha'aretz as one who does not don tefillin.
Ben Azzai defines an am ha'aretz as one who has no tzitzit on his garment.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef defines an am ha'aretz as one who has children but does not raise them to study Torah.
Acheirim defines an am ha'aretz as even one who reads and repeats but does not serve Torah scholars.
The baraita distinguishes a 'bor' (one who read but did not repeat) and applies a verse to one who neither read nor repeated.

items.text: Interpretation of 'im shonim al tit'arev'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'im shonim al tit'arev'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse 'im shonim al tit'arev' as referring to those who repeat halakhot. The Gemara clarifies that this is not obvious, as one might think it refers to those who repeat sin, as per Rav Huna's statement that repeating a sin makes it permissible. The verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse 'יְרָא אֶת ה׳ בְּנִי וָמֶלֶךְ עִם שׁוֹנִים אַל תִּתְעָרָב' as referring to those who repeat halakhot.
The Gemara asks why this interpretation is not obvious, since the verse could be understood differently.

The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might think 'שׁוֹנִים' refers to those who repeat sin, as per Rav Huna's statement that repeating a sin makes it permissible; the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Tannaim as 'destroyers of the world'
items.text_en: Tannaim as 'destroyers of the world'
items.desc_en: A tanna states that tannaim (reciters of Mishnah) are destroyers of the world. The Gemara objects, questioning how they could be destroyers. Ravina explains that they are called destroyers because they issue halakhic rulings from their Mishnah (without proper reasoning). A supporting baraita quotes Rabbi Yehoshua who initially objects but then agrees that they are called destroyers for this reason.

sub.desc_en: A tanna states that tannaim (reciters of Mishnah) are 'destroyers of the world'.
The Gemara objects: Could it enter your mind that they are literally 'destroyers of the world'?
Ravina explains that they are called 'destroyers' because they issue halakhic rulings directly from their Mishnah study without proper reasoning.
A supporting baraita quotes Rabbi Yehoshua who initially objects but then agrees that they are called 'destroyers' for this reason.

items.text: Three types of destroyers of the world: perushah, almanah shovavit, and minor
items.text_en: Three types of destroyers of the world: perushah, almanah shovavit, and minor
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three types of people who destroy the world: a virgin who prays excessively (בתולה צליינית), a widow who runs about (אלמנה שובבית), and a minor whose months have not been completed. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Yochanan who learned fear of sin from a virgin and reward from a widow. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a specific case like Yochani bat Retivi.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists three types of destroyers of the world: a praying virgin, a gadabout widow, and a minor whose months have not been completed.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan, who learned fear of sin from a virgin and reward from a widow, implying these are praiseworthy, not destructive.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers specifically to a case like Yochani bat Retivi, who was excessively pious in a destructive way.

items.text: Interpretations of 'minor whose months have not been completed'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'minor whose months have not been completed'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'minor whose months have not been completed': in the West they interpret it as a Torah scholar who kicks against his teachers. Rabbi Abba says it is a student who has not reached the level of ruling but rules anyway, citing a verse from Proverbs about many slain by a harlot, interpreted as referring to such a student and to one who has reached the level but does not rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the meaning of the phrase 'minor whose months have not been completed'.
In the West they interpret it as a Torah scholar who kicks against his teachers.
Rabbi Abba says it is a student who has not reached the level of ruling but rules anyway.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites a verse from Proverbs about many slain by a harlot, interpreted as referring to such a student and to one who has reached the level but does not rule.

items.text: Duration of lashes
items.text_en: Duration of lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the maximum number of lashes is forty, and notes that Rabbah taught this, but only when the person is healthy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the maximum number of lashes is forty years.
The Gemara objects: But Rabbah taught otherwise, implying a different duration.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbah's teaching applies only to healthy people (שוין).

items.text: Seven types of Pharisees
items.text_en: Seven types of Pharisees
items.desc_en: A baraita enumerates seven types of Pharisees, and the Gemara explains each type: the shoulder Pharisee, the waiting Pharisee, the bleeding Pharisee, the pestle Pharisee, the 'what is my duty' Pharisee, the Pharisee from love, and the Pharisee from fear.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing seven types of Pharisees: shoulder, waiting, bleeding, pestle, 'what is my duty', from love, and from fear.
The Gemara explains the first two types: the shoulder Pharisee acts like Shechem (circumcised for ulterior motives), and the waiting Pharisee knocks his feet together (pretending humility).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the bleeding Pharisee as one who bleeds himself against walls (to avoid looking at women).
Rabbah bar Sheila explains the pestle Pharisee as one who walks bent over like a pestle (exaggerated humility).
The Gemara objects: the 'what is my duty' Pharisee seems praiseworthy, not a negative type.
The Gemara resolves: the negative type is one who says 'what is my duty that I may do more' (excessive piety).
Abaye and Rava object to the baraita's inclusion of the Pharisee from love and from fear, citing a principle that one should study Torah even for ulterior motives.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav supports the objection: one should always engage in Torah and commandments even for ulterior motives, as from such motives one comes to act for their own sake.

items.text: Refining the 'what is my duty' Pharisee
items.text_en: Refining the 'what is my duty' Pharisee
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the inclusion of the 'what is my duty' Pharisee, as it seems praiseworthy, and resolves that it refers to one who says 'what is my additional duty' — implying excessive piety.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the 'what is my duty' Pharisee is listed among the bad types, since it seems praiseworthy.
The Gemara resolves that it refers to one who says 'what is my additional duty,' implying excessive piety beyond the law.

items.text: Removing love and fear Pharisees
items.text_en: Removing love and fear Pharisees
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava instruct the tanna not to include the Pharisees from love and fear, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even for ulterior motives, as this leads to pure motives.

sub.text: Abaye and Rava instructing the tanna
sub.text_en: Abaye and Rava instructing the tanna
sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava tell the tanna not to include the Pharisee from love and the Pharisee from fear in the list.

They support their instruction by citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even for ulterior motives, since from such engagement one comes to do them for their own sake.

items.text: Hypocrites and the court's vengeance
items.text_en: Hypocrites and the court's vengeance
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declares that hidden matters are hidden and revealed matters are revealed, and the great court will take vengeance on those who crush their heels. King Yannai tells his wife not to fear the Pharisees or non-Pharisees, but only the hypocrites who act like Zimri and seek reward like Pinchas.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declares that hidden matters are hidden and revealed matters are revealed, and the great court will take vengeance on those who crush their heels.
King Yannai tells his wife not to fear the Pharisees or non-Pharisees, but only the hypocrites who act like Zimri and seek reward like Pinchas.

items.text: Mishnah: Merit and the bitter waters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Merit and the bitter waters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Shimon says merit does not suspend the bitter waters, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says merit does suspend them, but the woman will not give birth or thrive, eventually dying the same death.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that merit does not suspend the bitter waters, and if it did, it would discredit the waters and give a bad name to pure women who drank.
Rabbi says that merit does suspend the bitter waters, but the woman does not give birth or improve, rather she wastes away and eventually dies the same death.

items.text: Meal offering defiled before sanctification
items.text_en: Meal offering defiled before sanctification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman's meal offering became defiled before being sanctified in a vessel, it is like all other meal offerings and may be redeemed; if after sanctification, it is burned. It then lists those whose meal offerings are burned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the meal-offering became impure before sanctification in a vessel, it is redeemed like all meal-offerings; if after sanctification, it is burned.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Women whose meal-offerings are burned
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Women whose meal-offerings are burned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a sotah's meal-offering is burned: when she says she is defiled, when witnesses testify to her defilement, when she refuses to drink, when her husband refuses to make her drink, or when he has intercourse with her on the way. It then states that all women married to priests have their meal-offerings burned, and distinguishes between an Israelite woman married to a priest (her offering is burned) and a priest's daughter married to an Israelite (her offering is eaten).

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between a priest and a priest's daughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between a priest and a priest's daughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates differences: a priest's daughter's meal-offering is eaten, a priest's is not; a priest's daughter can become profaned (by marriage to a disqualified man), a priest cannot; a priest's daughter may become impure for the dead, a priest may not; a priest eats most holy offerings, a priest's daughter does not.

items.text: Mishnah: Differences between a man and a woman
items.text_en: Mishnah: Differences between a man and a woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists further distinctions: a man uncovers his head and rends his garments (in mourning), a woman does not; a man can vow his son as a nazirite, a woman cannot; a man shaves for his father's naziriteship, a woman does not; a man betroths his daughter, a woman does not; a man sells his daughter, a woman does not; a man is stoned naked, a woman is not; a man is hanged, a woman is not; a man is sold for his theft, a woman is not.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on the meal-offerings of women married to priests
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on the meal-offerings of women married to priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that explains how the meal-offering of a woman married to a priest is offered: since the husband has a portion and the wife has a portion, the handful is offered by itself and the remainder is offered by itself (not eaten and not entirely burned).

items.text: Gemara: Objection and resolution via Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Gemara: Objection and resolution via Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: anything from the offering that is fit for the altar fires is subject to the prohibition of 'do not burn' (if offered improperly). It answers via Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one may burn such items for the sake of wood (not for the sake of a sweet savor).

items.text: Gemara: Alternative resolution via Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Alternative resolution via Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for Rabbi Eliezer, but for the Rabbis who reject that view, the practice follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who says the handful is offered by itself and the remainder is scattered on the ash-heap.

items.text: Conclusion of the dispute about the meal-offering of a sinner
items.text_en: Conclusion of the dispute about the meal-offering of a sinner
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon regarding a meal-offering of a sinner that is brought by a priest, because it is fit for offering. However, in the case of a woman's meal-offering, even the Rabbis concede that it is not burned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon regarding a meal-offering of a sinner brought by a priest, but in the case of a woman's meal-offering they concede it is not burned.

items.text: Reason for the Mishnah's law: a married Israelite woman does not eat offerings
items.text_en: Reason for the Mishnah's law: a married Israelite woman does not eat offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for the Mishnah's statement that a married Israelite woman does not eat offerings: the verse says 'And every meal-offering of a priest shall be wholly burnt, it shall not be eaten,' implying a priest, not a priestess.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's law that a married Israelite woman does not eat offerings.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'And every meal-offering of a priest shall be wholly burnt, it shall not be eaten,' interpreting it to mean a priest (כֹהֵן) and not a priestess (כֹּהֶנֶת).

items.text: Source that a priestess becomes profaned, but a priest does not
items.text_en: Source that a priestess becomes profaned, but a priest does not
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'And he shall not profane his seed among his people' that a priest's offspring becomes profaned, but he himself does not become profaned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: a priestess becomes profaned (by marrying a disqualified man), but a priest does not become profaned.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive this rule?

The Gemara answers: the verse 'וְלֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו' (And he shall not profane his seed among his people) teaches that his offspring becomes profaned, but he himself does not become profaned.

items.text: Source that a priestess becomes impure and a priest eats most holy offerings
items.text_en: Source that a priestess becomes impure and a priest eats most holy offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a priestess becomes impure from the dead because the verse says 'Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron,' implying sons, not daughters. A priest eats most holy offerings because the verse says 'Any male among the sons of Aaron may eat it.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a priestess becomes impure from the dead.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron' excludes daughters, so a priestess is not prohibited from impurity.
The Gemara cites the verse that a priest eats most holy offerings, as it says 'Any male among the sons of Aaron may eat it.'

items.text: Derivation of the difference between a man and a woman regarding leprosy
items.text_en: Derivation of the difference between a man and a woman regarding leprosy
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verse 'And the leprous person, in whom the plague is' that both a man and a woman are included. The word 'man' teaches that only a man lets his hair grow and rends his garments, not a woman.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'אִישׁ' (a man) to include a man in the laws of leprosy, and the verse 'וְהַצָּרוּעַ אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ' (and the leprous person, in whom the plague is) to include a woman.
The Gemara explains that the word 'אִישׁ' (man) teaches that only a man lets his hair grow and rends his garments, not a woman.

items.text: Laws of naziriteship: a man can dedicate his son, a woman cannot
items.text_en: Laws of naziriteship: a man can dedicate his son, a woman cannot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that it is a halacha in naziriteship that a man can shave for his father's naziriteship, but a woman cannot shave for her father's naziriteship. A man can dedicate his son as a nazirite, but a woman cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man can dedicate his son as a nazirite, but a woman cannot.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that it is a halacha (binding tradition) in naziriteship that a man can shave for his father's naziriteship, but a woman cannot.
Rabbi Yochanan reiterates that the rule about a man dedicating his son as a nazirite is a halacha (binding tradition) in naziriteship.

items.text: Laws of betrothal and sale of daughters
items.text_en: Laws of betrothal and sale of daughters
items.desc_en: A man can betroth his daughter, but a woman cannot betroth her daughter, as derived from the verse 'I have given my daughter to this man.' A man can sell his daughter, but a woman cannot sell her daughter, as derived from the verse 'When a man sells his daughter.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may betroth his daughter, but a woman may not betroth her daughter.
The Gemara derives the rule from the verse 'I have given my daughter to this man,' implying the father gives, not the mother.
The Mishnah states that a man may sell his daughter, but a woman may not sell her daughter.
The Gemara derives the rule from the verse 'When a man sells his daughter,' implying the father sells, not the mother.

items.text: Laws of stoning and hanging: a man is stoned naked and hanged, a woman is not
items.text_en: Laws of stoning and hanging: a man is stoned naked and hanged, a woman is not
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'And they shall stone him' that a man is stoned naked, but a woman is not stoned naked. From the verse 'And you shall hang him on a tree' that a man is hanged, but a woman is not hanged.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man is stoned naked but a woman is not.
The Gemara asks the reason for this distinction and cites the verse 'וְרָגְמוּ אוֹתוֹ' (and they shall stone him).
The Gemara objects: if the verse meant to exclude women from stoning entirely, that contradicts the verse that explicitly includes women in stoning.
The Gemara resolves: the term 'אוֹתוֹ' means he is stoned without his garment, but she is not stoned without her garment.
The Mishnah states that a man is hanged but a woman is not.
The Gemara asks the reason and cites the verse 'וְתָלִיתָ אוֹתוֹ עַל עֵץ' (and you shall hang him on a tree).
The Gemara answers: the verse says 'אוֹתוֹ' (him), excluding her.

items.text: Law of being sold for theft: a man is sold, a woman is not
items.text_en: Law of being sold for theft: a man is sold, a woman is not
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'And he shall be sold for his theft' that a man is sold for his theft, but a woman is not sold for her theft.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man is sold for his theft, but a woman is not sold for her theft.
The Gemara asks for the reason for this distinction.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'ונמכר בגנבתו' (Exodus 22:2), interpreting that he is sold for his theft, but she is not sold for her theft.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah: women who do not drink the bitter water
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah: women who do not drink the bitter water
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah, stating that an arusah (betrothed woman) and a shomeret yavam (a woman awaiting yibbum) do not drink the bitter water and do not receive a ketubah, as derived from the verse 'When a woman goes astray under her husband,' excluding an arusah and a shomeret yavam. The list continues with an almanah to a kohen gadol, a gerushah and a chalutzah to a common kohen, and a mamzeret.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah, stating that an arusah (betrothed woman) and a shomeret yavam (a woman awaiting yibbum) do not drink the bitter water and do not receive a ketubah.
The Gemara cites the verse 'אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׂטֶה אִשָּׁה תַּחַת אִישָׁהּ' (when a woman goes astray under her husband) to exclude an arusah and a shomeret yavam from the bitter water ritual.

The Mishnah continues listing women who do not drink: an almanah (widow) to a kohen gadol, a gerushah (divorcée) and a chalutzah (released from yibbum) to a common kohen, and a mamzeret (offspring of a forbidden union).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Women who do not drink and do not receive ketubah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Women who do not drink and do not receive ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories of women who neither drink the bitter water nor receive their ketubah, including those who admit impurity, those with witnesses, those who refuse to drink, and others. It also presents disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding widows whose husbands died before drinking, and between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding pregnant and nursing women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a female Netin (נתינה) married to an Israelite, or an Israelite woman married to a Mamzer (ממזר) or Netin (נתין), neither drinks the bitter water nor receives her ketubah (כתובה).
The Mishnah lists women who neither drink nor receive their ketubah (כתובה): one who admits impurity, one against whom witnesses testify she is impure, and one who refuses to drink.
The Mishnah states that if the husband says 'I will not make her drink' or if he had relations with her on the way, she receives her ketubah (כתובה) but does not drink.

The Mishnah presents the dispute: if the husbands died before the women drank, Beit Shammai (בית שמאי) say they receive the ketubah (כתובה) and do not drink, while Beit Hillel (בית הלל) say they either drink or forfeit their ketubah (כתובה).

The Mishnah records the dispute: Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) says a pregnant or nursing woman does not drink and does not receive her ketubah (כתובה), while the Sages (חכמים) say the husband can separate from her and take her back later.

The Mishnah states that an Aylonit (איילונית), an elderly woman, or one incapable of childbirth neither receives her ketubah (כתובה) nor drinks; Rabbi Elazar (רבי אלעזר) says the husband can marry another woman to fulfill procreation.
The Mishnah rules that all other women either drink or forfeit their ketubah (כתובה); the wife of a priest drinks and is permitted to her husband, and the wife of a eunuch drinks.
The Mishnah states that a husband can issue a warning (קינוי) regarding all forbidden relations, except with a minor or one who is not a man.

The Mishnah concludes: the court (בית דין) issues a warning (קינוי) for a husband who is deaf-mute, insane, or imprisoned, but only to disqualify her from her ketubah (כתובה); Rabbi Yosei (רבי יוסי) says even to make her drink when the husband is released.

items.text: Gemara's question: Source for kinuy with arusah and shomeret yavam
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Source for kinuy with arusah and shomeret yavam
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah implies a husband can issue a warning (kinuy) to his wife even if she does not drink, and asks for the source. It cites a baraita that derives the inclusion of an arusah and a shomeret yavam for kinuy from the verse 'דבר אל בני ישראל ואמרת'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's implication that a husband can issue a warning (קינוי) even if the wife does not drink.
A baraita is cited deriving from the verse 'דבר אל בני ישראל ואמרת' that an arusah (betrothed woman) and a shomeret yavam (a yevamah awaiting yibbum) are included in the law of קינוי (warning).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan on exclusions
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan on exclusions
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yonatan, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yoshiyah excludes an arusah from the sotah ritual using 'תחת אישך' but includes a shomeret yavam via 'איש איש', while Rabbi Yonatan excludes a shomeret yavam from 'תחת אישך' and an arusah from 'אשר תשטה אשה תחת אישה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yonatan's view.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yoshiyah excludes an arusah from the sotah ritual using 'תחת אישך' but includes a shomeret yavam via 'איש איש'.
The baraita continues: Rabbi Yonatan excludes a shomeret yavam from 'תחת אישך' and an arusah from 'אשר תשטה אשה תחת אישה'.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each Tanna's reasoning: one emphasizes the arusah because her betrothal is his and he can execute her, while the other emphasizes the shomeret yavam because she lacks mesirah to chuppah. It then asks what Rabbi Yonatan does with the extra 'איש איש', answering that it includes the wife of a deaf man, an insane man, and a blind man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one Tanna emphasizes the arusah because her betrothal is his and he can execute her.
The Gemara explains that the other Tanna emphasizes the shomeret yavam because she lacks mesirah to chuppah.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yonatan does with the extra phrase 'איש איש'.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yonatan uses it to include the wife of a deaf man, an insane man, and a blind man.

items.text: Shmuel's position on Rabbi Yoshiya
items.text_en: Shmuel's position on Rabbi Yoshiya
items.desc_en: Shmuel asserts that his own view aligns even with Rabbi Yoshiya, arguing that the need for a verse to include her implies she is not considered his wife at all.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asserts that his own view aligns even with Rabbi Yoshiya, arguing that the need for a verse to include her implies she is not considered his wife at all.

items.text: First inquiry: warning for a woman violating Jewish law
items.text_en: First inquiry: warning for a woman violating Jewish law
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does a woman who violates Jewish law require a warning to forfeit her ketubah, or not? The doubt is whether the warning is needed or if she can repent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does a woman who violates Jewish law (עוברת על דת) require a warning (התראה) to forfeit her ketubah, or not, considering the possibility of repentance?

items.text: Attempted proof from an arusah and a yevamah
items.text_en: Attempted proof from an arusah and a yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a warning is given to forfeit the ketubah, citing a mishnah that an arusah and a shomeret yavam do not drink but can be warned. Abaye and Rav Pappa reject this, explaining the warning is for other purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a warning is given to forfeit the ketubah, citing the mishnah that an arusah and a shomeret yavam do not drink but can be warned, and asks whether the warning is to forfeit the ketubah.
Abaye rejects the proof, explaining that the warning is to forbid her to him (the husband), not to forfeit the ketubah.
Rav Pappa rejects the proof, explaining that the warning is to enable her to drink the bitter water when she is married.
A baraita supports Rav Pappa's explanation, stating that one does not warn an arusah to drink as an arusah, but one warns her to drink when she is married.

items.text: Second attempted proof from forbidden marriages
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from forbidden marriages
items.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita about women in forbidden marriages who do not drink but can be warned, suggesting the warning is to forfeit the ketubah. Rav Yehuda from Disqarta rejects this, explaining it is to forbid her to the adulterer.

sub.desc_en: Rava brings a baraita listing women in forbidden marriages who do not drink the bitter water and do not receive a ketubah, inferring that the warning (קינוי) must be to forfeit the ketubah.
Rava argues that since these women are already forbidden to their husbands, the warning must be intended to forfeit their ketubah.
Rav Yehuda from Disqarta rejects Rava's proof, explaining that the warning is to forbid the woman to the adulterer just as she is forbidden to her husband.

items.text: Third attempted proof and resolution
items.text_en: Third attempted proof and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina from Sura brings a baraita that Beit Din warns for a husband who is deaf, insane, or imprisoned, explicitly to disqualify her from her ketubah. This proves a warning is needed. The Gemara explains why others did not cite this: there, she has no fear of her husband.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina from Sura brings a baraita about Beit Din warning for a husband who is deaf, insane, or imprisoned, explicitly to disqualify her from her ketubah, proving that a warning is needed.
The Gemara explains why the other Amoraim did not cite this baraita: there, the woman has no fear of her husband at all, so the case is different.

items.text: Second inquiry: husband's desire to keep her
items.text_en: Second inquiry: husband's desire to keep her
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if a husband who wants to keep his wife who violates Jewish law may do so. It attempts to prove from the baraita that Beit Din acts for a husband who cannot, implying that if he could, he would keep her, so Beit Din would not act against his will.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who wishes to keep his wife who violates Jewish law (עוברת על דת) may do so, or whether the Torah's concern is solely the husband's objection.

The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita listing those for whom Beit Din acts (e.g., a deaf or imprisoned husband) that if a husband could keep her, Beit Din would not act against his will, implying the husband cannot keep her.

items.text: Third inquiry: husband's forgiveness of warning
items.text_en: Third inquiry: husband's forgiveness of warning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if a husband can forgive his warning. It brings several attempted proofs, including from the baraita about Beit Din, from the practice of appointing two scholars, and from a statement by Rabbi Yoshiya in the name of Ze'ira, which concludes that a warning can be forgiven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who forgives his warning (קינוי) renders the warning void, or whether it remains in effect.

sub.text: Gemara's attempted proof from the baraita about Beit Din
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from the baraita about Beit Din
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a warning cannot be forgiven, citing the baraita that Beit Din appoints a warning for a husband who cannot do so himself, implying the warning is not subject to the husband's forgiveness.

sub.text: Gemara's attempted proof from the practice of appointing two scholars
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from the practice of appointing two scholars
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a warning cannot be forgiven, citing the practice of appointing two scholars to prevent the husband from being alone with his wife, which would be unnecessary if he could simply forgive the warning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yoshiya in the name of Ze'ira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiya in the name of Ze'ira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya reports in the name of Ze'ira that a husband who forgives his warning renders it void, and the Gemara concludes that this is the correct ruling.

items.text: Dispute about timing of forgiveness
items.text_en: Dispute about timing of forgiveness
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether forgiveness is valid before or after seclusion. The Gemara concludes it is not valid after seclusion, based on a proof from Rabbi Yosei's argument about the sotah having no remedy, which would not hold if forgiveness were possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about whether a husband's waiver of his warning (קינוי) is valid after seclusion (סתירה).
One authority (Rav Acha) holds that the waiver is valid before seclusion but not after.
The other authority (Ravina) holds that the waiver is valid even after seclusion.
The Gemara concludes that the view that the waiver is invalid after seclusion is more plausible, based on a proof from the Sages' response to Rabbi Yosei.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's argument that the husband should be believed about his wife's purity, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) from the case of a menstruant (נידה).
The Sages reject Rabbi Yosei's argument, noting that a menstruant has a remedy (permissibility after immersion), while a sotah has no remedy.

The Gemara argues that if the waiver were valid after seclusion, the sotah would have a remedy (the husband could waive and cohabit), contradicting the Sages' claim; therefore, the waiver is invalid after seclusion.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about husbands who died before their wives drank, with Beit Shammai holding that a document ready for collection is considered as already collected.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the Mishnah's dispute about husbands who died before their wives drank the bitter water.
The gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
The gemara explains that Beit Shammai holds the principle of שטר העומד לגבות כגבוי דמי (a document ready for collection is considered as already collected).

items.text: Beit Hillel's position on a loan document
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's position on a loan document
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel holds that a loan document standing to be collected is not considered as already collected, in contrast to Beit Shammai.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction regarding the Mishnah's 'pregnant friend'
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction regarding the Mishnah's 'pregnant friend'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abbuha states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a pregnant friend applies only to a barren woman or an elderly woman, but an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) is universally agreed not to drink nor receive her ketubah, based on the verse requiring her to be capable of conceiving seed.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about an arusah and a yevamah
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about an arusah and a yevamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: one who warns his betrothed or his yavam's wife, if she was secluded before he married her, she does not drink nor receive her ketubah, implying that even those capable of bearing seed may be exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Women who do not drink and do not receive ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women who do not drink and do not receive ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists women who neither drink the sotah waters nor receive their ketubah: a pregnant or nursing woman of another man, a man who marries a barren or old woman without prior children, and contrasts with cases where they do drink or lose ketubah. Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether such a marriage must be dissolved permanently or temporarily.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a pregnant or nursing woman of another man does not drink the sotah waters and does not receive her ketubah, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Meir explains that a man should not marry a pregnant or nursing woman of another man, and if he does, he must divorce her permanently.
The Sages respond that he must divorce her but may remarry her when the time comes.
The Mishnah states that a man who marries a barren or old woman without prior children does not make her drink and she does not receive her ketubah.
Rabbi Elazar adds that such a man can marry another woman to fulfill procreation.
The Mishnah contrasts with cases where the woman does drink or loses her ketubah, such as a betrothed woman or a yevamah.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Aylonit contradicts Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Aylonit contradicts Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah includes an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) among those who drink or lose ketubah, which is a refutation of Rav Nachman who held that an aylonit does not drink.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman by noting that the Mishnah explicitly includes an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) among those who either drink the bitter water or lose their ketubah, contradicting Rav Nachman's position that an aylonit does not drink.

items.text: Rav Nachman's defense: It is a dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's defense: It is a dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds that the Mishnah reflects one Tanna, but he follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar who says an aylonit does not drink, based on the verse 'and she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed' — excluding one who cannot conceive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds that the Mishnah reflects a dispute among Tannaim, and he aligns with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who rules that an aylonit does not drink and does not receive her ketubah, based on the verse 'ונקתה ונזרעה זרע' (she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed) — excluding one who cannot conceive.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that an aylonit does not drink the bitter waters, based on the verse 'and she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed' — excluding one who cannot conceive.

items.text: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse and Rabbi Yishmael's objection
items.text_en: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse and Rabbi Yishmael's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'and she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed'. It is needed for the teaching that if a barren woman drinks, she is visited with children (Rabbi Akiva). Rabbi Yishmael objects: if so, all barren women would be suspected and drink, but this one who was not suspected loses out? Rather, the verse teaches that if she gave birth in pain she will give birth easily, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'וְנִקְּתָה וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע' (and she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed).
The Gemara cites a baraita that Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse to mean that if a barren woman drinks, she is visited with children.
Rabbi Yishmael objects: if so, all barren women would be suspected and drink, but this one who was not suspected loses out.
Rabbi Yishmael resolves that the verse teaches that if she gave birth in pain she will give birth easily, etc.

items.text: Clarifications: Woman of a mamzer, convert, and aylonit
items.text_en: Clarifications: Woman of a mamzer, convert, and aylonit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to state these cases: for a mamzer's wife, one might think she does not drink to avoid increasing the number of mamzerim; for a convert's wife, one might think the verse 'speak to the children of Israel' excludes converts; but the word 'and you shall say' includes them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state the case of a mamzer's wife, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought she should not drink to avoid increasing the number of mamzerim, so the Mishnah teaches that she does drink.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state the cases of a convert's wife, a freed slave's wife, and an aylonit.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought the verse 'speak to the children of Israel' excludes converts, so the Mishnah teaches that they are included.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the exclusion is indeed correct, and converts should not drink.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'and you shall say' (וְאָמַרְתָּ) is an inclusion, teaching that converts are included.

items.text: Wife of a kohen drinks and is permitted to her husband
items.text_en: Wife of a kohen drinks and is permitted to her husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why it is obvious that a kohen's wife drinks; one might think that since a captured woman is forbidden to a kohen, this one who was captured (by suspicion) should also be forbidden. The Gemara then discusses the case of a woman who was raped (mitnaveh) and why she is permitted to her kohen husband despite the waters not testing her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why it is obvious that a kohen's wife drinks, suggesting that since a captured woman is forbidden to a kohen, this woman who was captured by suspicion should also be forbidden.

The Gemara questions why it is obvious that she is permitted to her husband, and Rav Huna explains the case is of a woman who was raped (mitnaveh), but the Gemara objects that the waters would have tested her.

Rav Huna clarifies that the case is of a woman raped through limbs (not full intercourse), so the waters do not test her, and one might think she is forbidden to a kohen, but the mishnah teaches she is permitted.

items.text: Wife of a eunuch drinks; jealousy can be expressed through any ervah
items.text_en: Wife of a eunuch drinks; jealousy can be expressed through any ervah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the wife of a eunuch drinks, despite the verse 'from beside your husband' implying a man capable of intercourse, and that one can be jealous through any forbidden relative (ervah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The wife of a eunuch drinks — this is obvious! Why is it stated?
The Gemara answers: Lest you say the verse 'from beside your husband' implies a man capable of intercourse, and this one is not, the mishnah teaches that she drinks.
The Gemara asks: One can be jealous through any forbidden relative (ערוה) — this is obvious! Why is it stated?
The Gemara answers: Lest you say these are not subject to jealousy (קנוי), the mishnah teaches that they are.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about the double 'nitma'ah'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about the double 'nitma'ah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the double mention of 'nitma'ah' (she became defiled) in the Torah applies to both the husband and the lover, or only to the lover when the woman is already forbidden to the husband. It concludes that the double mention teaches that it applies to both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible interpretation that the double mention of 'nitma'ah' (she became defiled) might apply only to the husband and the lover where the woman becomes forbidden through this act of adultery, but not to a case where she is already forbidden; the Gemara then rejects this, concluding that the double mention teaches it applies to both.

items.text: Exclusion of a minor (katan) and the case of a shachuf
items.text_en: Exclusion of a minor (katan) and the case of a shachuf
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's exclusion of a 'katan' (minor) is derived from the word 'ish' (man) in the verse. It then questions whether this excludes a shachuf (a man with crushed testicles), citing Shmuel's ruling that a shachuf can be the subject of a kinui and disqualifies from terumah. The Gemara clarifies that these rulings are not obvious, as one might think the shachuf is not capable of intercourse or producing seed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's exclusion of a minor and a non-man, deriving it from the word 'איש' (man), and then asks what this excludes, suggesting it might exclude a שָׁחוּף (man with crushed testicles).

The Gemara objects by citing שמואל (Shmuel) who ruled that a שָׁחוּף can be the subject of a קינוי (warning) and disqualifies from תרומה (priestly portion), contradicting the suggestion that the Mishnah excludes him.

The Gemara questions why שמואל's ruling about a שָׁחוּף being subject to a קינוי is not obvious, given the verse 'וְשָׁכַב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע' (and a man lay with her carnally) which might imply he is not capable of seed.
The Gemara answers that שמואל's ruling teaches us that a שָׁחוּף is indeed subject to a קינוי, despite not being capable of seed.

The Gemara questions why שמואל's ruling that a שָׁחוּף disqualifies from תרומה is not obvious, given the verse 'לֹא יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ' (he shall not profane his seed) which might imply only one with seed disqualifies.
The Gemara answers that שמואל's ruling teaches us that a שָׁחוּף disqualifies from תרומה even though he cannot produce seed.

items.text: Exclusion of a non-Jew (nochri) and the source for disqualification
items.text_en: Exclusion of a non-Jew (nochri) and the source for disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah excludes a nochri (non-Jew), citing Rav Hamnuna that a nochri can be the subject of a kinui and disqualifies from terumah. The Gemara explains that the disqualification is not obvious, as one might think it only applies to a 'bar havayah' (one capable of marriage), but Rabbi Yochanan teaches from the verse about a bat kohen that a nochri or slave who has relations with a kohenet disqualifies her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's exclusion of 'one who is not a man' refers to a non-Jew (נכרי).
Rav Hamnuna states that a non-Jew can be the subject of a kinui (warning) and disqualifies a woman from terumah.
The Gemara asks why the ruling about kinui is not obvious, and explains that it teaches that even though the woman is already forbidden to a non-Jew, the sota ritual still applies.
The Gemara asks why the ruling about disqualification from terumah is not obvious, and explains that it teaches that a non-Jew disqualifies, based on Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Yishmael, deriving from the verse 'וּבַת כֹּהֵן כִּי תִהְיֶה אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה' that a non-Jew or slave who has relations with a kohenet, Levite, or Israelite disqualifies her, since they lack the possibility of widowhood or divorce.

items.text: Exclusion of an animal (beheima) and the source for no zenut with an animal
items.text_en: Exclusion of an animal (beheima) and the source for no zenut with an animal
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa concludes that the Mishnah excludes an animal (beheima), as there is no concept of zenut (fornication) with an animal. Rava from Parzikya asks for the source, and the Gemara cites the verse about the 'etnan zona' (hire of a harlot) and the teaching that the etnan of a dog and the price of a harlot are permitted, implying no zenut with an animal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah excludes an animal (בהמה), because there is no concept of זנות (fornication) with an animal.
Rava from Parzikya asks Rav Ashi for the source of the rabbinic principle that there is no זנות (fornication) with an animal.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the verse and baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the verse and baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the אתנן זונה (hire of a harlot) and the baraita that the אתנן of a dog and the מחיר of a harlot are permitted, implying no זנות with an animal.

items.text: The purpose of 'shikvat zera' and the debate over kinui for improper relations
items.text_en: The purpose of 'shikvat zera' and the debate over kinui for improper relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'shikvat zera' (seed of intercourse), and Rav Sheshet says it excludes a kinui for relations not in the usual manner. Rava objects that 'mishkevei isha' (lyings of a woman) already implies the usual manner. Rava then suggests it excludes a kinui for relations via limbs (outer contact), but Abaye objects that this is mere licentiousness, which the Torah does not forbid. Abaye suggests it excludes a kinui for kissing, but this depends on a dispute about the definition of 'ha'ara'ah' (initial contact). The Gemara concludes that Rava's view is maintained, but the verse teaches that the husband's jealousy is relevant even for improper relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'shikvat zera' (seed of intercourse), and cites a baraita that it excludes 'something else'.
Rav Sheshet explains that 'shikvat zera' excludes a kinui (jealousy warning) for relations not in the usual manner.
Rava objects that the phrase 'mishkevei isha' (lyings of a woman) already implies the usual manner, so 'shikvat zera' is unnecessary for that exclusion.
Rava suggests that 'shikvat zera' excludes a kinui for relations via limbs (outer contact without penetration).
Abaye objects that such contact is mere licentiousness (פריצותא), which the Torah does not forbid, so the husband's jealousy would not apply.
Abaye suggests that 'shikvat zera' excludes a kinui for kissing.

The Gemara notes that Abaye's explanation works only for the view that 'ha'ara'ah' (initial contact) means insertion of the corona, making kissing insignificant; but for the view that 'ha'ara'ah' is kissing, the exclusion is problematic.

The Gemara concludes that Rava's view (relations via limbs) is maintained, and the verse teaches that the husband's jealousy applies even for improper relations, since the husband is particular about such conduct.

items.text: Shmuel's statement about a man's conduct
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement about a man's conduct
items.desc_en: Shmuel begins a statement about a man's conduct, but the text is cut off, likely continuing to the next amud.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel begins a statement about a person taking something, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on marrying a daughter of a promiscuous woman
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on marrying a daughter of a promiscuous woman
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about whether one should marry a daughter of a promiscuous woman (דומה) or the woman herself. Rav argues the daughter comes from a fit drop, while Rabbi Yochanan argues the daughter stands in a presumption of fitness.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one should marry a promiscuous woman (דומה) rather than her daughter, because the daughter comes from a fit drop while the mother comes from a unfit drop.

Rabbi Yochanan argues that one should marry the daughter of a promiscuous woman rather than the woman herself, because the daughter stands in a presumption of fitness (חזקת כשרות) while the mother does not.

items.text: Challenge and resolution by Rava
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution by Rava
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from a baraita that says one may marry a דומה. Rava deflects by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to a case where one already married her, and the text should read 'daughter of a דומה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states 'A man may marry a promiscuous woman (דומה),' which seems to contradict Rav's position.

Rava resolves the objection by arguing that the baraita does not mean לכתחילה (the ideal standard) but rather בדיעבד (after the fact), and therefore it should be read as referring to the daughter (בת דומה), not the mother.

items.text: Halakhic conclusion and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusion and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: The halakha is decided in favor of Rabbi Yochanan: one should marry the daughter of a promiscuous woman, not the woman herself. A baraita taught by Rav Taḥlifa before Rabbi Avahu supports this, stating that children of a promiscuous woman are fit because most intercourse follows the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan, citing a baraita taught by Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva before Rabbi Avahu that a promiscuous woman's children are fit because the majority of her sexual relations are with her husband.

sub.text: Baraita cited by Rav Taḥlifa before Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Baraita cited by Rav Taḥlifa before Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rav Taḥlifa before Rabbi Avahu supports the ruling: children of a promiscuous woman are fit because most intercourse follows the husband (רוב בעילות אחר הבעל).

items.text: Rav Amram's query about an excessively promiscuous woman
items.text_en: Rav Amram's query about an excessively promiscuous woman
items.desc_en: Rav Amram asks about a woman who is excessively promiscuous: if she conceives only near her period, the husband does not guard her; but if she conceives only near her immersion, since the husband knows her cycle, does he guard her or not? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram asks: if the woman was excessively promiscuous, what is the status of her children? He first dismisses the question according to the view that a woman only conceives close to her menstrual period, since the husband does not know her and does not guard her.

Rav Amram then reframes the question according to the view that a woman only conceives close to her immersion (after her menstrual period): since the husband knows her, does he guard her, or because she is excessively promiscuous does he not? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).
The gemara records that the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Baraita on the Sotah ritual for women whose husbands are unavailable
items.text_en: Baraita on the Sotah ritual for women whose husbands are unavailable
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'איש איש' to include women whose husbands are deaf, insane, blind, abroad, or imprisoned: the court can warn them to disqualify them from their ketubah. However, the court cannot make them drink the bitter water; Rabbi Yosei disagrees and says the court can make them drink, and when the husband returns he will administer the drink.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'איש איש' to include women whose husbands are deaf, insane, blind, abroad, or imprisoned, stating that the court warns them to disqualify them from their ketubah.
The Tanna Kamma argues that the court cannot make them drink the bitter water, as the verse requires the husband to bring his wife.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees and says the court can make them drink, and when the husband returns he will administer the drink.

items.text: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Sages require both 'וקינא' and 'והביא' by the husband, while Rabbi Yosei does not require both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the Rabbis require the sequence 'וקנא...והביא' (he warned and then he brought), while Rabbi Yose does not require this sequence.
The Gemara explains that the Sages require both 'וְקִנֵּא' (he warned) and 'וְהֵבִיא' (he brought) by the husband, while Rabbi Yosei does not require both.

items.text: Derivation of physical disqualifications for the Sotah ritual
items.text_en: Derivation of physical disqualifications for the Sotah ritual
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds 'אשר תשטה אשה תחת אישה' to equate the man and woman. Rav Sheshet derives that just as a blind husband cannot make her drink, so a blind woman cannot drink. Rav Ashi adds that a lame or amputated woman cannot drink, based on the verse.

sub.text: Baraita on the analogy between husband and wife
sub.text_en: Baraita on the analogy between husband and wife
sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'אשר תשטה אשה תחת אישה' (when a woman goes astray under her husband) to draw an analogy (הקישא) between the man and the woman.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the purpose of the analogy
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the purpose of the analogy
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what halachic purpose does this analogy serve?

Rav Sheshet answers: just as if the husband is blind he cannot make her drink, as it is written 'ונעלם מעיני אישה' (and it was hidden from the eyes of her husband), so too if the wife is blind she does not drink.
Rav Ashi offers a different application: just as a lame or maimed woman would not drink (because she cannot physically perform the ordeal), as it is written...

items.text: Opening: The priest's physical fitness for the sotah ritual
items.text_en: Opening: The priest's physical fitness for the sotah ritual
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the priest must be able to stand the woman before God and place the offering on her hands; if he is lame or missing a hand, he cannot administer the waters. Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that just as a mute woman cannot drink because she must say 'Amen, amen,' so too a mute priest cannot administer the waters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the priest must be able to stand the woman before God and place the offering on her hands; if he is lame or missing a hand, he cannot administer the waters.
Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that just as a mute woman cannot drink because she must say 'Amen, amen,' so too a mute priest cannot administer the waters.

items.text: Transition: Returning to the topic of the betrothed woman
items.text_en: Transition: Returning to the topic of the betrothed woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the earlier discussion about the betrothed woman (arusah) and the sotah waters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the earlier discussion about the betrothed woman (ארוסה) and the sotah waters.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: The waters test the lover and the woman is forbidden to both
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: The waters test the lover and the woman is forbidden to both
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from the double expression 'וּבָאוּ' that the waters test the lover as well as the woman. He further derives from the double 'נִטְמָאָה' that the woman is forbidden to both her husband and her lover. Rabbi Yehoshua confirms that this was the teaching of Zechariah ben HaKatzav, and Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) explains that the two occurrences of 'נִטְמָאָה' in the passage refer one to the husband and one to the lover.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives from the double expression 'וּבָאוּ' that the waters test the lover as well as the woman.
Rabbi Akiva further derives from the double 'נִטְמָאָה' that the woman is forbidden to both her husband and her lover.

Rabbi Yehoshua confirms that this was the teaching of Zechariah ben HaKatzav, and Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) explains that the two occurrences of 'נִטְמָאָה' in the passage refer one to the husband and one to the lover.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: A second-degree loaf imparts impurity to a third
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: A second-degree loaf imparts impurity to a third
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva expounds the verse 'כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹכוֹ יִטְמָא' to teach that a second-degree food (a loaf that touched a primary source) can impart impurity to a third-degree food. Rabbi Yehoshua laments that this would have amazed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who had said that a future generation would declare a third-degree loaf pure because there was no biblical source for its impurity, but now Rabbi Akiva provides such a source.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva expounds the verse 'וּכְלִי חֶרֶשׂ... כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹכוֹ יִטְמָא' to teach that a second-degree loaf (כיכר שני) can impart impurity to a third-degree food.

Rabbi Yehoshua laments that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who said a future generation would declare a third-degree loaf pure for lack of a biblical source, would be amazed that Rabbi Akiva now provides such a source from the verse.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: The Sabbath boundary of a Levitical city
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching: The Sabbath boundary of a Levitical city
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva reconciles two contradictory verses about the measurement outside a Levitical city: one says 2,000 cubits, the other says 1,000 cubits. He explains that the inner 1,000 cubits are the open land (migrash) and the outer 1,000 cubits (totaling 2,000) are the Sabbath boundary. Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, says the 1,000 cubits are the open land and the 2,000 cubits are fields and vineyards.
