sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva opens by citing two contradictory verses about the measurement outside a Levitical city: one says 2,000 cubits, the other says 1,000 cubits.
Rabbi Akiva resolves the contradiction: the inner 1,000 cubits are the open land (מִגְרָשׁ) and the outer 1,000 cubits (totaling 2,000) are the Sabbath boundary.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's alternative
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's alternative
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, offers an alternative interpretation: the 1,000 cubits are the open land and the 2,000 cubits are fields and vineyards.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Nechemiah: How Israel sang at the Red Sea
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Nechemiah: How Israel sang at the Red Sea
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva expounds the word 'לֵאמֹר' in the verse about Moses and Israel singing, teaching that Israel responded after Moses with each phrase like reciting Hallel. Rabbi Nechemiah argues that they recited it like the Shema (in unison), not like Hallel (responsively).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva expounds the word 'לֵאמֹר' in the verse about the song at the Red Sea, teaching that Israel responded responsively after Moses, phrase by phrase, like reciting Hallel.
Rabbi Nechemiah argues that Israel recited the song in unison like the Shema, not responsively like Hallel.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos: Job served God out of love
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos: Job served God out of love
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos teaches that Job served God out of love, citing the verse 'הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי לוֹ אֲיַחֵל' (Though He slay me, I will hope for Him). The Gemara notes that the matter is ambiguous, but the continuation 'עַד אֶגְוָע לֹא אָסִיר תֻּמָּתִי מִמֶּנִּי' proves he acted out of love. Rabbi Yehoshua then laments that this would have amazed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who had always taught that Job served out of fear, citing 'אִישׁ תָּם וְיָשָׁר יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים', but now his student's student (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos) teaches that he acted out of love.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos teaches that Job served God out of love, citing the verse 'הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי לוֹ אֲיַחֵל' and resolving the ambiguity with the continuation 'עַד אֶגְוָע לֹא אָסִיר תֻּמָּתִי מִמֶּנִּי'.

Rabbi Yehoshua laments that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who taught that Job served out of fear based on 'אִישׁ תָּם וְיָשָׁר יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים', would be amazed that his student's student now proves Job acted out of love.

items.text: Gemara's question: To whom does 'oto' refer?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: To whom does 'oto' refer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion: The word 'אוֹתוֹ' (him) in the Mishnah's statement 'the waters test him' — to whom does it refer? If it refers to the husband, what did the husband do? The Gemara raises a difficulty, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom the word 'אוֹתוֹ' (him) in the Mishnah refers, and raises the difficulty that if it refers to the husband, what did the husband do to warrant being tested.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does the water test the paramour?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does the water test the paramour?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sotah waters test the paramour if he has sin, citing a verse that the man must be free of sin for the waters to test his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sotah waters test the paramour if he has sin, citing a verse that the man must be free of sin for the waters to test his wife.

items.text: Answer: The Mishnah refers to the paramour
items.text_en: Answer: The Mishnah refers to the paramour
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's statement about 'him' refers to the paramour, and explains that the Mishnah uses 'her' in the first clause and 'him' in the second due to the context of the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah's 'him' refers to the paramour, why not teach it explicitly as in the latter clause?
The Gemara answers: it always refers to the paramour; the Mishnah uses 'her' in the first clause and 'him' in the second due to the context of the verses.

items.text: Inquiry about the derivation from 'וּבָאוּ'
items.text_en: Inquiry about the derivation from 'וּבָאוּ'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt whether the derivation is from the word 'בָּאוּ' repeated or from 'וּבָאוּ' with a vav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the verse use the word 'ובאו' (and they came) twice, or 'באו' (they came) and 'ובאו' (and they came)?

items.text: Resolution attempt from 'נִטְמָאָה'
items.text_en: Resolution attempt from 'נִטְמָאָה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the doubt by citing a verse about 'נִטְמָאָה' and 'וְנִטְמָאָה', but the doubt persists whether it is 'נִטְמָאָה' repeated or with a vav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the doubt by citing a baraita that equates the prohibition for the husband and the paramour, based on the verse 'נִטְמָאָה' and 'וְנִטְמָאָה'.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita refers to the word 'נִטְמָאָה' repeated twice or to the phrase 'נִטְמָאָה' and 'וְנִטְמָאָה', leaving the doubt unresolved.

items.text: Resolution from Rabbi's statement
items.text_en: Resolution from Rabbi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the doubt by citing Rabbi's statement that two occurrences of 'וְנִטְמָאָה' in the parashah indicate one for the husband and one for the paramour, implying Rabbi Akiva interprets the vavs.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi says that the two occurrences of 'ונטמאה' in the passage indicate one for the husband and one for the paramour, implying that Rabbi Akiva interprets the 'vav' (and) as significant.

items.text: Derivation of six verses for Rabbi Akiva and three for Rabbi
items.text_en: Derivation of six verses for Rabbi Akiva and three for Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Akiva, six verses are written: one for her warning, one for his warning, one for her action, one for his action, one for her knowledge, and one for his knowledge. According to Rabbi, only three verses are written: one for warning, one for action, and one for knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that according to Rabbi Akiva, six verses are written: one for her warning, one for his warning, one for her action, one for his action, one for her knowledge, and one for his knowledge.
The Gemara states that according to Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), only three verses are written: one for warning, one for action, and one for knowledge.

items.text: Derivation that waters test the paramour from 'לַצְבּוֹת בֶּטֶן'
items.text_en: Derivation that waters test the paramour from 'לַצְבּוֹת בֶּטֶן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'לַצְבּוֹת בֶּטֶן וְלַנְפִּל יָרֵךְ' that the waters test the paramour's belly and thigh, as the woman's belly and thigh are already mentioned elsewhere. The Gemara also addresses alternative interpretations and concludes that the verse implies both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives that the waters test the paramour as well.
The Gemara answers that it is derived from a baraita which interprets the verse 'לַצְבּוֹת בֶּטֶן וְלַנְפִּל יָרֵךְ' as referring to the belly and thigh of the paramour.

The Gemara objects that the other tanna (Rabbi Akiva) interprets the verse as teaching the priest to inform the woman that her belly will be afflicted first, to avoid casting aspersions on the bitter waters.

The Gemara rejects the objection by arguing that if the verse were only about the woman, it should have said 'her belly and her thigh'; the general wording 'the belly and the thigh' implies the paramour.

The Gemara resolves that if the verse were entirely for the paramour, it would have said 'his belly and his thigh'; the general wording teaches both: the paramour is punished and the priest informs the woman of the order of punishment.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition from Zecharyah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition from Zecharyah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that Zecharyah used to expound in this manner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that Zechariah ben HaKatzav would expound in this manner.

items.text: Tannaic dispute: Three occurrences for husband, paramour, and terumah
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute: Three occurrences for husband, paramour, and terumah
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that the three occurrences of 'אִם נִטְמְאָה', 'נִטְמָאָה', and 'וְנִטְמָאָה' are for the husband, the paramour, and terumah, according to Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught: the three occurrences of 'אם נטמאה', 'נטמאה', and 'ונטמאה' in the passage indicate one for the husband, one for the paramour, and one for terumah (priestly portion), according to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer for priesthood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer for priesthood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues through a kal vachomer that if a divorced woman, permitted to terumah, is forbidden to the priesthood, then a Sotah, forbidden to terumah, should certainly be forbidden to the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if a divorced woman, who is permitted to terumah, is forbidden to the priesthood, then this woman, who is forbidden to terumah, should certainly be forbidden to the priesthood.

items.text: Derivation that a doubtful Sotah is forbidden
items.text_en: Derivation that a doubtful Sotah is forbidden
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verses 'וְהִיא נִטְמָאָה' and 'וְהִיא לֹא נִטְמָאָה' teach that a Sotah in doubt is forbidden to drink, as the text indicates that if she is defiled she should not drink, and if not defiled, why make her drink? This shows that uncertainty renders her forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verses 'והיא נטמאה' and 'והיא לא נטמאה': if she was defiled, why does she drink? If she was not defiled, why does he make her drink? This teaches that a doubtful case is forbidden.

items.text: Kal vachomer from Sotah to creeping creatures
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from Sotah to creeping creatures
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives a kal vachomer: if for Sotah, where an unintentional act is not treated like intentional and coercion like willingness, yet uncertainty is treated as certainty, then for creeping creatures, where unintentional is treated like intentional and coercion like willingness, it is logical that uncertainty should be treated as certainty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives a קל וחומר (a fortiori) for sheratzim (creeping things): if in the case of a sotah, where an unintentional act is not treated like an intentional one, yet doubt is treated as certainty, then for sheratzim, where unintentional is treated like intentional, doubt should certainly be treated as certainty.

items.text: Derivation of impurity laws from Sotah
items.text_en: Derivation of impurity laws from Sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that just as the Sotah case involves a private domain and an object that can be interrogated, so too a creeping animal (sheretz) in a private domain and with the capacity to be interrogated is deemed impure in cases of doubt. This leads to a general rule: an object that can be interrogated in a private domain is impure, in the public domain it is pure, and an object that cannot be interrogated is always pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Sotah case is treated as certain (וַדַּאי) for the purpose of deriving impurity laws.
The Gemara derives from the Sotah case that a creeping animal (שֶׁרֶץ) in a private domain and with the capacity to be interrogated is treated as impure in cases of doubt.
The Gemara states the general rule: an object that can be interrogated in a private domain is impure, in the public domain it is pure, and an object that cannot be interrogated is always pure.

items.text: Questioning Rabbi Akiva's derivation for priesthood
items.text_en: Questioning Rabbi Akiva's derivation for priesthood
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's statement that Rabbi Akiva derived the laws of terumah from the Sotah, and then asks how Rabbi Akiva derived the laws for the priesthood. It suggests that perhaps the priesthood does not require a separate verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yishmael said that Rabbi Akiva derived terumah from Sotah, but does Rabbi Akiva also derive the priesthood from Sotah?
The Gemara suggests that perhaps Rabbi Akiva does not need a separate verse for the priesthood, implying it is derived from the same source or is unnecessary.

items.text: Continuation of the debate on the number of verses
items.text_en: Continuation of the debate on the number of verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues the argument between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael about how many verses are needed to derive the prohibitions for a sotah. It states that according to Rabbi Akiva, four verses are written, while according to Rabbi Yishmael, only three are needed, with the prohibition for kehunah derived via a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Torah treated a suspected sotah (ספק זונה) like a definite zonah (זונה) for the prohibition of terumah.
Rabbi Akiva holds that four verses are written: one for the husband, one for the paramour, one for kehunah (priesthood), and one for terumah.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that only three verses are written (for husband, paramour, and terumah), and the prohibition for kehunah is derived via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument).
The Gemara objects: how does Rabbi Yishmael know that the verse is needed for terumah and kehunah comes from a קל וחומר, perhaps the verse is for kehunah and terumah is permitted?
Rabbi Yishmael answers: it is logical that terumah is analogous to husband and paramour, as all apply during life (מחיים), excluding kehunah which applies after death.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva does not accept this analogy to husband and paramour.
Alternatively, even if Rabbi Akiva accepts the analogy, he holds that the Torah wrote a verse for something that could have been derived by קל וחומר (a fortiori argument).
Rav Giddel in the name of Rav cites a verse to derive that an item with intent to be asked (יש בו דעת לישאל) is treated differently from one without such intent regarding doubt about impurity.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the end of the verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the end of the verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the end of the verse, which implies that only a definitely pure person may eat, but a doubtful one may not.
The Gemara resolves: the first part refers to a case with intent to be asked (יש בו דעת לישאל), the second to one without such intent.
The Gemara explains that both Rav Giddel's teaching and the derivation from sotah are necessary, as each covers a different case.
The Gemara adds that without Rav Giddel's teaching, one might have thought that sotah requires intent of both the toucher and the touched, so both sources are needed.
The Gemara shifts to a new topic: on that day Rabbi Akiva taught about earthenware vessels.
The Gemara asks: since an earthenware vessel has no inner cavity (אין לו), why is it impure?
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers: from the Torah it has no impurity, but from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) it does, comparing a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) to a second-degree food.
The Gemara objects: the comparison can be refuted because a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) is a primary source of impurity (אב הטומאה).
The Gemara begins a response with 'תֵּיתֵי' (let it come), but the argument is cut off.

items.text: Clarification of the verses for Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Clarification of the verses for Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that for Rabbi Akiva, four verses are needed: one for the husband, one for the adulterer, one for kehunah, and one for terumah. For Rabbi Yishmael, only three verses are needed: one for the husband, one for the adulterer, and one for terumah, with kehunah derived via a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for Rabbi Akiva, four verses are written: one for the husband, one for the adulterer, one for kehunah, and one for terumah.
The Gemara states that for Rabbi Yishmael, only three verses are written: one for the husband, one for the adulterer, and one for terumah, while kehunah is derived via a kal vachomer.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's assumption that the verse is needed for terumah and kehunah is derived via kal vachomer. Perhaps the verse is needed for kehunah, and terumah is permitted? The Gemara answers that it is logical to compare terumah to the husband and adulterer, which apply during life, excluding kehunah which applies after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yishmael: perhaps the verse is needed for kehunah (priesthood), and terumah (priestly portion) is permitted without a verse.
The Gemara answers that it is logical to compare terumah to the husband and adulterer, which apply during life, excluding kehunah which applies after death.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's response and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's response and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva does not accept the comparison to the husband and adulterer. Alternatively, even if he does accept it, he holds that the Torah writes a verse even for something that could be derived via a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Akiva does not accept the comparison (דּוּמְיָא) to the husband and adulterer.

sub.text: Alternative explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Alternative explanation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: Alternatively, even if Rabbi Akiva does accept the comparison, he holds that the Torah wrote a verse even for something that could be derived via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument).

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement about doubtful impurity
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement about doubtful impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav that the law regarding an item that has the capacity to be asked (i.e., a person) versus one that does not (i.e., an inanimate object) is derived from a verse. The verse implies that only a definite impurity prohibits, but a doubtful impurity permits. However, the end of the verse seems to contradict this, so the Gemara concludes that the distinction is between cases where there is capacity to ask and where there is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel states in the name of Rav that the distinction between an item with capacity to be asked (a person) and one without (an object) regarding doubtful impurity is derived from the verse 'והבשר אשר יגע בכל טמא לא יאכל' (the meat that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten), implying that only definite impurity prohibits, but doubtful impurity permits.

The Gemara objects by citing the end of the verse 'והבשר כל טהור יאכל בשר' (the meat, every pure person may eat meat), which implies that only definite purity permits, but doubtful impurity prohibits, contradicting the initial inference.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by concluding that the first part of the verse refers to a case where there is capacity to ask (a person), and the second part to a case where there is no capacity to ask (an inanimate object), thus harmonizing the two inferences.

items.text: Need for both Rav Giddel's statement and the sotah derivation
items.text_en: Need for both Rav Giddel's statement and the sotah derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rav Giddel's statement and the derivation from sotah are necessary. If only from Rav Giddel, one might think the law applies in both private and public domains, so the sotah derivation is needed. If only from sotah, one might think it requires the knowledge of both the one who touches and the one being touched, so Rav Giddel's statement is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rav Giddel's statement and the derivation from sotah are necessary to teach the full law.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching about a clay vessel and the third degree of impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching about a clay vessel and the third degree of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that on that day, Rabbi Akiva taught about a clay vessel that has no inner space, yet is impure. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that from the Torah it has no impurity, but from a kal vachomer it does: just as a tevul yom (who is permitted in chullin) invalidates terumah, a second-degree food (which is invalid in chullin) should certainly make a third degree in terumah. The Gemara raises a refutation that tevul yom is a primary source of impurity, but then begins to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that on that day, Rabbi Akiva taught about a clay vessel that has no inner space yet is impure.
The Gemara asks: since the vessel has no inner space, why is it impure?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that from the Torah it has no impurity, but from a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) it does: just as a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) who is permitted in חולין (non-sacred food) invalidates תרומה (priestly portion), a second-degree food that is invalid in חולין should certainly make a third degree in תרומה.
The Gemara raises a refutation: the kal vachomer can be challenged because a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) is an אב הטומאה (primary source of impurity), unlike a second-degree food.
The Gemara begins to answer the refutation, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Initial kal vachomer for second-degree food in terumah
items.text_en: Initial kal vachomer for second-degree food in terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: just as a tevul yom of a sheretz (which is a primary source of impurity) and a clay vessel (which imparts impurity through its airspace) are both permitted in chullin but disqualify terumah, so too a second-degree food (כיכר שני) should disqualify terumah. The argument concludes with the common element (הצד השוה) that they are permitted in chullin and disqualify terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that a second-degree food (כיכר שני) should disqualify terumah, based on the common element (הצד השוה) of tevul yom of a sheretz and a clay vessel, which are permitted in chullin but disqualify terumah.
An anonymous objection (דור אחר) refutes the kal vachomer by noting that the common element (הצד השוה) has a stringent aspect (צד חמור) that undermines the analogy.
The Gemara notes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai does not refute the kal vachomer based on the stringent aspect (צד חמור), implying he accepts the argument.

items.text: Objection to the kal vachomer and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response
items.text_en: Objection to the kal vachomer and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's response
items.desc_en: Another generation (דור אחר) objects that the common element has a stringent aspect (צד חמור). Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai does not raise this objection, indicating his acceptance of the argument.

sub.desc_en: Another generation (דור אחר) objects to the kal vachomer (קל וחומר) argument, pointing out that the common element (צד השוה) has a stringent aspect (צד חמור).

sub.text: Gemara's statement about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai does not raise this objection, indicating his acceptance of the argument.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's derivation of fourth degree in sacred food
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's derivation of fourth degree in sacred food
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei derives that a fourth-degree food (רביעי) in sacred food is invalid through a kal vachomer: if a person lacking atonement (מחוסר כיפורים), who is permitted in terumah, is invalid in sacred food, then a third-degree food (שלישי), which is invalid in terumah, should certainly produce a fourth degree in sacred food. The Gemara explains that third-degree in sacred food is from the Torah (based on the verse 'והבשר אשר יגע בכל טמא לא יאכל'), and fourth-degree is from the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a person lacking atonement (מחוסר כיפורים), who is permitted in terumah, is invalid in sacred food, then a third-degree food (שלישי), which is invalid in terumah, should certainly produce a fourth-degree (רביעי) in sacred food.
The Gemara summarizes that the third-degree in sacred food is derived from the Torah, while the fourth-degree is derived from the kal vachomer.

The Gemara provides the scriptural source for the third-degree in sacred food from the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בְּכׇל טָמֵא לֹא יֵאָכֵל' (the meat that touches any impure thing shall not be eaten), explaining that it refers to a second-degree food touching it, and reiterates that the fourth-degree comes from the kal vachomer.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's critique of Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's critique of Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that he does not understand Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, because a counterexample exists: food that comes from a tevul yom (אוכל הבא מחמת טבול יום) is invalid in terumah but does not produce a fourth degree in sacred food. The baraita cites Abba Shaul, Rabbi Meir, and the Sages regarding the status of tevul yom in sacred food: Abba Shaul says it imparts impurity to two and disqualifies one, Rabbi Meir says it imparts impurity to one and disqualifies one, and the Sages say it disqualifies sacred food just as it disqualifies terumah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that he does not understand Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer (קל וחומר) reasoning, because a counterexample exists: food that comes from a טבול יום (tevul yom, one who immersed that day) is invalid in תרומה (terumah, priestly portion) but does not produce a fourth degree of impurity in sacred food.
The baraita cites Abba Shaul, who says that a טבול יום (tevul yom) in sacred food imparts impurity to two levels (שניים) and disqualifies one (פוסל אחד).
The baraita cites Rabbi Meir, who says that a טבול יום (tevul yom) in sacred food imparts impurity to one level (אחד) and disqualifies one (פוסל אחד).
The baraita cites the Sages, who say that a טבול יום (tevul yom) disqualifies sacred food just as it disqualifies תרומה (terumah), without creating a fourth degree.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges: how do we know Rabbi Yosei holds like the Sages? Perhaps he holds like Abba Shaul, who says tevul yom imparts impurity to two and disqualifies one. The Gemara responds: if he held like Abba Shaul, he could have derived the fourth degree in sacred food from food that comes from a tevul yom, since tevul yom itself is permitted in chullin yet produces a fourth degree in sacred food.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yosei holds like the Sages, suggesting he might hold like Abba Shaul who says tevul yom imparts impurity to two and disqualifies one.

The Gemara responds that if Rabbi Yosei held like Abba Shaul, he could have derived the fourth degree in sacred food from food that comes from a tevul yom, since tevul yom itself is permitted in chullin yet produces a fourth degree in sacred food.

items.text: Gemara's initial argument and rebuttal
items.text_en: Gemara's initial argument and rebuttal
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if a third-degree impurity from a second-degree source can create a fourth in sacred food, then a second-degree impurity should create a third in unconsecrated food. It then anticipates a potential refutation based on a טבול יום being a primary source, but notes that the case of מחוסר כיפורים already addresses this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if a third-degree impurity derived from a second-degree source can create a fourth in sacred food, then a second-degree impurity should create a third in unconsecrated food.
The Gemara anticipates a potential refutation based on a טבול יום being a primary source, but notes that the case of מחוסר כיפורים already addresses this, so the objection is dismissed.

items.text: Rav Asi/Rabbah ben Isi's statement in Rav's name
items.text_en: Rav Asi/Rabbah ben Isi's statement in Rav's name
items.desc_en: Rav Asi (or Rabbah ben Isi) reports in Rav's name that five Tannaim—Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Eliezer—all agree that a second-degree impurity does not create a third-degree impurity in unconsecrated food.

sub.text: Rav Asi (or Rabbah ben Isi) in Rav's name
sub.text_en: Rav Asi (or Rabbah ben Isi) in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi (or Rabbah ben Isi) reports in Rav's name that five Tannaim—Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Eliezer—all agree that a second-degree impurity does not create a third-degree impurity in unconsecrated food.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir states that items requiring immersion by rabbinic decree are permitted in unconsecrated food, implying that second-degree impurity does not create a third in חולין.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Mishnah for Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Mishnah for Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules that items requiring rabbinic immersion are permitted in unconsecrated food (חולין) and second tithe (מעשר), while the Sages forbid them in second tithe, demonstrating that Rabbi Meir holds second-degree impurity does not create a third in חולין.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara references a previously stated teaching of Rabbi Yosei, which implies that if a second-degree impurity could create a third in חולין, it would lead to a fourth in תרומה and a fifth in קודש, which is not the case.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yosei's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yosei's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's previously stated position that if a second-degree impurity could create a third in חולין, it would lead to a fourth in תרומה and a fifth in קודש, which is not the case.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua rules that eating a first-degree and then a second-degree food makes the eater second-degree, and a third-degree food makes him second-degree in קודש but not in תרומה. The Gemara explains this applies to חולין made on the level of תרומה, implying no third-degree in חולין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua rules that eating a first-degree and then a second-degree food makes the eater second-degree, and a third-degree food makes him second-degree in קודש but not in תרומה.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling applies to חולין made on the level of תרומה.
The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to חולין prepared on the level of תרומה, not on the level of קודש.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a second-degree food does not create a third-degree in חולין.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar states that the first-degree impurity in קודש, חולין, and תרומה all have the same effect: in קודש it renders two items impure and disqualifies one, in תרומה it renders one impure and disqualifies one, and in חולין it disqualifies one. This implies no second-degree creates a third in חולין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Elazar's position by citing a baraita.

Rabbi Elazar states that the first-degree impurity in קודש, חולין, and תרומה all have the same effect: in קודש it renders two items impure and disqualifies one, in תרומה it renders one impure and disqualifies one, and in חולין it disqualifies one, implying no second-degree creates a third in חולין.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer discusses taking חלה from a pure dough for an impure one, requiring a piece of dough less than an egg-bulk to connect them. This implies that impurity does not spread in חולין beyond the first degree, consistent with no second-degree creating a third.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that חלה (priestly dough portion) may be taken from a pure dough for an impure one by placing a piece smaller than an egg-bulk between them, implying that impurity does not spread in חולין (non-sacred food) beyond the first degree.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Sages prohibit something, setting up the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Sages prohibit something, setting up the Gemara's discussion.

items.text: Initial interpretation of the dispute
items.text_en: Initial interpretation of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes the dispute is about whether a second-degree impurity makes a third-degree in unconsecrated food (חולין).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Eliezer permits an egg-bulk of pure dough in the middle.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the initial assumption
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the initial assumption
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the initial assumption was that both the mishna and baraita refer to first-degree impure dough, and that non-sacred food untithed for חלה (ḥalla) is not treated like חלה (ḥalla).
The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about whether a second-degree impurity can impart third-degree impurity to non-sacred items, with one opinion holding it cannot.
The Gemara presents the opposing opinion that a second-degree impurity can impart third-degree impurity to non-sacred items.

items.text: Rav Mari's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Mari's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana rejects the initial assumption, arguing that all agree there is no second making third in חולין; the dispute is about whether חולין הטבולין לחלה are like challah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana rejects the initial assumption, arguing that all agree there is no second making third in חולין; the dispute is about whether חולין הטבולין לחלה are like challah.

items.text: Alternative resolution
items.text_en: Alternative resolution
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: all agree that חולין הטבולין לחלה are not like challah and there is no second making third in חולין; the dispute is about whether it is permitted to cause impurity to unconsecrated food in the Land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: everyone agrees that חולין הטבולין לחלה is not like challah and that a second-degree impurity does not make a third-degree in ordinary food, and the dispute is about whether it is permitted to cause impurity to ordinary food in the Land of Israel.
One opinion holds that it is permitted to cause impurity to unconsecrated food in the Land of Israel.
The other opinion holds that it is forbidden to cause impurity to unconsecrated food in the Land of Israel.

items.text: Transition to the song at the sea
items.text_en: Transition to the song at the sea
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about the status of Sabbath boundaries (תחומין) as biblical or rabbinic, then moves to the baraita about Rabbi Akiva's lecture on the song at the sea.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about whether Sabbath boundaries (תחומין) are biblical or rabbinic, citing the baraita about Rabbi Akiva's lecture.

items.text: Three opinions on how Israel recited the song
items.text_en: Three opinions on how Israel recited the song
items.desc_en: The baraita presents three Tannaic views: Rabbi Akiva says they responded with refrains like the Hallel reader; Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says they repeated every phrase; Rabbi Nechemya says they recited together like a prayer leader.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Akiva's view that Israel recited the song like an adult reading Hallel, with the people repeating only the chapter headings after Moses.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili states that Israel recited the song like a minor reading Hallel, repeating every single word after Moses.
Rabbi Nechemya says that Israel recited the song like a prayer leader beginning the Shema, with Moses starting and the people joining in unison.

items.text: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical derivation: Rabbi Akiva interprets 'לֵאמֹר' as referring to the first phrase; Rabbi Eliezer interprets it as every phrase; Rabbi Nechemya derives from 'וַיֹּאמְרוּ' that they all spoke together and 'לֵאמֹר' that Moses began.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With regard to what do they disagree?
Rabbi Akiva holds that the word 'לֵאמֹר' (saying) refers only to the first phrase.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that 'לֵאמֹר' (saying) refers to every single word.
Rabbi Nechemya holds that 'וַיֹּאמְרוּ' (and they said) indicates they all spoke together, and 'לֵאמֹר' (saying) means that Moses began first.

items.text: Additional baraita on infants' song
items.text_en: Additional baraita on infants' song
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili describes how even infants miraculously sang, and Rabbi Meir adds that even fetuses in the womb sang, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili taught that when Israel came up from the sea, even infants and nursing babies saw the Divine Presence and said 'זה אלי ואנוהו' (This is my God and I will glorify Him), as it is written 'מפי עוללים ויונקים יסדת עז' (Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings You have established strength).
Rabbi Meir adds that even fetuses in the womb sang, citing a verse (the verse is cut off at the end of the daf).

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse about the sea splitting
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse about the sea splitting
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Israelites could see the Divine Presence at the sea if they were not worthy, and Rabbi Tanchum answers that the sea became like a transparent mirror for them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Israelites could see the Divine Presence at the sea if they were not worthy, citing the verse 'בְּמַקְהֵלוֹת בָּרְכוּ אֱלֹהִים' (In assemblies bless God).
Rabbi Tanchum answers that the sea became like a transparent mirror (אספקלריא המאירה) for them, enabling them to see the Divine Presence.

items.text: Analysis of the spelling of 'lo' in Job's verse
items.text_en: Analysis of the spelling of 'lo' in Job's verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos's statement about Job, questioning whether the word 'lo' is spelled with an aleph (meaning 'not') or a vav (meaning 'to him'), and concludes that the spelling can imply both meanings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hurkanos's statement about Job and questions whether the word 'lo' is spelled with an aleph (meaning 'not') or a vav (meaning 'to him').
The Gemara objects by citing a verse where 'lo' is spelled with an aleph but clearly means 'to him', challenging the assumption that spelling alone determines meaning.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'lo' in Job's verse is ambiguous and can be interpreted both ways, meaning both 'not' and 'to him'.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's comparison of Job and Abraham
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's comparison of Job and Abraham
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir argues that since both Job and Abraham are described as 'fearing God', Job's fear must also be from love, as Abraham's was, and proves Abraham's love from the verse 'seed of Abraham my lover'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir opens a baraita comparing the phrase 'ירא אלהים' (fearing God) used for Job and Abraham, arguing that Job's fear must also be from love (מאהבה).
Rabbi Meir proves that Abraham's fear was from love by citing the verse 'זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אֹהֲבִי' (seed of Abraham my lover).

items.text: The difference between acting from love and from fear
items.text_en: The difference between acting from love and from fear
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains that acting from love is greater than from fear, as love is rewarded for thousands of generations while fear is only for a thousand, and the Gemara resolves a contradiction in verses about the duration of reward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between one who acts from love and one who acts from fear.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar answers that one who acts from love is greater, as love is rewarded for two thousand generations while fear is only for a thousand.
The Gemara cites verses: one verse promises reward for thousands (אלפים) to those who love God, while another promises reward for a thousand (אלף) to those who keep His commandments.
The Gemara objects that the second verse also mentions 'to those who love Him' alongside 'to those who keep His commandments,' both for a thousand generations.
The Gemara resolves that each verse is interpreted according to its immediate context: one refers to love alone, the other to fear alone.

items.text: Rava's dream interpretation for two students
items.text_en: Rava's dream interpretation for two students
items.desc_en: Two students tell Rava about their dreams, one reciting a verse about those who fear God and the other about those who love His name, and Rava declares them both complete righteous, one from love and one from fear.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces two students sitting before Rava, one of whom reports a dream verse about those who fear God.
The second student reports his dream verse about those who love God's name.
Rava declares both students complete righteous ones, one acting from love and the other from fear.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah (heading)
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah (heading)
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase 'Hadran alach' (we return to you), indicating the start of a new discussion on the Sotah laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase 'Hadran alach' (we return to you), indicating the start of a new discussion on the Sotah laws.

items.text: Mishnah: Testimony in the Sotah case
items.text_en: Mishnah: Testimony in the Sotah case
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents disputes about testimony regarding a Sotah: Rabbi Eliezer says even hearsay from a bird suffices to divorce her, Rabbi Yehoshua requires witnesses who discuss the matter, and the Gemara discusses the reliability of various witnesses and derives a kal vachomer about testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling of רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) that if a husband warned his wife and she secluded herself, even hearsay from a flying bird obligates him to divorce her and pay her marriage contract.
The Mishnah presents the position of רבי יהושע (Rabbi Yehoshua), who requires that gossiping women who spin by moonlight discuss the matter before he divorces her.
The Mishnah rules that if one witness testifies that he saw her defiled, she does not drink the bitter water, and even a slave or maidservant is credible to disqualify her from her marriage contract.

The Mishnah lists female relatives (mother-in-law, daughter-in-law, rival wife, yevama, husband's daughter) who are credible only to prevent her from drinking the bitter water, not to disqualify her from her marriage contract.
The Mishnah raises a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference): if first testimony (seclusion) requires two witnesses, then final testimony (defilement) should also require two witnesses.
The Mishnah resolves the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'ועד אין בה' (and there be no witness against her), teaching that any testimony suffices for defilement.
The Mishnah begins a reverse kal vachomer: now that one witness suffices for defilement, the first testimony (seclusion) should also be established by one witness.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Derivation that first testimony requires two witnesses
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Derivation that first testimony requires two witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah argues that since the second testimony (which prohibits her forever) is established by one witness, the first testimony (which does not prohibit forever) should logically also be established by one witness. The Gemara counters with a verse: 'for he found in her a matter of nakedness' and compares it to 'by the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established', concluding that here too two witnesses are required.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that since the second testimony (which prohibits her forever) is established by one witness, the first testimony (which does not prohibit forever) should logically also be established by one witness.

The Gemara counters with a verse: 'for he found in her a matter of nakedness' and compares it to 'by the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established', concluding that here too two witnesses are required.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of conflicting testimonies
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of conflicting testimonies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: if one witness says she was defiled and another says she was not, or a woman says defiled and another says not, she drinks. If one says defiled and two say not, she drinks. If two say defiled and one says not, she does not drink.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: one witness says she was defiled and another says not, or a woman says defiled and another says not — she drinks.
The Mishnah adds: if one says defiled and two say not, she drinks; if two say defiled and one says not, she does not drink.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the derivation and the source for impurity without warning or seclusion
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the derivation and the source for impurity without warning or seclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation: the verse 'for he found in her a matter of nakedness' should teach 'in her' and not in warning, 'in her' and not in seclusion. It then asks: from where do we derive that a single witness is not believed for mere impurity without warning and seclusion? It answers by a verbal analogy of 'matter' from elsewhere, requiring two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation: the verse 'for he found in her a matter of nakedness' should teach 'in her' and not in warning, 'in her' and not in seclusion.
The Gemara clarifies that the derivation indeed teaches 'in her' and not in warning, 'in her' and not in seclusion.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a single witness is not believed for mere impurity without warning and seclusion?
The Gemara answers by a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'matter' from elsewhere, requiring two witnesses.

items.text: Gemara: Source that a single witness is believed in the absence of contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara: Source that a single witness is believed in the absence of contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's case where one witness says defiled and another says not implies that without contradiction, a single witness is believed. It derives this from the verse 'and there is no witness against her'—the verse speaks of two witnesses, but 'one witness' teaches that wherever 'witness' is stated, it means two unless specified as 'one'. The Torah then says: since there are not two, but one, and 'she was not seized', she is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the Mishnah's case where one witness says defiled and another says not implies that without contradiction, a single witness is believed.
The Gemara asks for the source that a single witness is believed in the absence of contradiction.

The baraita derives from the verse 'וְעֵד אֵין בָּהּ' (and there is no witness against her) that the verse speaks of two witnesses, and the word 'אֶחָד' (one) teaches that wherever 'עֵד' (witness) is stated, it means two unless specified as 'one'.
The Gemara concludes that since there are not two witnesses but one, and 'וְהִיא לֹא נִתְפָּשָׂה' (she was not seized), she is prohibited.

items.text: Ulla's objection and resolution: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Ulla's objection and resolution: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: Ulla objects: since by Torah law a single witness is believed, how can another witness contradict him? For wherever the Torah believed one witness, it is as if there are two, and the words of one cannot stand against two. Therefore, Ulla teaches the Mishnah differently: in the case of one vs. one, she does not drink. Rabbi Yitzchak agrees, but Rabbi Chiyya says she drinks. The Gemara resolves: the dispute is whether the witnesses came simultaneously or sequentially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a second witness can contradict the first, since wherever the Torah believed one witness, it is as if there are two, and the words of one cannot stand against two.
Ulla teaches the Mishnah differently: in the case of one witness vs. one, she does not drink; Rabbi Yitzchak agrees, but Rabbi Chiyya says she drinks.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: the case where the witnesses came simultaneously (בבת אחת) is different from the case where they came sequentially (בזה אחר זה).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Chiyya and resolution: The Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Chiyya and resolution: The Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiyya from the Mishnah: if one says defiled and two say not, she drinks—implying that one vs. one she does not drink. Rabbi Chiyya retorts: from the latter clause, two say defiled and one says not, she does not drink—implying one vs. one she drinks. The Gemara resolves: the entire Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses, and it follows Rabbi Nechemya, who says that where the Torah believed one witness, follow the majority of opinions, and two women are like two men. Alternatively, some say that wherever a single qualified witness comes initially, even a hundred women are like one witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiyya from the Mishnah: the case of one witness saying defiled and two saying not defiled implies that one vs. one she would not drink, contradicting Rabbi Chiyya's position.

Rabbi Chiyya retorts by pointing to the latter clause of the Mishnah: two say defiled and one says not, she does not drink, which would imply that one vs. one she drinks, so the Mishnah is internally inconsistent if taken literally.

The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses and follows Rabbi Nechemya, who rules that where the Torah believed one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, and two women count as two men.
An alternative explanation is offered: wherever a single qualified witness comes initially, even a hundred women are considered like one witness, so the Mishnah's cases are consistent.

items.text: Conclusion of Rabbi Nechemya's ruling on sotah testimony
items.text_en: Conclusion of Rabbi Nechemya's ruling on sotah testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case of a woman who came initially and reconciles it with Rabbi Nechemya's view that wherever the Torah trusts one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, treating two women regarding one woman like two men regarding one man. It then clarifies why two cases of invalid witnesses are needed, teaching that we follow the majority even for leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah is dealing with, and answers that it involves a woman who came initially.

The Gemara reconciles the case with Rabbi Nechemya's view that wherever the Torah trusts one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, treating two women regarding one woman like two men regarding one man, but two women regarding one man is considered equally divided.
The Gemara explains why two cases of invalid witnesses are needed: to teach that we follow the majority even for leniency, not only for stringency.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah: 'Mi shekinei'
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah: 'Mi shekinei'
items.desc_en: The phrase 'Hadaran alach mi shekinei' marks the conclusion of the previous chapter and a return to the Mishnah that lists passages recited in any language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the conclusion of the previous chapter and a return to the Mishnah that lists passages recited in any language.

items.text: Mishnah: Passages in any language vs. only in Hebrew
items.text_en: Mishnah: Passages in any language vs. only in Hebrew
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists passages that may be recited in any language: the sotah passage, ma'aser confession, Shema, prayer, Grace after Meals, oath of testimony, and oath of deposit. Then it lists those that must be in Hebrew: bikurim recitation, chalitzah, blessings and curses, priestly blessing, High Priest's blessing, the king's passage, the eglah arufah passage, and the anointed for war when speaking to the people.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing passages that may be recited in any language: the sotah passage, ma'aser confession, Shema, prayer, Grace after Meals, oath of testimony, and oath of deposit.

The Mishnah then lists passages that must be recited in Hebrew: bikurim recitation, chalitzah, blessings and curses, priestly blessing, High Priest's blessing, the king's passage, the eglah arufah passage, and the anointed for war when speaking to the people.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for bikurim and chalitzah
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for bikurim and chalitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that bikurim must be in Hebrew by a verbal analogy: 've'anita ve'amarta' here and 've'anu haLeviim ve'amru' there, just as there it is in Hebrew, so too here. Similarly for chalitzah, using the same analogy. Rabbi Yehuda adds that 've'antah ve'amrah cachah' requires her to say it in that very language (Hebrew).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how bikurim is recited in Hebrew.
The Gemara derives bikurim in Hebrew via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from 'וְעָנִיתָ וְאָמַרְתָּ' to 'וְעָנוּ הַלְוִיִּם וְאָמְרוּ'.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that the verse 'וְעָנְתָה וְאָמְרָה כָּכָה' requires chalitzah to be said specifically in Hebrew.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for blessings and curses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for blessings and curses
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the ceremony of blessings and curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, identifying the location as Shechem via a verbal analogy from 'Elonei Moreh'. It details the arrangement of the tribes, priests, Levites, and the ark, and the procedure of turning toward each mountain, reciting blessings and curses, with the people answering 'Amen'. Finally, it mentions bringing stones, building an altar, plastering it, and writing the Torah in seventy languages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks how the ceremony of blessings and curses is performed.
The Gemara describes the location as Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal near Shechem, derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'אלוני מורה' (Elonei Moreh) in the story of Abraham.
The Gemara details the arrangement: six tribes on each mountain, with priests, Levites, and the ark in the middle, citing a verse from Joshua.
The Gemara describes the procedure: turning toward Mount Gerizim for blessings and toward Mount Ebal for curses, with the people answering 'Amen'.
The Gemara describes the subsequent actions: bringing stones, building an altar, plastering it, and writing the Torah in seventy languages, citing the verse 'באר היטב' (explain well).

items.text: Derivation that the sotah passage may be recited in any language
items.text_en: Derivation that the sotah passage may be recited in any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the law that the sotah passage may be recited in any language, and answers from the verse 'And the priest shall say to the woman'—implying in any language he speaks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the sotah passage may be recited in any language?
The Gemara answers: It is derived from the verse 'And the priest shall say to the woman'—implying in any language he speaks.

items.text: Tannaic baraita on what the sotah is informed about
items.text_en: Tannaic baraita on what the sotah is informed about
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the sotah is informed in a language she understands about what she drinks and why, and about what she is suspected of being defiled, all to prevent slander against the bitter waters.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the sotah is informed in any language she understands about what she drinks and in what vessel, and about what she was defiled and how.
The baraita specifies that 'what she drinks' refers to the matter of קינוי (jealousy warning) and סתירה (seclusion), and 'in what vessel' — a clay jug.

The baraita specifies that 'what she was defiled' refers to matters of jest and childishness, and 'how' — whether accidentally or intentionally, under duress or willingly; all this to prevent slander against the bitter waters.

items.text: Derivation that viduy maaser may be recited in any language
items.text_en: Derivation that viduy maaser may be recited in any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that viduy maaser may be recited in any language from a verbal analogy of 'saying' from the sotah. Rav Zevid challenges Abaye to derive it from the Levites' recitation in the Holy Tongue, but the Gemara rejects this because the Levites' recitation involves both 'answering' and 'saying', whereas viduy maaser involves only 'saying'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where it is derived that viduy maaser may be recited in any language, and answers with a verbal analogy from the sotah.
Rav Zevid challenges Abaye, suggesting that the verbal analogy should be drawn from the Levites' recitation, which is in the Holy Tongue.
The Gemara resolves that a verbal analogy of 'saying' alone is derived from 'saying' alone, not from 'answering' and 'saying' together, thus rejecting the Levites as a source.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's principle: praise softly, grief loudly
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's principle: praise softly, grief loudly
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that a person should recite his praise in a low voice (from viduy maaser) and his grief in a loud voice (from mikra bikkurim). The Gemara questions the loud voice for grief, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that prayer was instituted silently to avoid embarrassing sinners, and resolves that it is not 'grief' but 'distress'—a metzora must announce his impurity so others pray for him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states the principle that a person should recite his praise in a low voice and his disgrace in a loud voice.

The Gemara explains the biblical sources for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's principle: praise in a low voice is derived from viduy maaser (the confession of tithes), and disgrace in a loud voice is derived from mikra bikkurim (the declaration of first fruits).

The Gemara objects: How can disgrace be recited in a loud voice? Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that prayer was instituted silently to avoid embarrassing sinners, as the Torah did not distinguish the place of a sin-offering from a burnt-offering.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the principle: do not say 'his disgrace' but rather 'his distress'—a metzora (leper) must announce his impurity loudly so that many will pray for mercy on his behalf.

items.text: Discussion of silent prayer and the distinction between sin-offering and burnt-offering
items.text_en: Discussion of silent prayer and the distinction between sin-offering and burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara revisits Rabbi Yochanan's statement about silent prayer to avoid embarrassing sinners, noting that the Torah does not distinguish location between sin-offering and burnt-offering. Objections are raised about differences in blood application and gender, but each is dismissed: the priest knows the difference, the animal's fat covers the gender, and the sinner's own shame or need for atonement justifies the distinction.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that silent prayer was instituted to avoid embarrassing sinners, as the Torah did not distinguish location between a sin-offering and a burnt-offering.
The Gemara objects that there is a distinction: the blood of a sin-offering is applied above the red line, while the blood of a burnt-offering is applied below.
The Gemara answers that only the priest knows this distinction, so it does not publicly embarrass the sinner.
The Gemara objects that a sin-offering is female and a burnt-offering is male, which is publicly visible.
The Gemara answers that the gender is concealed by the animal's fat tail.
The Gemara objects that this works for a lamb, but what about a female goat which has no fat tail to conceal its gender?
The Gemara answers that the sinner himself is embarrassed because he should have brought a lamb but brought a goat instead.
The Gemara objects that for a sin-offering for idolatry, which must be a goat, there is no alternative, so what can be said?
The Gemara resolves that the sinner should be embarrassed and go, so that he may attain atonement.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on keriat shema in any language
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on keriat shema in any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that keriat shema may be recited in any language from the verse 'Shema Yisrael'. A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi holds it must be in Hebrew (based on 'vehayu'—as they are), while the Sages permit any language (based on 'shema'—in any language you hear). Each side addresses the other's prooftexts, with additional derivations for the order of recitation and the requirement to make the words audible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for reciting the Shema in any language, deriving it from the verse 'Shema Yisrael' meaning in any language you hear.
A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi holds the Shema must be recited in Hebrew (as written), while the Sages permit any language.
Rabbi derives from the verse 'והיו' (and they shall be) that the words must remain in their original Hebrew form.
The Sages derive from the word 'שמע' (hear) that the Shema may be recited in any language you understand.
The Gemara objects: the Sages must also address the verse 'והיו', and they explain it teaches the order of recitation (not to read backwards).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi derives the order of recitation, and answers that he learns it from the words 'דברים' and 'הדברים', while the Sages do not derive from these terms.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi must also address the word 'שמע', and explains that he uses it to require making the words audible to one's own ears, while the Sages follow the opinion that one who recites without hearing himself has fulfilled the obligation.

items.text: Beginning of a new sugya: Does Rabbi hold that one who recites shema without hearing it fulfills the obligation?
items.text_en: Beginning of a new sugya: Does Rabbi hold that one who recites shema without hearing it fulfills the obligation?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze whether Rabbi holds that one who recites shema without hearing it has fulfilled the obligation, based on the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi holds that one who recites the Shema without hearing it fulfills the obligation, based on the previous discussion.

items.text: Derivation that the entire Torah may be said in any language
items.text_en: Derivation that the entire Torah may be said in any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the Torah were only in Hebrew, the word 'וְהָיוּ' would be superfluous; it is needed because of 'שְׁמַע'. Conversely, if it could be in any language, 'שְׁמַע' would be superfluous; it is needed because of 'וְהָיוּ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah would need the word 'וְהָיוּ' if it were only in Hebrew, implying it must be said in any language.
The Gemara answers that 'וְהָיוּ' is needed because of the word 'שְׁמַע' (which requires Hebrew).
The Gemara alternatively questions why the Torah would need 'שְׁמַע' if it could be in any language, implying it must be in Hebrew.
The Gemara answers that 'שְׁמַע' is needed because of the word 'וְהָיוּ' (which requires any language).

items.text: Prayer may be in any language
items.text_en: Prayer may be in any language
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that prayer is supplication and may be recited in any language the individual wishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that prayer, being supplication, may be recited in any language the individual wishes.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding prayer in Aramaic
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding prayer in Aramaic
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan state that one should not ask personal needs in Aramaic because ministering angels do not understand it. The Gemara resolves that this applies to an individual, but a congregation may pray in any language. A baraita about a Bat Kol speaking Aramaic is countered by saying a Bat Kol is different, or that it was Gabriel who taught seventy languages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the Mishnah's ruling that prayer can be said in any language, citing Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan who forbid asking personal needs in Aramaic because ministering angels do not understand it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an individual, who should not pray in Aramaic, and a congregation, which may pray in any language.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita where a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) spoke in Aramaic, implying that angels do understand Aramaic.
The Gemara offers a first answer: a Bat Kol is different because its purpose is to be heard, so it speaks in a language people understand.
The Gemara offers a second answer: the voice was not an angel but the angel Gabriel, who knows all seventy languages, so it could speak Aramaic.

items.text: Grace after meals and oaths may be in any language
items.text_en: Grace after meals and oaths may be in any language
items.desc_en: Grace after meals is derived from the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ וּבֵרַכְתָּ' and may be in any language. The oath of testimony is derived from 'וְשָׁמְעָה קוֹל אָלָה' and may be in any language the witness hears. The oath of deposit is derived via a verbal analogy from the oath of testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse for Grace after Meals (ברכת המזון) to show it may be recited in any language.
The Gemara cites the verse for the oath of testimony (שבועת העדות) to show it may be administered in any language the witness understands.
The Gemara derives the oath of deposit (שבועת הפקדון) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תֶּחְטָא' in the oath of testimony.

items.text: Recitation of first fruits and halitzah must be in Hebrew
items.text_en: Recitation of first fruits and halitzah must be in Hebrew
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that must be said in Hebrew. For first fruits, a verbal analogy from 'וְעָנִיתָ' to the Levites' declaration shows it must be in Hebrew. For the Levites themselves, a verbal analogy from 'קוֹל' to Moses shows they speak in Hebrew.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that must be recited in Hebrew, beginning with the recitation over first fruits and חליצה (ḥalitza).
The Gemara derives that the recitation over first fruits must be in Hebrew via a verbal analogy from 'וְעָנִיתָ' (and you shall speak) to the Levites' declaration, which is in Hebrew.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the Levites themselves answered in Hebrew?
The Gemara answers: It is derived from a verbal analogy between the word 'קוֹל' (voice) here and the word 'קוֹל' in the verse about Moses, where God answered in Hebrew.

items.text: Dispute about the word 'כָּכָה' in halitzah
items.text_en: Dispute about the word 'כָּכָה' in halitzah
items.desc_en: The Rabbis interpret 'כָּכָה' as referring to an action that is indispensable, while Rabbi Yehuda derives additional laws from 'כֹּה' and 'כָּכָה'. The Rabbis do not derive anything from 'כֹּה' and 'כָּכָה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the word 'כָּכָה' (so) in the halitzah verse, and answers that they require it to teach that an action mentioned in the portion is indispensable.
It states that Rabbi Yehuda derives additional laws from the words 'כֹּה' (ko) and 'כָּכָה' (kakha).
It states that the Rabbis do not derive anything from the difference between 'כֹּה' and 'כָּכָה'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's use of 've'anta ve'amra'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's use of 've'anta ve'amra'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the phrase 've'anta ve'amra' (and she shall answer and say), explaining that it is needed to teach the Levites that the declaration is in the holy tongue. It then rejects a possible derivation from Moses by noting that the analogy is based on 'aniyah' (answering) not 'kol' (voice).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the phrase 'וְעָנְתָה וְאָמְרָה' (and she shall answer and say), given that he already derives the requirement of holy tongue from other terms.
The Gemara answers that the phrase is needed to teach the Levites that the declaration is in the holy tongue.

The Gemara objects that one could derive the requirement from Moses via a verbal analogy on 'קוֹל' (voice), and then rejects this by noting that the analogy is based on 'עֲנִיָּיה' (answering), not 'קוֹל'.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's rule
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's rule
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that wherever 'koh', 'kakhah', 'aniyah', and 'amirah' are said, it is in the holy tongue, with examples from the priestly blessing, chalitzah, and the Levites.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that wherever 'koh', 'kakhah', 'aniyah', and 'amirah' are said, it is in the holy tongue, with examples from the priestly blessing, chalitzah, and the Levites.

items.text: Location of blessings and curses
items.text_en: Location of blessings and curses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses how the blessings and curses were performed after crossing the Jordan. A baraita interprets the verses describing the location, with Rabbi Yehuda explaining 'be'ever hayarden' as beyond the Jordan, and the other phrases identifying the place as Shechem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking how the blessings and curses were performed after crossing the Jordan.

A baraita cites verses to locate the site, with Rabbi Yehuda interpreting 'be'ever hayarden' as beyond the Jordan and the Tanna Kamma explaining 'acharei derech mevo hashemesh' as the place where the sun shines.
The baraita continues interpreting the remaining phrases, identifying the location as Shechem via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse about Abraham.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei's dispute with Kutim
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei's dispute with Kutim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei recounts how he refuted the Kutim (Samaritans) by pointing out that they claim 'Elonei Moreh' is Shechem, but they have no tradition for it, while the Jews learn it through a gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei recounts that he refuted the Kutim (Samaritans) by accusing them of falsifying their Torah.
He argues that both sides agree 'Elonei Moreh' is Shechem, but the Jews derive this through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), while the Kutim have no tradition for it.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar offers a different interpretation of the verses, arguing that 'be'ever hayarden' means near the Jordan, and then raises difficulties with the other phrases, such as the land being that of the Hivites and the mountains not being in the Arabah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'be'ever hayarden' as near the Jordan, arguing that if it meant beyond the Jordan, the verse would have used a different phrase.
Rabbi Elazar raises a difficulty: the phrase 'be'eretz hakena'ani' describes land that actually belongs to the Hivites, not the Canaanites.
Rabbi Elazar raises two further difficulties: the mountains are not in the Arabah, and the people did not see the Gilgal at that time.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov explains that the verses are not describing the location but instructing the people on how to travel: on the road, in settled areas, and in the plain, not in fields, deserts, or mountains.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov explains that the verses instruct the people to travel on the road, in settled areas, and in the plain, not in fields, deserts, or mountains.

items.text: How Israel crossed the Jordan
items.text_en: How Israel crossed the Jordan
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the crossing of the Jordan: the ark traveled first instead of after two camps, and the priests carried it instead of the Levites. Rabbi Yosei adds that priests carried the ark in three places: crossing the Jordan, circling Jericho, and returning it to its place.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes how Israel crossed the Jordan: the ark traveled first instead of after two camps, and priests carried it instead of Levites.
Rabbi Yosei adds that priests carried the ark in three places: crossing the Jordan, circling Jericho, and returning it to its place.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the water height
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the water height
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that when the priests' feet immersed in the Jordan, the waters rose to a height of twelve mil by twelve mil, corresponding to the Israelite camp.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that when the priests' feet immersed in the Jordan, the waters rose to a height of twelve mil by twelve mil, corresponding to the Israelite camp.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon objects that if the water was only twelve mil high, it would flood the people. Instead, he explains that the water piled up in heaps over three hundred mil high, visible to all kings.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon objects that if the water was only twelve mil high, it would flood the people, since water is lighter than a person.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: He explains that the water piled up in heaps over three hundred mil high, visible to all kings, as the verse states.

items.text: Rahab's testimony as support
items.text_en: Rahab's testimony as support
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rahab's words to Joshua's messengers, confirming that the miracle was known to all the Canaanite kings.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites Rachav the prostitute's words to Joshua's spies, confirming that the nations heard of the miracle and their hearts melted.

items.text: Joshua's warning while still in the Jordan
items.text_en: Joshua's warning while still in the Jordan
items.desc_en: While still in the Jordan, Joshua tells the people that they cross on condition that they dispossess the inhabitants; otherwise, the waters will flood them, including him.

sub.desc_en: While still in the Jordan, Joshua tells the people they cross on condition that they dispossess the land's inhabitants, or the waters will sweep them away—including him.

items.text: Joshua's command to take stones as a sign
items.text_en: Joshua's command to take stones as a sign
items.desc_en: Joshua commands each tribe to take a stone on his shoulder as a sign for future generations that the fathers crossed the Jordan.

sub.desc_en: Joshua commands each tribe to lift a stone onto his shoulder as a sign for future children that their fathers crossed the Jordan.

items.text: Joshua's command for stones from the priests' feet
items.text_en: Joshua's command for stones from the priests' feet
items.desc_en: Joshua commands taking twelve stones from the priests' feet and placing them at the lodging place, specifying that it is only that night's lodging.

sub.text: Joshua's command about stones from the Jordan
sub.text_en: Joshua's command about stones from the Jordan
sub.desc_en: Joshua commands taking twelve stones from the priests' standing place and depositing them at the lodging site, limiting the command to that specific lodging.

items.text: Dispute about the weight of the stones and the cluster of grapes
items.text_en: Dispute about the weight of the stones and the cluster of grapes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda reports that Abba Chalafta and others measured each stone as forty se'ah. The Gemara calculates the weight of the cluster of grapes carried by the spies, with Rabbi Yitzchak describing how eight men carried the cluster, one a pomegranate, one a fig, while Joshua and Caleb carried nothing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda reports that Abba Chalafta and others measured each stone from the Jordan as weighing forty se'ah, and notes the general principle that a person's load is one-third of their carrying capacity.
The Gemara uses this measurement to calculate the weight of the cluster of grapes carried by the spies, interpreting the verse 'וַיִּשָּׂאֻהוּ בַמּוֹט בִּשְׁנָיִם' as indicating two poles.

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that eight men carried the cluster, one carried a pomegranate, one a fig, while Joshua and Caleb carried nothing, either because they were important or because they were not part of that plan.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha about the interpretation of Rabbi Yehuda's statement, but the text is cut off.

sub.text: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
