sub.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha
sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha regarding the interpretation of Rabbi Yehuda's statement.

items.text: Dispute about how the spies crossed the Jordan
items.text_en: Dispute about how the spies crossed the Jordan
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and another opinion about whether the spies crossed the Jordan in a single line or one after another, based on whether people or water are lighter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the spies crossed the Jordan one after another.
Another opinion holds that both views agree the spies crossed in a single line, but they disagree about whether people or water are lighter.

items.text: Resh Lakish on God's command to send spies
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on God's command to send spies
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the phrase 'Send for yourself' as meaning 'from your own understanding,' and notes that the verse 'it was good in my eyes' implies it was not good in God's eyes.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets 'שְׁלַח לְךָ' (send for yourself) as meaning 'from your own understanding,' implying God allowed Moses to choose the spies himself.
The gemara questions why Moses would choose a bad portion for himself, given the implication that he chose the spies.
Resh Lakish answers by citing the verse 'וַיִּיטַב בְּעֵינַי הַדָּבָר' (it was good in my eyes), explaining that it was good in Moses' eyes but not in God's eyes.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba on the spies' intention
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba on the spies' intention
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba explains that the spies intended to shame the land of Israel, as indicated by the word 'yachperu' (dig) which is related to shame.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba explains that the spies intended to shame the land of Israel, as indicated by the word 'yachperu' (dig) which is related to shame.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yochanan on the spies' names
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yochanan on the spies' names
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states a tradition that the spies were named according to their deeds, giving the example of Sthur ben Michael. Rabbi Yochanan adds Nachbi ben Vofsi as another example, explaining the meanings of their names.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states a tradition that the spies were named according to their deeds, giving the example of Sthur ben Michael and explaining the meaning of his name.
Rabbi Yochanan adds Nachbi ben Vofsi as another example, explaining the meanings of his name components.

items.text: Caleb's prayer and Joshua's blessing
items.text_en: Caleb's prayer and Joshua's blessing
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'and he came to Hebron' (singular) indicates Caleb separated from the spies and prayed at the patriarchs' graves. Moses had already prayed for Joshua, as implied by the name Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses the singular 'וַיָּבֹא' (and he came) instead of the plural 'וַיָּבֹאוּ' (and they came).
Rava explains that Caleb separated from the spies and prostrated himself at the patriarchs' graves, praying for deliverance from the spies' counsel.
The Gemara adds that Moses had already prayed for Joshua, as implied by the name Yehoshua (יָהּ יוֹשִׁיעֲךָ), and cites the verse about Caleb having a different spirit.

items.text: Interpretations of the giants' names
items.text_en: Interpretations of the giants' names
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two interpretations: one based on their actions (Achiman, Sheshai, Talmai) and another based on the cities they built (Anath, Alush, Talbush).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the names Achiman, Sheshai, and Talmai based on their actions: Achiman as the most skilled, Sheshai as making the land like pits, and Talmai as making the land like furrows.

The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: the names refer to cities they built — Anath, Alush, and Talbush — and the phrase 'yelidei ha'anak' indicates they made the sun appear as a necklace due to their height.

items.text: The building of Hebron and its fertility
items.text_en: The building of Hebron and its fertility
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse 'Hebron was built seven years before Zoan,' explaining it means it was more fertile, despite being rocky. A contradiction is raised about Hebron being a source of fat sheep, resolved by saying the rocky land produces good pasture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'built' regarding Hebron, asking if it means literal building, given the chronological impossibility of building a younger son's city before an older son's.
The Gemara explains that 'built' means Hebron was more fertile (built up) than Zoan, being seven times more fertile despite being rocky.
The Gemara objects that Hebron is described as rocky, yet a baraita says it was a source of fat sheep, implying fertility.

sub.text: Rav Avya or Rabba bar bar Chanan's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Avya or Rabba bar bar Chanan's resolution
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that precisely because the land is rocky, it produces good pasture that fattens sheep.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching on the spies' journey
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching on the spies' journey
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai interprets the verse 'And they went and came' to equate the spies' going with their coming, both being for evil counsel.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai interprets the verse 'And they went and came' to equate the spies' going with their coming, both being for evil counsel.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on slander without truth
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on slander without truth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir teaches that any slander that does not begin with a kernel of truth will not endure.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir teaches that any slander that does not begin with a kernel of truth will not endure.

items.text: Caleb's silencing and Joshua's speech
items.text_en: Caleb's silencing and Joshua's speech
items.desc_en: Rabba explains that Caleb silenced the people with words. Joshua initially hesitated to speak, but then praised Moses' miracles and encouraged the people to conquer the land.

sub.desc_en: Rabba explains that Caleb silenced the people by inciting them with words.
The gemara notes that when Joshua began to speak, the people objected, saying 'Will this severed head speak?'
Joshua cleverly begins by asking if only this miracle was performed by Moses, leading the people to think he is speaking in Moses' disgrace, and they fall silent.

Joshua then lists Moses' miracles — the exodus from Egypt, splitting the sea, and the manna — and argues that if Moses commanded them to build ladders to heaven they would obey, so surely they should conquer the land.

items.text: The spies' claim about God's inability
items.text_en: The spies' claim about God's inability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa interprets the spies' statement 'for he is stronger than us' as a blasphemous claim that even the Master of the house cannot remove His vessels.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse where the spies say 'we cannot go up against the people.'

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa interprets the spies' statement 'for he is stronger than us' (כי חזק הוא ממנו) as a blasphemous claim that even the Master of the house (God) cannot remove His vessels from Canaan.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of 'a land that devours its inhabitants'
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of 'a land that devours its inhabitants'
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that God intended the land's devouring for good—to cause the Canaanites to die and distract others—but the spies interpreted it as evil.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces the idea that God intended the land's devouring for good, but the spies interpreted it as evil.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of God's good intention
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of God's good intention
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that God caused the Canaanite leaders to die wherever the spies went, so the Canaanites would be distracted and not inquire about the spies.
An alternative explanation is that Job died at that time, and the entire world was occupied with his eulogy, providing the distraction.
Rava concludes that the spies, in contrast, interpreted the phenomenon as evil, saying 'a land that devours its inhabitants'.

items.text: The spies' lie about being like grasshoppers
items.text_en: The spies' lie about being like grasshoppers
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya questions how the spies knew they were like grasshoppers in the eyes of the Canaanites. The Gemara explains that they heard the Canaanites comparing them to ants.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya questions how the spies knew that the Canaanites saw them as grasshoppers, since the spies could only know their own perception.
The Gemara explains that the spies heard Canaanites comparing them to ants while the spies were hiding in trees, so they knew the Canaanites' perception.

items.text: The weeping on Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: The weeping on Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the night the spies returned was the eve of Tisha B'Av, and God decreed that because they wept for nothing, it would be a day of weeping for generations.

sub.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the night the spies wept was the eve of Tisha B'Av, and God decreed that because they wept for nothing, it would be a day of weeping for generations.

items.text: The punishment of the spies
items.text_en: The punishment of the spies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba describes the people throwing stones upward. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and others detail the spies' unusual death: their tongues were extended, and worms went in and out. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says they died of croup.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba explains that the people threw stones upward toward heaven, showing their rebellion against God.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states that the spies died an unusual death.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa citing Rabbi Sheila
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa citing Rabbi Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa in the name of Rabbi Sheila describes the spies' tongues being extended to their navels with worms entering and exiting.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the spies died of croup (אסכרה), a throat disease.

items.text: The Ark crossing the Jordan and Uzza's sin
items.text_en: The Ark crossing the Jordan and Uzza's sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when the last Israelite crossed the Jordan, the waters returned. The Ark carried its bearers, and Uzza was punished for touching it, as God said: 'The Ark carried its bearers, should it not carry itself?'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that when the last Israelite crossed the Jordan, the waters returned to their place.
The Gemara describes that the Ark carried its bearers and crossed, as the verse states.
The Gemara concludes that Uzza was punished for touching the Ark, as God said: 'The Ark carried its bearers, should it not carry itself?'

items.text: Dispute on Uzza's sin
items.text_en: Dispute on Uzza's sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree: one says Uzza was punished for negligence (shalu), the other for relieving himself in front of the Ark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse describing God's anger at Uzza for touching the Ark.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree on the nature of Uzza's sin: one says it was negligence (שָׁלוּ), the other says he relieved himself in front of the Ark.

items.text: Uzza's portion in the World to Come
items.text_en: Uzza's portion in the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan deduces from the verse 'with the Ark of God' that Uzza has a share in the World to Come, just as the Ark is eternal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan deduces from the verse 'with the Ark of God' that Uzza has a share in the World to Come, just as the Ark is eternal.

items.text: David's anger and punishment for calling Torah 'songs'
items.text_en: David's anger and punishment for calling Torah 'songs'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says David's face changed like a cake. The Gemara questions the use of 'anger' without 'nose'. Rava teaches that David was punished for calling Torah 'songs', and God caused him to err regarding the Ark's transport.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that David's face changed like a cake (חררה) when he became angry over Uzzah's death.
The Gemara questions why David's anger is singled out, noting that elsewhere the word 'אף' (nose/anger) accompanies 'ויחר' (and he was angry), but here it is absent.
Rava teaches that David was punished because he called Torah words 'songs' (זמירות), citing the verse 'זמירות היו לי חוקיך'.
God rebukes David for calling Torah 'songs' and causes him to err regarding the Ark's transport, despite even schoolchildren knowing that the Kohathites carried the Ark on shoulders, not on a cart.

items.text: The people of Beit Shemesh and the Ark
items.text_en: The people of Beit Shemesh and the Ark
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Elazar dispute whether the people of Beit Shemesh were struck for reaping and bowing or for speaking inappropriately.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why the people of Beit Shemesh were struck: was it merely for looking at the Ark?

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Elazar dispute: one says they were reaping and bowing (a disrespectful act), the other says they spoke inappropriate words.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about the seventy men
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about the seventy men
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse describing the death of seventy men out of fifty thousand. Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Elazar debate whether there were seventy men each worth fifty thousand, or fifty thousand men each worth seventy Sanhedrins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who told you to interpret the verse in this way and who caused you to be appeased.
Rabbi Avahu interprets the verse as seventy men each worth fifty thousand.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse as fifty thousand men each worth seventy Sanhedrins.

items.text: Sacrifices during the Ark's journey
items.text_en: Sacrifices during the Ark's journey
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the sacrifices offered when the Ark moved. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel suggests a sacrifice for each step, but Rav Chisda objects that this would fill the land with altars, and offers an alternative interpretation: a sacrifice for every six steps, and additional sacrifices for every six sets of six steps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verses describing David's sacrifices when the Ark moved: a bull and a fatling for six steps, and seven bulls and seven rams.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel explains that David offered a bull and a fatling for each step, and seven bulls and seven rams for every six steps.
Rav Chisda objects that Rav Pappa's interpretation would require altars all over the land, and instead proposes that David offered a bull and a fatling for every six steps.
Rav Chisda concludes that the seven bulls and seven rams were offered for every six sets of six steps.

items.text: The name of the stone: Kidon and Nachon
items.text_en: The name of the stone: Kidon and Nachon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the stone used by David was initially called Kidon (a javelin) and later Nachon (established), indicating a change in its status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the two different names for the stone in the biblical verses: Kidon and Nachon.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that initially the stone was called Kidon (a javelin, implying danger) and later Nachon (established, implying stability).

items.text: Three types of stones
items.text_en: Three types of stones
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates three sets of stones: one set up by Moses in Moab, one by Joshua in the Jordan, and one in Gilgal, each with a biblical source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates three sets of stones: one set up by Moses in Moab, one by Joshua in the Jordan, and one in Gilgal, each with a biblical source.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on writing the Torah
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on writing the Torah
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate how the Torah was written on stones. Rabbi Yehuda says it was written on stones and then plastered, while Rabbi Shimon says it was written on plaster with the text below for the nations to learn. Rabbi Shimon argues that the nations could have learned but did not, leading to their punishment. Rava bar Sheila explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from a verse, and Rabbi Yehuda's view is that the nations have no remedy but burning, like lime.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a question about how Israel wrote the Torah, and Rabbi Yehuda answers that they wrote it on stones and then plastered them with lime.

Rabbi Shimon objects to Rabbi Yehuda: how could the nations have learned the Torah if it was covered with lime? Rabbi Yehuda answers that God gave them extra intelligence, they sent scribes to scrape off the lime and copy it, and for this their decree was sealed for destruction because they could have learned but did not.
Rabbi Shimon states his own view: they wrote the Torah on lime and wrote below for the nations 'they shall teach you to do' — teaching that if they had repented, they would have been accepted.
Rava bar Sheila explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse 'nations will be burnt lime' — referring to the matter of lime.
Rabbi Yehuda explains his view by analogy: just as lime has no remedy but burning, so the nations have no remedy but burning.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Shimon from a baraita
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Shimon from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a baraita that includes Canaanites outside the land as eligible for acceptance if they repent aligns with Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna's view is supported by a baraita that includes Canaanites outside the land as eligible for acceptance if they repent.

items.text: Attribution of the previous Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Attribution of the previous Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Mishnah as following Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Mishnah as following Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

items.text: The miracles of the day and the ceremony
items.text_en: The miracles of the day and the ceremony
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the miracles that occurred when Israel crossed the Jordan, including the journey to the mountains and the writing of the Torah in seventy languages. It describes the building of the altar, sacrifices, and the folding of the stones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by listing the miracles of the day, including the crossing of the Jordan and the journey to Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, with a prooftext that no one could stand before Israel.
The Gemara cites a verse to distinguish between the first entry (under Joshua) and the second entry (under Ezra), showing that the same fear fell upon the nations.
The Gemara concludes that Israel was worthy of a miracle in the second entry as in the first, but sin prevented it.
The Gemara describes the building of the altar, the plastering, and the writing of the entire Torah in seventy languages, citing the verse 'באר היטב' (explain well).
The Gemara concludes the list of events: sacrifices, eating, drinking, blessing and cursing, folding the stones, and lodging in Gilgal, with a prooftext.

items.text: Clarification of the lodging place
items.text_en: Clarification of the lodging place
items.desc_en: The Gemara limits the placement of the stones to the specific lodging place mentioned in the verse, not any lodging place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that the stones could be placed in any lodging place, not just the specific one.
The Gemara answers with a scriptural limitation: the verse specifies 'where you lodged that night,' restricting the placement to that specific lodging place.

items.text: The hornet did not cross the Jordan
items.text_en: The hornet did not cross the Jordan
items.desc_en: A Tanna states that the hornet did not cross with Israel. The Gemara questions this from a verse. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains that the hornet stood at the Jordan's edge and shot venom at the Amorites, blinding and castrating them. Rav Pappa says there were two hornets: one from Moses' time that did not cross, and one from Joshua's time that did.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that the hornet (צרעה) did not cross the Jordan with Israel.
The Gemara questions the Tanna's statement, citing the verse 'וְשָׁלַחְתִּי אֶת הַצִּרְעָה לְפָנֶיךָ' (I will send the hornet before you), which implies it did cross.

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains that the hornet stood at the Jordan's edge and shot venom (מָרָה) at the Amorites, blinding them from above and castrating them from below, as derived from the verse about destroying fruit above and roots below.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by positing two hornets: one from Moses' time that did not cross, and one from Joshua's time that did.

items.text: The division of the tribes on the mountains
items.text_en: The division of the tribes on the mountains
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of 'and its half' in the Mishnah. Rav Kahana explains that just as the tribes are divided here (on the mountains), so they are divided on the stones of the ephod.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'and its half' regarding the division of the tribes.
Rav Kahana explains that the division of the tribes on the mountains parallels their division on the stones of the ephod.

items.text: The arrangement of the tribes on the ephod stones
items.text_en: The arrangement of the tribes on the ephod stones
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the two stones on the high priest's shoulders, each with six tribal names. The second stone lists the names according to birth order, but the first does not because Judah is given precedence. The total letters are fifty, twenty-five on each stone. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel offers an alternative view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the two precious stones on the high priest's shoulders, each bearing six tribal names.

The baraita explains that the second stone lists the names according to birth order, but the first does not because Judah is given precedence, and notes that the total letters are fifty, twenty-five on each stone.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's alternative view
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel's alternative view
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel offers an alternative view regarding the arrangement of the names on the stones.

items.text: Arrangement of tribes on the ephod stones
items.text_en: Arrangement of tribes on the ephod stones
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the tribes were not arranged on the ephod stones in the same order as in the census, but rather in the order of the second census: Leah's sons in order, Rachel's sons one on each side, and the handmaids' sons in the middle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the tribes were arranged on the ephod stones according to the second census order, not the first: Leah's sons in order, Rachel's sons one on each side, and the handmaids' sons in the middle.

items.text: Interpretation of 'according to their generations'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'according to their generations'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'according to their generations' means the names given by their father Jacob, not those given by Moses. This refutes Rav Kahana's earlier position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to interpret the phrase 'according to their generations' in the context of the stones of the ephod.
The Gemara answers that 'according to their generations' means the names given by their father Jacob, not the names given by Moses, citing examples of the names Reuben, Simeon, Dan, and Gad.
The Gemara declares this a refutation of Rav Kahana's earlier position.

items.text: Explanation of 'and its half' regarding Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal
items.text_en: Explanation of 'and its half' regarding Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the half of the tribes on Mount Gerizim was larger because although Levi was below, the sons of Joseph were with them, as per the verse where Joshua tells Joseph's descendants to go up to the forest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the meaning of 'and its half' is in the context of the tribes' arrangement on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
A Tanna teaches that the half facing Mount Gerizim was larger than the half facing Mount Ebal because the tribe of Levi was below (on Mount Gerizim).
The Gemara objects that if Levi was below, that would reduce the count, not increase it.
The Gemara resolves that although Levi was below, the sons of Joseph were also with them, as per the verse where Joshua tells Joseph's descendants to go up to the forest.

items.text: Joseph's descendants and the evil eye
items.text_en: Joseph's descendants and the evil eye
items.desc_en: Joshua told Joseph's descendants to hide in the forests to avoid the evil eye, but they replied that the evil eye has no power over them, as per the verse 'a fruitful son above the eye' and Rabbi Abahu's interpretation. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina adds a proof from the blessing 'and they shall multiply like fish in the midst of the land.'

sub.desc_en: Joshua tells the descendants of Joseph to hide in the forests so that the evil eye will not control them.
The sons of Joseph reply that the evil eye has no power over Joseph's seed, citing the verse 'a fruitful son above the eye'.
Rabbi Abahu interprets the verse homiletically: read not 'עלי עין' (above the eye) but 'עולי עין' (those who rise above the eye), indicating immunity to the evil eye.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's proof
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina adds a proof from the blessing 'and they shall multiply like fish in the midst of the land,' comparing Joseph's descendants to fish hidden from the evil eye.

items.text: The fifty letters and the extra letter in Joseph's name
items.text_en: The fifty letters and the extra letter in Joseph's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the count of fifty letters in the names of the tribes on the breastplate, noting it is only forty-nine. Rabbi Yitzchak says Joseph had an extra letter added, as per the verse 'testimony in Yehosef'. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, requiring 'according to their generations', and explains that Benjamin's name is written fully as 'Binyamin' here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the count of fifty letters in the names of the tribes on the breastplate, noting it is only forty-nine.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that Joseph had an extra letter added to his name, as per the verse 'עֵדוּת בִּיהוֹסֵף' (testimony in Yehosef).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, requiring that the names be 'according to their generations' (כְּתוֹלְדֹתָם), which would not allow an extra letter in Joseph's name.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that Benjamin's name is written fully as 'בִּנְיָמִין' here, with the extra letter making up the count.

items.text: Joseph and Judah: sanctifying God's name
items.text_en: Joseph and Judah: sanctifying God's name
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida says that Joseph, who sanctified God's name in private, had a letter from God's name added to his name; Judah, who sanctified God's name in public, was entirely named after God.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna quoting Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida states that Joseph, who sanctified God's name in private, had a letter from God's name added to his name, while Judah, who sanctified God's name in public, was entirely named after God.

items.text: Joseph's temptation and resistance
items.text_en: Joseph's temptation and resistance
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife: both intended sin, but Joseph saw his father's image and was warned that his name would be erased from the ephod. He resisted, his seed spilled, and he merited to be engraved on the ephod stones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife, citing the verse and presenting the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the meaning of 'לעשות מלאכתו'.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the servants were absent due to their idolatrous festival, and Potiphar's wife feigned illness to be alone with Joseph.
The Gemara recounts that Joseph saw his father's image in the window, who warned him that his name would be erased from the ephod stones if he sinned.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir explains that Joseph's bow returned to its strength and his seed spilled from his fingernails due to his resistance.
The Gemara concludes that Joseph's merit of resisting temptation caused him to be engraved on the ephod stones and to become the shepherd of Israel.

items.text: Joseph's potential twelve tribes and Benjamin's sons
items.text_en: Joseph's potential twelve tribes and Benjamin's sons
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Joseph was worthy to produce twelve tribes, but his seed spilled, so they came from Benjamin instead, and all were named after Joseph. The names of Benjamin's sons are then expounded.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Joseph was worthy to produce twelve tribes, but his seed spilled, so they came from Benjamin instead, and all were named after Joseph.
The baraita expounds the names of Benjamin's sons: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, and Gera.
The baraita concludes the exposition of Benjamin's sons' names, with an alternative explanation for 'Va'ard'.

items.text: Joseph's knowledge of seventy languages and the oath
items.text_en: Joseph's knowledge of seventy languages and the oath
items.desc_en: Pharaoh's astrologers objected to Joseph's rule, so Gabriel taught him seventy languages, but he didn't learn until God added a letter to his name. Later, Joseph asked Pharaoh to release him from his oath to bury Jacob in Canaan, and Pharaoh agreed.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan recounts that when Pharaoh appointed Joseph, his astrologers objected that a slave bought for twenty silver coins should not rule over them.

Pharaoh replies that he sees royal qualities in Joseph, and when the astrologers demand that Joseph know seventy languages, Gabriel teaches him, but Joseph only learns after God adds a letter from His name to Joseph's name.
Joseph speaks in Hebrew, which Pharaoh does not understand, so Joseph teaches him Hebrew and makes him swear not to reveal the secret.

When Joseph asks to be released from his oath to bury Jacob in Canaan, Pharaoh tells him to seek annulment of his oath, and Joseph counters that Pharaoh should also annul his own oath, but Pharaoh ultimately permits Joseph to go.

items.text: Judah's sanctification of God's name at the sea
items.text_en: Judah's sanctification of God's name at the sea
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain Judah's sanctification of God's name in public, describing how the tribes argued at the sea about who would descend first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the source for Judah's sanctification of God's name.
Rabbi Meir teaches that when Israel stood at the sea, the tribes argued about who would descend first, and Judah jumped in.

items.text: Benjamin entered the sea first
items.text_en: Benjamin entered the sea first
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tradition that the tribe of Benjamin entered the sea first, citing a verse that is reinterpreted to support this. As a reward, Benjamin merited to host the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the tribe of Benjamin entered the sea first, citing a verse reinterpreted through a wordplay, and that the princes of Judah stoned them.
The Gemara concludes that as a reward, Benjamin merited to host the Divine Presence, citing a verse about the Temple being between his shoulders.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's objection: Nachshon ben Aminadav entered first
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's objection: Nachshon ben Aminadav entered first
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda disputes the previous tradition, arguing that no tribe wanted to enter first, and Nachshon ben Aminadav of Judah jumped into the sea. He cites verses from Psalms that Nachshon recited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects to the tradition that Benjamin entered first, asserting that no tribe wanted to enter and Nachshon ben Aminadav of Judah jumped first, citing a verse from Hosea.
Rabbi Yehuda cites Psalms verses that Nachshon recited when he entered the sea, as a prophetic support for his account.

items.text: Moses' prayer and Judah's reward
items.text_en: Moses' prayer and Judah's reward
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how Moses prayed at length while the Israelites were in danger, and God rebuked him. As a reward for Nachshon's action, Judah merited kingship over Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes how Moses prayed at length while the Israelites were in danger, and God rebuked him for delaying.
Moses responds to God's rebuke, and God instructs him to raise his staff and stretch out his hand over the sea.
The Gemara concludes that as a reward for Nachshon's action, Judah merited kingship over Israel, citing the verse that the sea saw and fled.

items.text: Positions of the Levites on Mount Gerizim and Ebal
items.text_en: Positions of the Levites on Mount Gerizim and Ebal
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded regarding the placement of the Levites during the blessings and curses. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the elders of the priesthood and Levites were below, while the rest were above. Rabbi Yoshiya says all fit for service were below.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that it is impossible to place Levi below or above, as verses contradict each other.
He resolves that the elders of the priesthood and Levites stood below, and the rest above.
Rabbi Yoshiya says that all fit for service stood below, and the rest above.

items.text: Rabbi's opinion: All were below, and the meaning of 'upon'
items.text_en: Rabbi's opinion: All were below, and the meaning of 'upon'
items.desc_en: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) argues that all the Levites were below, and they turned their faces toward Mount Gerizim for blessings and toward Mount Ebal for curses. He then explains that the word 'upon' (על) in the verse means 'adjacent to', citing a proof from the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi says that all stood below, turning their faces toward Mount Gerizim for blessing and toward Mount Ebal for curse, interpreting 'על' as 'adjacent to'.
A baraita supports Rabbi's interpretation by citing verses where 'על' means 'adjacent to' rather than 'on top of'.
The Gemara answers that 'עַל' means 'adjacent to' (בסמוך).

A baraita is cited where Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) proves from the verse 'וְנָתַתָּ עַל הַמַּעֲרֶכֶת' (and you shall place pure frankincense upon the arrangement) and from 'וְסַכֹּתָ עַל הָאָרֹן' (and you shall cover the ark) that 'עַל' means 'adjacent to'.

items.text: The blessings and curses: general and specific
items.text_en: The blessings and curses: general and specific
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the blessings and curses were recited in both general and specific terms, to teach, learn, observe, and perform.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that the blessings and curses were recited in general and specific terms, for learning, teaching, observing, and performing.

items.text: Counting the covenants for each commandment
items.text_en: Counting the covenants for each commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that there are forty-eight covenants for each commandment, based on the three locations (Sinai, Ohel Moed, and Arvot Moav) where the Torah was given, each with multiple covenants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that there are forty-eight covenants for each commandment, based on the three locations (Sinai, Ohel Moed, and Arvot Moav) where the Torah was given, each with multiple covenants.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's alternative view on locations
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's alternative view on locations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon excludes Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal from the count and includes the Tent of Meeting in the wilderness instead.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon excludes Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal from the count of covenant sites and includes the Tent of Meeting in the wilderness instead.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding where the general principles and details of the commandments were stated. Rabbi Yishmael says general principles at Sinai and details in the Tent of Meeting; Rabbi Akiva says both were at Sinai, repeated in the Tent of Meeting, and reiterated in Arvot Moav.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says general principles were stated at Sinai and details in the Tent of Meeting; Rabbi Akiva says both were at Sinai, repeated in the Tent of Meeting, and reiterated in Arvot Moav.
The Gemara concludes that every commandment in the Torah has forty-eight covenants established upon it, regardless of the dispute's details.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's expanded count
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's expanded count
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, citing Rabbi Shimon, states that for each commandment there are forty-eight covenants, each multiplied by the number of Israelites (603,550), resulting in a vast number of covenants per individual.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, citing Rabbi Shimon, states that for each commandment there are forty-eight covenants, each multiplied by the number of Israelites (603,550), resulting in a vast number of covenants per individual.

items.text: The difference between the two opinions
items.text_en: The difference between the two opinions
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya explains that the difference between the earlier opinion and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's is whether the count includes the guarantor and the guarantor's guarantor (ערב וערב דערב).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two opinions regarding the number of covenants.
Rav Mesharshiya answers that the difference lies in whether the count includes the guarantor and the guarantor's guarantor (ערב וערב דערב).

items.text: Interpretation of the curses regarding adultery and idolatry
items.text_en: Interpretation of the curses regarding adultery and idolatry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani, the interpreter of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, teaches that the entire section of curses was said only about an adulterer and adulteress. The curse against making a graven image is interpreted as referring to one who commits adultery and fathers a child who then worships idols.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani, interpreter of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani, interpreter of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani teaches that the entire section of curses was said only about an adulterer and adulteress.
The gemara asks why the verse 'אָרוּר הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה פֶסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה' (Cursed is the man who makes a graven image) is needed, since the curse itself suffices.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani explains that the verse refers to one who commits adultery and fathers a child who then goes to worship idols, and curses the parents who caused this.

items.text: Details of the blessings and curses at Gerizim and Ebal
items.text_en: Details of the blessings and curses at Gerizim and Ebal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse teaches that the blessing should precede the curse, but not all blessings precede all curses. It also derives that the blessing is analogous to the curse in several respects: both are performed by Levites, in a loud voice, in the Holy Tongue, with general and specific formulations, and both are answered with 'Amen'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse about placing the blessing on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal, and explains that the verse comes to teach that the blessing should precede the curse, not the location.
The baraita clarifies that only one blessing precedes each curse, not all blessings before all curses, based on the singular form 'blessing' and 'curse'.

The baraita derives that the blessing is analogous to the curse in five respects: both are performed by Levites, in a loud voice, in the Holy Tongue, with general and specific formulations, and both are answered with 'Amen'.

items.text: Mishnah: The Priestly Blessing
items.text_en: Mishnah: The Priestly Blessing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing the Priestly Blessing, stating that in the country it is recited as three blessings, but in the Temple as one blessing, and in the Temple the priests pronounce the Divine Name as it is written.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking how the Priestly Blessing is recited, stating that in the country it is said as three blessings, but in the Temple as one blessing, and in the Temple the priests pronounce the Divine Name as it is written.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the practice of the priestly blessing: in the Temple the priests raise their hands above their heads, except the High Priest who does not raise above the frontplate; in the provinces they raise them to shoulder height. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the High Priest also raises above the frontplate, citing the verse about Aaron.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the practice of priestly blessing: in the Temple priests raise hands above their heads, except the High Priest who does not raise above the frontplate; Rabbi Yehuda argues that the High Priest also raises above the frontplate, citing the verse about Aaron.

items.text: Gemara: Language of the blessing
items.text_en: Gemara: Language of the blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse "כה תברכו" that the blessing must be recited in the holy language (Hebrew), using a gezerah shavah to the blessing at Mount Gerizim. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the word "כה" itself indicates the specific language.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the priestly blessing must be recited in the holy language (Hebrew).
The Gemara questions whether the blessing may be recited in any language or specifically in Hebrew.
The Gemara answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as the blessing at Mount Gerizim was in Hebrew, so too this blessing must be in Hebrew.

items.text: Gemara: Standing during the blessing
items.text_en: Gemara: Standing during the blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the blessing must be recited while standing, again using a gezerah shavah to the blessing at Mount Gerizim. Rabbi Natan adds a proof from the verse about serving and blessing, linking standing to the service of the priests.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the priestly blessing must be recited while standing, derived via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from the blessing at Mount Gerizim.

Rabbi Natan argues that the requirement to stand is unnecessary from the גזירה שוה, as a verse linking service and blessing teaches that just as service is performed while standing, so too the blessing.

items.text: Gemara: Raising of hands (Nesiat Kapayim)
items.text_en: Gemara: Raising of hands (Nesiat Kapayim)
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the blessing requires raising the hands, using a gezerah shavah to Aaron's blessing. Rabbi Yonatan raises a difficulty: perhaps the comparison also implies it is only for the High Priest on a festival? Rabbi Natan answers that the verse "הוא ובניו כל הימים" teaches that all priests, all days, perform the blessing with raised hands, and the blessing is linked to service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives that the priestly blessing requires raising the hands (נשיאות כפים) via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from Aaron's blessing.
Rabbi Yonatan raises a difficulty: perhaps the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) would also limit the blessing to the High Priest, on a festival, and during public service, as in the case of Aaron.

Rabbi Natan resolves the difficulty by citing the verse 'הוא ובניו כל הימים' (he and his sons all the days), which teaches that all priests, all days, perform the blessing with raised hands, and the blessing is linked to service.

items.text: Gemara: The explicit name and location
items.text_en: Gemara: The explicit name and location
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the blessing uses the explicit divine name (שם המפורש) in the Temple, based on the verse "ושמו את שמי". It then limits this to the Temple (בית הבחירה) using a gezerah shavah. Rabbi Yoshiya offers an alternative derivation from a verse about God's name and the chosen place.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Priestly Benediction is recited with the explicit divine name (שם המפורש), deriving this from the verse 'ושמו את שמי' (and they shall put My name), meaning My unique name.

The Gemara raises the possibility that the explicit name is also used outside the Temple (בגבולין), and then answers via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse 'לשום את שמו שם' (to put His name there) that it is limited to the Temple (בית הבחירה).

רבי יאשיה (Rabbi Yoshiya) offers an alternative derivation, arguing that the verse 'בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי' (in every place where I cause My name to be mentioned) is transposed to mean that God mentions His name only in the Temple, where He comes to bless.

items.text: Gemara: Who is included in the blessing
items.text_en: Gemara: Who is included in the blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the phrase "אמור להם" that the blessing includes not only Israelites but also converts, women, and freed slaves.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (So you shall bless the children of Israel) and then asks: from where do we include converts, women, and freed slaves? It answers: the phrase 'אָמוֹר לָהֶם' (you shall say to them) includes all of them.

items.text: Gemara: Facing the congregation and loud voice
items.text_en: Gemara: Facing the congregation and loud voice
items.desc_en: Two baraitot derive that the blessing must be recited face to face (not with backs turned) and in a loud voice, both from the phrase "אמור להם" — as one speaks to a friend.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the phrase 'אמור להם' that the priestly blessing must be recited face to face, like one speaking to a friend.
A second baraita derives from the same phrase that the blessing must be recited in a loud voice, again likening it to speaking to a friend.

items.text: Gemara: Who may call the priests and who may recite
items.text_en: Gemara: Who may call the priests and who may recite
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rav Chisda state traditions: the call "Kohanim" is said to two or more priests, not to one; and a priest calls "Kohanim", not an Israelite, based on the verse "אמור להם".

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a tradition: one calls two priests 'כֹּהֲנִים' (priests) but does not call one 'כֹּהֵן' (priest), from 'אָמוֹר לָהֶם' (say to them) implying at least two; Rav Chisda adds that a priest calls 'כֹּהֲנִים' but an Israelite does not call 'כֹּהֲנִים', from 'אָמוֹר לָהֶם' (say to them) implying the speaker is a priest.
Rav Chisda adds a tradition: a priest calls 'Kohanim', not an Israelite, based on the same verse 'אמור להם' (speak to them), implying the speaker is also a priest.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on the source of wine for the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on the source of wine for the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Abaye's opinion that the wine for the priestly blessing must come from the priests themselves, not from the community.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Abaye's opinion that the wine for the priestly blessing comes from the priests themselves, not Rav Chisda's.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic) for the following statements
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic) for the following statements
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided to aid in remembering the upcoming teachings of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic (סִימַן) listing key topics: desire for blessing, the platform (דּוּכָן), service, the cup, the stingy eye, and the heifer.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teachings on the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teachings on the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that God desires the priestly blessing, and that a priest who blesses is himself blessed. He also states that a priest who does not ascend to the platform to bless violates three positive commandments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that God desires the priestly blessing, citing the verse 'וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַאֲנִי אֲבָרְכֵם' (and they shall place My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that a priest who blesses is himself blessed, and one who does not bless is not blessed, citing the verse 'וַאֲבָרְכָה מְבָרְכֶיךָ' (and I will bless those who bless you).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that a priest who does not ascend the platform to recite the priestly blessing violates three positive commandments: 'כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ' (so you shall bless), 'אָמוֹר לָהֶם' (you shall say to them), and 'וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי' (they shall place My name).

items.text: Rav's concern about a priest's lineage and resolution
items.text_en: Rav's concern about a priest's lineage and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav expresses concern that a priest who does not ascend to the platform might be a son of a divorcée or a חלוצה. The Gemara resolves that there is no dispute: one who ascends occasionally is permitted, while one who never ascends is suspect.

sub.desc_en: Rav expresses concern that a priest who does not ascend to the platform might be a son of a divorcée or a חלוצה (woman who performed חליצה).
The Gemara resolves that there is no dispute: one who ascends occasionally is permitted, while one who never ascends is suspect.

items.text: Priest who does not ascend during the service and exceptions
items.text_en: Priest who does not ascend during the service and exceptions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that a priest who does not ascend for the blessing during the service may not ascend later. The Gemara questions this from the practice of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and resolves with a baraita that distinguishes between one who has not yet moved his feet and one who has.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that a priest who does not ascend for the blessing during the service may not ascend later, deriving this from the parallel to Aaron's service.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi would ascend for the blessing even though they had not performed the service, contradicting the rule.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi had already moved their feet from their place, and a baraita of Rabbi Oshaya teaches that the rule only applies to one who has not yet moved his feet.
The Gemara cites a supporting baraita about one who promises to lift his hands and returns to prayer, showing that moving slightly is sufficient to allow ascent.

items.text: Teachings on the generous eye and the עגלה ערופה
items.text_en: Teachings on the generous eye and the עגלה ערופה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the cup of blessing is given only to a generous person, that even birds recognize a stingy person, and that one who benefits from a stingy person violates a negative commandment. He also states that the עגלה ערופה comes only because of stinginess, as the elders declare they did not send the murdered man away without food or escort.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that the cup of blessing (כוס של ברכה) is given only to a generous person (טוב עין), citing a verse and a homiletic reading.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi proves that even birds recognize a stingy person (צר עין), citing a verse from Proverbs.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one who benefits from a stingy person violates a negative commandment (לאו), and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that he violates two negative commandments.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi concludes that the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer) comes only because of stinginess (צר עין), as the elders declare they did not send the murdered man away without food or escort.

items.text: Synagogue entirely of priests and the status of those behind them
items.text_en: Synagogue entirely of priests and the status of those behind them
items.desc_en: Ada in the name of Rabbi Simlai teaches that in a synagogue entirely of priests, all ascend to the platform. Rabbi Zeira says they bless their brothers in the fields. The Gemara resolves contradictions about whether those behind the priests are included in the blessing, distinguishing between those who are compelled and those who are not, and between a quorum of ten remaining and not.

sub.text: Ada in the name of Rabbi Simlai
sub.text_en: Ada in the name of Rabbi Simlai
sub.desc_en: Ada in the name of Rabbi Simlai teaches that in a synagogue entirely of priests, all ascend to the platform, and Rabbi Zeira says they bless their brothers in the fields.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita of Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya that those behind the priests are not included in the blessing.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between those who are compelled to stand behind the priests and those who are not.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rav Shimi mi'Birtah d'Shichori
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rav Shimi mi'Birtah d'Shichori
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita of Rav Shimi mi'Birtah d'Shichori that in a synagogue entirely of priests, some ascend and some answer 'Amen', contradicting the earlier teaching that all ascend.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where a quorum of ten remains to answer 'Amen' and where it does not.

items.text: Inquiry about partitions and sides regarding the blessing
items.text_en: Inquiry about partitions and sides regarding the blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that those behind the priests are not included in the blessing, but a partition does not separate Israel from their Father in heaven. An inquiry is raised about those standing at the sides, and Abba Mar bar Rav Ashi brings a proof from a mishna about sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita of Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya that those behind the priests are not included in the blessing.
The Gemara asks whether a partition (מחיצה) separates those behind the priests from the blessing, noting that a wall or a long row does not.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers that even a partition of iron does not separate Israel from their Father in heaven, implying it does not block the blessing.
The Gemara raises an inquiry about those standing at the sides (צדדין) of the priests.

sub.text: Abba Mar bar Rav Ashi's proof
sub.text_en: Abba Mar bar Rav Ashi's proof
sub.desc_en: Abba Mar bar Rav Ashi brings a proof from a mishna about sprinkling (הזאה) to resolve the inquiry about those at the sides.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of sprinkling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a priest sprinkled the blood of the red heifer in the wrong order (behind before in front), the sprinkling is invalid; if he sprinkled on the sides of the front, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a priest sprinkled the blood of the red heifer in the wrong order (behind before in front), the sprinkling is invalid; if he sprinkled on the sides of the front, it is valid.

items.text: Gemara: Prohibition on speaking during Torah reading
items.text_en: Gemara: Prohibition on speaking during Torah reading
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna derives from a verse that once the Torah scroll is opened, it is forbidden to speak even about halakha, as the verse implies silence. Rabbi Zeira cites a different verse to support this.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna rules that once the Torah scroll is opened, it is forbidden to speak even about halakha, deriving from the verse 'and when he opened it, all the people stood' that standing implies silence.
Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda cites a different verse — 'and the ears of all the people were toward the Torah scroll' — to support the prohibition on speaking during Torah reading.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Hand-washing before priestly blessing
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Hand-washing before priestly blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that any priest who did not wash his hands may not raise his hands for the priestly blessing, citing a verse that links lifting hands with holiness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a priest who did not wash his hands may not perform the priestly blessing, citing the verse 'שאו ידיכם קודש וברכו את ה׳' (Lift your hands in holiness and bless the Lord).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua's practices for longevity
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua's practices for longevity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua tells his students that he merited long life because he never treated the synagogue disrespectfully, never stepped over people's heads, and never raised his hands for the priestly blessing without a blessing.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua what he did to merit long life.

Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua lists three practices: never treating the synagogue disrespectfully, never stepping over people's heads, and never raising his hands for the priestly blessing without a blessing.

items.text: The blessing before the priestly blessing
items.text_en: The blessing before the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing is recited before the priestly blessing. Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda answers: the blessing that sanctifies with the holiness of Aaron and commands to bless Israel with love.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing is recited before the priestly blessing.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda answers that the blessing is 'אשר קדשנו בקדושתו של אהרן וצונו לברך את עמו ישראל באהבה' (Who sanctified us with the holiness of Aaron and commanded us to bless His people Israel with love).

items.text: Prayers when starting and finishing the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Prayers when starting and finishing the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara records what the priest says when he begins the blessing (a prayer that the blessing have no stumbling block) and when he turns his face from the congregation (a plea that God fulfill His decree).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what prayer the priest recites when he begins the priestly blessing.
Rav Chisda (transmitted by Rav Ukva) answers that the priest prays that the blessing contain no stumbling block or sin.
The Gemara asks what prayer the priest recites when he turns his face away from the congregation after the blessing.
Rav Chisda instructs Rav Ukva to teach that the priest prays: 'Master of the Universe, we have done what You decreed upon us; do for us [what You promised].'

items.text: Opening citation from the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Opening citation from the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: The daf begins with a verse from the Torah that the priests recite as part of the blessing.

sub.text: Opening citation from the priestly blessing
sub.text_en: Opening citation from the priestly blessing
sub.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from the Torah that the priests recite as part of the blessing.

items.text: Rav Chisda's rulings on the timing of responses during the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's rulings on the timing of responses during the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda, transmitted by Rabbi Zeira, sets forth a series of rules governing when the priests, the reader, and the congregation may begin their respective parts, ensuring that each response follows the completion of the previous one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that the priests may not bend their fingers (to form the blessing hand) until they turn their faces away from the congregation.
Rabbi Zeira transmits Rav Chisda's rule that the reader may not call 'Priests' until the congregation's 'Amen' has concluded.

Rav Chisda rules that the priests may not begin the blessing until the reader's call finishes, the congregation may not answer 'Amen' until the blessing finishes, and the priests may not begin the next blessing until the 'Amen' finishes.

Rabbi Zeira transmits Rav Chisda's rule that the priests may not turn their faces from the congregation until the prayer leader begins 'שים שלום' (Grant Peace), and may not leave until the prayer leader finishes it.

Rabbi Zeira transmits Rav Chisda's final rule: the congregation may not answer 'Amen' until the reader's blessing finishes, the reader may not read Torah until the 'Amen' finishes, the translator may not begin translation until the verse finishes, and the reader may not begin another verse until the translation finishes.

items.text: Rabbi Tanchum's ruling on the haftarah reader
items.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum's ruling on the haftarah reader
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that the one who reads the haftarah must first read from the Torah, and may not begin the haftarah until the Torah scroll is rolled up.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that the haftarah reader must first read from the Torah and may not begin the haftarah until the Torah scroll is rolled up.

items.text: Rabbi Tanchum on the prayer leader and the ark
items.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum on the prayer leader and the ark
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that the prayer leader may not remove the Torah scroll from the ark in public, out of respect for the congregation.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that the prayer leader may not remove the Torah scroll from the ark in public, out of respect for the congregation.

items.text: Dispute about when the congregation may leave
items.text_en: Dispute about when the congregation may leave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the congregation may not leave until the Torah scroll is placed in its place, while Shmuel says until the reader leaves. The Gemara resolves the dispute by noting they refer to different situations: one where there is another exit, and one where there is not.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that the congregation may not leave until the Torah scroll is taken and placed in its place.
Shmuel objects, stating that the congregation may leave only when the reader leaves.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that the two opinions refer to different situations: one where there is another exit, and one where there is not.
Rava supports the resolution by citing the verse 'אַחֲרֵי ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם תֵּלֵכוּ' (after the Lord your God you shall walk), implying one should follow the Torah scroll.

items.text: Verses recited during the priestly blessing
items.text_en: Verses recited during the priestly blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda specifies the verses the congregation recites when the priests bless the people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verses the congregation recites during the priestly blessing.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda specifies three verses from Psalms that the congregation recites.

items.text: Verses for Musaf on Shabbat and the principle for concluding
items.text_en: Verses for Musaf on Shabbat and the principle for concluding
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi states the verses recited during Musaf on Shabbat. The Gemara questions why a particular verse is not included, and Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi explains that since the section began with blessings of God, it concludes with blessings of God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verses are recited during Musaf on Shabbat, and Rabbi Asi answers with a list of psalms.
Rabbi Asi specifies the verses recited: 'שיר המעלות הנה ברכו את ה׳' and 'ברוך ה׳ מציון'.'
The Gemara objects that the verse 'יברכך ה׳ מציון' should also be included since it appears in the same context.

sub.text: Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi
sub.text_en: Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi
sub.desc_en: Yehuda the son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi resolves that since the section began with blessings of God, it concludes with blessings of God, excluding the verse that begins with a blessing of man.

items.text: Verses for Mincha on a fast day
items.text_en: Verses for Mincha on a fast day
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov states the verses recited during the Mincha service on a fast day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verses are recited during the Mincha service on a fast day.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers with the specific verses recited: 'אִם עֲוֹנֵינוּ עָנוּ בָנוּ...', 'מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל...', and 'לָמָּה תִהְיֶה כְּאִישׁ נִדְהָם...'.

items.text: Verses for Ne'ilah on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Verses for Ne'ilah on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verse is recited during the Ne'ilah service of Yom Kippur. Mar Zutra (or some say in a baraita) answers with a series of verses from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what verse is recited during the Ne'ilah service of Yom Kippur.
Mar Zutra (or some say in a baraita) answers with a series of verses from Psalms: 'Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed' and subsequent verses.

items.text: Where to recite the verses
items.text_en: Where to recite the verses
items.desc_en: There is a dispute about where these verses are said during the blessing. Rav Yosef says between each blessing, Rav Sheshet says during the mention of God's name. A further dispute between Rav Mari and Rav Zevid: one says verse by verse, the other says all at once.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where these verses are recited during the blessing.
Rav Yosef says the verses are recited between each blessing.
Rav Sheshet says the verses are recited during the mention of God's name.
Rav Mari says the verses are recited verse by verse.
Rav Zevid says all the verses are recited together at once.

items.text: Debate on reciting verses outside the Temple
items.text_en: Debate on reciting verses outside the Temple
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says one who recites these verses outside the Temple is mistaken. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa supports this, arguing that even in the Temple they should not be said, as a servant who is blessed should listen. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina argues they should be said outside the Temple, as a servant who is blessed should show a happy face. Rabbi Avahu initially said them but stopped after seeing Rabbi Abba from Akko did not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba rules that one who recites these verses outside the Temple (בגבולין) is merely mistaken.
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa supports the restriction, arguing that even in the Temple they should not be said, because a servant who is blessed should listen attentively.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina objects, arguing that outside the Temple they should be said, because a servant who is blessed should show a happy face.
Rabbi Avahu reports that he initially recited them but stopped after seeing Rabbi Abba from Akko did not.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's humility
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu initially thought himself humble, but after seeing Rabbi Abba from Akko state one reason while his spokesman stated another without complaint, he realized he was not truly humble. The story illustrates Rabbi Avahu's humility through an incident involving his wife and his spokesman's wife.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that he initially considered himself humble.
Rabbi Avahu recounts that after seeing Rabbi Abba from Akko state one reason while his spokesman stated another without complaint, he realized he was not truly humble.

The Gemara asks what Rabbi Avahu's humility consisted of, and relates a story where his wife complained about his spokesman's wife's disrespect, and Rabbi Avahu responded that it does not matter, as from him and from him the Most High is praised.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's deference and a story of rivalry
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's deference and a story of rivalry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu declined to be appointed head because Rabbi Abba from Akko had many creditors. A story is told of Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba visiting a place; Rabbi Avahu drew crowds with aggadah while Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba taught halakha, causing the latter distress. Rabbi Avahu consoled him with a parable, and despite escorting him, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba remained upset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Avahu was appointed by the rabbis to lead, but he declined because Rabbi Abba from Akko had many creditors.

A story is told of Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba visiting a place; Rabbi Avahu drew crowds with aggadah while Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba taught halakha, causing the latter distress, and Rabbi Avahu consoled him with a parable.
Despite Rabbi Avahu's daily escort and special honor on that day, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba remained upset.

items.text: Congregation's response during Modim
items.text_en: Congregation's response during Modim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the congregation says when the prayer leader says Modim. Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Simai, the Nehardeans, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov offer different versions. Rav Pappa concludes that one should say all of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the congregation says when the prayer leader recites the Modim blessing.
Rav proposes that the congregation says: 'We thank You, Hashem our God, for we thank You.'
Shmuel proposes: 'God of all flesh, for we thank You.'
Rabbi Simai proposes: 'Our Creator, Creator of the beginning, for we thank You.'

sub.text: Nehardeans' answer in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.text_en: Nehardeans' answer in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans transmit in Rabbi Simai's name a longer version: 'Blessings and thanks to Your great name, for You have kept us alive and sustained us, for we thank You.'

Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds a concluding section: 'So may You keep us alive, favor us, gather us, and bring our exiles to Your holy courts, to keep Your statutes and do Your will wholeheartedly, for we thank You.'
Rav Pappa rules that one should recite all of the proposed versions together.

items.text: Respect for the congregation
items.text_en: Respect for the congregation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak emphasizes always having awe of the congregation, as the priests face the people. Rav Nachman derives this from David's words. The rabbis derive from here that priests may not ascend the platform in sandals, one of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments. Rav Ashi explains the reason is not respect but fear of a broken strap causing suspicion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that one must always have awe of the congregation, as the priests face the people and their backs are toward the Divine Presence.
Rav Nachman derives the same principle from David's words, where David said that if the people listen to him they are his brothers, but if not they are his subjects whom he rules with a stick.
The rabbis derive from here that priests may not ascend the platform in sandals, one of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments, and the gemara suggests the reason is respect for the congregation.

Rav Ashi rejects the reason of respect, explaining that the enactment was due to concern that a broken sandal strap might cause the priest to go tie it, leading people to suspect he is a בן גרושה (son of a divorced woman) or בן חלוצה (son of a halutzah).

items.text: Transition to Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the beginning of the next Mishnah: 'And in the Temple, one blessing, etc.' This serves as a transition to the next topic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: 'And in the Temple, one blessing...' etc.

items.text: Why no 'Amen' in the Temple
items.text_en: Why no 'Amen' in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'Amen' was not answered in the Temple because the response to each blessing was a praise of God, as derived from Nehemiah 9:5. A baraita provides the scriptural basis for this practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the detailed procedure is necessary, and answers that it is because 'Amen' is not answered in the Temple.
A baraita cites Nehemiah 9:5 to prove that in the Temple, instead of 'Amen', each blessing is answered with a praise of God.

items.text: Mishnah: High Priest's reading procedure
items.text_en: Mishnah: High Priest's reading procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the High Priest reads the Torah on Yom Kippur: the Torah is passed from the synagogue attendant to the head of the synagogue, then to the deputy, and finally to the High Priest. He reads specific portions, rolls the scroll, and recites eight blessings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking how the High Priest's blessings are performed, describing the chain of passing the Torah scroll from the synagogue attendant to the head of the synagogue.
The Mishnah continues the chain: the head of the synagogue gives the scroll to the deputy, who gives it to the High Priest.
The Mishnah describes how the High Priest stands to receive the scroll, reads specific Torah portions, rolls the scroll, and recites an additional portion by heart.

The Mishnah lists the eight blessings the High Priest recites after the Torah reading: on the Torah, the service, thanksgiving, forgiveness of sin, the Temple, Israel, the priests, Jerusalem, and the rest is prayer.

items.text: Gemara: Honor for a student in the presence of a rabbi
items.text_en: Gemara: Honor for a student in the presence of a rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that honor is given to a student in the presence of a rabbi, as the Torah is passed through several intermediaries. Abaye counters that all this is solely for the honor of the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that honor is divided for a student in the presence of a rabbi.
Abaye counters that all this is solely for the honor of the High Priest.

items.text: Gemara: Standing in the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Gemara: Standing in the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'stands and receives', implying that sitting is possible, but sitting in the Temple courtyard is prohibited except for kings of the House of David. Rav Chisda resolves that this occurred in the Women's Courtyard, where sitting is permitted. A challenge is raised from a baraita that states the reading was in the courtyard, with a dispute about whether it was on the Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'stands and receives', implying that sitting is possible, but sitting in the Temple courtyard is prohibited except for kings of the House of David.
Rav Chisda resolves that the reading occurred in the Women's Courtyard, where sitting is permitted.
A challenge is raised from a baraita that states the reading was in the courtyard, with a dispute about whether it was on the Temple Mount.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Location of the reading
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Location of the reading
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the king reads from the Torah in the Women's Courtyard. Rav Chisda identifies the location as the עזרת נשים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the verse describing the king's reading location as before the water gate.
Rav Chisda identifies the location as the Women's Courtyard (עזרת נשים).

items.text: Gemara: Skipping portions in the Torah
items.text_en: Gemara: Skipping portions in the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance of skipping from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Ba'asor', citing a baraita that forbids skipping in the Torah. Abaye resolves the contradiction twice: first by distinguishing between when the translator pauses, then by distinguishing between one topic and two topics. The baraita is then cited in full, including the rule for skipping in the Twelve Minor Prophets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah allows skipping from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Ba'asor', but a baraita forbids skipping in the Torah.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the translator pauses and when he does not.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states skipping is forbidden in the Torah entirely, not just when the translator does not pause.
Abaye offers a second resolution: the Mishnah deals with one topic, while the baraita forbids skipping between two topics.
A baraita is cited in full, confirming that skipping in the Torah is permitted within one topic and in the Twelve Minor Prophets, provided the translator does not pause.

items.text: Gemara: Rolling the Torah scroll
items.text_en: Gemara: Rolling the Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes rolling the Torah scroll and placing it in one's bosom. The Gemara explains this is done to avoid disparaging the Torah scroll.
