sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah scroll is rolled and placed in one's bosom to avoid disparaging the scroll.

items.text: Gemara: Reading from a scroll by heart
items.text_en: Gemara: Reading from a scroll by heart
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on the tenth of Tishrei, the High Priest reads from the Torah by heart. The Gemara asks why not roll the scroll or bring another scroll. Rav Sheishes answers that one does not roll a Torah scroll in public. Rav Huna bar Yehuda and Reish Lakish offer reasons: due to the slight to the first scroll, and to avoid an unnecessary blessing. The Gemara questions the concern for slight, citing a case where three scrolls are used, and distinguishes between one person using two scrolls and three people using three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the High Priest reads by heart instead of rolling the scroll to the passage.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheishes
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheishes
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishes answers that one does not roll a Torah scroll in public.
The Gemara asks why not bring another scroll instead of reading by heart.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers that using a second scroll would slight the first.
Reish Lakish answers that it is to avoid an unnecessary blessing.
The Gemara objects that we do not seem to worry about slighting a scroll, citing Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's case of three scrolls on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh Tevet.
The Gemara resolves that three people using three scrolls causes no slight, but one person using two scrolls does.

items.text: Gemara: The blessings recited by the king
items.text_en: Gemara: The blessings recited by the king
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the king recites eight blessings. The Gemara cites a baraita detailing the blessings: for the Torah, the service, thanksgiving, forgiveness of sin, the Temple, the priests, Israel, and Jerusalem. The remaining prayer is described as supplication, and the king concludes with 'Shome'a Tefillah'. Afterwards, each person brings a Torah scroll from home to read, to show their strength to the public.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the eight blessings the king recites: for the Torah, the service, thanksgiving, forgiveness of sin, the Temple, the priests, Israel, and Jerusalem.

The baraita explains that the remaining prayer is supplication, the king concludes with 'שׁוֹמֵעַ תְּפִלָּה' (He who hears prayer), and then each person brings a Torah scroll from home to read publicly to display their strength.

items.text: Mishnah: The ceremony of the king's reading
items.text_en: Mishnah: The ceremony of the king's reading
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the ceremony of the king's reading (Hakhel): after the first day of Sukkot in the eighth year, a wooden platform is built in the Temple courtyard. The king receives the Torah scroll from the High Priest through a chain of officials, stands to receive it, and reads while seated. The story of Agrippas is recounted, who stood and read, and was praised. The king reads specific portions, and recites the blessings, substituting the festival blessing for forgiveness of sin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the timing and setup of the king's reading ceremony: after the first day of Sukkot in the eighth year, a wooden platform is built in the Temple courtyard.
The Mishnah details the chain of transmission of the Torah scroll from the synagogue attendant to the king, and notes that the king stands to receive it but reads while seated.
The Mishnah recounts the story of King Agrippas, who stood and read, was praised by the Sages, and was comforted when he wept upon reaching the verse about appointing a foreigner.
The Mishnah lists the specific Torah portions the king reads: from the beginning of Deuteronomy through the Shema, the blessings and curses, and the section of the king.
The Mishnah concludes that the king recites the same blessings as the High Priest, but substitutes the festival blessing for the blessing of forgiveness of sin.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the timing of Hakhel
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the timing of Hakhel
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's 'eighth' refers to the eighth year, not the eighth day. It then asks why all the phrases in the verse (Deut. 31:10-11) are necessary, and explains each one: 'At the end' excludes counting from now, 'of the year of release' excludes the end of the release year, 'during the festival' excludes the beginning of the year, 'of Sukkot' excludes the last festival day, and 'when all Israel comes' teaches it is when they come for the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'on the eighth' and corrects it to 'in the eighth year'.
The Gemara asks why all the phrases in the verse (Deut. 31:10-11) are necessary.
The Gemara explains that 'At the end' alone would imply counting from now, so the Torah added 'of the release year' to exclude that.
The Gemara explains that 'of the release year' alone would imply the end of the release year, so the Torah added 'during the festival' to exclude that.
The Gemara explains that 'during the festival' alone would imply the beginning of the year, so the Torah added 'of Sukkot' to exclude that.
The Gemara explains that 'of Sukkot' alone would include the last festival day, so the Torah added 'when all Israel comes' to teach it is when they come for the festival.

items.text: Gemara's question on honor for a student in the presence of the rabbi
items.text_en: Gemara's question on honor for a student in the presence of the rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's procedure that honor is given to a student in the presence of the rabbi, but Abaye explains that the entire procedure is for the honor of the king.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's procedure that honor is given to a student in the presence of the rabbi.
Abaye explains that the entire procedure is for the honor of the king, not for the student.

items.text: The king's standing and sitting while reading the Torah
items.text_en: The king's standing and sitting while reading the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Agrippas could sit in the Temple courtyard, given the rule that only kings of David's line may sit there. Rav Chisda resolves that this occurred in the Women's Courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the king stands to receive the Torah scroll and then sits to read, but the Gemara notes that Agrippas stood throughout.
The Gemara questions how Agrippas could sit in the Temple courtyard, given the rule that only kings of David's line may sit there.
Rav Chisda resolves that Agrippas's sitting occurred in the Women's Courtyard, where sitting is permitted.

items.text: Praise for Agrippas and the exception for a mitzvah
items.text_en: Praise for Agrippas and the exception for a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages praised Agrippas for standing, given that a king cannot waive his honor. It answers that a mitzvah is different, and the praise was for the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages praised Agrippas for standing, given that a king cannot waive his honor, citing Rav Ashi's principle that a king's honor is not waivable.
The Gemara answers that a mitzvah is different, so the praise was for the mitzvah, not for the king's standing.

items.text: The sin of flattery toward Agrippas
items.text_en: The sin of flattery toward Agrippas
items.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Natan states that when the reader reached the verse about not appointing a foreigner, the enemies of Israel were condemned because they flattered Agrippas by not correcting him.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Natan
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Natan
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Natan states that when the reader reached the verse about not appointing a foreigner, the enemies of Israel were condemned because they flattered Agrippas by not correcting him.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta on the corruption of flattery
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta on the corruption of flattery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta teaches that since flattery prevailed, justice has been perverted and people can no longer claim their deeds are greater than others'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta teaches that since flattery (חנופה) prevailed, justice has been perverted, deeds corrupted, and no one can claim their deeds are greater than another's.

items.text: Permissibility of flattering the wicked in this world
items.text_en: Permissibility of flattering the wicked in this world
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ma'arva and Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi permit flattering the wicked in this world, citing a verse. Resh Lakish derives the same from Jacob's encounter with Esau, and Rabbi Levi's parable illustrates that flattery can deter harm.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ma'arva / Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ma'arva / Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ma'arva (or Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi) permits flattering the wicked in this world, citing the verse 'לֹא יִקָּרֵא עוֹד לְנָבָל נָדִיב' (no longer will a scoundrel be called noble) as proof that in this world it is permitted.

Resh Lakish derives the same permission from Jacob's words to Esau: 'כִּרְאֹת פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים וַתִּרְצֵנִי' (for seeing your face is like seeing the face of God, and you have accepted me), implying flattery was used.

Rabbi Levi offers a parable: Jacob's encounter with Esau is like a man who recognizes his friend intends to kill him, so he says 'taste this dish I tasted in the king's house,' causing the friend to fear the king and refrain from killing.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's series of curses for flatterers
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's series of curses for flatterers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar delivers four statements: a flatterer brings wrath, his prayer is unheard, he falls into Gehinnom, and he eventually falls into the hands of his victim or his descendants.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar opens with the first curse: a flatterer brings wrath upon the world and his prayer is unheard.
A mnemonic (סימן) lists key words for the series: wrath, fetus, Gehinnom, in his hand, menstruant, exile.
Rabbi Elazar's second statement: a flatterer is cursed even by fetuses in the womb, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar's third statement: a flatterer falls into Gehinnom, citing a verse about fire consuming straw.
Rabbi Elazar's fourth statement: a flatterer eventually falls into the hands of his victim or his descendants, citing the verse from Jeremiah.

items.text: Opening verse and introduction to flattery
items.text_en: Opening verse and introduction to flattery
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about Jeremiah being seized at the Benjamin gate, introducing the theme of flattery in a community.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Jeremiah being seized at the Benjamin gate, introducing the theme of flattery.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar on flattery and exile
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar on flattery and exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that any community with flattery is as repulsive as a menstruating woman and will ultimately go into exile, citing verses with the word 'galmud'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that any community with flattery is as repulsive as a נִדָּה (menstruating woman), citing the verse 'עֲדַת חָנֵף גַּלְמוּד' and explaining that in coastal cities they call a נִדָּה 'גַּלְמוּדָה' (separated from her husband).
Rabbi Elazar adds that a community with flattery will ultimately go into exile, linking the verse 'עֲדַת חָנֵף גַּלְמוּד' to the verse about exile in Isaiah.

items.text: Four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence
items.text_en: Four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba lists four groups—scoffers, flatterers, liars, and slanderers—that do not receive the Divine Presence, each supported by a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba lists four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence: scoffers, flatterers, liars, and slanderers.

sub.text: Supporting verses for first three groups
sub.text_en: Supporting verses for first three groups
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for scoffers, flatterers, and liars: Job 34:30, Psalms 5:5, and Psalms 101:7 respectively.
The Gemara cites Psalms 5:5 for slanderers, interpreting 'רָע' as evil speech.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula 'Hadran alach' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: The priest anointed for war speaks in the Holy Tongue
items.text_en: Mishnah: The priest anointed for war speaks in the Holy Tongue
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the priest anointed for war speaks to the people in the Holy Tongue, and the Gemara explains the content of his speech, including the distinction between fighting brothers and enemies, and the encouragement not to fear.

sub.text: Mishnah's statement about the anointed for war
sub.text_en: Mishnah's statement about the anointed for war
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the anointed for war (משוח מלחמה) spoke to the people in the Holy Tongue, citing the verse 'וְנִגַּשׁ הַכֹּהֵן... וְדִבֶּר אֶל הָעָם'.
The Mishnah explains that the verse says 'עַל אוֹיְבֵיכֶם' (against your enemies) and not against your brothers, citing the story of the men of Shomron who showed mercy to captives.

sub.text: Mishnah's explanation of the four exhortations
sub.text_en: Mishnah's explanation of the four exhortations
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah explains each of the four exhortations: 'אַל יֵרַךְ לְבַבְכֶם' (from horse neighing), 'אַל תִּירְאוּ' (from shield clashing), 'אַל תַּחְפְּזוּ' (from horn sounds), 'אַל תַּעַרְצוּ' (from shouting).
The Mishnah contrasts the enemy's reliance on human victory with Israel's reliance on God, citing Goliath and Shovach as examples, and identifies 'הַהֹלֵךְ עִמָּכֶם' as the camp of the Ark.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of Holy Tongue from verbal analogy
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of Holy Tongue from verbal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's source is and answers via a verbal analogy: 'vedibber' here is like 'yedabber' by Moses, where it was in the Holy Tongue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's proof is, and answers that it derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'וְדִבֶּר' here and 'מֹשֶׁה יְדַבֵּר' at Sinai, where it was in the Holy Tongue.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah derives the requirement of Holy Tongue via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'vedibber' used by Moses.

items.text: Who is the priest? Not any priest, but an appointed one
items.text_en: Who is the priest? Not any priest, but an appointed one
items.desc_en: A baraitha teaches that the priest is not any priest but an appointed one, derived from a comparison to the appointed officers. The Gemara rejects the possibility of the High Priest or the deputy (Segan), explaining that the deputy is not an appointed officer but a replacement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the priest who speaks is a designated appointee (ממונה), derived from a comparison to the officers (שוטרים).

The Gemara objects that the High Priest also has a king over him, but resolves that the comparison is about his service (עבודתו); the deputy (סגן) is not considered a 'ממונה' because he only substitutes if the High Priest becomes disqualified, as taught by Rabbi Chanina.
The Gemara objects: the High Priest also has a king over him; it answers that the comparison is specifically regarding his service (עבודתו).
The Gemara objects: perhaps the priest is the deputy (סגן)? It answers that the deputy is not an appointed officer.
A baraita citing Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim explains that the deputy (סגן) is appointed only to replace the High Priest if he becomes disqualified, not as a permanent appointee over him.

items.text: The content of the priest's speech: Shema and encouragement
items.text_en: The content of the priest's speech: Shema and encouragement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains why the priest says 'Shema Yisrael'—even if only reciting the Shema morning and evening, they will not be delivered. A baraitha adds that the priest speaks twice: once at the border and once in battle.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the priest specifically says 'Shema Yisrael' in his speech to the soldiers.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that God tells Israel: even if you only fulfilled the mitzvah of reciting the Shema (קריאת שמע) morning and evening, you will not be delivered into their hands.
A baraita teaches that the priest speaks to the soldiers twice: once at the border (בספר) and once in battle, and the gemara begins to quote what he says at the border.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The speech of the battle-arrayers
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The speech of the battle-arrayers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the words of the battle-arrayers who encourage the troops not to fear, corresponding to four tactics of the nations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the speech of the battle-arrayers who encourage the troops not to fear, corresponding to four tactics of the nations.

items.text: Goliath's arrogance and downfall
items.text_en: Goliath's arrogance and downfall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Goliath stood with brazenness before God, and God caused him to fall by the hand of David. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir lists three places where Goliath's mouth trapped him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Goliath stood with brazenness before God, calling God 'איש' (a man), and God caused him to fall by the hand of David, who is also called 'בן איש' (son of a man).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir lists three places where Goliath's mouth trapped him: his challenge to send a man, his boast about defeating an opponent, and his insult to David about coming with sticks, which David turned back on him by invoking God's name.

items.text: Goliath's timing and duration
items.text_en: Goliath's timing and duration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets Goliath's morning and evening appearances as an attempt to disrupt the recitation of Shema, and his forty days correspond to the forty days the Torah was given.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Goliath's morning and evening appearances were meant to disrupt the recitation of the Shema (קריאת שמע), and his forty days correspond to the forty days the Torah was given.

items.text: Interpretations of 'the middleman'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'the middleman'
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim offer explanations for the term 'the middleman' describing Goliath: built without blemish, intermediate among his brothers, built like a structure, or a hundred cubits and one span.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'הבינים' (the middleman) means in the description of Goliath.
Rav explains that 'הבינים' means Goliath was built without any blemish.
Shmuel explains that 'הבינים' means Goliath was the intermediate among his brothers.
Bei Rabbi Sheila explains that 'הבינים' means Goliath was built like a structure.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'הבינים' means Goliath was a hundred cubits and one span tall.

items.text: Derogatory interpretations of Goliath's name and lineage
items.text_en: Derogatory interpretations of Goliath's name and lineage
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that everyone trod upon Goliath's mother like a winepress, and that everyone had relations with his mother, based on wordplay.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef interprets Goliath's name as indicating that everyone trod upon his mother like a winepress.
Rav Yosef notes the variant reading 'מערות' (caves) and 'מערכות' (battle arrays), and interprets that everyone had relations with Goliath's mother.

items.text: The names Harafah and Orpah
items.text_en: The names Harafah and Orpah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Orpah's original name was Harafah or Orpah, each explaining the alternative name through wordplay involving threshing or striking from behind.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes the textual discrepancy between the name 'Harafah' and 'Orpah' in the verses.
Rav says her original name was Harafah, and she was called Orpah because everyone struck her from behind (like an עורף, nape).
Shmuel says her original name was Orpah, and she was called Harafah because everyone threshed her like groats (הריפות), citing two verses as support.

items.text: The four giants born to Harafah
items.text_en: The four giants born to Harafah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the four giants born to Harafah in Gath as Saf, Madon, Goliath, and Yishbi beNov.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the four giants born to Harafah in Gath as Saf, Madon, Goliath, and Yishbi beNov.

items.text: The reward of Orpah and the descendants of Ruth
items.text_en: The reward of Orpah and the descendants of Ruth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rava explain that the four giants descended from Orpah were a reward for her tears, while Ruth's descendants (David) defeated them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the four giants falling by David's hand and links it to Orpah's kiss and Ruth's clinging.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that the children of the one who kissed (Orpah) will fall by the hand of the children of the one who clung (Ruth).
Rava explains that Orpah's four tears earned her four giant descendants, as the verse says 'they lifted their voice and wept again'.

items.text: The lesson from Goliath's incomplete praise
items.text_en: The lesson from Goliath's incomplete praise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar notes that the verse understates Goliath's weaponry, teaching that one should not recount the praise of the wicked, except to highlight David's greatness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a textual discrepancy: the verse is written as 'חץ חניתו' (arrow of his spear) but read as 'עץ חניתו' (wood of his spear).
Rabbi Elazar explains that the understatement shows we have not yet reached half the praise of that wicked man (Goliath).
The Gemara derives a general principle: it is forbidden to recount the praise of the wicked.
The Gemara objects: should one not even begin to mention the wicked at all?
The Gemara resolves: the mention is permitted here because it serves to highlight David's greatness.

items.text: The names Shovach and Shofach
items.text_en: The names Shovach and Shofach
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the original name of the Ammonite general, explaining the alternative name through wordplay involving a dovecote or pouring out.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes the textual variant between the names Shovach and Shofach for the Ammonite general.
One of the sages (Rav) says his original name was Shofach, and he was called Shovach because he was built like a dovecote (שובך).
The other sage (Shmuel) says his original name was Shovach, and he was called Shofach because anyone who saw him was poured out (נשפך) before him like a flask (קיתון).

items.text: Interpretation of 'his quiver is like an open grave'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'his quiver is like an open grave'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi) debate whether the verse describes heaps of slain or heaps of dung, and Rav Mari deduces a practical lesson about bowel disease.

sub.text: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi) — first opinion
sub.text_en: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi) — first opinion
sub.desc_en: One opinion interprets the verse 'his quiver is like an open grave' as describing heaps of slain when they shoot arrows, and the phrase 'all of them are mighty' precludes the possibility that they are merely skilled in battle.

sub.text: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi) — second opinion
sub.text_en: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi) — second opinion
sub.desc_en: The other opinion interprets the verse as describing heaps of dung when they relieve themselves, and the phrase 'all of them are mighty' precludes the possibility that they suffer from bowel disease.
Rav Mari deduces from the second opinion that a person with excessive feces has bowel disease, and the practical implication is that he should exert himself (to relieve himself).

items.text: Interpretation of 'anxiety in a man's heart'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'anxiety in a man's heart'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate whether the verse means one should remove anxiety from his mind or share it with others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'דְּאָגָה בְלֶב אִישׁ יַשְׁחֶנָּה' (Anxiety in a man's heart depresses it).
Rabbi Ami interprets the verse to mean one should remove anxiety from his mind (יַשִּׂחֶנָּה מִדַּעְתּוֹ).
Rabbi Asi interprets the verse to mean one should share his anxiety with others (יְשִׂיחֶנָּה לַאֲחֵרִים).

items.text: The reason for the battle-arrayers' speech
items.text_en: The reason for the battle-arrayers' speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the battle-arrayers' speech is because God and all His attributes are involved in the war.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the battle-arrayers' speech is because God and all His attributes are involved in the war.

items.text: Pinchas's lineage and the war against Midian
items.text_en: Pinchas's lineage and the war against Midian
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Pinchas went to war to avenge his maternal grandfather Joseph, but questions how Pinchas could be descended from Joseph given that his mother was from Putiel. It resolves that one of his maternal grandparents was from Joseph and the other from Jethro, as hinted by the dual meaning of 'Putiel'.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna explains that the items mentioned in the verse—the Sanhedrin, Pinchas as the anointed for war, the Ark, and the trumpets—were all present in the war against Midian.

The Tanna states that Pinchas went to war to avenge his maternal grandfather Joseph, and the Gemara questions how Pinchas could descend from Joseph given that his mother was from Putiel, resolving that 'Putiel' hints at both Joseph and Jethro.

The Gemara explains that the tribes disparaged Pinchas as 'ben Puti,' but resolves that one of his maternal grandparents was from Joseph and the other from Jethro, as hinted by the dual meaning of 'Putiel.'

items.text: Mishnah: Those who return from war and those who do not
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who return from war and those who do not
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the exemptions from war: one who built a new house and not dedicated it, planted a vineyard and not redeemed it, or betrothed a woman and not married her. It details what constitutes a house, vineyard, and betrothal, and then lists those who do not return (e.g., building a gatehouse, porch, or balcony) and those who never leave (e.g., one who dedicated his house or married his betrothed).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the verse about the officers speaking to the people regarding one who built a new house and has not dedicated it, and lists various types of buildings and acquisitions that are included.
The Mishnah continues with the case of one who planted a vineyard and has not redeemed it, including various types of planting and acquisition.

The Mishnah discusses the case of one who betrothed a woman, including various marital situations, and states that all these individuals hear the priest's words and return, while providing water, food, and repairing roads.

The Mishnah lists those who do not return from war, including builders of certain structures, planters of certain trees, and those in forbidden marriages, with additional opinions from Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer.

The Mishnah lists those who do not move from their place, including those who have dedicated their house, redeemed their vineyard, or married their betrothed or yevama, and they are not provided with water, food, or road repairs.

items.text: Gemara: The roles of the priest and officer in announcing exemptions
items.text_en: Gemara: The roles of the priest and officer in announcing exemptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the priest speaks and the officer makes the announcements audible, based on verses. It resolves conflicting baraitot by explaining that from 'and he shall approach' until 'and they shall speak' the priest both speaks and announces, from 'and they shall speak' until 'and they shall add' the priest speaks and the officer announces, and from 'and they shall add' onward the officer both speaks and announces.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the officers spoke their own words, and resolves that the verse refers to the words of the anointed for war.

Abaye resolves three conflicting baraitot by explaining that from 'ונגש' to 'ודברו' the priest speaks and the priest announces, from 'ודברו' to 'ויספו' the priest speaks and the officer announces, and from 'ויספו' onward the officer speaks and the officer announces.
The Gemara cites three conflicting baraitot about who speaks and who announces.

Abaye resolves the contradictions by assigning each baraita to a different stage of the announcements: from 'and he shall approach' until 'and they shall speak' the priest speaks and the priest announces; from 'and they shall speak' until 'and they shall add' the priest speaks and the officer announces; from 'and they shall add' onward the officer speaks and the officer announces.

items.text: Gemara: Exegesis of the exemptions for house and vineyard
items.text_en: Gemara: Exegesis of the exemptions for house and vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that one who bought, inherited, or received a house as a gift also returns, and that a house includes structures like a straw house, cattle shed, woodshed, and storeroom, but excludes a gatehouse, porch, and balcony. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov limits 'house' to its literal meaning, and the phrase 'not dedicated' excludes a robber. The Gemara suggests this disagrees with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who interprets 'soft-hearted' as one who is afraid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that one who bought, inherited, or received a house as a gift is also included in the exemption.
The baraita expands 'house' to include structures like a straw house, cattle shed, wood shed, and storage house, but excludes a gatehouse, portico, and porch, limiting to dwellings.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interprets 'house' literally and derives from 'לא חנכו' that a stolen house is excluded.
The Gemara notes that this baraita disagrees with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who interprets 'רך הלבב' as one who is afraid.

items.text: Clarification of the thief's exemption
items.text_en: Clarification of the thief's exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the thief is exempt if he repented and paid the value, but since the animal came to him through theft, he does not return it as a purchaser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the thief's exemption from returning to war should apply only to sins still in his possession, not to a stolen animal he has already returned.

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, the thief repented and paid the value, but since the animal originally came to him through theft, he does not return it as a purchaser.

items.text: Derivation of the exemption for planting a vineyard
items.text_en: Derivation of the exemption for planting a vineyard
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verse that only one who plants a vineyard is exempt, but one who buys, inherits, or receives as a gift is also exempt. The term 'vineyard' includes five fruit trees but excludes four fruit trees and five barren trees.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and derives that the exemption applies not only to one who plants a vineyard but also to one who buys, inherits, or receives it as a gift.
The baraita further derives that the term 'כרם' (vineyard) includes five fruit trees but excludes four fruit trees and five barren trees.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion and the contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion and the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says 'vineyard' literally, and excludes layering and grafting. This contradicts the Mishnah which includes them. Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between forbidden and permitted grafting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that 'כרם (vineyard)' is literal, and the exemption 'לא חלל' excludes layering (מבריך) and grafting (מרכיב).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly includes layering and grafting alongside planting.

Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to forbidden grafting (הרכבת איסור), while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's exemption applies to permitted grafting (הרכבת היתר).

items.text: Discussion of permitted grafting and orlah
items.text_en: Discussion of permitted grafting and orlah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the case of permitted grafting: a young branch on an old tree is nullified, but a young branch on another young tree is not nullified if planted for a fence or beams. The distinction is that the latter can be reconsidered for fruit, while the former cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a case of permitted grafting, and initially suggests a young branch on another young branch, but rejects it because the first young branch would still require orlah observance; instead it proposes a young branch on an old tree.
Rabbi Abahu objects that a young branch grafted onto an old tree is nullified and exempt from orlah, so this cannot be the case of permitted grafting.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the case is actually a young branch on another young branch, but the first was planted for a fence or beams, which is exempt from orlah.
The Gemara asks why a young branch on an old tree is nullified but a young branch on another young tree is not.

The Gemara resolves that in the old-tree case the branch cannot be reconsidered for fruit, but in the young-tree case it can, and supports this with a baraita that self-grown shoots are obligated in orlah.

items.text: The case of a shared vineyard and military exemption
items.text_en: The case of a shared vineyard and military exemption
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a vineyard of two partners does not exempt them from military service, unlike five brothers where one died, because each is not called 'his vineyard'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita cannot be explained as referring to a vineyard belonging to two partners, where each one returns to his own share.
Rav Pappa answers that this teaches a principle: a vineyard belonging to two partners does not exempt them from military service.
The Gemara objects: why is this different from the case of five brothers where one died in battle, where all return?
The Gemara resolves: there each brother is called 'his wife', but here each partner is not called 'his vineyard'.

items.text: Alternative resolution: layering a tree on vegetables
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: layering a tree on vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the case as layering a tree on vegetables, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits and the Sages forbid. Rav Dimi cites Rabbi Yochanan that the Tanna is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who interprets 'planted' literally.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes an alternative resolution: the case involves layering a tree on vegetables, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits it and the Sages forbid it.
Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Tanna is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who interprets 'planted' literally, excluding layering and grafting.

items.text: Halakhot of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Halakhot of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi transmits several rulings in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: a young branch less than a handbreadth is obligated in orlah; a corpse occupies four cubits for Shema; a woman raised among brothers is forbidden to marry them; gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah in the field are subject to tithes; and a young branch less than a handbreadth does not sanctify seeds.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan identifies the earlier baraita as the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who interprets 'planted' literally to exclude layering and grafting.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi transmits a ruling that a young vine less than a handbreadth is obligated in orlah all its years, but this applies only to a small cluster; an entire vineyard of such vines generates publicity and is exempt.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi transmits a ruling that a corpse occupies four cubits for the recitation of Shema, citing the verse 'Whoever mocks the poor blasphemes his Maker'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak transmits a ruling that a stepdaughter raised among brothers is forbidden to marry them because she appears as their sister, but the Gemara comments that the matter generates publicity and is not actually prohibited.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak transmits a ruling that gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and peah gathered into the granary are obligated for tithes, but Ulla limits this to the field; in the city, the matter generates publicity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak transmits a ruling that a young vine less than a handbreadth does not sanctify seeds planted next to it, but this applies only to a small cluster; an entire vineyard of such vines does sanctify.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The text begins another ruling in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Discussion of the grave courtyard and its dimensions
items.text_en: Discussion of the grave courtyard and its dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dimensions of a grave courtyard that render it impure, citing a Tannaic dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. It then clarifies the conditions regarding the opening's position and whether the courtyard is enclosed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the rule that a corpse occupies four cubits for impurity.
A baraita is cited: a grave courtyard that has four cubits renders one inside pure, according to Beit Shammai.
Beit Hillel states that the courtyard need only be four handbreadths.
The Gemara clarifies: the dispute applies when the opening is from above, but if from the side, all agree it is four cubits.
The Gemara objects: the opposite seems logical — from the side one can exit directly, from above one must pass through the opening and create a tent.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita should be reversed — the dispute is when the opening is from the side, but from above all agree it is four cubits.
The Gemara qualifies: this applies only to a grave courtyard with partitions, but an ordinary corpse occupies four cubits.

items.text: Baraita on those exempt due to betrothal
items.text_en: Baraita on those exempt due to betrothal
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the exemption for one who betrothed a woman applies to a virgin, a widow, a yevamah, and even if five brothers are in battle and one dies, all return. It also lists those who are exempt because they cannot marry, such as a widow to a High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the exemption for one who betrothed a woman applies to a virgin, a widow, a yevamah, and even if five brothers are in battle and one dies, all return; it also lists those exempt because they cannot marry, such as a widow to a High Priest.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the baraita aligns with Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who interprets 'fearful and fainthearted' as one afraid of sins. It resolves that even according to him, the exemption applies only to those who have actually consummated the marriage, as per Rabbah's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the baraita contradicts Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, who interprets 'fearful and fainthearted' as one afraid of sins he has committed.

The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, the exemption applies only after consummation, based on Rabbah's principle that one is not liable until he actually consummates the forbidden marriage.

items.text: Derashot on the order of building, planting, and marrying
items.text_en: Derashot on the order of building, planting, and marrying
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds on the verses about building a house, planting a vineyard, and betrothing a woman, teaching proper conduct. Various interpretations are given, including allegorical readings of the verses as referring to Torah study and good deeds.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that the Torah's order of building, planting, and betrothing teaches proper conduct: one should build a house, plant a vineyard, and then marry.
The Gemara cites King Solomon's verse from Proverbs to support the Tanna Kamma's order of building, planting, and marrying.
An anonymous interpretation reads the verse allegorically: preparing outside work refers to מקרא (Scripture), the field refers to משנה (Mishnah), and building the house refers to גמרא (Gemara).

Another anonymous interpretation reads the verse as: preparing outside work refers to מקרא (Scripture) and משנה (Mishnah), the field refers to גמרא (Gemara), and building the house refers to good deeds.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yossi HaGelili interprets the verse as: preparing outside work refers to מקרא (Scripture), משנה (Mishnah), and גמרא (Gemara); the field refers to good deeds; and building the house refers to expounding and receiving reward.

items.text: Those who do not return and the addition of a dimos
items.text_en: Those who do not return and the addition of a dimos
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who do not return, and a baraita adds that if one added a dimos to a house, he returns. Rabbi Eliezer says that one who builds a brick house in Sharon does not return because it is renovated twice a week.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who do not return from the war, beginning with one who builds a gatehouse.
A baraita adds that if one added a dimos (a room or extension) to the house, he returns from the war.
Rabbi Eliezer states that one who builds a brick house in the Sharon region does not return because it is renovated twice a week.
A baraita explains that the reason is that they renovate such a house twice a week, so it is considered a new house each time.

items.text: Derasha on 'new wife' and the exemption
items.text_en: Derasha on 'new wife' and the exemption
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds on the verse 'new wife', teaching that it includes a widow and divorcee, but excludes one who remarries his divorcee. The exemption is only for a woman who is new to him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse 'אישה חדשה' (a new wife) to include a widow and divorcee, but exclude one who remarries his divorcee, since she is not new to him.

items.text: Derasha on 'he shall not go out' and 'he shall not pass'
items.text_en: Derasha on 'he shall not go out' and 'he shall not pass'
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds on the verse 'he shall not go out in the army', teaching that he is also exempt from providing supplies. It clarifies that the exemption applies only to those who have completed the act, and the two prohibitions teach that he violates two negative commandments.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'he shall not go out in the army' and deducing that he is also exempt from providing supplies, based on the additional verse 'and he shall not pass over it for any matter'.

The baraita raises a possible inclusion: one might think the exemption extends to those who built a house but did not dedicate it, planted a vineyard but did not redeem it, or betrothed a woman but did not marry her.
The baraita answers that the word 'עָלָיו' (upon him) limits the exemption to those who have completed the act, excluding those who have not yet done so.
The baraita resolves that since both prohibitions are written, 'he shall not go out' and 'he shall not pass', the two verses teach that he violates two negative commandments.

items.text: Dispute on 'fearful and fainthearted' and the procedure for sending back
items.text_en: Dispute on 'fearful and fainthearted' and the procedure for sending back
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yossi HaGelili on the meaning of 'fearful and fainthearted'. Rabbi Yossi adds a list of forbidden marriages. The Gemara then describes the procedure of appointing officers to prevent soldiers from retreating.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the verse about the officers continuing to speak, and Rabbi Akiva interprets 'fearful and fainthearted' literally as one who cannot bear the battle.

Rabbi Yossi HaGelili gives an alternative interpretation: the 'fearful and fainthearted' is one who fears sins he has committed, and therefore the Torah attached all these exemptions so he could return on their account.
Rabbi Yossi lists forbidden marriages (e.g., a widow to a High Priest, a divorcee to a common priest) and declares that one who has contracted such a marriage is the 'fearful and fainthearted'.

The Mishnah concludes by describing the procedure: after the officers finish speaking, commanders are appointed, and guards with iron axes are stationed at the rear to prevent retreat, with authority to strike the legs of anyone trying to flee.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions from battle
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions from battle
items.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that the priest's speech to the soldiers is because the beginning of flight is defeat, citing verses. It then states that these exemptions apply only to discretionary wars, but for obligatory wars everyone goes out, even a bridegroom from his chamber and a bride from her canopy. Rabbi Yehuda says the opposite: the exemptions apply to obligatory wars, but for mandatory wars everyone goes out.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by explaining that the beginning of flight is defeat, citing verses from the story of the Philistines.

The Tanna Kamma states that the exemptions from battle apply only to discretionary wars (מלחמות הרשות), but for obligatory wars (מלחמות מצוה) everyone goes out, even a bridegroom from his chamber and a bride from her canopy.
Rabbi Yehuda reverses the ruling: the exemptions apply to obligatory wars (מלחמות מצוה), but for mandatory wars (מלחמות חובה) everyone goes out.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the difference between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the difference between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the opinions of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili regarding the types of wars. It answers that the difference is a rabbinic transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the opinions of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili regarding the types of wars.
The Gemara answers that the difference is a rabbinic transgression (עבירה דרבנן).

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili from a baraita
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who converses between one set of tefillin and another commits a transgression and returns from the war. It asks whose opinion this follows, and concludes it follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: whose opinion does the baraita about one who converses between tefillin follow?
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

items.text: Another baraita: one who retreats due to fear returns
items.text_en: Another baraita: one who retreats due to fear returns
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by the baraita that one who hears the sound of horns and retreats, or the clashing of shields and retreats, or the whetting of swords and water flows to his knees, returns from battle. It suggests it follows Rabbi Akiva and not Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but rejects this, saying even Rabbi Yosei HaGelili agrees because of the verse 'lest he melt the heart of his brothers as his heart'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by the baraita that one who retreats due to fear returns from battle.
The Gemara suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva and not Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, stating that even Rabbi Yosei HaGelili agrees because of the verse 'lest he melt the heart of his brothers as his heart'.

items.text: Textual correction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Textual correction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'because the beginning of flight is defeat' and suggests it should be 'because the beginning of defeat is flight'. It concludes to say 'because the beginning of defeat is flight'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'because the beginning of flight is defeat' and argues it should be 'because the beginning of defeat is flight'.
The Gemara resolves the textual issue by correcting the Mishnah to read 'because the beginning of defeat is flight'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the 'discretionary' war of the Rabbis is the 'obligatory' war of Rabbi Yehuda, and the 'obligatory' war of the Rabbis is the 'mandatory' war of Rabbi Yehuda. Rava adds that the wars of Joshua for conquest are, according to all, mandatory, and the wars of the house of David for expansion are, according to all, discretionary. The dispute is about wars to subdue non-Jews so they do not come upon them, which one calls obligatory and the other discretionary. The practical difference is for one who is engaged in a mitzvah, who is exempt from another mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan equates the Rabbis' 'discretionary war' (מלחמת הרשות) with Rabbi Yehuda's 'obligatory war' (מלחמת מצוה), and the Rabbis' 'obligatory war' with Rabbi Yehuda's 'mandatory war' (מלחמת חובה).

Rava clarifies that all agree Joshua's conquest wars are mandatory and David's expansion wars are discretionary; the dispute concerns wars to subdue non-Jews from attacking, with the practical difference being exemption from another מצוה (commandment) for one already engaged in a מצוה.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara states 'We have returned to you, anointed for war', marking the end of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'We have returned to you, anointed for war'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Eglah Arufah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Eglah Arufah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins the laws of the heifer whose neck is broken, stating it is recited in Hebrew, citing the verse. Three judges from the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem go out; Rabbi Yehuda says five, deriving from the words 'your elders' and 'your judges'. If the body is found hidden in a pile, hanging on a tree, or floating on water, they do not perform the rite. If found near a border, a city with a majority of non-Jews, or a city without a court, they do not perform it. Measurement is only to a city that has a court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the laws of the heifer whose neck is broken (עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה), stating it is recited in Hebrew, citing the verse, and presenting the dispute between the Tanna Kamma (three judges) and Rabbi Yehuda (five judges).
The Mishnah lists cases where the rite is not performed: if the body is hidden in a pile, hanging on a tree, or floating on water, each excluded by a specific word in the verse.

The Mishnah concludes with additional exclusions: if the body is found near a border, a city with a majority of non-Jews, or a city without a court, the rite is not performed; measurement is only to a city that has a court.

items.text: Gemara: Source for Hebrew in eglah arufah
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for Hebrew in eglah arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means. Rabbi Abahu explains: it says 'and they shall answer and say', and elsewhere it says 'and the Levites shall answer and say'; just as the response there is in Hebrew, so too here it is in Hebrew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by citing the verse without explicit proof for Hebrew.

רבי אבהו (Rabbi Abahu) explains that the Mishnah derives Hebrew from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'וְעָנוּ וְאָמְרוּ' (and they shall answer and say) here and the same phrase by the Levites on Mount Ebal, where it is explicitly in Hebrew.
The Mishnah then describes the procedure for עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken): three from the Great Sanhedrin go out, and רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) says five.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the number of judges
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the number of judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda derives five judges from 'your elders' (two) and 'your judges' (two) plus one to avoid an even-numbered court. Rabbi Shimon says only three: 'your elders' (two) plus one. The Gemara explains the derivation: Rabbi Shimon uses 'your judges' to require the most distinguished of your judges. Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'elders' and 'your elders' that they must be distinguished. Rabbi Shimon counters that if it said 'elders' he would think even market elders, so 'your elders' is needed; and if only 'your elders', he would think even a small Sanhedrin, so 'your judges' teaches the most distinguished. Rabbi Yehuda learns a gezerah shavah from 'elders' of the congregation, that just as there they are the distinguished of the congregation, so too here. The Gemara then questions why 'your elders and your judges' is needed if the gezerah shavah teaches everything, and answers that the vav of 'and your judges' is for the count.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse and presenting Rabbi Yehuda's position: 'your elders' (two) and 'your judges' (two) plus one to avoid an even court yields five judges.
Rabbi Shimon states his position: 'your elders' (two) plus one to avoid an even court yields three judges.
The Gemara asks: But for Rabbi Shimon, isn't 'and your judges' written? The Gemara answers that he requires that phrase for the distinguished among your judges.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives the requirement for distinguished judges from the extra wording 'your elders' (not just 'elders').

Rabbi Shimon explains his reasoning: if the verse said only 'elders', he would think even market elders; 'your elders' excludes that; if only 'your elders', he would think even a small Sanhedrin, so 'your judges' teaches the most distinguished.
Rabbi Yehuda learns from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'elders' here and 'elders of the congregation' that just as there they are the distinguished of the congregation, so too here.
The Gemara questions: If Rabbi Yehuda derives from the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), why does he need the phrase 'your elders and your judges' at all?
The Gemara resolves: Rather, the vav in 'and your judges' is for the count (adding two judges), and Rabbi Shimon does not accept this derivation.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the number of judges
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the number of judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verses 'ויצאו' and 'ומדדו' would add extra judges, but resolves that these verses are needed for other teachings: 'ויצאו' excludes agents, and 'ומדדו' mandates measuring even if the corpse is found near the city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verses 'ויצאו' and 'ומדדו' would add extra judges, making nine according to Rabbi Yehuda or seven according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara resolves that those verses are needed for other teachings: 'ויצאו' excludes agents, and 'ומדדו' mandates measuring even if the corpse is found near the city.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who interprets 'זקניך' as the Sanhedrin and 'שופטיך' as the king and high priest, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who interprets 'זקניך' as the Sanhedrin and 'שופטיך' as the king and high priest, citing verses.

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position on the Sanhedrin
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position on the Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disputes only regarding the king and high priest, but agrees with either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon regarding the Sanhedrin, or whether he disputes even the Sanhedrin, requiring the entire Sanhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry whether Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov disputes only regarding the king and high priest, but agrees with either Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon regarding the Sanhedrin, or whether he disputes even the Sanhedrin, requiring the entire Sanhedrin.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof and Abaye's alternative
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof and Abaye's alternative
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef brings a baraita about a rebellious elder who disputes the court when they left for measuring the heifer, implying the entire Sanhedrin left, supporting Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Abaye counters that it might refer to adding to the city or courtyards, which requires a court of seventy-one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita about a rebellious elder who disputes the court at Beit Pagei, deriving that the place determines the halakha.
The Gemara asks how many members went out, concluding that all of them must have gone out.
The Gemara questions whether they left for an optional matter, citing a verse that limits leaving the Sanhedrin.
The Gemara concludes they left for a mitzva, likely the heifer measurement, supporting Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Abaye objects that the mitzva might be expanding the city or courtyards, which requires a court of seventy-one.
A baraita supports Rav Yosef, explicitly mentioning the heifer measurement and city expansion as reasons for the Sanhedrin to leave.

items.text: Dispute about a hidden corpse or sheaf
items.text_en: Dispute about a hidden corpse or sheaf
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of a corpse hidden in a pile or hanging on a tree is analyzed. Rav explains that the verse 'כי ימצא חלל' excludes a hidden corpse, while the sheaf case is different. The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding 'טָמוּן' is resolved through scriptural exegesis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about a hidden corpse aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view and not with the Sages.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda excludes a concealed sheaf from the law of forgotten sheaves, while the Sages include it via the phrase 'in the field'.
Rav responds that even according to the Sages, the Mishnah's ruling is derived from the context of the verse, and the sheaf case is also derived from its own context.

The Gemara explains: the verse 'כי ימצא חלל' (if a slain person is found) implies any location, but 'באדמה' (in the ground) excludes a hidden corpse; for sheaves, the context of harvest requires revealed objects, so 'בשדה' includes hidden ones.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yehuda too, the analogy to harvest should exclude hidden sheaves; the Gemara answers: yes, indeed.
The Gemara asks: if so, what does Rabbi Yehuda learn from 'בשדה'? It is needed to include forgotten standing grain; the Sages derive that from the broader verse.

Rabbi Yehuda uses the phrase to exclude sheaves that floated into another's field, as per Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Elazar; the Sages derive this from the difference between 'בשדה' and 'בשדך', while Rabbi Yehuda does not learn from that distinction.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about floating sheaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about floating sheaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether sheaves that floated into one's own field are considered in the field. Rav Kahana suggests a proof from Rabbi Avahu's statement, but the Gemara refines the case to include even placed sheaves in a friend's field, with 'צָפוּ' being the typical scenario.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether sheaves that floated into one's own field are considered as being in the field for the law of שכחה (forgotten sheaves).
Rav Kahana suggests a proof from Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Elazar, who excludes sheaves that floated into a friend's field, implying that floating into one's own field is included.

The Gemara objects that the proof is flawed: if the exclusion applies only to floating sheaves in a friend's field, then even placed sheaves in a friend's field would be excluded, but the verse 'בְּשָׂדֶךָ' (your field) is absent there.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Avahu's statement actually applies even to placed sheaves in a friend's field, and the mention of 'צָפוּ' (floating) is merely the typical scenario, not a limiting condition.

items.text: Baraita about a sheaf placed on another
items.text_en: Baraita about a sheaf placed on another
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a sheaf placed on another and forgotten: the bottom is שכחה, the top is not. Rabbi Shimon says neither is. The Gemara explains that the top is considered 'like floating' and the case is about one who acquired the sheaf, so it applies even in the field.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a sheaf picked up to be taken to the city and placed on another and forgotten — the bottom one is שכחה (forgotten sheaf), the top one is not; Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says both are not, the bottom because it is hidden (טָמוּן) and the top because it is floating (צָף).
The Gemara distinguishes: there, since he took possession of the sheaf, he acquired it, so the top is not considered שכחה; the baraita mentions 'on top of another' only because of the bottom sheaf.

The Gemara objects: but the baraita says 'because it is floating (צָף)', not 'because he acquired it'! The Gemara resolves: read it as 'because it is like floating (כְּצָף)', i.e., the top sheaf is considered as if floating and thus not שכחה.

items.text: Abaye's question about two corpses stacked
items.text_en: Abaye's question about two corpses stacked
items.desc_en: Abaye is asked about two corpses stacked: from which does one measure? The possibilities are: from the top (since the bottom is hidden), from the bottom (since the top is floating), or neither. The answer is not provided in the text.

sub.desc_en: Abaye declares himself as sharp as בן עזאי (ben Azzai) in the markets of טבריה (Tiberias), ready to answer any question.
A certain Sage asks Abaye: If two corpses are found one on top of the other, from which does one measure the distance to the cities?
Abaye considers the first possibility: a corpse of the same type as the one below is considered concealed, not floating, so one measures from the upper corpse.
Abaye considers the second possibility: a corpse of the same type is considered floating, not concealed, so one measures from the lower corpse.
Abaye considers the third possibility: a corpse of the same type is both concealed and floating, so one measures from neither, and the ritual is not performed.
Abaye begins to respond to the Sage, but the text cuts off before providing the answer.

items.text: Analysis of the Tosefta about the Omer and the dispute about 'tamun' (hidden)
items.text_en: Analysis of the Tosefta about the Omer and the dispute about 'tamun' (hidden)
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a Tosefta about an omer that was placed on top of another and forgotten. It suggests that the Tanna'im in the Tosefta follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that 'in the field' excludes a hidden item. The Gemara then debates whether they disagree about whether 'min bemino' (same species) is considered hidden, concluding that all agree it is hidden, and the dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta about an omer placed on top of another and forgotten, where the lower one is considered forgotten (שכחה) and the upper one is not, with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon ruling both are exempt because the lower is hidden (טָמוּן) and the upper is floating (צָף).
The Gemara suggests that these Tanna'im follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that 'in the field' (בשדה) excludes a hidden item (טָמוּן).
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about whether 'min bemino' (same species) is considered hidden (טָמוּן) or not.

The Gemara rejects this, explaining that all agree 'min bemino' is hidden, and the dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, with the Rabbis following the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda following Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects that if so, why specify 'on top of another' — even on dirt or a pebble it would be the same.
The Gemara resolves that indeed it applies even to dirt, and the case was chosen to show the strength of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that even 'min bemino' is considered hidden.

items.text: Derashot on the word 'halal' and exceptions to the eglah arufah
items.text_en: Derashot on the word 'halal' and exceptions to the eglah arufah
items.desc_en: A baraisa expounds the verse 'halal' to exclude a strangled person, a convulsing person, one hidden in a pile, one hanging on a tree, and one floating on water. Rabbi Elazar argues that if the corpse is 'halal' (pierced) in any of these cases, they perform the ritual. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda challenges him, and the Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar relies on an extra 'halal' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa expounds the verse 'חלל' (pierced) to exclude various cases from the eglah arufah ritual: a strangled person, a convulsing person, one hidden in a pile, one hanging on a tree, and one floating on water.
Rabbi Elazar argues that in all these cases, if the corpse is actually 'חלל' (pierced), they perform the eglah arufah ritual.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda challenges Rabbi Elazar: if a strangled person is found in a garbage heap, you agree they do not perform the ritual, so the same exclusions should apply to the other cases.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar relies on an extra occurrence of the word 'חלל' in the verse to include these cases.

items.text: The law of a corpse found near a border city or a city without a court
items.text_en: The law of a corpse found near a border city or a city without a court
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the corpse is found near a border city or a city with a majority of non-Jews, measurement is not performed. The Gemara explains the scriptural derivation from 'ki yimatzei' (when it is found) excluding a 'found' (common) case. It then discusses the case of a city without a court, teaching that they measure to the nearest city with a court, as derived from 'ziknei ha'ir hahi'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a corpse is found near a border city or a city with a majority of non-Jews, measurement is not performed, and the Gemara explains the scriptural derivation from 'כי ימצא' (when it is found) excluding a 'found' (common) case.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that measurement is only to a city with a court, since it is obvious from the earlier clause about a city without a court.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches a new law: if a corpse is found near a city without a court, they bypass that city and measure to the nearest city with a court, as derived from the verse 'ולקחו זקני העיר ההיא' (and the elders of that city shall take).

items.text: Mishnah: Corpse equidistant between two cities, Jerusalem exempt, and head separate from body
items.text_en: Mishnah: Corpse equidistant between two cities, Jerusalem exempt, and head separate from body
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents disputes: Rabbi Eliezer says if the corpse is exactly between two cities, both bring two calves; Jerusalem does not bring a calf because it was not divided among the tribes; if the head is in one place and the body in another, Rabbi Eliezer says the head is brought to the body, while Rabbi Akiva says the body is brought to the head. The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning that it is possible to be precise and the verse says 'kerovah' (near), even if multiple are near.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a corpse is found exactly between two cities, both bring two calves, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Mishnah adds that Jerusalem does not bring a calf because it was not divided among the tribes.
The Mishnah presents disputes about whether the head is brought to the body or vice versa, and from where measurements are taken.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: it is possible to be precise, and the verse says 'קרובה' (near), even if multiple are near.
The Gemara explains that Jerusalem does not bring a calf because the verse says 'לְרִשְׁתָּהּ' (to its inheritance), and Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about where to bring the head or the body for burial
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about where to bring the head or the body for burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is not about measurement but about where the met mitzvah acquires its place for burial. Rabbi Yitzchak explains: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the body falls in its place and the head wanders, so the head is brought to the body; Rabbi Akiva holds that the head falls where it falls and the body runs after it, so the body is brought to the head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is about, and rejects the possibility that it concerns measurement.

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the dispute is about where the met mitzvah (abandoned corpse) acquires its place for burial: Rabbi Eliezer holds the body falls in place and the head wanders, so the head is brought to the body; Rabbi Akiva holds the head falls where it falls and the body runs after it, so the body is brought to the head.

items.text: Dispute about the point of measurement: navel, nose, or neck
items.text_en: Dispute about the point of measurement: navel, nose, or neck
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute about from where to measure: one holds that the primary source of life is the nose, another holds it is the navel. It cites Tanna'im about the formation of a fetus: from the head or the navel. It concludes that even Abba Shaul, who says formation is from the navel, agrees that life is in the nose, as per the verse 'all in whose nostrils is the breath of life'. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says from the neck, based on the verse 'to put it on the necks of the slain wicked'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva regarding the point from which to measure.
One opinion holds that the primary source of life is the nose, so measurement is from the nose.
The other opinion holds that the primary source of life is the navel, so measurement is from the navel.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Tanna'im dispute the origin of fetal formation: one says from the head, Abba Shaul says from the navel.
The Gemara resolves that even Abba Shaul, who says formation is from the navel, agrees that life is in the nose, as per the verse 'all in whose nostrils is the breath of life'.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says measurement is from the neck, citing the verse 'to put it on the necks of the slain wicked'.

items.text: Mishnah: The ritual of the eglah arufah and the declaration of the elders
items.text_en: Mishnah: The ritual of the eglah arufah and the declaration of the elders
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure: the elders of Jerusalem leave, the elders of the city bring a heifer that has not been worked, take it to a rugged valley, and behead it. The place becomes forbidden for planting and work. The elders wash their hands and declare 'our hands did not shed this blood', meaning they did not send him away without food or leave him without escort.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the initial procedure: the Jerusalem elders depart, the city elders bring a heifer that has not been worked, take it to a rugged valley, behead it, and the place becomes forbidden for planting and work but permitted for certain tasks.
The Mishnah continues: the city elders wash their hands and declare that they did not shed the blood, meaning they did not send him away without food or leave him without escort.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the priests' declaration over the heifer and notes that the Holy Spirit assures them that the blood will be atoned for.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the priests' declaration over the heifer and notes that the Holy Spirit assures them that the blood will be atoned for.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answer on blemishes
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer on blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a blemish does not disqualify the heifer, using a קל וחומר from the red heifer. It answers that the verse 'אֲשֶׁר אֵין בָּהּ מוּם' limits blemish disqualification to the red heifer. It then raises a challenge regarding other labors, citing Rav Yehuda's ruling, and resolves it via a גזירה שווה of 'עֹל'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a blemish should not disqualify the עגלה (heifer) via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the red heifer.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אֲשֶׁר אֵין בָּהּ מוּם' limits blemish disqualification to the red heifer alone.
The Gemara objects that if the limitation applies, then other labors should not disqualify the red heifer either.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that placing a sack yoke on the red heifer disqualifies it, while the עגלה requires actual pulling.

The Gemara resolves that the red heifer's other labors are derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'עֹל' from the עגלה, and the limitation 'בָּהּ' excludes the עגלה from blemish disqualification.

items.text: Derivation of labors disqualifying consecrated animals
items.text_en: Derivation of labors disqualifying consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether labors disqualify consecrated animals, using a קל וחומר from the heifer. It is refuted because the heifer has years disqualifying it. The Gemara then cites verses to show that labors do not disqualify consecrated animals, but a concern for labors done after consecration requires a separate verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the word 'בָּהּ' (in it) also appears in the heifer verse, so why not exclude labors there too?
The Gemara explains that the word 'בָּהּ' in the heifer verse is needed to exclude consecrated animals from disqualification by labors.
The Gemara questions whether the exclusion of consecrated animals from labor disqualification is derived from here, since it is already derived elsewhere.
The Gemara cites another verse to show that labors performed by a non-priest do not disqualify consecrated animals.
The Gemara resolves that both verses are necessary: one for labors performed when the animal was unconsecrated, the other for labors performed after consecration.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the baraita on labors
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling and the baraita on labors
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rav Yehuda's ruling that placing a sack on the red heifer disqualifies it, but for the heifer only if it pulls. A baraita challenges this, deriving that all labors disqualify the red heifer via a קל וחומר from the heifer. The Gemara explains the phrase 'אִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר' as addressing a potential refutation, and concludes with a גזירה שווה that includes the requirement of pulling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that placing a sack on the red heifer disqualifies it, but for the heifer only if it pulls.
A baraita is cited that derives from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that all labors disqualify the red heifer, just as they disqualify the heifer.

The Gemara asks what the phrase 'אִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר' (if you wish to say) means, explaining it introduces a potential refutation based on the heifer's disqualification by years or on consecrated animals.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'עֹל' (yoke) used in both contexts, concluding that all labors disqualify and require pulling.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the source for labors
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the source for labors
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute is between Tannaim: one derives labors from the heifer, another from the red heifer's own verse. Two baraitot are cited, each using a כלל ופרט and a ריבוי to include all labors, but limiting the disqualification of other labors to the time of labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute is between Tannaim: one derives the disqualification of other labors from the heifer whose neck is broken, another from the red heifer's own verse.

A baraita teaches that regarding the red heifer, the verse 'עֹל' (yoke) is expanded by 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא עָלָה עָלֶיהָ עֹל' to include all labors, but other labors disqualify only during the time of labor, while a yoke disqualifies even not during labor.
The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as a כלל ופרט (generalization and detail), which would exclude all labors except a yoke.
The Gemara answers that the word 'אֲשֶׁר' is a ריבוי (amplification), so the verse is not a simple כלל ופרט but includes all labors.
