A baraita similarly teaches regarding the heifer whose neck is broken: the verse 'עֹל' is expanded by 'אֲשֶׁר לֹא עֻבַּד בָּהּ' to include all labors, but other labors disqualify only during the time of labor, while a yoke disqualifies even not during labor.
The Gemara again objects that the verse could be interpreted as a כלל ופרט, which would exclude all labors except a yoke.
The Gemara answers that the word 'אֲשֶׁר' is a ריבוי (amplification), so the verse includes all labors.

items.text: Measurement of the yoke's pulling
items.text_en: Measurement of the yoke's pulling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Yochanan about the measure of pulling the yoke. Rabbi Yochanan answers: the width of a yoke. A question arises whether it is length or width, and a certain rabbi clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan meant a handbreadth in width, which also teaches the standard size of a yoke for sales.

sub.desc_en: רבי אבהו (Rabbi Avahu) asks רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) what is the measure of pulling the yoke that disqualifies the heifer; Rabbi Yochanan answers: the full size of a yoke.

A dilemma arises among the Sages whether the measure is along the length or the width; a certain Sage named רבי יעקב (Rabbi Yaakov) clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan said the pulling is measured by its width, which is a handbreadth.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan did not simply say 'a handbreadth' instead of mentioning the yoke; it answers that he thereby teaches the standard size of a yoke — a handbreadth.
The Gemara notes that this measurement is relevant for commercial transactions of yokes.

items.text: Reason for the heifer and definition of 'אֵיתָן'
items.text_en: Reason for the heifer and definition of 'אֵיתָן'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul explains why the Torah requires a heifer in a rough valley: it atones for one who prevented another from doing mitzvot. The Gemara clarifies that 'פֵּירוֹת' refers to mitzvot, not children. It then defines 'אֵיתָן' as hard, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul explains that the Torah requires a heifer in a rough valley because God says: let something that did not produce fruit be atoned in a place that does not produce fruit, to atone for one who prevented another from doing mitzvot.
The Gemara asks what 'פֵּירוֹת' (fruit) means, and rejects the possibility that it refers to procreation (פריה ורביה), because then an old man or a eunuch would also require a heifer.
The Gemara answers that 'פֵּירוֹת' refers to mitzvot (commandments).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'אֵיתָן' (hard) and introduces a baraita that defines 'אֵיתָן' as hard, citing a verse.

items.text: Definition of 'eitan' as old
items.text_en: Definition of 'eitan' as old
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses to prove that 'eitan' means old, with Acheirim adding a proof from Jeremiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites two verses (Numbers 24:21 and Micah 6:2) to establish that 'eitan' means old.
Acheirim adds a proof from Jeremiah 5:15 that 'eitan' means old, citing the phrase 'an ancient nation.'

items.text: Reason for chopping from behind
items.text_en: Reason for chopping from behind
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the heifer is chopped from behind, deriving it from a gezerah shavah with the bird sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the heifer is chopped from behind with a cleaver.
The Gemara explains the reason: a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the bird sin-offering teaches that the heifer is chopped from behind.

items.text: Dispute on whether the prohibition applies retroactively or prospectively
items.text_en: Dispute on whether the prohibition applies retroactively or prospectively
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan argue whether the verse 'which shall not be worked nor sown' refers to the past or future. Rava clarifies that both agree on the future, but dispute the past, with each citing a different reading of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Yoshiya interprets the verse as referring to the past, Rabbi Yonatan as referring to the future.
Rava clarifies that both agree on the future (להבא), and their dispute is only about the past (לשעבר), each citing a different reading of the word 'אשר'.

items.text: Permitted activities and the derivation of the prohibition
items.text_en: Permitted activities and the derivation of the prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that only activities that directly affect the ground are prohibited, excluding flax-beating and stone-clearing. The Gemara then considers a possible kal vachomer or a klal ufrat derivation, concluding that 'asher' is a ribbui.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that only activities directly affecting the ground are prohibited, excluding flax-beating and stone-clearing, and derives this from the verse 'which shall not be worked'.
The Gemara explains that the specific mention of 'sowing' teaches that only activities that are in the body of the ground are prohibited, excluding flax-beating and stone-clearing.
The Gemara objects that one could interpret the verse as a כלל ופרט (general and specific), which would limit the prohibition to sowing alone.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'אשר' (which) is a ריבוי (amplification), extending the prohibition to all forms of work.

items.text: Hand-washing and the declaration of the elders
items.text_en: Hand-washing and the declaration of the elders
items.desc_en: A baraisa explains that the elders wash their hands at the place of the heifer's neck-breaking. The Gemara then clarifies that their declaration 'our hands did not shed this blood' means they did not fail to provide food or escort.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the elders wash their hands at the place of the heifer's neck-breaking, derived from the verse's repetition of 'עֲרוּפָה' (the neck-broken one).
The Gemara questions how the elders could declare 'our hands did not shed this blood,' since it is unthinkable that a court would commit murder.
The Gemara explains that the declaration means they did not fail to provide food or escort for the victim.

items.text: The importance of escorting (levaya) and the story of the Canaanite
items.text_en: The importance of escorting (levaya) and the story of the Canaanite
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that one is compelled to provide escort, as its reward is unlimited. The Gemara brings the story of the Canaanite who showed the spies the city entrance and was saved, and a kal vachomer for escorting. A dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan about how he showed them is resolved with a baraisa supporting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Meir stating that one is compelled to provide escort (לויה), as its reward is unlimited, and cites the story of the Canaanite who showed the spies the city entrance and was saved along with his family.

A baraita elaborates on the reward of the Canaanite: the city Luz, where he settled, was never destroyed by Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar, and even the angel of death cannot enter it; its elders go outside to die.

The Gemara draws a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if the Canaanite, who only gestured without speaking or walking, earned salvation for himself and his descendants, then one who escorts by foot certainly earns great reward.
The Gemara asks how the Canaanite showed the entrance, and records a dispute: Chizkiya says he twisted his mouth, Rabbi Yochanan says he showed with his finger.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view, stating that because the Canaanite showed them with his finger, he earned salvation for himself and his descendants until the end of all generations.

items.text: Various teachings on the reward and measure of escorting
items.text_en: Various teachings on the reward and measure of escorting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Torah study serves as an escort, and that Pharaoh's four steps of escorting Abraham led to 400 years of servitude. Rav Yehuda says escorting four amot in the city protects from harm. A baraisa details distances for escorting a rabbi, and stories of Rabbis escorting each other are recounted.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) teaches that one walking without an escort should engage in Torah study, citing the verse 'כי לוית חן הם לראשך' (for they shall be a chaplet of grace to your head).

רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) further teaches that because Pharaoh escorted Abraham four steps, his descendants were enslaved for 400 years, citing the verse 'ועבדום וענו אתם ארבע מאות שנה' (and they shall serve them and afflict them 400 years).
רב יהודה (Rav Yehuda) in the name of רב (Rav) states that anyone who escorts a friend four cubits in the city will not be harmed.
The Gemara relates that רבינא (Ravina) escorted רבא בר יצחק (Rava bar Yitzchak) four cubits in the city, and although he encountered danger, he was saved.

A ברייתתא (baraita) teaches the distances for escorting: a teacher escorts a student to the outskirts of the city, a friend to the Shabbat boundary, and a student has no measure for escorting his teacher.
The Gemara asks: How far should a student escort his teacher? רב ששת (Rav Sheshet) answers: up to a parasang.
The Gemara qualifies: this applies only to a non-primary teacher, but for one's primary teacher, the distance is three parasangs.
The Gemara relates that רב כהנא (Rav Kahana) escorted רב שימי בר אשי (Rav Shimi bar Ashi) to the palm grove of Babylonia, where he asked if those palm trees date from the time of Adam the first man.

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: רב שימי בר אשי (Rav Shimi bar Ashi) responds by citing רבי יוסי בר חנינא (Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina), who explains that lands Adam decreed for settlement were settled, and those he did not decree were not settled.
The Gemara relates that רב מרדכי (Rav Mordechai) escorted רב אשי (Rav Ashi) from הגרוניא (Hagronya) to בי כיפי (Bei Keifei), and some say to בי דורא (Bei Dura).

items.text: The story of Elisha and the bears
items.text_en: The story of Elisha and the bears
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir says that one who does not escort is like a murderer, citing Elisha who was not escorted and cursed the youths. The Gemara explains the youths' sin, and various opinions on what Elisha saw that led him to curse them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir states that one who does not escort or be escorted is like a murderer, citing the story of Elisha and the bears.
The Gemara explains that the youths taunted Elisha saying 'Go up, baldhead,' accusing him of making the place bald (destroying their livelihood).
The Gemara asks what is meant by the phrase 'young lads' (נערים קטנים) in the verse.
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'נערים' means they were emptied (מנוערים) of mitzvot, and 'קטנים' means they were small in faith.
A baraita adds that they were actually youths but debased themselves like children.
Rav Yosef objects that perhaps the description 'נערים קטנים' refers to their place of origin, citing a parallel verse where 'נערה קטנה' is used.
Rabbi Pedat answers that there the place is not specified, but here the place is specified, so the description must be about their character.
The Gemara asks what Elisha saw that led him to curse the youths.
Rav says Elisha saw something tangible, citing a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that wherever the sages set their eyes, death or poverty results.
Shmuel says Elisha saw that all of them were conceived on Yom Kippur (a sin).
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says Elisha saw that they wore their hair in a gentile style (בלורית).
Rabbi Yochanan says Elisha saw that they had no moisture of mitzvah (no merit).
The Gemara asks: perhaps their descendants had merit?
Rabbi Elazar answers that neither they nor their descendants had merit until the end of all generations.
The Gemara cites the verse that two bears came out of the forest and mauled forty-two of the youths.

items.text: The nature of the miracle of the bears
items.text_en: The nature of the miracle of the bears
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether the attack of the bears on the youths was a single miracle or a miracle within a miracle. One holds that there was a forest but no bears, the other that there was neither forest nor bears, and the bears were created from fear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the debate between Rav and Shmuel regarding the nature of the miracle of the bears: one says it was a single miracle (a forest existed but no bears), the other says it was a miracle within a miracle (neither forest nor bears existed, and the bears were created from fear).

items.text: Balak's sacrifices and the reward of Ruth
items.text_en: Balak's sacrifices and the reward of Ruth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that because Balak offered forty-two sacrifices, forty-two children of Israel were killed. The Gemara questions this, citing Rav Yehudah who said that even for insincere Torah study one receives reward, and Balak's sacrifices led to the birth of Ruth, from whom Solomon descended.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that because Balak offered forty-two sacrifices, forty-two Israelite children were killed.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina's statement, implying it seems problematic.
Rav Yehudah citing Rav teaches that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even insincerely, and Balak's reward was the birth of Ruth, from whom Solomon descended.
Rabbi Yosei ben Choni adds that Ruth was the daughter of Eglon, who was Balak's son, reinforcing the connection.
The Gemara resolves that despite the reward, Balak's intention was for a curse, so the punishment was justified.

items.text: The goodness of the city and the three graces
items.text_en: The goodness of the city and the three graces
items.desc_en: The verse describes the city's water as bad and the land as barren, yet the people said the city was good. Rabbi Chanin explains that this refers to the grace of the place upon its inhabitants. Rabbi Yochanan lists three types of grace: place, wife, and purchase.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions how the city could be called good when its water was bad and land barren.
Rabbi Chanin explains that the goodness refers to the grace (חן) of the place upon its inhabitants.
Rabbi Yochanan generalizes that there are three types of grace: of place, of wife, and of purchase.

items.text: Elisha's three illnesses
items.text_en: Elisha's three illnesses
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that Elisha suffered three illnesses: one for inciting the bears against the children, one for pushing Gehazi away with both hands, and one from which he died.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three illnesses that Elisha suffered: one for inciting the bears, one for pushing Gehazi away with both hands, and one from which he died.

items.text: The principle of left hand repelling, right hand drawing near
items.text_en: The principle of left hand repelling, right hand drawing near
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one should always repel with the left hand and draw near with the right, unlike Elisha who pushed Gehazi away with both hands, and unlike Joshua ben Perachiah who pushed Jesus the Nazarene away with both hands.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that one should always repel with the left hand and draw near with the right, unlike Elisha who pushed Gehazi away with both hands, and unlike Joshua ben Perachiah who pushed Jesus the Nazarene away with both hands.

items.text: Gehazi's sin and punishment
items.text_en: Gehazi's sin and punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Gehazi took gifts from Naaman against Elisha's will. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Elisha was studying the eight creeping things at that time and told Gehazi that the time had come to receive their reward, and Naaman's leprosy would cling to him. Rabbi Yochanan identifies the four leprous men as Gehazi and his three sons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Elisha and Gehazi, citing the verse where Naaman offers gifts and Elisha rebukes Gehazi for taking them.
The Gemara questions how Gehazi could be accused of taking all those items when he only took silver and garments.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Elisha was studying the eight creeping things and told Gehazi that the time had come to receive their reward, so Naaman's leprosy would cling to him.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the four leprous men mentioned in the verse as Gehazi and his three sons.

items.text: Elisha's attempt to bring Gehazi back in repentance
items.text_en: Elisha's attempt to bring Gehazi back in repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Elisha went to Damascus to bring Gehazi back in repentance, but Gehazi refused, citing a tradition that one who sins and causes the public to sin is not given the opportunity to repent. The Gemara offers various explanations of what Gehazi did to cause public sin: he hung a magnetic stone for Jeroboam's sin, or engraved the Divine Name on its mouth, or pushed the Sages away.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Elisha went to Damascus.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Elisha went to bring Gehazi back in repentance, but Gehazi refused.
Gehazi cites a tradition from Elisha that one who sins and causes the public to sin is not given the opportunity to repent.
The Gemara asks what Gehazi did to cause the public to sin.
Some say Gehazi hung a magnetic stone for Jeroboam's sin and suspended it between heaven and earth.
Others say Gehazi engraved the Divine Name on the stone's mouth, and it would recite the first two commandments.
Others say Gehazi pushed the Sages away from Elisha, as implied by the verse that only now the place was too cramped for them.

items.text: Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus the Nazarene
items.text_en: Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus the Nazarene
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Joshua ben Perachiah fled to Alexandria due to persecution, and upon his return, he praised the innkeeper's hospitality. Jesus misinterpreted his praise as referring to the innkeeper's wife, leading Joshua to excommunicate him. Despite daily attempts at reconciliation, Jesus was not accepted back, and eventually turned to idolatry, sinning and causing the public to sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Joshua ben Perachiah, recounting how he fled to Alexandria during King Yannai's persecution of the rabbis, and how Shimon ben Shetach sent him a coded message indicating it was safe to return.

Upon returning, Joshua praised the innkeeper's hospitality; Jesus misinterpreted this as referring to the innkeeper's wife, leading Joshua to excommunicate him with four hundred shofars and refuse daily attempts at reconciliation.

Joshua attempted to accept Jesus back but a gesture was misinterpreted; Jesus then engaged in idolatry, and when Joshua called him to repent, Jesus cited the principle that one who sins and causes the public to sin is not given the opportunity to repent, as Jesus ultimately led Israel astray.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that regarding the evil inclination, a child, and a woman, one should repel with the left hand and draw near with the right.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states a principle: regarding the evil inclination (יצר), a child (תינוק), and a woman (אשה), one should repel with the left hand and draw near with the right.

items.text: Mishnah: The heifer whose neck is broken and the cessation of rituals
items.text_en: Mishnah: The heifer whose neck is broken and the cessation of rituals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the laws of the heifer whose neck is broken: if the murderer is found before the heifer is killed, it goes out to pasture; after it is killed, it is buried. It details cases of conflicting testimony. It then states that when murderers increased, the heifer ceremony ceased; when adulterers increased, the bitter waters ceased; and when the great sages died, the clusters (of Torah) ceased, and Yochanan the High Priest abolished the confession of the tithe and the awakeners and knockers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of the heifer whose neck is broken: if the murderer is found before the heifer is killed, it goes out to pasture; after it is killed, it is buried; if found after the heifer is killed, the murderer is executed.
The Mishnah details cases of conflicting testimony regarding the murderer, specifying when the heifer ceremony is still performed and when it is not.

The Mishnah states that when murderers increased, the heifer ceremony ceased, and notes the case of Eliezer ben Dinah, also called Techinah ben Perishah, who was later called 'ben haRatzchan' (son of the murderer).
The Mishnah states that when adulterers increased, the bitter waters ceased, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai abolished them, citing a verse.

The Mishnah concludes that when Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yehudah died, the clusters (of Torah) ceased, and Yochanan the High Priest abolished the confession of the tithe, the awakeners, and the knockers.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that until Yosei ben Yoezer's time, a hammer would strike in Jerusalem, and in his time there was no need to ask about demai (doubtfully tithed produce).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that until Yosei ben Yoezer's time, a hammer would strike in Jerusalem, and in his time there was no need to ask about demai (doubtfully tithed produce).

items.text: Gemara: Source for single witness in eglah arufah
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for single witness in eglah arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if the heifer is beheaded and then the murderer is found, it does not atone. It then discusses the Mishnah's case where one witness says he saw the murderer and two say he did not, deriving from a verse that a single witness is believed to prevent the beheading.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the heifer is beheaded and then the murderer is found, the beheading does not atone, derived from the verse 'וְלָאָרֶץ לֹא יְכֻפַּר לַדָּם אֲשֶׁר שֻׁפַּךְ בָּהּ כִּי אִם בְּדַם שֹׁפְכוֹ' (and the land shall not be atoned for the blood that was shed in it except by the blood of the one who shed it).

The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that when one witness says he saw the murderer and two say he did not, the reason they behead is because the two contradict him, implying that without contradiction, a single witness is believed to prevent the beheading.

sub.text: Baraita with Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita with Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Tanna Kamma derives from 'לֹא נוֹדַע מִי הִכָּהוּ' (it is not known who struck him) that if it is known who struck him, even by one witness at the end of the world, they would not behead; Rabbi Akiva adds that a Sanhedrin that saw a killer but did not recognize him would not behead, derived from 'וְעֵינֵינוּ לֹא רָאוּ' (and our eyes did not see), even though they saw.

items.text: Ulla's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Ulla's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one witness can contradict another, citing Ulla's principle that where the Torah believes one witness, it is like two, so one cannot contradict two. Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak resolve that the Mishnah means they would not behead. Rabbi Chiya says they would behead, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between simultaneous and sequential testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since a single witness is believed, how can another single witness contradict him, given Ulla's principle that where the Torah believes one witness it is like two, and one cannot stand against two?
Ulla answers: read the Mishnah as saying 'they would not behead' (לֹא הָיוּ עוֹרְפִין), and Rabbi Yitzchak agrees.
Rabbi Chiya objects: read the Mishnah as saying 'they would behead' (הָיוּ עוֹרְפִין), which contradicts Ulla's principle.
The Gemara resolves: no contradiction — one case is simultaneous testimony, the other is sequential.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Chiya from Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Chiya from Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiya from the Mishnah: if one witness says he saw and two say he did not, they behead, implying that one against one would not behead. But the latter clause implies the opposite, creating a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiya from the Mishnah: if one witness says he saw and two say he did not, they behead, implying that one against one would not behead, which contradicts Rabbi Chiya.
The Gemara counters: according to your reasoning, the latter clause implies the opposite — that one against one would behead, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Resolution: Disqualified witnesses and Rabbi Nechemya
items.text_en: Resolution: Disqualified witnesses and Rabbi Nechemya
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses (e.g., women), following Rabbi Nechemya's principle that where the Torah believes one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, treating two women as two men. A second version explains that the case involves a woman from the start, and Rabbi Nechemya distinguishes between two women against one woman (equal) and two women against one man (majority). The Gemara explains why both cases of disqualified witnesses are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah deals with disqualified witnesses (e.g., women), following Rabbi Nechemya's principle that where the Torah believes one witness, we follow the majority of opinions, treating two women against one man as two men against one man.

An alternative version states that when a valid witness comes first, even one hundred women are like one witness; the case involves a woman from the start, and Rabbi Nechemya distinguishes between two women against one woman (equal) and two women against one man (half and half).
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs two cases of disqualified witnesses.
The Gemara answers that both cases are needed to teach that we follow the majority of opinions even when it leads to a lenient ruling, not only when it leads to a stringent one.

items.text: Baraita: Cessation of eglah arufah
items.text_en: Baraita: Cessation of eglah arufah
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that when murderers multiplied, the eglah arufah ceased because it only comes for uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that when murderers increased, the heifer ritual was abolished because it only comes for doubt.

items.text: Baraita: Cessation of sotah waters
items.text_en: Baraita: Cessation of sotah waters
items.desc_en: A baraita states that when adulterers multiplied, the sotah waters ceased, as the verse requires the husband to be free of sin. The Gemara expands that the sin of children and daughters also affects, and even the sin of a single woman. Rabbi Elazar explains that if the people are scrupulous, the waters test their wives.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְנִקָּה הָאִישׁ מֵעָוֹן' to establish that the sotah waters test the wife only when the husband is free of sin.
The Gemara asks what the additional verse 'וְאוֹמֵר' comes to teach, suggesting it might include the sin of children and daughters.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'לֹא אֶפְקוֹד עַל בְּנוֹתֵיכֶם' to show that the sin of children and daughters also affects the waters.
The Gemara further questions whether the sin of a single woman (פנויה) also affects the waters.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'כִּי הֵם עִם הַזֹּנוֹת יְפָרֵדוּ' to include the sin of a single woman.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse 'וְעָם לֹא יָבִין יִלָּבֵט' teaches that if the people are scrupulous, the waters test their wives; otherwise, they do not.

items.text: List of societal declines
items.text_en: List of societal declines
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various societal declines: when those who seek favor multiplied, justice was perverted; when those who show partiality multiplied, the yoke of heaven was removed; when whisperers multiplied, the Shechinah departed; and many other moral and religious deteriorations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the list of societal declines: when those who seek favor multiplied, justice was perverted and the yoke of heaven was removed.
The Mishnah continues: when whisperers multiplied, the Shechinah departed; when those who follow their greed multiplied, moral inversion increased.
The Mishnah continues: when those who draw spittle multiplied, arrogance increased and Torah declined; when the arrogant multiplied, daughters married them.

The Gemara objects: but the Master said that an arrogant person is not accepted even in his own home, so how could daughters marry them? It answers that initially they jump to marry him, but eventually he is degraded before them.
The Mishnah continues: when those who impose burdens multiplied, bribery and injustice increased; when those who accept favors multiplied, anarchy reigned; when the stingy multiplied, lending ceased.

The Mishnah concludes the list: when women with stretched necks and winking eyes multiplied, the bitter waters ceased; when gift-takers multiplied, days shortened; when the proud multiplied, disputes increased; when students of Shammai and Hillel who did not serve properly multiplied, Torah became two Torahs; when those who accept charity from gentiles multiplied, Israel was lowered.

items.text: Explanation of 'eshkolot' and Yosei ben Yoezer
items.text_en: Explanation of 'eshkolot' and Yosei ben Yoezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'eshkolot' as a man who contains everything. It then discusses Yosei ben Yoezer and Yochanan the High Priest who abolished the confession of the tithe, because it was not given properly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'eshkolot' and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers: a man who contains everything; then it asks why Yohanan the High Priest abolished the confession of tithe, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers: because it was not given properly, as the Torah required giving to Levites.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains 'eshkolot' as a man who contains everything.
The Gemara asks why Yochanan the High Priest abolished the confession of the tithe.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that the tithe was abolished because it was not given properly to the Levites.

items.text: Question about Yochanan's enactment regarding tithes
items.text_en: Question about Yochanan's enactment regarding tithes
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Yochanan could give the first tithe to the priests if people were not separating tithes at all. Resh Lakish explains that any house that does not confess over the first tithe will not confess over the other tithes, and Abaye explains the reason is that the verse begins with it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Yochanan could give the first tithe to the priests if people were not separating tithes at all.
Reish Lakish explains that any house that does not confess over the first tithe will not confess over the other tithes.
Abaye explains that the reason is that the verse begins with the first tithe.

items.text: Yochanan's decree on demai and cancellation of confession
items.text_en: Yochanan's decree on demai and cancellation of confession
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that people were indeed separating some tithes, citing a baraita that Yochanan saw only terumah was universally separated, while first and second tithes were only partially observed. He therefore instituted that buyers from am ha'aretz must separate first and second tithes, and he cancelled the confession for haverim and decreed on demai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the assumption that people were separating tithes, given that Yochanan cancelled the confession and decreed on demai.
A baraita is cited describing Yochanan's survey that only terumah was universally separated, while first and second tithes were only partially observed.
Yochanan tells the people that just as terumah carries a death penalty, so too does terumat ma'aser and tevel.
Yochanan institutes that a buyer from an am ha'aretz must separate first and second tithes, with specific rules for terumat ma'aser and second tithe.
The Gemara summarizes that Yochanan enacted two things: cancelling the confession for haverim and decreeing on demai of am ha'aretz.

items.text: Cancellation of the 'awakeners' and 'strikers'
items.text_en: Cancellation of the 'awakeners' and 'strikers'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Yochanan also cancelled the 'awakeners'—Levites who said 'Awake, why do You sleep, God'—and the 'strikers' who would strike the calf between its horns to make blood fall in its eyes, which appeared as a blemish. He instituted rings in the ground instead.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Yochanan the High Priest also cancelled the 'awakeners'.
The Gemara asks what the 'awakeners' were.

Rachbah explains that the 'awakeners' were Levites who recited 'Awake, why do You sleep, God' on the platform, and Yochanan objected because God never sleeps, but the verse is appropriate when Israel suffers.
The Mishnah states that Yochanan also cancelled the 'strikers'.
The Gemara asks what the 'strikers' were.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the 'strikers' would scratch the calf between its horns to make blood fall in its eyes, and Yochanan cancelled it because it appeared as a blemish.
A baraita adds that they would beat the calf with sticks like idolatry, and Yochanan said they were feeding neveilot (neveilot) to the altar, and instituted rings in the ground instead.

items.text: Other enactments of Yochanan
items.text_en: Other enactments of Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that until Yochanan's days, a hammer would strike in Jerusalem on Chol HaMoed, and no one needed to ask about demai, as previously stated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that until Yochanan's days, a hammer would strike in Jerusalem on Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara adds that in all his days, no one needed to ask about demai, as previously stated.

items.text: Mishnah: Things that ceased with the Sanhedrin and Temple
items.text_en: Mishnah: Things that ceased with the Sanhedrin and Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that when the Sanhedrin ceased, song ceased from wedding feasts; when the prophets died, Urim and Tumim ceased; when the Temple was destroyed, the shamir and honeycomb ceased, and faithful men ended. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and the Sages add further calamities.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that when the Sanhedrin ceased, song ceased from wedding feasts, citing a verse.
The Mishnah continues listing calamities: when the first prophets died, the Urim and Tumim ceased; when the Temple was destroyed, the shamir, honeycomb, and faithful men ceased, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel testifies in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua that since the Temple's destruction, every day is cursed, dew is not for blessing, and the taste of fruits is removed.
Rabbi Yosei adds that the oil of fruits was also removed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that purity removed taste and smell, and tithes removed the oil of grain.
The Sages conclude that licentiousness and sorcery destroyed everything.

items.text: Gemara: Source for song ceasing with Sanhedrin and prohibition of music
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for song ceasing with Sanhedrin and prohibition of music
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua derives from a verse that song ceased with the Sanhedrin. Rav says the ear that hears song should be uprooted. Rava says song in a house leads to destruction. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Ashi explain the verse, and Mar bar Rav Ashi adds a metaphor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the verse about song ceasing refers to the abolition of the Sanhedrin.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua cites the verse 'זְקֵנִים מִשַּׁעַר שָׁבָתוּ בַּחוּרִים מִנְּגִינָתָם' (Elders have ceased from the gate, young men from their music) to prove the connection.
Rav declares that an ear that hears song should be uprooted.
Rava states that song in a house leads to destruction at its threshold, citing the verse 'קוֹל יְשׁוֹרֵר בַּחַלּוֹן חֹרֶב בַּסַּף כִּי אַרְזָה עֵרָה'.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'כִּי אַרְזָה עֵרָה' (for the cedar is laid bare).
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that even a house paneled with cedar will collapse, interpreting the verse as a metaphor for destruction.
Rav Ashi derives from the verse that destruction begins at the threshold, and offers an alternative proof from the verse 'וּשְׁאִיָּה יֻכַּת שָׁעַר' (and ruin is at the gate).
Mar bar Rav Ashi adds a metaphor: he saw a house goring like an ox, meaning destruction strikes suddenly.

items.text: Distinctions in types of song and their effects
items.text_en: Distinctions in types of song and their effects
items.desc_en: Rav Huna distinguishes between permitted song of boatmen and plowmen and forbidden song of weavers. He abolished song, causing prices to drop, but Rav Chisda belittled it and prices rose. Rav Yosef discusses the impropriety of men singing and women responding, and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the song of boatmen and plowmen is permitted, but the song of weavers is forbidden.

sub.text: Narrative about Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Narrative about Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Huna abolished song, causing prices to drop, but Rav Chisda belittled it, causing prices to rise.
Rav Yosef states that men singing and women responding is licentiousness, and women singing and men responding is like fire in flax, and the practical difference is which to abolish first.

items.text: Five calamities brought by drinking with music
items.text_en: Five calamities brought by drinking with music
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that drinking with four types of musical instruments brings five calamities: exile, famine, forgetfulness of Torah, degradation of God, and degradation of Israel, as derived from verses in Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that drinking with four types of musical instruments brings five calamities, citing the verse from Isaiah.
Rabbi Yochanan expounds the five calamities from the continuation of the verse: exile, famine, forgetfulness of Torah, degradation of God, and degradation of Israel.

items.text: Debate on the identity of 'first prophets' and the cessation of Urim and Tumim
items.text_en: Debate on the identity of 'first prophets' and the cessation of Urim and Tumim
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a verse about the grave expanding, then asks who are the 'first prophets' whose death led to the cessation of prophecy. Rav Huna identifies them as David, Samuel, and Solomon; Rav Nachman objects that in David's time the Urim and Tumim sometimes worked and sometimes didn't. A baraita is cited stating that after the First Temple's destruction, the Urim and Tumim ceased, and a potential contradiction from the time of Zerubbabel is resolved by explaining that the statement was aspirational.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the 'first prophets' whose death caused the grave to expand.
Rav Huna identifies the 'first prophets' as David, Samuel, and Solomon.
Rav Nachman objects that in David's time the Urim and Tumim sometimes answered and sometimes did not, citing the case of Evyatar.
Rabbah bar Shmuel challenges by citing a verse about Zechariah, suggesting it refers to Urim and Tumim.
The Gemara rejects the challenge, explaining that the verse refers to prophets, not Urim and Tumim.
A baraita is cited stating that after the First Temple's destruction, Urim and Tumim ceased.
The Gemara resolves a potential contradiction from the time of Zerubbabel by explaining that the statement was aspirational, like saying 'until the dead rise and the Messiah comes'.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative identification and stories of Bat Kol
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative identification and stories of Bat Kol
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reinterprets 'first prophets' to exclude Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who were the last prophets. After their death, the Holy Spirit ceased, but a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) was still used. Two stories illustrate this: one in Jericho where Hillel the Elder was deemed worthy of the Shekhinah, and another in Yavneh where Shmuel HaKatan was similarly recognized. Shmuel HaKatan's deathbed prophecy about future calamities is recounted, and it is noted that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava could not be eulogized due to the circumstances of his death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reinterprets 'first prophets' to exclude Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who were the last prophets.
A baraita states that after the death of Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the Holy Spirit ceased, but a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) was still used.

sub.text: Story of Bat Kol in Jericho
sub.text_en: Story of Bat Kol in Jericho
sub.desc_en: A Bat Kol in Jericho declared Hillel the Elder worthy of the Shekhinah, and at his death he was eulogized as a pious and humble disciple of Ezra.

sub.text: Story of Bat Kol in Yavneh
sub.text_en: Story of Bat Kol in Yavneh
sub.desc_en: A Bat Kol in Yavneh declared Shmuel HaKatan worthy of the Shekhinah, and at his death he was eulogized as a humble and pious disciple of Hillel.
Shmuel HaKatan prophesied at his death about future calamities: Shimon and Yishmael to the sword, their companions to slaughter, and the rest of the people to plunder.
The gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava could not be eulogized with the same praise because he was killed by the government, and one does not eulogize those executed by the state.

items.text: The shamir worm: its nature and use in building the Temple
items.text_en: The shamir worm: its nature and use in building the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the Temple's destruction, the shamir worm ceased. A baraita explains that the shamir was used by Solomon to build the Temple without iron tools, as per the verse 'the house was built of stone made ready at the quarry'. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya debate whether the stones were cut outside or inside; Rabbi resolves the dispute by applying each opinion to different stones. The shamir's size (like a barleycorn), its creation during the six days of creation, and its preservation in lead tubes with barley bran are described.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the shamir worm used by Solomon to build the Temple, citing the verse 'the house was built of stone made ready at the quarry' as the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi Nechemya objects, citing the verse 'all these were costly stones, sawed with a saw', and explains that the absence of iron noise in the Temple means the stones were shaped outside and brought in.
Rabbi resolves the dispute by applying Rabbi Yehuda's view to the Temple stones and Rabbi Nechemya's view to the stones of Solomon's own house.

The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Nechemya, what was the shamir used for, since the stones were cut with saws? It answers with a baraita that the shamir was used for engraving the stones of the ephod, as writing with ink and showing the shamir from outside caused the stones to split.

The baraita describes the process: the stones were written on with ink, then the shamir was shown from outside, causing them to split like a fig tree in summer or a crack in the rainy season, without loss.

Another baraita describes the shamir's size (like a barleycorn), its creation during the six days of creation, its indestructibility, and its preservation wrapped in woolen sponges and placed in a lead tube filled with barley bran.

items.text: Cessation of fine wine, glass, and 'nofet tzufim' after the First Temple
items.text_en: Cessation of fine wine, glass, and 'nofet tzufim' after the First Temple
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that after the First Temple's destruction, fine wine (shira p'randa) and white glass ceased. A baraita adds iron chariots and, according to some, congealed wine from Senir. The term 'nofet tzufim' is debated: Rav says it is fine flour floating on a sieve, Levi says it is two loaves that expand in the oven, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it is honey from Zifiya, as translated by Rav Sheshet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that after the destruction of the First Temple, fine wine (שִׁירָא פְּרַנְדָּא) and white glass ceased.
A baraita supports Rabbi Ami, adding iron chariots and, according to some, congealed wine from Senir that resembles fig cakes.
The gemara asks the meaning of the term 'נוֹפֶת צוּפִים' (nofet tzufim).
Rav explains that 'נוֹפֶת צוּפִים' is fine flour that floats on a sieve, resembling dough kneaded with honey and oil.
Levi says it refers to two loaves that stick in the oven and expand until they touch each other.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi identifies it as honey from Zifiya, as translated by Rav Sheshet: bees that fly and bring honey from mountain herbs.

items.text: Debate on the meaning of 'zifim' honey and the 'zifim' people
items.text_en: Debate on the meaning of 'zifim' honey and the 'zifim' people
items.desc_en: A Mishnah about liquids that are pure except for 'devash zifim' and 'hatzapichim' is cited. Rabbi Yochanan explains 'zifim' as honey that is adulterated (mezayyefin), while Reish Lakish says it is named after the place Zif. A similar debate applies to the 'zifim' who spoke to Saul: Rabbi Yochanan says they were people who falsified their words, while Rabbi Elazar says they were from the place Zif.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that anything poured is pure except for 'devash zifim' and 'hatzapichim'.
The Gemara asks what 'zifim' means in the context of honey.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) explains that 'zifim' honey is honey that is adulterated (mezayyefin).
ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) says the honey is named after the place Zif, citing the verse 'זיף וטלם ובעלות' (Ziph and Telem and Bealoth).
The Gemara brings a parallel verse about 'zifim' who spoke to Saul, to apply the same debate.
The Gemara asks what 'zifim' means in the context of the people who spoke to Saul.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) says the 'zifim' were people who falsified their words.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) says they are called after their place Zif, citing the same verse.

items.text: The cessation of 'anshei amanah' and the meaning of 'ketanei amanah'
items.text_en: The cessation of 'anshei amanah' and the meaning of 'ketanei amanah'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that 'anshei amanah' (men of faith) ceased. Rabbi Yitzchak explains these are people who trust in God, citing Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol that one who has bread and worries about tomorrow is of little faith. Rabbi Elazar connects this to the verse 'who despises the day of small things', saying that the smallness of faith caused the righteous to have their table diminished in the future. Rava interprets 'ketanei amanah' as the small ones among the wicked of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that 'anshei amanah' (men of faith) ceased.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'anshei amanah' are people who believe in the Holy One, Blessed be He.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol says that one who has bread in his basket and asks what he will eat tomorrow is among those of little faith.
Rabbi Elazar connects the concept to the verse 'who despises the day of small things', explaining that the smallness of faith caused the righteous to have their table diminished in the future.
Rava interprets 'ketanei amanah' as the small ones among the wicked of Israel.

items.text: Opening continuation: the wicked who devour their father's judgment
items.text_en: Opening continuation: the wicked who devour their father's judgment
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues its discussion of the wicked who cause their father to be judged, noting that in the future they will complain that God gave them the means to sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the wicked who devour their father's judgment will complain to God that He gave them the means to sin.

items.text: Three teachings of Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah on Torah study and its significance
items.text_en: Three teachings of Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah on Torah study and its significance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah delivers three statements: David's prayer prevented Israel from becoming sellers of many things; Habakkuk's prayer enabled two scholars to study under one cloak; two scholars walking without Torah discourse deserve burning; two scholars in one city who do not ease each other in halakhah lead to one dying and one exiled.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's first statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's first statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah states that without David's prayer, all Israel would have become sellers of many things, citing the verse 'שִׁיתָה ה׳ מוֹרָה לָהֶם'.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's second statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's second statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah states that without Habakkuk's prayer, two Torah scholars would have had to share one cloak, interpreting the verse 'ה׳ שָׁמַעְתִּי שִׁמְעֲךָ' with a homiletic reading of 'בְּקֶרֶב שָׁנִים' as 'בְּקֵרוּב שְׁנַיִם'.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's third statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's third statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah states that two Torah scholars walking without words of Torah deserve to be burned, citing the verse about Elijah and Elisha where the presence of speech prevented fire.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's fourth statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah's fourth statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a bar Yeverechyah states that two Torah scholars in one city who do not ease each other in halakhah (הלכה) lead to one dying and one exiled, interpreting 'בִּבְלִי דַעַת' as without Torah.

items.text: Teachings on the Torah scholar's reward and divine favor
items.text_en: Teachings on the Torah scholar's reward and divine favor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya teaches that a Torah scholar who studies under duress has his prayer heard. Rabbi Avahu says such a scholar is satisfied from the Divine Presence; Rabbi Acha bar Chanina adds that the curtain is not shut before him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya teaches that a Torah scholar who studies under duress has his prayer heard, citing a verse.
Rabbi Avahu adds that such a scholar is satisfied from the Divine Presence, citing a verse.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina adds that the curtain is not shut before such a scholar, citing a verse.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the daily curse and the world's sustenance
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the daily curse and the world's sustenance
items.desc_en: Rava explains that each day's curse is greater than the previous, and the world endures only because of the Kedushah of the sidra and the 'Yehei Shmeih Rabbah' of the aggadah.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that each day's curse is greater than the previous day's, citing a verse and explaining that the 'morning' and 'evening' refer to the passing day.
The Gemara asks: if the curse is so severe, how does the world endure at all?
Rava answers that the world endures only because of the Kedushah of the sidra and the 'Yehei Shmeih Rabbah' of the aggadah, citing a verse to support this.

items.text: Baraita: Decline in produce taste and oil due to the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Baraita: Decline in produce taste and oil due to the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that with the destruction of the Temple, purity nullified taste and smell, and tithes nullified the oil of grain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that with the destruction of the Temple, beneficial dew ceased and the taste of fruits was lost.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains that purity (טהרה) nullified taste and smell, and tithes (מעשר) nullified the oil of grain.

items.text: Stories of fathers and sons illustrating familial affection and rivalry
items.text_en: Stories of fathers and sons illustrating familial affection and rivalry
items.desc_en: Two anecdotes: Rav Huna gives a fragrant herb to his son Rabbah, then to his son Abba, who rejoices but pains his father; Rav Acha bar Yaakov is raised by his grandson who later refuses to serve him, saying he is not obligated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna finds a fragrant herb, gives it to his son Rabbah, then to his son Abba, who rejoices but pains his father, illustrating the folk saying about paternal vs. filial love.

sub.text: Narrator (story of Rav Acha bar Yaakov)
sub.text_en: Narrator (story of Rav Acha bar Yaakov)
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov raises his grandson Rav Yaakov bar barteih, who later refuses to serve him, saying he is not obligated, illustrating the folk saying about a grandson's ingratitude.

items.text: Mishnah: Decrees from the Roman wars and laments for the deaths of sages
items.text_en: Mishnah: Decrees from the Roman wars and laments for the deaths of sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists decrees from the wars of Vespasian, Titus, and the final war, and then laments that after the deaths of Rabbi Meir, Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, Rabbi Yosei Katanat, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabban Gamliel the Elder, Rabbi Yishmael ben Piavi, and Rabbi, various virtues and studies ceased.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the decree from the war of Vespasian: they decreed against wreaths for bridegrooms and against the אירוס (a type of wedding custom).
The Mishnah continues: in the war of Titus, they decreed against wreaths for brides and that a man should not teach his son Greek.
The Mishnah states: in the final war, they decreed that a bride should not go out in a litter within the city, but our rabbis permitted it.

The Mishnah laments that with the deaths of Rabbi Meir, Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, and Rabbi Yosei Katanat, various virtues and studies ceased, and explains why Rabbi Yosei was called 'Katanat'.

The Mishnah concludes that with the deaths of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabban Gamliel the Elder, Rabbi Yishmael ben Piavi, and Rabbi, the splendor of wisdom, honor of Torah, purity and abstinence, splendor of the priesthood, and humility and fear of sin ceased.

items.text: Gemara: Tosefta and baraita on the decline after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Gemara: Tosefta and baraita on the decline after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and Rabbi Eliezer the Great, describing how at the Temple's destruction, friends and freemen were shamed, the powerful and eloquent prevailed, and wisdom declined so that the wise became like scribes, scribes like synagogue servants, and servants like the common people.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta introduces Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's teaching that after the Temple's destruction, friends and freemen were shamed, the powerful and eloquent prevailed, and no one sought or inquired.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair concludes that there is no one to rely on except the Father in Heaven.
Rabbi Eliezer the Great adds that from the Temple's destruction, the wise became like scribes, scribes like synagogue servants, and servants like the common people.

items.text: Baraita on the footsteps of the Messiah
items.text_en: Baraita on the footsteps of the Messiah
items.desc_en: The baraita describes the moral and social decay preceding the messianic era: insolence increases, the vine gives its fruit but wine is costly, the kingdom turns to heresy, the study hall becomes a place of licentiousness, Galilee is destroyed, the Gablan is desolate, border dwellers wander without mercy, wisdom of scribes becomes foul, sin-fearers are despised, truth is absent, youths shame elders, elders stand before children, and the family is turned upside down. The only support is our Father in heaven.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the signs of moral decay preceding the messianic era, culminating in the sole support being our Father in heaven.

items.text: Dispute about types of incense
items.text_en: Dispute about types of incense
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's prohibition of a certain incense. Rav limits the prohibition to sulfur and salt, but allows myrtle and rose. Shmuel forbids myrtle and rose but allows reed and hilt. Levi forbids even reed and hilt, and his baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's prohibition of incense to sulfur and salt, permitting myrtle and rose.
Shmuel forbids myrtle and rose but permits reed and hilt.
Levi forbids even reed and hilt, and his baraita supports this.

items.text: Definition of 'Irus' and the story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Definition of 'Irus' and the story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'Irus' from the Mishnah. Rabbi Elazar defines it as a table with one leg. Rabbah bar Rav Huna made a tambourine for his son, and his father broke it, fearing it would be confused with a one-legged table, instructing him to make it from a jug or a basket.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of the term 'Irus' mentioned in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Elazar defines 'Irus' as a one-legged table.

sub.text: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbah bar Rav Huna made a tambourine for his son, and his father Rav Huna broke it, fearing it would be confused with a one-legged table, instructing him to make it from a jug or a basket.

items.text: Decrees on bridal crowns and wedding canopies
items.text_en: Decrees on bridal crowns and wedding canopies
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's decree on bridal crowns during the war of Titus. Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines it as a 'city of gold'. A baraita confirms this but allows a cap of wool. Similarly, a decree was made on wedding canopies, defined as gilded canopies, but one may make a simple canopy and hang whatever one wishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'bridal crowns'.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines the bridal crown as a 'city of gold' (a gold headpiece shaped like a city).
A baraita confirms the definition of bridal crowns as a 'city of gold', but permits making a cap of wool instead.
A Tanna adds that a decree was also made on wedding canopies.
The Gemara asks what is meant by 'wedding canopies'.
The Gemara defines wedding canopies as gilded canopies.
A baraita confirms the definition of wedding canopies as gilded canopies, but permits making a simple canopy and hanging whatever one wishes.

items.text: The story of the Hasmonean civil war and the ban on Greek wisdom
items.text_en: The story of the Hasmonean civil war and the ban on Greek wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story behind the Mishnah's ban on teaching Greek to one's son. During the siege between Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, a sage who knew Greek wisdom advised the besiegers to stop the daily sacrifices. They sent a pig instead, causing the land to quake. At that moment, they cursed anyone who raises pigs or teaches Greek wisdom. The year is identified by a mishnah about the omer and two loaves.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the siege between Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, describing the daily practice of sending money for sacrifices.
A sage who knew Greek wisdom advises the besiegers that as long as the daily sacrifices continue, they will not be defeated.
The besiegers send a pig instead of the sacrifice, causing the land of Israel to quake.
At that moment they cursed anyone who raises pigs or teaches Greek wisdom, and the year is identified by a mishnah about the omer and two loaves.

items.text: Clarification: Greek language vs. Greek wisdom, and the exception for the house of Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Clarification: Greek language vs. Greek wisdom, and the exception for the house of Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ban on Greek wisdom, citing Rabbi and Rav Yosef who permit Greek language. It distinguishes between Greek language and Greek wisdom. It then asks if Greek wisdom is forbidden, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that 500 children in his father's house learned Greek wisdom. The answer is that the house of Rabban Gamliel was an exception because they were close to the government, as a baraita permits a close relative to cut hair in the Roman style.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ban on Greek wisdom by citing Rabbi who said that in Eretz Yisrael one should speak either Hebrew or Greek, and Rav Yosef who said the same for Babylonia with Aramaic or Persian.
The Gemara distinguishes between Greek language (לשון יוונית) and Greek wisdom (חכמת יוונית), implying the ban applies only to the latter.
The Gemara questions whether Greek wisdom is indeed forbidden, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that 500 children in his father's house learned Greek wisdom.
The Gemara resolves that the house of Rabban Gamliel was an exception because they were close to the government, citing a baraita that permits a close relative to cut hair in the Roman style.

items.text: Decree on the bridal palanquin
items.text_en: Decree on the bridal palanquin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in the last war, a decree was made that a bride should not go out in a palanquin. The Gemara explains the reason: for modesty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in the last war, a decree was made that a bride should not go out in a palanquin.
The Gemara explains that the reason for the decree is for modesty (צניעות).

items.text: List of sages whose deaths marked the loss of virtues
items.text_en: List of sages whose deaths marked the loss of virtues
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's death, wisdom ceased. The Gemara lists other sages: after Rabbi Eliezer, the Torah scroll was hidden; after Rabbi Yehoshua, counsel and thought ceased; after Rabbi Akiva, the arms of Torah ceased; after Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, the crown of wisdom ceased; after Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, men of deed ceased; after Abba Yosef ben Ktonta, the pious ceased; after Ben Azzai, the diligent ceased; after Ben Zoma, the expounders ceased; after Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, locusts came and troubles multiplied; after Rabbi, troubles doubled. Rav Yosef and Rav Nachman each told the tanna not to teach humility and fear of sin, respectively, because they themselves possessed those qualities.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's death, wisdom ceased, and the Gemara lists subsequent sages whose deaths marked the loss of specific virtues.

The baraita continues listing sages: after Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah the crown of wisdom ceased, after Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa men of deed ceased, after Abba Yosef ben Ktonta the pious ceased, with an explanation of his name.
The baraita continues: after Ben Azzai the diligent ceased, after Ben Zoma the expounders ceased, after Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel locusts came and troubles multiplied, after Rabbi troubles doubled.
Rav Yosef and Rav Nachman each told the tanna not to teach humility and fear of sin, respectively, because they themselves possessed those qualities.
